steps.text: Receive every information relating to the commission of a cognizable offence irrespective of the area in which the offence was committed; it may be given to the Station House Officer (SHO) orally, in writing, or through electronic communication [Section 173(1) BNSS].

details.text: There is no hard and fast rule that the informant must be the aggrieved person or victim; information may be given by any person.
details.citation: Kerala Police - Standard Operating Procedure: Investigation & Prosecution in General (SOP Series), State Police Chief, 01.11.2020

details.text: It is not necessary that first information be given only by a person with entire knowledge of the facts; it may be merely hearsay [Shew Pru v. King, AIR 1941 Rang 209].

details.text: The practice of insisting on written information about a cognizable offence before registering a case is not correct and should be dispensed with.

steps.text: The complaint of a cognizable offence shall compulsorily be registered; registration of the FIR is mandatory even if the offence occurred outside the territorial jurisdiction of the police station, and refusal on the jurisdiction ground is prohibited.
legal_basis: Section 173(1) BNSS 2023
Section 199(c) BNS 2023 (officer's penal liability for default)

details.text: A police officer who defaults in registering an offence under BNS Sections 64, 65, 66, 67, 68, 70, 71, 74, 76, 77, 79, 124, 143, 144 is himself liable for a punishable offence under Section 199(c) BNS.
details.citation: Twenty-Nine Standard Operating Procedures - C.I.D. Crime & Railways, Gujarat Police, circular PRC/Circular-SOP-1/656/2024 dated 29/10/2024

details.text: The Section 199(c) BNS punishment for an officer who fails to record information under Section 173(1) BNSS in relation to those offences is rigorous imprisonment for not less than six months, extendable to two years, and fine.
details.citation: BPR&D - Final SOP on Preliminary Enquiry, 2023 (Section 173(3) BNSS)

details.text: The officer has no power to refuse to enter received information about a cognizable offence in the FIR; refusal is possible only if the information is vague and not adequate enough to enable commencement of an investigation.
details.citation: Kerala Police - Standard Operating Procedure: Investigation & Prosecution in General (SOP Series), State Police Chief, 01.11.2020

details.text: The FIR is not an encyclopedia: it is enough if the officer, on the information given, suspects the commission of a cognizable offence — he need not be convinced or satisfied that one has been committed.
details.citation: Kerala Police - Standard Operating Procedure: Investigation & Prosecution in General (SOP Series), State Police Chief, 01.11.2020

details.text: Do not defer registration on the plea of verifying the truth of the information, and do not withhold recording of the FIR for the collection of further details.
details.citation: Kerala Police - Standard Operating Procedure: Investigation & Prosecution in General (SOP Series), State Police Chief, 01.11.2020

details.text: Refusal to record an FIR because the place of crime is outside territorial jurisdiction amounts to dereliction of duty; the officer must record the case and forward it (AIR 1993 SC 2644).
details.citation: Kerala Police - Standard Operating Procedure: Investigation & Prosecution in General (SOP Series), State Police Chief, 01.11.2020

details.text: A police officer cannot refuse to record the FIR on the ground of having no territorial jurisdiction over the place of offence.
details.citation: Kerala Police - Standard Operating Procedure: Investigation & Prosecution in General (SOP Series), State Police Chief, 01.11.2020

details.text: Refusal to record the FIR for the specified sexual/acid-attack offences is punishable under Section 166A IPC [now BNS 199].
details.citation: Kerala Police - Standard Operating Procedure: Investigation & Prosecution in General (SOP Series), State Police Chief, 01.11.2020

details.text: The informant/victim/aggrieved party has no right to withdraw the case once the FIR is registered.
details.citation: Kerala Police - Standard Operating Procedure: Investigation & Prosecution in General (SOP Series), State Police Chief, 01.11.2020

steps.title: Register every cognizable complaint compulsorily

steps.text: Before registering, verify whether the offence disclosed is cognizable or non-cognizable: an FIR (including a Zero FIR) can be registered only for a cognizable offence.

Section 174 BNSS 2023

details.text: The essential condition for recording an FIR is information relating to the commission of a cognizable offence; if the information discloses more offences than one, at least one must be cognizable for direct registration by the officer in charge.
details.citation: Kerala Police - Standard Operating Procedure: Investigation & Prosecution in General (SOP Series), State Police Chief, 01.11.2020

details.text: Take care that the informant is not exaggerating the occurrence or giving the colour of a cognizable offence to a non-cognizable incident; informants tend to give coloured statements out of excitement or prejudice.
details.citation: Kerala Police - Standard Operating Procedure: Investigation & Prosecution in General (SOP Series), State Police Chief, 01.11.2020

steps.title: Verify the offence is cognizable before registering
steps.triage_why: This is a pre-registration verification step; the case is already registered.

steps.text: If the information is given orally, reduce it to writing (by the SHO or under his supervision), read it over to the informant, and obtain the informant's signature on every such written complaint; enter its substance in the prescribed station book [Section 173(1)(i) BNSS].
legal_basis: Section 173(1)(i) BNSS 2023

details.text: Record in plain and simple words, in the language of the victim as far as possible.
details.citation: Kerala Police - Standard Operating Procedure: Investigation & Prosecution in General (SOP Series), State Police Chief, 01.11.2020

details.text: The idea behind reading over the recorded information and obtaining the informant's signature is to ensure that what has been reduced to writing is a true and faithful version of the information given.
details.citation: Kerala Police - Standard Operating Procedure: Investigation & Prosecution in General (SOP Series), State Police Chief, 01.11.2020

details.text: If the informant cannot sign, take his right/left hand thumb impression; if he cannot speak the regional language, seek the service of an interpreter; read the recorded statement over to an illiterate informant 2-3 times.
details.citation: Kerala Police - Standard Operating Procedure: Investigation & Prosecution in General (SOP Series), State Police Chief, 01.11.2020

details.text: If after recording the information the informant refuses to sign the report, he may be prosecuted for the offence under Section 180 IPC.
details.citation: Kerala Police - Standard Operating Procedure: Investigation & Prosecution in General (SOP Series), State Police Chief, 01.11.2020

details.text: Absence of the informant's signature on the FIR does not vitiate or nullify it; the FIR is still admissible in evidence.
details.citation: Kerala Police - Standard Operating Procedure: Investigation & Prosecution in General (SOP Series), State Police Chief, 01.11.2020

details.text: The officer in charge, even if outside the police station building, can record the first information, forward it for registering an FIR at the police station, and commence and continue the investigation.
details.citation: Kerala Police - Standard Operating Procedure: Investigation & Prosecution in General (SOP Series), State Police Chief, 01.11.2020

details.text: If the officer in charge who registered the case is not the SHO, he shall forthwith inform the SHO to exercise the discretionary powers.
details.citation: Kerala Police - Standard Operating Procedure: Investigation & Prosecution in General (SOP Series), State Police Chief, 01.11.2020

details.text: At a Police Out-Post the officer in charge cannot prepare an FIR (he is not a Station House Officer): he enters the facts in the Out-Post general diary and sends the report or the informant as expeditiously as possible to the police station; in an emergency he proceeds to the scene, takes steps to arrest the accused and recover stolen property pending the SHO's arrival, and sees to the proper guarding of the scene.
details.citation: Kerala Police - Standard Operating Procedure: Investigation & Prosecution in General (SOP Series), State Police Chief, 01.11.2020

Read the written information over to the informant.

steps.title: Reduce oral information to writing and sign it
steps.triage_why: Statutory requirement under BNSS 173(1)(i); failure to properly reduce oral complaints to writing and obtain signatures can invalidate the FIR.
steps.case_action: If the information is given orally, reduce it to writing (by the SHO or under his supervision), read it over to Samarth Manishkumar Choksi, and obtain Samarth Manishkumar Choksi's signature on every such written complaint; enter its substance in the prescribed station book [Section 173(1)(i) BNSS].

steps.text: Record the FIR as a truthful, complete first account — neither minimized nor exaggerated: note the time of occurrence (occurrence and reporting times must be logical), motive, preparation and previous/subsequent conduct of the accused if known, the modus operandi, identity or physical features of the accused with the circumstances of identification (light, distance, line of visibility), names of eyewitnesses, injuries seen on the informant or witnesses, and the correct value and identifying marks of property involved.

details.text: Cover the eleven 'W's for a comprehensive FIR: what information, informant's capacity (eyewitness/victim/hearsay), who committed, who is the victim, when, where, why (motive), which way it happened (role of each accused, weapon), who else was present, what was taken away, what traces were left.
details.citation: Kerala Police - Standard Operating Procedure: Investigation & Prosecution in General (SOP Series), State Police Chief, 01.11.2020

details.text: Enter serially the names of known/suspected/unknown accused with full particulars; record eyewitness names and the names of persons to whom the complainant reported the accused's names immediately after the occurrence — if available first-hand information is not noted, the defence may term it fabrication and afterthought.
details.citation: Kerala Police - Standard Operating Procedure: Investigation & Prosecution in General (SOP Series), State Police Chief, 01.11.2020

details.text: The informant should distinguish between what he saw, knew and heard; where a particular person is suspected, clearly specify the facts on which the suspicion is based.
details.citation: Kerala Police - Standard Operating Procedure: Investigation & Prosecution in General (SOP Series), State Police Chief, 01.11.2020

details.text: Explain any delay in lodging the FIR believably in the FIR itself (8th column); unexplained delay creates suspicion of afterthought, though delay in filing an FIR in a rape case cannot be used against the prosecution.
details.citation: Kerala Police - Standard Operating Procedure: Investigation & Prosecution in General (SOP Series), State Police Chief, 01.11.2020

details.text: Do not interpolate anything after the FIR has been written; avoid scoring out what has been written — in unavoidable cases draw a line across the words keeping them legible and the recording officer should initial it.
details.citation: Kerala Police - Standard Operating Procedure: Investigation & Prosecution in General (SOP Series), State Police Chief, 01.11.2020

details.text: Do not avoid the crucial facts of the First Information Statement while filling the 12th column of the FIR, and do not include in column 12 information that was not stated in the first information.
details.citation: Kerala Police - Standard Operating Procedure: Investigation & Prosecution in General (SOP Series), State Police Chief, 01.11.2020

details.text: Mention correctly the value of property stolen, damaged or lost — do not lessen it to improve statistics — and clearly note special identifying marks with a detailed description.
details.citation: Kerala Police - Standard Operating Procedure: Investigation & Prosecution in General (SOP Series), State Police Chief, 01.11.2020

details.text: If the incident happened after sunset, explain the source of light; record the direction and distance of the place of occurrence from the police station in the last part of the statement; record the informant's contact number and e-mail ID; if the victim does not come to give the statement, explain the reason for his absence.
details.citation: Kerala Police - Standard Operating Procedure: Investigation & Prosecution in General (SOP Series), State Police Chief, 01.11.2020

details.text: If the informant knows the names of the occurrence/ocular witnesses, record them in the First Information Statement.
details.citation: Kerala Police - Standard Operating Procedure: Investigation & Prosecution in General (SOP Series), State Police Chief, 01.11.2020

steps.title: Capture every required particular in the FIR
steps.triage_why: Good investigative practice for a complete record, but the legal validity of the prosecution does not depend on the 'completeness' of the FIR as much as its existence.

steps.text: Treat the informant properly while taking the FIR: allow nobody to prompt statements, do not distort or exaggerate the information given, never jump to conclusions, do not make the informant wait long, do not insult, abuse or ridicule him, do not deprive him of the public utilities at the police station for his primary needs, put a stressed informant at ease, brief him about his rights and the services rendered by the police, and if an injured person comes to the station, do not record the statement there — direct him to hospital immediately and record the statement at the hospital.

details.text: Be humble, polite and simple, using very polite language with senior citizens; if a written complaint has omissions, clarify the relevant details and then record the information; put the stressed informant at ease before recording.
details.citation: Kerala Police - Standard Operating Procedure: Investigation & Prosecution in General (SOP Series), State Police Chief, 01.11.2020

details.text: While taking the statement of an injured person, note the position of the injury.
details.citation: Kerala Police - Standard Operating Procedure: Investigation & Prosecution in General (SOP Series), State Police Chief, 01.11.2020

steps.text: Do not conduct a preliminary inquiry: (a) in any offence outside the band of imprisonment of three years or more but less than seven years; (b) in any offence under the SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, as barred by Section 18A of that Act; (c) for a complaint made by the complainant before a Magistrate having jurisdiction (complaint case); (d) at the time of registering a Zero FIR by a non-jurisdictional police station; and (e) when registration of an FIR has been ordered by a Court or a competent authority.
legal_basis: Section 173(3) BNSS 2023
Section 18A, SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act 1989
Section 199(c) BNS 2023

details.text: Also do not conduct a preliminary enquiry for the offences mentioned in Section 199(c) BNS (BNS 64, 65, 66, 67, 68, 70, 71, 74, 76, 77, 79, 124, 143, 144) even though they fall within the three-to-seven-year punishment range of Section 173(3) BNSS — failure to record information for these offences is itself punishable for the officer.
details.citation: BPR&D - Final SOP on Preliminary Enquiry, 2023 (Section 173(3) BNSS)

details.text: In cases under the SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act 1989, register the FIR without any preliminary enquiry whatsoever.

details.text: Do not conduct a preliminary enquiry for offences mentioned in Section 199(c) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita even though they fall within the three-to-seven-year punishment range of Section 173(3) BNSS.

legal_basis: Section 302 IPC [now BNS 103(1)] — punishment for murder: death, or imprisonment for life, and also liable to fine

Section 304B IPC [now BNS 80] — dowry death, where the death of a woman is caused by any burns or bodily injury or occurs otherwise than under normal circumstances within seven years of her marriage and it is shown that soon before her death she was subjected to cruelty or harassment by her husband or any relative of her husband for or in connection with any demand for dowry
Section 174 CrPC [now BNSS 194] — police to enquire and report on suicide etc.; report signed and forwarded forthwith to the District Magistrate or Sub-divisional Magistrate

Section 176 CrPC [now BNSS 196] — inquiry by Magistrate into cause of death; power to disinter and examine a body; relatives to be informed and allowed to remain present ('relative' means parents, children, brothers, sisters and spouse)
Section 327 IPC [now BNS 119(1)] — voluntarily causing hurt to extort property, or to constrain to an illegal act (imprisonment up to ten years and fine)
Section 323 IPC [now BNS 115(2)] — punishment for voluntarily causing hurt (except the case provided for by s.334 IPC): imprisonment up to one year, or fine up to one thousand rupees, or both
Section 284 IPC [now BNS 286] — punishment for careless handling of poisonous substances

Sections 299, 302, 304A, 306, 307, 309, 324, 326, 328 and 489A IPC [now BNS 100, 103, 106(1), 108, 109, no direct BNS equivalent for 309 (BNS 226 covers only attempt to suicide to compel or restrain a public servant), 118(1), 118(2), 123 and 178 respectively] — offences relating to administration of poisonous substances
Poisons Act 1919; Drugs Act 1940; Drugs and Magic Remedies Act 1954; Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act 1985; Pharmacy Act 1948 — possession, sale and control of poisons

steps.title: Locate latent fingerprints before searching the scene
steps.triage_why: Latent fingerprints are fragile evidence. Touching items before dusting leads to permanent degradation/loss of the accused's prints at the scene.

steps.text: Search the scene by an orderly, recognised pattern so no material evidence is missed: Line/Strip method (large and outdoor scenes - walk end to end and return); Grid method (double line search, large scenes such as fields); Wheel/Ray method (small circular scenes - from the centre outward along radii); Spiral method (outdoor scenes without barriers - ever-widening circle from the core); Zone method (houses/buildings - divide into four quadrants and examine each).

details.text: The most practical method is to begin the search at the point where the body is first discovered and extend the search in an outward direction until the entire room or location has been covered.

steps.text: For every offence punishable with seven years or more, the officer in charge of the police station shall cause a forensic expert to visit the crime scene to collect forensic evidence, and shall cause videography of the process on a mobile phone or other electronic device (BNSS 176(3)); where the State lacks a forensic facility, the State Government notifies utilization of another State's facility.

steps.deadline: Mandatory from the date notified by the State Government, which must be notified as early as possible but not later than five years (BNSS 176(3))

steps.applies_when: Offence punishable with imprisonment of seven years or more

details.text: Role allocation: if only the police first responder is present/equipped, the first responder performs the scene photography/videography per SOP; if only the forensic team is present (fully equipped), it performs the recording; if both are functional and well equipped, the first responder records where there is a time lag in the forensic team reaching the scene, and where there is no time lag the forensic team takes the lead and performs the complete SOP.

details.text: Rationale: forensic experts are limited in number and stationed at district headquarters and delay disturbs the scene, so the first responder's own videography/photography preserves the scene authentically; specific and expert photography for better erudition of evidence follows, done by forensic science experts with distinct training.

steps.text: Know and apply the statutory contexts requiring audio-video recording: (1) BNSS 105 - search and seizure processes (mandatory); (2) BNSS 173 - FIR registration: for victims of BNS 64-71, 74-79 and 124 offences who are mentally/physically disabled, record the information at the informant's residence or chosen place in the presence of an interpreter/special educator, with videography of the recording MANDATORY; (3) BNSS 176 - rape victim's statement at her residence or place of choice, if possible by a woman police officer, optionally recordable by audio-video means including mobile phone; (4) BNSS 180 - witness statements may also be recorded by audio-video means (optional); (5) BNSS 185 - police search must compulsorily be recorded by audio-video means, desirably by mobile phone.

details.text: The crime scene itself is to be recorded through any audio-video electronic means, preferably mobile phone - a major change of the new criminal laws to improve evidence quality, overcome contradictory witness testimony and defeat allegations of tampering.

bsa_refs.title: Admissibility of electronic records
bsa_refs.summary: This is the operative provision for proving electronic records. Operating notwithstanding anything contained in this Adhiniyam, sub-section (1) deems any information contained in an electronic record which is printed on paper, stored, recorded or copied in optical or magnetic media or semiconductor memory and produced by a computer or any communication device, or otherwise stored, recorded or copied in any electronic form (the 'computer output'), to be also a document, if the conditions mentioned in this section are satisfied in relation to the information and computer in question, and makes that output admissible in any proceedings, without further proof or production of the original, as evidence of any contents of the original or of any fact stated therein of which direct evidence would be admissible. What sub-section (1) deems is that the computer output is ALSO a document: it does not deem the output to be the original, and it settles nothing about the truth or the weight of what the record contains. Both the deeming and the admissibility are conditional on the section's conditions being satisfied. (The supplied Gazette text reads 'as evidence or any contents of the original'; that is an apparent typographical error for 'as evidence of any contents of the original', and the latter reading is used here.) Sub-section (2) lays down the four conditions in clauses (a) to (d): production of the output by the computer or communication device during the period over which it was used regularly to create, store or process information for the purposes of any activity regularly carried on over that period by the person having lawful control over its use; regular feeding into the device, in the ordinary course of those activities, of information of the kind contained in the record or of the kind from which it is derived; the device operating properly throughout the material part of that period, or any period in which it was not operating properly or was out of operation during that part not being such as to affect the electronic record or the accuracy of its contents; and the information in the record reproducing or being derived from such information fed in. Sub-section (3) treats all the computers or communication devices used for that purpose during that period, whether in standalone mode, on a computer system, on a computer network, on a computer resource enabling information creation or providing information processing and storage, or through an intermediary, as constituting for the purposes of this section a single computer or communication device, and references in the section are construed accordingly. Sub-section (4) is the certificate provision: in any proceeding where it is desired to give a statement in evidence by virtue of this section, a certificate doing ANY of the following three things shall be submitted along with the electronic record at each instance where it is being submitted for admission, namely (a) identifying the electronic record containing the statement and describing the manner in which it was produced, (b) giving such particulars of any device involved in the production of that record as may be appropriate for the purpose of showing that it was produced by a computer or a communication device referred to in clauses (a) to (e) of sub-section (3), and (c) dealing with any of the matters to which the conditions mentioned in sub-section (2) relate. The certificate must purport to be signed by a person in charge of the computer or communication device or the management of the relevant activities (whichever is appropriate) AND an expert, that is, two signatories, and it shall be evidence of any matter stated in the certificate; for the purposes of that sub-section it is sufficient for a matter to be stated to the best of the knowledge and belief of the person stating it, in the certificate specified in the Schedule (the form of which is not part of the text supplied here). Sub-section (5) clarifies that information is taken to be supplied to the computer or communication device if it is supplied in any appropriate form, whether directly or, with or without human intervention, by means of any appropriate equipment; and that a computer output is taken to have been produced by the device whether produced by it directly or, with or without human intervention, by means of any appropriate equipment or by other electronic means as referred to in clauses (a) to (e) of sub-section (3).
key_requirements: Sub-section (1) operates notwithstanding anything contained in this Adhiniyam.

Information contained in an electronic record which is printed on paper, stored, recorded or copied in optical or magnetic media or semiconductor memory and produced by a computer or any communication device, or otherwise stored, recorded or copied in any electronic form (the computer output), shall be deemed to be also a document, if the conditions mentioned in this section are satisfied in relation to the information and computer in question.

Such computer output shall be admissible in any proceedings, without further proof or production of the original, as evidence of any contents of the original or of any fact stated therein of which direct evidence would be admissible (the supplied Gazette text reads 'as evidence or any contents of the original', an apparent typographical error for 'as evidence of any contents of the original', and the latter reading is used here).

The computer output containing the information must have been produced by the computer or communication device during the period over which that device was used regularly to create, store or process information for the purposes of any activity regularly carried on over that period by the person having lawful control over its use.

During the said period, information of the kind contained in the electronic record, or of the kind from which the information so contained is derived, must have been regularly fed into the computer or communication device in the ordinary course of the said activities.

Throughout the material part of the said period the computer or communication device must have been operating properly, or, if not, any period in which it was not operating properly or was out of operation during that part of the period must not have been such as to affect the electronic record or the accuracy of its contents.
The information contained in the electronic record must reproduce or be derived from such information fed into the computer or communication device in the ordinary course of the said activities.

Where the function of creating, storing or processing information for the purposes of the activity was regularly performed by means of one or more computers or communication devices, whether in standalone mode, on a computer system, on a computer network, on a computer resource enabling information creation or providing information processing and storage, or through an intermediary, all the computers or communication devices used for that purpose during that period shall be treated for the purposes of this section as constituting a single computer or communication device.

In any proceeding where it is desired to give a statement in evidence by virtue of this section, a certificate doing any of the things listed in clauses (a) to (c) of sub-section (4) shall be submitted along with the electronic record.
The certificate shall be submitted along with the electronic record at each instance where it is being submitted for admission.
Clause (a) of sub-section (4): identifying the electronic record containing the statement and describing the manner in which it was produced.

Clause (b) of sub-section (4): giving such particulars of any device involved in the production of that electronic record as may be appropriate for the purpose of showing that the electronic record was produced by a computer or a communication device referred to in clauses (a) to (e) of sub-section (3).
Clause (c) of sub-section (4): dealing with any of the matters to which the conditions mentioned in sub-section (2) relate.
The certificate must purport to be signed by a person in charge of the computer or communication device or the management of the relevant activities (whichever is appropriate) and an expert.
The certificate shall be evidence of any matter stated in the certificate.
For the purposes of sub-section (4) it shall be sufficient for a matter to be stated to the best of the knowledge and belief of the person stating it in the certificate specified in the Schedule.

Information shall be taken to be supplied to a computer or communication device if it is supplied thereto in any appropriate form and whether it is so supplied directly or (with or without human intervention) by means of any appropriate equipment.

A computer output shall be taken to have been produced by a computer or communication device whether it was produced by it directly or (with or without human intervention) by means of any appropriate equipment or by other electronic means as referred to in clauses (a) to (e) of sub-section (3).
bsa_refs.investigation_relevance: Wherever the IO relies on this section to put computer output in evidence - CDRs, CCTV footage, device extractions, printouts, server logs - the record must travel with a sub-section (4) certificate, and it must go with the record each and every time the record is submitted for admission, not merely once at charge-sheet stage. On the text the certificate is one 'doing any of' three things: identifying the record and describing how it was produced, giving particulars of any device involved, and dealing with any of the matters to which the sub-section (2) conditions relate; the statute requires any of the three, but the safe practice is to cover all three. The certificate must purport to be signed by two people, a person in charge of the computer or communication device or the management of the relevant activities (whichever is appropriate) and an expert, and it is the certificate specified in the Schedule, so the IO should line up both signatories before the record is tendered; a matter may be stated in it to the best of the knowledge and belief of the person stating it. At seizure, therefore, the IO should record the facts the signatories will later have to certify: regular use of the device over the relevant period for the activity, who had lawful control over its use, regular feeding of information of that kind in the ordinary course, and the proper working of the device (or that any malfunction or downtime in the material part of the period did not affect the record or the accuracy of its contents). Note the limits of sub-section (1): where the conditions are met it deems the computer output to be also a document and lets it in without further proof or production of the original, but it does not make the output the original and it settles nothing about the truth or weight of the contents.
time_limits: s.63(2)(a): no fixed number of days is prescribed - the relevant period is the period over which the computer or communication device was used regularly to create, store or process information for the purposes of the activity regularly carried on over that period.

s.63(2)(c): the computer or communication device must have been operating properly 'throughout the material part of the said period', or any period in which it was not operating properly or was out of operation during that part must not have been such as to affect the electronic record or the accuracy of its contents. This qualification belongs to clause (c) alone and does not relax clauses (a), (b) or (d).
s.63(4): the certificate must be submitted along with the electronic record 'at each instance where it is being submitted for admission' - a repeating timing requirement, not a one-time filing.

bsa_refs.source_note: The Gazette text of sub-section (1) prints "as evidence or any contents of the original". The reading is plainly "as evidence of any contents", which is how the key requirement states it and how the repealed s.65B of the Evidence Act read; the quotation reproduces the print exactly. Flag it if a defence takes a point on it.

steps.title: Establish Positions by Photographing an Undisturbed Scene
steps.triage_why: Crime scene documentation must occur before alteration; once the body or weapons are moved, the original spatial relationship (crucial for reconstruction) is lost forever.

steps.text: Photograph/videograph in three ranges: (1) overall wide-angle coverage of the whole scene and the surrounding area (for outdoor scenes drone cameras may be used); (2) mid-range/orientation shots showing the relation and location of each piece of evidence to the others and to its surroundings; (3) close-up/macro shots of each item taken TWICE - once WITH a scale/ruler and once WITHOUT - so the defence cannot allege the scene was altered or that anything was concealed. Photograph the dead body (if present) to show location, injuries and condition; photograph each piece of evidence where found to establish its relationship to the victim; shoot evidence from straight above to eliminate distance distortion; and photograph blood patterns with a scale from different angles.

details.text: The blood-stain pattern at the scene can indicate the type of weapon of offence.
details.citation: Directorate of Forensic Science Services, Ministry of Home Affairs, Govt of India - Standard Operating Procedure for Crime Scene Investigation

details.text: In cases of murder or suicide a medical officer should accompany the police to the scene whenever possible and inspect the body and its surroundings before they are disturbed.
details.citation: Directorate of Forensic Science Services, Ministry of Home Affairs, Govt of India - Standard Operating Procedure for Crime Scene Investigation

details.text: Take colour photographs (colour photography is mandatory in UAPA cases); point the photographs at the evidence in the scene (tyre marks, footprints, perishable evidence); take long-distance shots to show the location (a drone may be utilized in certain cases), intermediate-distance shots to show relative positions, and close-up shots of injuries, footprints, dagger, firearms etc.; prefer the Department Photographer/Videographer, else private photographers at Government-fixed rates; in police encounter death cases photography/videography by BOTH private and department photographers is mandatory.
details.citation: Kerala Police - Standard Operating Procedure: Investigation & Prosecution in General (SOP Series), State Police Chief, 01.11.2020

details.text: Scales/measuring tapes may be used while taking photographs from short distances.
details.citation: Kerala Police - Standard Operating Procedure: Investigation & Prosecution in General (SOP Series), State Police Chief, 01.11.2020

details.text: Ensure proper lighting; take a complete set of pictures - aerial, long-range, mid-range and close-ups; include entry and exit routes, victims and evidence as far as possible; photograph/video transient marks such as blood stains, fingerprints and footprints as soon as possible; work from the exterior to the interior and from general to specific focus; prefer close-up photography for footprints, fingerprints, shoeprints, tyre tracks and injuries; take photographs and video with a scale when appropriate.
details.citation: BPR&D - SOP on Audio-Video Recording under the New Criminal Laws (BNSS/BSA)

details.text: When photographing injuries hold the camera at a 90-degree angle to the injury and take (1) a general-scene or full-frame photo/video of the person, (2) a shot showing the relationship of the injury to the subject's body, and (3) a close-up of the injury WITH and WITHOUT the evidence ruler.
details.citation: BPR&D - SOP on Audio-Video Recording under the New Criminal Laws (BNSS/BSA)

details.text: Give proper attention to the quality of videography/photography so it can be used for comparison purposes or to calculate precise measurements - latent prints, exemplars/standards, other ridge detail impressions, bloodstains, bullet strikes, transfer patterns, tool marks, bite marks, pattern injuries, and tire or footwear impressions.
details.citation: BPR&D - SOP on Audio-Video Recording under the New Criminal Laws (BNSS/BSA)

steps.triage_why: Scale and orientation shots are necessary to prove the exact location of evidence; without them, the physical evidence may be challenged as being out of context.

steps.text: Prepare a crime scene sketch - generally rough, but in heinous crimes also to scale: measure distances accurately and leave nothing of importance out; show the exact position of one or two permanent fixtures to help ascertain distances to major articles, exhibits and marks (blood stains, vehicle track marks); note the relationship of the various pieces of evidence to the surroundings; indicate the compass north point obtained by compass; and mention the title, case reference, date, time, and name and signature of the IO in the corner.

details.text: The IO's sketch map is relevant under ss.7 & 9 Evidence Act [now BSA] as based on actual spot observation; record the scale, indicate direction, and have the person who prepares it sign it (two independent witnesses may be cited); the services of revenue officials may be sought; draw it on good quality A3/A4 paper; establish the scene boundary mentioning distances from identifying fixed points/pillars/marks.
details.citation: Kerala Police - Standard Operating Procedure: Investigation & Prosecution in General (SOP Series), State Police Chief, 01.11.2020

details.text: Never avoid making a sketch in cases such as road accident, murder and gunshot fire; include the relative positions of objects, fittings, fixtures, furniture, vehicle, dead body and weapons, and mention road, wall, river, well, building, railway track and trees; measure exact inter-distances with a tape and do not rely on approximation; North should be toward the top shown by an arrow head; indicate identity marks such as tattoo, injuries and other atypical marks on the body as figures; always mention case number, section, police station, date, time and place of occurrence.
details.citation: Director, Forensic Science Laboratory, UP Police - Crime Scene (Protocol) Management (English section)

details.text: Always use appropriate and conventional symbols, letters and digits of a legend to avoid crowding the sketch.
details.citation: Director, Forensic Science Laboratory, UP Police - Crime Scene (Protocol) Management (English section)

details.text: Draw the site plan of the place of occurrence correctly, indicating the directions from where the accused persons came and left, the surrounding areas of the scene of crime, where the incident took place, from where the exhibits were lifted, and the source of light during night. If the scene of crime, the place where the accused in the vehicle were last seen, or any other relevant exhibits are at different locations, prepare separate site plans.
details.citation: Delhi Police Academy - Compendium of Scenarios for Investigating Officers, 2024

details.text: Prepare the demarcation memo of the place of occurrence, the site plan of the place of occurrence and the site plan of the place of recovery.

details.text: Show the point of source of light in the site plan of the place of occurrence if the same was prepared in the night.

ticks.do: Prepare a crime scene sketch, generally rough, but in heinous crimes also to scale.
Measure distances accurately and leave nothing of importance out.
Show the exact position of one or two permanent fixtures to help ascertain distances to major articles, exhibits and marks (blood stains, vehicle track marks).
Note the relationship of the various pieces of evidence to the surroundings.
Indicate the compass north point obtained by compass.
Mention in the corner the title, case reference, date, time, and name and signature of the IO.

steps.title: Draw and Annotate the Crime Scene Sketch
steps.triage_why: A scaled sketch is mandatory in heinous crimes (murder) to establish the geometry of the scene and the position of the deceased/weapons.

steps.text: Review the preliminary survey to determine the documentation needed (photography, video, sketch, measurements, notes) and maintain the documentation as a permanent record. Prepare notes and reports in chronological order containing facts only - no opinions, no analysis and no conclusions - and give a general description of the scene exactly as the IO sees it during the preliminary survey.

details.text: Document the scene; there are three ways by which it can be documented: by photography/videography of the scene, or drawing the sketch map of the scene, or preparing a descriptive mahazar.
details.citation: Kerala Police - Standard Operating Procedure: Investigation & Prosecution in General (SOP Series), State Police Chief, 01.11.2020

details.text: Never omit to include in the crime scene report the significant and important positive OR negative findings of preliminary examinations encountered during investigation, and always include photographs, sketches and maps in the report.
details.citation: Director, Forensic Science Laboratory, UP Police - Crime Scene (Protocol) Management (English section)

details.text: In burn cases, never forget to incorporate the condition of doors and windows and the position of bolts and stoppers in the panchnama of the scene of occurrence.
details.citation: Director, Forensic Science Laboratory, UP Police - Crime Scene (Protocol) Management (English section)

details.text: Document all observations at the scene of crime very meticulously, paying attention to every detail; reliance on memory should be strictly avoided.
details.citation: LNJN National Institute of Criminology and Forensic Science, MHA - A Forensic Guide for Crime Investigators: Standard Operating Procedures (marked Restricted)

details.text: Use the documentation to identify the location of evidentiary items that may later be lost, contaminated or destroyed.

bsa_refs.title: Admissibility of electronic records
bsa_refs.summary: This is the operative provision for proving electronic records. Operating notwithstanding anything contained in this Adhiniyam, sub-section (1) deems any information contained in an electronic record which is printed on paper, stored, recorded or copied in optical or magnetic media or semiconductor memory and produced by a computer or any communication device, or otherwise stored, recorded or copied in any electronic form (the 'computer output'), to be also a document, if the conditions mentioned in this section are satisfied in relation to the information and computer in question, and makes that output admissible in any proceedings, without further proof or production of the original, as evidence of any contents of the original or of any fact stated therein of which direct evidence would be admissible. What sub-section (1) deems is that the computer output is ALSO a document: it does not deem the output to be the original, and it settles nothing about the truth or the weight of what the record contains. Both the deeming and the admissibility are conditional on the section's conditions being satisfied. (The supplied Gazette text reads 'as evidence or any contents of the original'; that is an apparent typographical error for 'as evidence of any contents of the original', and the latter reading is used here.) Sub-section (2) lays down the four conditions in clauses (a) to (d): production of the output by the computer or communication device during the period over which it was used regularly to create, store or process information for the purposes of any activity regularly carried on over that period by the person having lawful control over its use; regular feeding into the device, in the ordinary course of those activities, of information of the kind contained in the record or of the kind from which it is derived; the device operating properly throughout the material part of that period, or any period in which it was not operating properly or was out of operation during that part not being such as to affect the electronic record or the accuracy of its contents; and the information in the record reproducing or being derived from such information fed in. Sub-section (3) treats all the computers or communication devices used for that purpose during that period, whether in standalone mode, on a computer system, on a computer network, on a computer resource enabling information creation or providing information processing and storage, or through an intermediary, as constituting for the purposes of this section a single computer or communication device, and references in the section are construed accordingly. Sub-section (4) is the certificate provision: in any proceeding where it is desired to give a statement in evidence by virtue of this section, a certificate doing ANY of the following three things shall be submitted along with the electronic record at each instance where it is being submitted for admission, namely (a) identifying the electronic record containing the statement and describing the manner in which it was produced, (b) giving such particulars of any device involved in the production of that record as may be appropriate for the purpose of showing that it was produced by a computer or a communication device referred to in clauses (a) to (e) of sub-section (3), and (c) dealing with any of the matters to which the conditions mentioned in sub-section (2) relate. The certificate must purport to be signed by a person in charge of the computer or communication device or the management of the relevant activities (whichever is appropriate) AND an expert, that is, two signatories, and it shall be evidence of any matter stated in the certificate; for the purposes of that sub-section it is sufficient for a matter to be stated to the best of the knowledge and belief of the person stating it, in the certificate specified in the Schedule (the form of which is not part of the text supplied here). Sub-section (5) clarifies that information is taken to be supplied to the computer or communication device if it is supplied in any appropriate form, whether directly or, with or without human intervention, by means of any appropriate equipment; and that a computer output is taken to have been produced by the device whether produced by it directly or, with or without human intervention, by means of any appropriate equipment or by other electronic means as referred to in clauses (a) to (e) of sub-section (3).
key_requirements: Sub-section (1) operates notwithstanding anything contained in this Adhiniyam.

Information contained in an electronic record which is printed on paper, stored, recorded or copied in optical or magnetic media or semiconductor memory and produced by a computer or any communication device, or otherwise stored, recorded or copied in any electronic form (the computer output), shall be deemed to be also a document, if the conditions mentioned in this section are satisfied in relation to the information and computer in question.

Such computer output shall be admissible in any proceedings, without further proof or production of the original, as evidence of any contents of the original or of any fact stated therein of which direct evidence would be admissible (the supplied Gazette text reads 'as evidence or any contents of the original', an apparent typographical error for 'as evidence of any contents of the original', and the latter reading is used here).

The computer output containing the information must have been produced by the computer or communication device during the period over which that device was used regularly to create, store or process information for the purposes of any activity regularly carried on over that period by the person having lawful control over its use.

During the said period, information of the kind contained in the electronic record, or of the kind from which the information so contained is derived, must have been regularly fed into the computer or communication device in the ordinary course of the said activities.

Throughout the material part of the said period the computer or communication device must have been operating properly, or, if not, any period in which it was not operating properly or was out of operation during that part of the period must not have been such as to affect the electronic record or the accuracy of its contents.
The information contained in the electronic record must reproduce or be derived from such information fed into the computer or communication device in the ordinary course of the said activities.

Where the function of creating, storing or processing information for the purposes of the activity was regularly performed by means of one or more computers or communication devices, whether in standalone mode, on a computer system, on a computer network, on a computer resource enabling information creation or providing information processing and storage, or through an intermediary, all the computers or communication devices used for that purpose during that period shall be treated for the purposes of this section as constituting a single computer or communication device.

In any proceeding where it is desired to give a statement in evidence by virtue of this section, a certificate doing any of the things listed in clauses (a) to (c) of sub-section (4) shall be submitted along with the electronic record.
The certificate shall be submitted along with the electronic record at each instance where it is being submitted for admission.
Clause (a) of sub-section (4): identifying the electronic record containing the statement and describing the manner in which it was produced.

Clause (b) of sub-section (4): giving such particulars of any device involved in the production of that electronic record as may be appropriate for the purpose of showing that the electronic record was produced by a computer or a communication device referred to in clauses (a) to (e) of sub-section (3).
Clause (c) of sub-section (4): dealing with any of the matters to which the conditions mentioned in sub-section (2) relate.
The certificate must purport to be signed by a person in charge of the computer or communication device or the management of the relevant activities (whichever is appropriate) and an expert.
The certificate shall be evidence of any matter stated in the certificate.
For the purposes of sub-section (4) it shall be sufficient for a matter to be stated to the best of the knowledge and belief of the person stating it in the certificate specified in the Schedule.

Information shall be taken to be supplied to a computer or communication device if it is supplied thereto in any appropriate form and whether it is so supplied directly or (with or without human intervention) by means of any appropriate equipment.

A computer output shall be taken to have been produced by a computer or communication device whether it was produced by it directly or (with or without human intervention) by means of any appropriate equipment or by other electronic means as referred to in clauses (a) to (e) of sub-section (3).
bsa_refs.investigation_relevance: Wherever the IO relies on this section to put computer output in evidence - CDRs, CCTV footage, device extractions, printouts, server logs - the record must travel with a sub-section (4) certificate, and it must go with the record each and every time the record is submitted for admission, not merely once at charge-sheet stage. On the text the certificate is one 'doing any of' three things: identifying the record and describing how it was produced, giving particulars of any device involved, and dealing with any of the matters to which the sub-section (2) conditions relate; the statute requires any of the three, but the safe practice is to cover all three. The certificate must purport to be signed by two people, a person in charge of the computer or communication device or the management of the relevant activities (whichever is appropriate) and an expert, and it is the certificate specified in the Schedule, so the IO should line up both signatories before the record is tendered; a matter may be stated in it to the best of the knowledge and belief of the person stating it. At seizure, therefore, the IO should record the facts the signatories will later have to certify: regular use of the device over the relevant period for the activity, who had lawful control over its use, regular feeding of information of that kind in the ordinary course, and the proper working of the device (or that any malfunction or downtime in the material part of the period did not affect the record or the accuracy of its contents). Note the limits of sub-section (1): where the conditions are met it deems the computer output to be also a document and lets it in without further proof or production of the original, but it does not make the output the original and it settles nothing about the truth or weight of the contents.
time_limits: s.63(2)(a): no fixed number of days is prescribed - the relevant period is the period over which the computer or communication device was used regularly to create, store or process information for the purposes of the activity regularly carried on over that period.

s.63(2)(c): the computer or communication device must have been operating properly 'throughout the material part of the said period', or any period in which it was not operating properly or was out of operation during that part must not have been such as to affect the electronic record or the accuracy of its contents. This qualification belongs to clause (c) alone and does not relax clauses (a), (b) or (d).
s.63(4): the certificate must be submitted along with the electronic record 'at each instance where it is being submitted for admission' - a repeating timing requirement, not a one-time filing.

bsa_refs.title: Proof of signature and handwriting of person alleged to have signed or written document produced
bsa_refs.summary: This section states the proof rule for a document said to bear a person's signature or handwriting. Where a document is alleged to be signed by, or to have been written wholly or in part by, any person, the signature or the handwriting of so much of the document as is alleged to be in that person's handwriting must be proved to be in his handwriting. The obligation is mandatory, and it is limited to the portion alleged to be that person's: nothing beyond that portion has to be proved under this section. The section does not itself prescribe the manner in which that proof is to be given, and it names no act to be done by any investigating officer; it operates as a rule of proof on whoever tenders the document and on the Court in receiving it.
key_requirements: If a document is alleged to be signed or to have been written wholly or in part by any person, the signature or the handwriting must be proved to be in his handwriting.
The proof requirement extends only to so much of the document as is alleged to be in that person's handwriting.
bsa_refs.investigation_relevance: Whenever the case rests on a signed or handwritten document - a disputed cheque, a receipt, a threat letter, a register entry, a signed agreement - the IO must build the material that will later establish the signature or handwriting as that person's, because the document does not prove itself. Note the limit: only the part alleged to be in that person's hand needs proving, so the IO should identify precisely which words, entries or signature are attributed to the accused or witness. The section itself prescribes no mode of proof and no step for the IO; nothing about specimen writings, comparison or expert opinion appears in this text, so any such step must be sourced from another provision and not from this one.

steps.text: Protect all evidence against loss, contamination, cross-transfer (suspect to victim, victim to suspect, scene to scene, item to item) and deterioration, and take care while picking and packing that no article is inadvertently contaminated with extraneous material. bsa_refs.title: Admissibility of electronic records
bsa_refs.summary: This is the operative provision for proving electronic records. Operating notwithstanding anything contained in this Adhiniyam, sub-section (1) deems any information contained in an electronic record which is printed on paper, stored, recorded or copied in optical or magnetic media or semiconductor memory and produced by a computer or any communication device, or otherwise stored, recorded or copied in any electronic form (the 'computer output'), to be also a document, if the conditions mentioned in this section are satisfied in relation to the information and computer in question, and makes that output admissible in any proceedings, without further proof or production of the original, as evidence of any contents of the original or of any fact stated therein of which direct evidence would be admissible. What sub-section (1) deems is that the computer output is ALSO a document: it does not deem the output to be the original, and it settles nothing about the truth or the weight of what the record contains. Both the deeming and the admissibility are conditional on the section's conditions being satisfied. (The supplied Gazette text reads 'as evidence or any contents of the original'; that is an apparent typographical error for 'as evidence of any contents of the original', and the latter reading is used here.) Sub-section (2) lays down the four conditions in clauses (a) to (d): production of the output by the computer or communication device during the period over which it was used regularly to create, store or process information for the purposes of any activity regularly carried on over that period by the person having lawful control over its use; regular feeding into the device, in the ordinary course of those activities, of information of the kind contained in the record or of the kind from which it is derived; the device operating properly throughout the material part of that period, or any period in which it was not operating properly or was out of operation during that part not being such as to affect the electronic record or the accuracy of its contents; and the information in the record reproducing or being derived from such information fed in. Sub-section (3) treats all the computers or communication devices used for that purpose during that period, whether in standalone mode, on a computer system, on a computer network, on a computer resource enabling information creation or providing information processing and storage, or through an intermediary, as constituting for the purposes of this section a single computer or communication device, and references in the section are construed accordingly. Sub-section (4) is the certificate provision: in any proceeding where it is desired to give a statement in evidence by virtue of this section, a certificate doing ANY of the following three things shall be submitted along with the electronic record at each instance where it is being submitted for admission, namely (a) identifying the electronic record containing the statement and describing the manner in which it was produced, (b) giving such particulars of any device involved in the production of that record as may be appropriate for the purpose of showing that it was produced by a computer or a communication device referred to in clauses (a) to (e) of sub-section (3), and (c) dealing with any of the matters to which the conditions mentioned in sub-section (2) relate. The certificate must purport to be signed by a person in charge of the computer or communication device or the management of the relevant activities (whichever is appropriate) AND an expert, that is, two signatories, and it shall be evidence of any matter stated in the certificate; for the purposes of that sub-section it is sufficient for a matter to be stated to the best of the knowledge and belief of the person stating it, in the certificate specified in the Schedule (the form of which is not part of the text supplied here). Sub-section (5) clarifies that information is taken to be supplied to the computer or communication device if it is supplied in any appropriate form, whether directly or, with or without human intervention, by means of any appropriate equipment; and that a computer output is taken to have been produced by the device whether produced by it directly or, with or without human intervention, by means of any appropriate equipment or by other electronic means as referred to in clauses (a) to (e) of sub-section (3).
key_requirements: Sub-section (1) operates notwithstanding anything contained in this Adhiniyam.

Information contained in an electronic record which is printed on paper, stored, recorded or copied in optical or magnetic media or semiconductor memory and produced by a computer or any communication device, or otherwise stored, recorded or copied in any electronic form (the computer output), shall be deemed to be also a document, if the conditions mentioned in this section are satisfied in relation to the information and computer in question.

Such computer output shall be admissible in any proceedings, without further proof or production of the original, as evidence of any contents of the original or of any fact stated therein of which direct evidence would be admissible (the supplied Gazette text reads 'as evidence or any contents of the original', an apparent typographical error for 'as evidence of any contents of the original', and the latter reading is used here).

The computer output containing the information must have been produced by the computer or communication device during the period over which that device was used regularly to create, store or process information for the purposes of any activity regularly carried on over that period by the person having lawful control over its use.

During the said period, information of the kind contained in the electronic record, or of the kind from which the information so contained is derived, must have been regularly fed into the computer or communication device in the ordinary course of the said activities.

Throughout the material part of the said period the computer or communication device must have been operating properly, or, if not, any period in which it was not operating properly or was out of operation during that part of the period must not have been such as to affect the electronic record or the accuracy of its contents.
The information contained in the electronic record must reproduce or be derived from such information fed into the computer or communication device in the ordinary course of the said activities.

Where the function of creating, storing or processing information for the purposes of the activity was regularly performed by means of one or more computers or communication devices, whether in standalone mode, on a computer system, on a computer network, on a computer resource enabling information creation or providing information processing and storage, or through an intermediary, all the computers or communication devices used for that purpose during that period shall be treated for the purposes of this section as constituting a single computer or communication device.

In any proceeding where it is desired to give a statement in evidence by virtue of this section, a certificate doing any of the things listed in clauses (a) to (c) of sub-section (4) shall be submitted along with the electronic record.
The certificate shall be submitted along with the electronic record at each instance where it is being submitted for admission.
Clause (a) of sub-section (4): identifying the electronic record containing the statement and describing the manner in which it was produced.

Clause (b) of sub-section (4): giving such particulars of any device involved in the production of that electronic record as may be appropriate for the purpose of showing that the electronic record was produced by a computer or a communication device referred to in clauses (a) to (e) of sub-section (3).
Clause (c) of sub-section (4): dealing with any of the matters to which the conditions mentioned in sub-section (2) relate.
The certificate must purport to be signed by a person in charge of the computer or communication device or the management of the relevant activities (whichever is appropriate) and an expert.
The certificate shall be evidence of any matter stated in the certificate.
For the purposes of sub-section (4) it shall be sufficient for a matter to be stated to the best of the knowledge and belief of the person stating it in the certificate specified in the Schedule.

Information shall be taken to be supplied to a computer or communication device if it is supplied thereto in any appropriate form and whether it is so supplied directly or (with or without human intervention) by means of any appropriate equipment.

A computer output shall be taken to have been produced by a computer or communication device whether it was produced by it directly or (with or without human intervention) by means of any appropriate equipment or by other electronic means as referred to in clauses (a) to (e) of sub-section (3).
bsa_refs.investigation_relevance: Wherever the IO relies on this section to put computer output in evidence - CDRs, CCTV footage, device extractions, printouts, server logs - the record must travel with a sub-section (4) certificate, and it must go with the record each and every time the record is submitted for admission, not merely once at charge-sheet stage. On the text the certificate is one 'doing any of' three things: identifying the record and describing how it was produced, giving particulars of any device involved, and dealing with any of the matters to which the sub-section (2) conditions relate; the statute requires any of the three, but the safe practice is to cover all three. The certificate must purport to be signed by two people, a person in charge of the computer or communication device or the management of the relevant activities (whichever is appropriate) and an expert, and it is the certificate specified in the Schedule, so the IO should line up both signatories before the record is tendered; a matter may be stated in it to the best of the knowledge and belief of the person stating it. At seizure, therefore, the IO should record the facts the signatories will later have to certify: regular use of the device over the relevant period for the activity, who had lawful control over its use, regular feeding of information of that kind in the ordinary course, and the proper working of the device (or that any malfunction or downtime in the material part of the period did not affect the record or the accuracy of its contents). Note the limits of sub-section (1): where the conditions are met it deems the computer output to be also a document and lets it in without further proof or production of the original, but it does not make the output the original and it settles nothing about the truth or weight of the contents.
time_limits: s.63(2)(a): no fixed number of days is prescribed - the relevant period is the period over which the computer or communication device was used regularly to create, store or process information for the purposes of the activity regularly carried on over that period.

s.63(2)(c): the computer or communication device must have been operating properly 'throughout the material part of the said period', or any period in which it was not operating properly or was out of operation during that part must not have been such as to affect the electronic record or the accuracy of its contents. This qualification belongs to clause (c) alone and does not relax clauses (a), (b) or (d).
s.63(4): the certificate must be submitted along with the electronic record 'at each instance where it is being submitted for admission' - a repeating timing requirement, not a one-time filing.

steps.text: Maintain a written chain of custody for every recording and every sealed evidence package from creation/seizure until handover to the forensic laboratory and to the court: once packed and sealed in front of the witnesses, keep a clear written chain of custody record for each package, documenting the name and signature of every person (including internal staff) who takes possession of or transports the evidence, the date of transfer, and the evidence's label or serial number, using the Chain of Custody Form (Case Details; Device Details; transfer-by-transfer Chain of Custody Documentation). Keep the record in a secure and reliable system with appropriate access controls and audit trails so it remains in 'proper custody' (BSA Explanation to ss.80 and 81, and s.93); send the sealed package for forensic examination without undue delay; and at the time of chargesheet submit the chain of custody with the chargesheet u/s 193 BNSS.

bsa_refs.title: Presumption as to Gazettes, newspapers, and other documents
bsa_refs.summary: This section tells the Court to presume, without further proof, that certain classes of document are genuine. The classes are documents purporting to be the Official Gazette, documents purporting to be a newspaper or journal, and documents purporting to be a document that some law directs a person to keep. The presumption is conditional: the document must be kept substantially in the form required by law and must be produced from proper custody. The Explanation defines proper custody as the place where, and the person with whom, the document is required by law to be kept, and it saves custody that is otherwise irregular where a legitimate origin is proved or the circumstances make that origin probable. The Explanation is stated to operate both for this section and for section 92.
key_requirements: The Court shall presume the genuineness of every document purporting to be the Official Gazette or to be a newspaper or journal.
The Court shall presume the genuineness of every document purporting to be a document directed by any law to be kept by any person.
The presumption operates only if such document is kept substantially in the form required by law.
The presumption operates only if the document is produced from proper custody.
A document is in proper custody if it is in the place in which, and looked after by the person with whom, such document is required to be kept.
No custody is improper if it is proved to have had a legitimate origin, or if the circumstances of the particular case are such as to render that origin probable.
The proper custody definition in the Explanation applies for the purposes of this section and section 92.
bsa_refs.investigation_relevance: When the case file relies on a Gazette notification, a newspaper or journal issue, or a register or record that some law requires a person to maintain, the IO should obtain the copy from the office or official who is legally required to keep it and record that source in the seizure memo or panchnama, because the Court's presumption of genuineness attaches only to a document produced from proper custody and kept substantially in the legally required form. Where the document was picked up from a private or unexplained source, the IO must be ready to prove a legitimate origin or circumstances making that origin probable, otherwise genuineness will have to be proved by ordinary evidence.

bsa_refs.title: Presumption as to Gazettes in electronic or digital record
bsa_refs.summary: This is the electronic counterpart of section 80. The Court shall presume the genuineness of every electronic or digital record purporting to be the Official Gazette, and of every electronic or digital record purporting to be a record that some law directs a person to keep. As in section 80, the presumption is conditional on the record being kept substantially in the form required by law and being produced from proper custody. The Explanation defines proper custody for electronic records as the place where, and the person with whom, the document is required to be kept, and preserves custody whose origin is legitimate or probably legitimate. The Explanation is stated to operate for this section and for section 93.
key_requirements: The Court shall presume the genuineness of every electronic or digital record purporting to be the Official Gazette.
The Court shall presume the genuineness of every electronic or digital record purporting to be a record directed by any law to be kept by any person.
The presumption operates only if such electronic or digital record is kept substantially in the form required by law.
The presumption operates only if the record is produced from proper custody.
Electronic records are in proper custody if they are in the place in which, and looked after by the person with whom, such document is required to be kept.
No custody is improper if it is proved to have had a legitimate origin, or the circumstances of the particular case are such as to render that origin probable.
The proper custody definition in the Explanation applies for the purposes of this section and section 93.
bsa_refs.investigation_relevance: Where the IO relies on an electronic Gazette copy or on an electronic record that a law requires some person or office to maintain, the record should be obtained from that official custodian and the source and custodian recorded, since the presumption of genuineness turns on the record being produced from proper custody and kept substantially in the legally required form. A copy collected from an unofficial mirror or a private device does not automatically get the presumption, and the IO will then have to show a legitimate or probable origin for that custody.

bsa_refs.title: Presumption as to electronic records five years old
bsa_refs.summary: Presumption as to electronic records five years old. Where an electronic record purporting or proved to be five years old is produced from any custody which the Court in the particular case considers proper, the Court may presume that an electronic signature which purports to be the electronic signature of a particular person was so affixed by him or any person authorised by him in this behalf. The modality is permissive: the text says the Court may presume, not shall presume, so nothing follows automatically once age and custody are shown. Both conditions, the five-year age and custody the Court considers proper, must be satisfied before the presumption is even available, and the Court's view of proper custody is formed in the particular case. The Explanation states that the Explanation to section 81 shall also apply to this section; section 93 itself does not set out what that Explanation contains.
key_requirements: The presumption is available only where the electronic record purports, or is proved, to be five years old.
The presumption is available only where the record is produced from custody which the Court in the particular case considers proper.

Where those conditions are met the Court may presume that the electronic signature which purports to be that of a particular person was so affixed by him or any person authorised by him in this behalf.
The Explanation to section 81 shall also apply to this section.
bsa_refs.investigation_relevance: Where the case relies on an electronic record carrying an electronic signature, the presumption under this section is reachable only if the record purports, or can be proved, to be five years old and is produced from a custody the Court in the particular case accepts as proper. The IO should therefore preserve and be able to account for the custody of such records, and should be in a position to show which of the two routes to age applies, since proof of age is not the only route where the record itself purports to be five years old. The presumption is discretionary, so the IO should not treat authorship of the electronic signature as settled: independent material linking the signature to that person, or to a person authorised by him, should still be collected.
time_limits: Five years: the presumption becomes available only for an electronic record purporting or proved to be five years old. The section fixes no other period and no outer limit.
