steps.text: Submit a certificate under BSA s.63(4) with the electronic record at EACH instance it is produced for admission: it must identify the electronic record containing the statement and describe the manner in which it was produced, give particulars of any device involved in its production, and deal with the s.63(2) conditions; it is signed BOTH by the person in charge of the computer or communication device or of the management of the relevant activities (Schedule Part A) AND by an expert (Part B), matters being stated to the best of knowledge and belief in the format specified in the Schedule. Certification does not require the OWNER of the device but the person who actually manages the device regularly at the relevant time. Never submit digital evidence to court without this certificate.

details.text: Certification is required for BOTH categories: (1) digital recordings made under the new laws - AV recording of statements of victim and witnesses u/s 180 BNSS (preferable), AV recording of search and seizure (mandatory), and other procedural compliances such as identification parade and property disposal (preferable); and (2) digital devices routinely seized during investigation (mobiles, social media accounts, emails, computers, CCTV cameras) - each certified doubly, by the handler (or manager) and by an expert.
details.citation: BPR&D - SOP on Audio-Video Recording under the New Criminal Laws (BNSS/BSA)

details.text: Part A ('to be given by party') is signed by the owner/handler or operator/first responder/manager. Where videography by the first-responder police team was actually done by a constable, the Part A certificate may be given by the head constable of that same first-responder team which routinely manages the police station's AV recording, or by the records head-mohrir under whom the record is downloaded and archived - but the chain of custody form must clearly mention the change of hands and the reasons. For seizure of digital evidence the Part A giver is the owner/operator/handler or manager or person in charge of the device in contention. Part B is signed by an 'expert' - a person occupying a responsible official position who is witness to the chain of events (e.g. the SHO; where the first responder recorded the video, the forensic team in-charge may give Part B).

bsa_refs.title: Opinions of experts
bsa_refs.summary: Section 39 makes expert opinion a relevant fact. s.39(1) provides that when the Court has to form an opinion on a point of foreign law, of science or art, or any other field, or as to identity of handwriting or finger impressions, the opinions of persons specially skilled in that subject are relevant facts, and it labels such persons "experts". s.39(2) deals separately with electronic material: where the Court has to form an opinion on any matter relating to information transmitted or stored in any computer resource or any other electronic or digital form, the opinion of the Examiner of Electronic Evidence referred to in section 79A of the Information Technology Act, 2000 is a relevant fact. The Explanation to s.39(2) provides that such an Examiner of Electronic Evidence shall be an expert. The illustrations cover opinion on symptoms produced by a poison, opinion on symptoms showing unsoundness of mind and the accused's capacity to know the nature of the act, and comparison of a disputed document with another document proved or admitted to have been written by the same person.
key_requirements: The opinions of persons specially skilled in foreign law, science or art, any other field, or in questions as to identity of handwriting or finger impressions are relevant facts when the Court has to form an opinion on that point.
Persons specially skilled in such a field are called experts.

Where the Court has to form an opinion on any matter relating to information transmitted or stored in any computer resource or any other electronic or digital form, the opinion of the Examiner of Electronic Evidence referred to in section 79A of the Information Technology Act, 2000 is a relevant fact.
For the purposes of sub-section (2), an Examiner of Electronic Evidence shall be an expert.
bsa_refs.investigation_relevance: The IO should route every scientific, medical, ballistic, chemical, handwriting or finger-impression question to a person specially skilled in that field and place the basis of that skill on record, since it is skill in the subject that makes the opinion relevant. For anything transmitted or stored in a computer resource or in any other electronic or digital form, the opinion that s.39(2) makes relevant is that of an Examiner of Electronic Evidence notified under section 79A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, so electronic exhibits should be sent to such an Examiner; and, as illustration (c) shows, a handwriting comparison requires the IO to also supply a specimen document that is proved or admitted to have been written by the suspected author.

bsa_refs.title: Admissibility of electronic records
bsa_refs.summary: This is the operative provision for proving electronic records. Operating notwithstanding anything contained in this Adhiniyam, sub-section (1) deems any information contained in an electronic record which is printed on paper, stored, recorded or copied in optical or magnetic media or semiconductor memory and produced by a computer or any communication device, or otherwise stored, recorded or copied in any electronic form (the 'computer output'), to be also a document, if the conditions mentioned in this section are satisfied in relation to the information and computer in question, and makes that output admissible in any proceedings, without further proof or production of the original, as evidence of any contents of the original or of any fact stated therein of which direct evidence would be admissible. What sub-section (1) deems is that the computer output is ALSO a document: it does not deem the output to be the original, and it settles nothing about the truth or the weight of what the record contains. Both the deeming and the admissibility are conditional on the section's conditions being satisfied. (The supplied Gazette text reads 'as evidence or any contents of the original'; that is an apparent typographical error for 'as evidence of any contents of the original', and the latter reading is used here.) Sub-section (2) lays down the four conditions in clauses (a) to (d): production of the output by the computer or communication device during the period over which it was used regularly to create, store or process information for the purposes of any activity regularly carried on over that period by the person having lawful control over its use; regular feeding into the device, in the ordinary course of those activities, of information of the kind contained in the record or of the kind from which it is derived; the device operating properly throughout the material part of that period, or any period in which it was not operating properly or was out of operation during that part not being such as to affect the electronic record or the accuracy of its contents; and the information in the record reproducing or being derived from such information fed in. Sub-section (3) treats all the computers or communication devices used for that purpose during that period, whether in standalone mode, on a computer system, on a computer network, on a computer resource enabling information creation or providing information processing and storage, or through an intermediary, as constituting for the purposes of this section a single computer or communication device, and references in the section are construed accordingly. Sub-section (4) is the certificate provision: in any proceeding where it is desired to give a statement in evidence by virtue of this section, a certificate doing ANY of the following three things shall be submitted along with the electronic record at each instance where it is being submitted for admission, namely (a) identifying the electronic record containing the statement and describing the manner in which it was produced, (b) giving such particulars of any device involved in the production of that record as may be appropriate for the purpose of showing that it was produced by a computer or a communication device referred to in clauses (a) to (e) of sub-section (3), and (c) dealing with any of the matters to which the conditions mentioned in sub-section (2) relate. The certificate must purport to be signed by a person in charge of the computer or communication device or the management of the relevant activities (whichever is appropriate) AND an expert, that is, two signatories, and it shall be evidence of any matter stated in the certificate; for the purposes of that sub-section it is sufficient for a matter to be stated to the best of the knowledge and belief of the person stating it, in the certificate specified in the Schedule (the form of which is not part of the text supplied here). Sub-section (5) clarifies that information is taken to be supplied to the computer or communication device if it is supplied in any appropriate form, whether directly or, with or without human intervention, by means of any appropriate equipment; and that a computer output is taken to have been produced by the device whether produced by it directly or, with or without human intervention, by means of any appropriate equipment or by other electronic means as referred to in clauses (a) to (e) of sub-section (3).
key_requirements: Sub-section (1) operates notwithstanding anything contained in this Adhiniyam.

Information contained in an electronic record which is printed on paper, stored, recorded or copied in optical or magnetic media or semiconductor memory and produced by a computer or any communication device, or otherwise stored, recorded or copied in any electronic form (the computer output), shall be deemed to be also a document, if the conditions mentioned in this section are satisfied in relation to the information and computer in question.

Such computer output shall be admissible in any proceedings, without further proof or production of the original, as evidence of any contents of the original or of any fact stated therein of which direct evidence would be admissible (the supplied Gazette text reads 'as evidence or any contents of the original', an apparent typographical error for 'as evidence of any contents of the original', and the latter reading is used here).

The computer output containing the information must have been produced by the computer or communication device during the period over which that device was used regularly to create, store or process information for the purposes of any activity regularly carried on over that period by the person having lawful control over its use.

During the said period, information of the kind contained in the electronic record, or of the kind from which the information so contained is derived, must have been regularly fed into the computer or communication device in the ordinary course of the said activities.

Throughout the material part of the said period the computer or communication device must have been operating properly, or, if not, any period in which it was not operating properly or was out of operation during that part of the period must not have been such as to affect the electronic record or the accuracy of its contents.
The information contained in the electronic record must reproduce or be derived from such information fed into the computer or communication device in the ordinary course of the said activities.

Where the function of creating, storing or processing information for the purposes of the activity was regularly performed by means of one or more computers or communication devices, whether in standalone mode, on a computer system, on a computer network, on a computer resource enabling information creation or providing information processing and storage, or through an intermediary, all the computers or communication devices used for that purpose during that period shall be treated for the purposes of this section as constituting a single computer or communication device.

In any proceeding where it is desired to give a statement in evidence by virtue of this section, a certificate doing any of the things listed in clauses (a) to (c) of sub-section (4) shall be submitted along with the electronic record.
The certificate shall be submitted along with the electronic record at each instance where it is being submitted for admission.
Clause (a) of sub-section (4): identifying the electronic record containing the statement and describing the manner in which it was produced.

Clause (b) of sub-section (4): giving such particulars of any device involved in the production of that electronic record as may be appropriate for the purpose of showing that the electronic record was produced by a computer or a communication device referred to in clauses (a) to (e) of sub-section (3).
Clause (c) of sub-section (4): dealing with any of the matters to which the conditions mentioned in sub-section (2) relate.
The certificate must purport to be signed by a person in charge of the computer or communication device or the management of the relevant activities (whichever is appropriate) and an expert.
The certificate shall be evidence of any matter stated in the certificate.
For the purposes of sub-section (4) it shall be sufficient for a matter to be stated to the best of the knowledge and belief of the person stating it in the certificate specified in the Schedule.

Information shall be taken to be supplied to a computer or communication device if it is supplied thereto in any appropriate form and whether it is so supplied directly or (with or without human intervention) by means of any appropriate equipment.

A computer output shall be taken to have been produced by a computer or communication device whether it was produced by it directly or (with or without human intervention) by means of any appropriate equipment or by other electronic means as referred to in clauses (a) to (e) of sub-section (3).
bsa_refs.investigation_relevance: Wherever the IO relies on this section to put computer output in evidence - CDRs, CCTV footage, device extractions, printouts, server logs - the record must travel with a sub-section (4) certificate, and it must go with the record each and every time the record is submitted for admission, not merely once at charge-sheet stage. On the text the certificate is one 'doing any of' three things: identifying the record and describing how it was produced, giving particulars of any device involved, and dealing with any of the matters to which the sub-section (2) conditions relate; the statute requires any of the three, but the safe practice is to cover all three. The certificate must purport to be signed by two people, a person in charge of the computer or communication device or the management of the relevant activities (whichever is appropriate) and an expert, and it is the certificate specified in the Schedule, so the IO should line up both signatories before the record is tendered; a matter may be stated in it to the best of the knowledge and belief of the person stating it. At seizure, therefore, the IO should record the facts the signatories will later have to certify: regular use of the device over the relevant period for the activity, who had lawful control over its use, regular feeding of information of that kind in the ordinary course, and the proper working of the device (or that any malfunction or downtime in the material part of the period did not affect the record or the accuracy of its contents). Note the limits of sub-section (1): where the conditions are met it deems the computer output to be also a document and lets it in without further proof or production of the original, but it does not make the output the original and it settles nothing about the truth or weight of the contents.
time_limits: s.63(2)(a): no fixed number of days is prescribed - the relevant period is the period over which the computer or communication device was used regularly to create, store or process information for the purposes of the activity regularly carried on over that period.

s.63(2)(c): the computer or communication device must have been operating properly 'throughout the material part of the said period', or any period in which it was not operating properly or was out of operation during that part must not have been such as to affect the electronic record or the accuracy of its contents. This qualification belongs to clause (c) alone and does not relax clauses (a), (b) or (d).
s.63(4): the certificate must be submitted along with the electronic record 'at each instance where it is being submitted for admission' - a repeating timing requirement, not a one-time filing.

the conditions mentioned in this section are satisfied in relation to the information and

shall be admissible in any proceedings, without further proof or
production of the original, as evidence or any contents of the original or of any fact stated
therein of which direct evidence would be admissible.

(a) the computer output containing the information was produced by the
computer or communication device during the period over which the computer or
communication device was used regularly to create, store or process information
for the purposes of any activity regularly carried on over that period by the
person having lawful control over the use of the computer or communication
device;

(b) during the said period, information of the kind contained in the electronic
record or of the kind from which the information so contained is derived was regularly
fed into the computer or communication device
in the ordinary course of the said
activities;

(c) throughout the material part of the said period, the computer or
communication device was operating properly or, if not, then in respect of any

accuracy of its contents; and

(d)
the information contained in the electronic record reproduces or is

(3) Where over any period, the function of creating, storing or processing information
for the purposes of any activity regularly carried on over that period as mentioned in
clause (a) of sub-section (2) was regularly performed by means of one or more computers or

(a) in standalone mode; or
(b) on a computer system; or
(c) on a computer network; or
(d) on a computer resource enabling information creation or providing information
processing and storage; or
(e) through an intermediary,
all the computers or communication devices used for that purpose during that period shall
be treated for the purposes of this section as constituting a single computer or communication
device;

(4) In any proceeding where it is desired to give a statement in evidence by virtue of
this section, a certificate doing any of the following things shall be submitted along with the
electronic record at each instance where it is being submitted for admission, namely:—

a certificate doing any of the following things shall be submitted along with the
electronic record at each instance where it is being submitted for admission,

(a) identifying the electronic record containing the statement and describing
the manner in which it was produced;

(c) dealing with any of the matters to which the conditions mentioned in
sub-section (2) relate,

and purporting to be signed by a person in charge of the computer or communication
device or the management of the relevant activities (whichever is appropriate) and an expert
shall be evidence of any matter stated in the certificate

for the purposes of this
sub-section it shall be sufficient for a matter to be stated to the best of the knowledge and
belief of the person stating it in the certificate specified in the Schedule.

(a) information shall be taken to be supplied to a computer or communication

steps.text: Create the permanent record: the evidence specialist (or designated officer) copies the files, WITHOUT opening them, onto a write-once-read-many (WORM) 'master negative' storage device which is the permanent record, is kept in a secured location or designated desktop, does not become part of the investigative case files and is never removed from departmental custody; copy the master negative (again without opening) onto a 'negative duplicate / mirror image' working device, one per criminal case, confirming the images were correctly transferred; any copy for review by the IO, prosecutor or defence is made afresh from the negative duplicate; any enhancement of digital image files is documented by the evidence specialist and recorded on a separate device; and keep all originals in a designated/partitioned drive in a separate file which is not touched by anyone once it is hashed, with working copies kept separately.

bsa_refs.title: Primary evidence
bsa_refs.summary: Section 57 defines primary evidence as the document itself produced for the inspection of the Court, and then extends that definition through seven Explanations. Explanation 1 makes each part of a document executed in several parts primary evidence of the document. Explanation 2 makes each counterpart, executed by one or some of the parties only, primary evidence as against the parties executing it. Explanation 3 applies only where a number of documents are all made by one uniform process, as in the case of printing, lithography or photography: each is then primary evidence of the contents of the rest, but where they are all copies of a common original they are not primary evidence of the contents of the original. Explanations 4 to 7 carry the definition into electronic material: where an electronic or digital record is created or stored and that storage occurs simultaneously or sequentially in multiple files, each such file is primary evidence (Explanation 4); an electronic or digital record produced from proper custody is primary evidence unless it is disputed (Explanation 5); where a video recording is simultaneously stored in electronic form and transmitted or broadcast or transferred to another, each of the stored recordings is primary evidence (Explanation 6); and where an electronic or digital record is stored in multiple storage spaces in a computer resource, each such automated storage, including temporary files, is primary evidence (Explanation 7). An Illustration applies Explanation 3 to placards all printed at one time from one original. The section says what counts as primary evidence; it does not say that contents can be proved only in that way, and the 'unless it is disputed' qualification belongs to Explanation 5 alone.
key_requirements: Primary evidence means the document itself produced for the inspection of the Court.
Where a document is executed in several parts, each part is primary evidence of the document.
Where a document is executed in counterpart, each counterpart executed by one or some of the parties only is primary evidence as against the parties executing it.
Where a number of documents are all made by one uniform process, as in printing, lithography or photography, each is primary evidence of the contents of the rest.
Where such documents are all copies of a common original, they are not primary evidence of the contents of the original.
Where an electronic or digital record is created or stored and that storage occurs simultaneously or sequentially in multiple files, each such file is primary evidence.
Where an electronic or digital record is produced from proper custody, it is primary evidence unless it is disputed.
Where a video recording is simultaneously stored in electronic form and transmitted or broadcast or transferred to another, each of the stored recordings is primary evidence.
Where an electronic or digital record is stored in multiple storage spaces in a computer resource, each such automated storage, including temporary files, is primary evidence.
bsa_refs.investigation_relevance: The IO should seize and produce the document or the device itself wherever that is possible, and should record custody carefully, because under Explanation 5 an electronic or digital record produced from proper custody is primary evidence unless it is disputed. Under Explanations 4 and 7, where an electronic or digital record is created or stored and that storage occurs simultaneously or sequentially in multiple files, or where the record is stored in multiple storage spaces in a computer resource, each such file and each such automated storage, including temporary files, is primary evidence. Explanation 6 is narrower and both of its conditions must be met: it covers a video recording simultaneously stored in electronic form and transmitted or broadcast or transferred to another, and it is each of those stored recordings that is primary evidence; a recording copied afterwards from a stored file is not within Explanation 6, whatever its position under the other Explanations may be. The seizure memo and forwarding note should therefore identify exactly which file, device or storage space is being relied on and how it came into existence. On documents, Explanation 3 operates only where a number of documents are all made by one uniform process, such as printing, lithography or photography; each is then primary evidence of the contents of the rest, but where they are all copies of a common original none of them is primary evidence of the contents of the original. That does not make such a copy worthless, since this section says only what is primary evidence: the contents of the original may still be proved by the original itself, or by secondary evidence where the law permits it, so a copy should not be dropped from the case file merely because it cannot stand as primary evidence of the original.

steps.text: On completion of the operation, bring the recording device to the police station and transfer the AV recording to the local designated desktop (directly through device insertion, or by cable or Bluetooth) WITHOUT opening the files; mention this transfer in the chain of custody form and do the hashing. Hash BOTH the primary evidence (original media) and the mirrored copy and match the hash values to prove they contain the same data, and document the hashing; depict all transfers in chain of custody forms duly signed by the responder and the evidence expert. When seizing digital evidence/devices, do the hashing through write-blocking devices to make it alter-proof. Algorithms: MD5 is less secure with collision risk and SHA-1 is being phased out; the SHA-2 family (SHA-256/384/512) is recommended.

details.text: At the conclusion of the tour of duty, turn in the camera's memory card by placing it in an evidence envelope with identifying case information, sealed, and deliver the sealed envelope to the evidence specialist; download the unaltered images into a limited-access computer file using departmentally approved writing software that does not permit re-writing or alteration of recorded images.

steps.title: Keep the scene unaltered until recording finishes
steps.triage_why: Altering the scene or body before recording destroys the spatial context of the crime, which is vital for reconstructing the homicide.

steps.text: Never overlook stains of blood, semen, urine, smears, paint, fibres or hair — preserve the bits of objects affected; never omit to collect suspicious pieces of cloth, fibre, hair, paper or documents; always note the presence of bottles, containers, glasses and utensils and their condition (filled, half filled, empty, stained) where a poisonous substance or alcohol is expected or suspected; never hesitate to preserve objects which look useless at the time unless absolutely sure about them, as they could be vital at later stages; do not exclude details about furniture, doors, windows, curtains, tapestry, carpet, upholstery, flooring, fixtures and fittings.

steps.text: Use photography as part of the documentation for all physical crime scenes: photograph the dead body (if present) to show its location, injuries and condition; photograph each piece of evidence to illustrate where it was found and to establish its relationship to the victim; take photographs from straight above to eliminate potential distance distortions; photograph blood patterns along with a scale from different angles — the bloodstain pattern can indicate the type of weapon of offence.

details.text: Record the scene of all important and heinous crimes by black and white as well as colour photography; never fail to photograph the entry and exit points; always include the relative positions of building, road, boundary wall, fence, shrubbery, doors, windows, pole and trees; take close-up photographs of injuries, ligature marks, traces of resistance, scratches, tears, contusion and abrasion on the victim's body; always use a scale when photographing tool marks, tyre marks, skid marks, footprints and shoeprints; the photograph must be a truthful representation of a material and relevant object, showing the relationship of objects to one another against a recognizable background; maintain a record of photographs including time, date, case number, police station, place and name of photographer.

details.text: Never fail to photograph the dead body in homicides, suspicious deaths, strangulation, burning, hanging, drowning and road accident cases, and always take a sufficient number of photographs of the dead body from all possible angles covering injuries and marks.

steps.text: Air dry articles bearing wet or damp biological material at room temperature before final packaging; under no circumstances should wet or moist items remain in plastic or paper containers for more than two hours; never dry stained material by heating, by a hot air blower or heater, or by placing the article in bright/direct sunlight — hang clothing and similar items in a room with adequate air circulation; never pack clothing or objects carrying wet bloodstains (and clothes whether dry or wet) in airtight containers or polythene/plastic bags.

conflicts.description: dna_guidelines p.6 allows a wet or moist item to remain in a container for no more than 2 hours; the up_pictorial_forensic_sop short-term storage table (p.20) allows 'wet bloody items (if they cannot be dried)' to be held at temperature-controlled conditions (15.5-24 degrees C) for less than 24 hours.
conflicts.resolution: The national 2-hour rule governs wherever the item can be dried — drying is the primary obligation. The state matrix's window applies only to the residual class of wet bloody items that CANNOT be dried, for which the same table marks frozen as best and refrigerated as acceptable; it does not license leaving a dryable item wet for 24 hours.

ticks.do: Air dry articles bearing wet or damp biological material at room temperature before final packaging.
Do not leave wet or moist items in plastic or paper containers for more than two hours under any circumstances.
Never dry stained material by heating, by a hot air blower or heater, or by placing the article in bright or direct sunlight.
Hang clothing and similar items in a room with adequate air circulation.
Never pack clothing or objects carrying wet bloodstains, and clothes whether dry or wet, in airtight containers or polythene or plastic bags.

steps.title: Dry and pack wet biological exhibits safely
steps.triage_why: Wet biological evidence in plastic grows mold/bacteria rapidly, destroying DNA profiles and rendering the evidence useless.

steps.text: Identify and secure each item of evidence in a container at the crime scene and avoid excessive handling of evidence after it is collected; use paper bags / paper sheets / paper envelopes for biological evidence and never use printed paper, as the ink may contaminate the exhibits; pack and label each article separately and never pack more than one item together; label each exhibit with FIR number and date, section of law, name of IO, police station, district and state, duly signed and sealed by the IO; number the labels consecutively with the signature of the forwarding officer, doing the labelling on the cover and not on the evidence itself; enclose all packets belonging to one case in one box or an outer covering.

steps.title: Secure, package and label crime scene exhibits
steps.triage_why: Improper packaging (e.g., printed paper) can contaminate samples, and poor labeling leads to evidence being rejected by the court.

steps.text: Collect liquid blood at the scene in an EDTA tube using a disposable syringe or dropper (from a pool of blood: lift into an EDTA vial and simultaneously lift the sample on sterile-tipped foam surface swabs), OR transfer onto a gauze piece / FTA card, air dry and keep in a paper packet/envelope; submit to the laboratory within 24 hours of collection, keeping liquid blood samples in a thermos flask or thermocol box stuffed with ice or a coolant pack during transport; collect a fresh/wet blood clot in a sterile tube with an equal volume of normal saline or PBS (PBS is preferred for DNA evidence samples).
steps.deadline: Submit liquid blood within 24 hours of collection (dna_guidelines p.10); the state tips warn that beyond 48 hours the sample may become useless (up_crime_inv_tips p.1)

details.text: Lift liquid blood onto a gauze pad or other sterile cotton cloth and let it air-dry at room temperature; cool or freeze the dried gauze sample as soon as possible and deliver it to the laboratory as quickly as possible — if the delay exceeds 48 hours the sample may become useless; if the laboratory is nearby, send the stain-bearing object immediately.
details.citation: UP Police - Crime Investigation Tips/Guidance for Investigating Officers - TRANSLATED FROM HINDI

details.text: If the victim is so badly injured that a transfusion is necessary, try to obtain — or initiate the necessary procedure to obtain — the pre-transfusion specimen collected by the hospital; hospitals do not keep these specimens long, so act promptly.
details.citation: UP Police - Crime Investigation Tips/Guidance for Investigating Officers - TRANSLATED FROM HINDI

details.text: Ensure that blood-stained clothing worn by the person is air-dried and refrigerated so that it remains available as a secondary standard; refrigerate — do not freeze — liquid blood standards, collect the standard on a sterile gauze pad or swab, air dry it and pack it in paper (never a plastic container), and send liquid standards to the laboratory as quickly as possible.

conflicts.description: Anticoagulant/container: dna_guidelines (pp.6, 10, 16) and up_pictorial_forensic_sop p.19 prescribe EDTA vials for blood; up_crime_inv_tips p.2 prescribes a yellow-stoppered (ACD) or purple-stoppered vacutainer for the standard specimen drawn by the pathologist from the heart.
conflicts.resolution: EDTA vials govern (national DNA guideline, corroborated by the UP discipline matrix, which additionally requires the donor's name and date of collection on the vial and an ice container). The ACD vacutainer is recorded as the older state-tips practice. Grey-stoppered BA (blood-alcohol) tubes remain a distinct container for blood-alcohol work.

conflicts.description: Freezing: up_crime_inv_tips p.1 says to cool or freeze the sample as soon as possible, while the up_pictorial_forensic_sop storage tables (p.20) mark 'Never' against Liquid Blood in the Frozen column in BOTH the short-term and long-term tables, and up_crime_inv_tips p.3 itself says to refrigerate and not freeze blood standards.
conflicts.resolution: Never freeze liquid blood (matrix tables p.20, corroborated by tips p.3). The tips' p.1 'cool or freeze' applies only to the air-dried gauze-lifted sample, not to liquid blood.

conflicts.description: Transport temperature: dna_guidelines p.10 prescribes a thermos flask or thermocol box with ice/coolant pack, while dna_guidelines p.16 prescribes a 'dry ice storage box maintaining the temperature at least 4 degrees C'; the state matrix (p.20) bars freezing liquid blood outright.
conflicts.resolution: The 4 degrees C floor printed in the national guideline governs: transport chilled at refrigeration temperature (2-8 degrees C per the matrix) and never allow liquid blood to freeze; the printed phrase 'dry ice storage box' is retained as printed but is subordinate to the 4 degrees C requirement and the matrix's 'Never' entry.

steps.text: Place wet or semi-dry tissue, organs or foetal remains (e.g. mutilated remains) in a clean plastic container and immediately store under freezing conditions WITHOUT any preservative for DNA analysis — never add preservatives like formalin (saline is used as preservative only where the sample is for toxicology/drug testing); pack samples separately; transport in a thermocol box with dry ice / coolant pack and vaccine carrier and submit within 24 hours of collection; if there is any delay in transportation, store the packed sample in a freezer.
steps.deadline: Submit within 24 hours of collection (dna_guidelines p.11)

steps.text: All liquid blood of victims and accused should be in EDTA vials with the details written and signed by the doctor on each vial and separate packaging for each; only liquid blood in EDTA vials should be transported in a dry ice storage box, maintaining the temperature at least 4 degrees C until submission in the laboratory; evidence samples of the victim for DNA examination are vaginal swabs, a slide of vaginal smear and undergarments, along with the victim's reference blood sample in an EDTA vial / gauze / FTA card; evidence samples of the accused are blood samples in EDTA vials / gauze / FTA card and any other swabs such as a penile swab taken by the doctor during medical examination.

details.text: Biological materials from a dead body or a living person should always be collected by the medical officer only; remember the tiniest part of a biological material could be vital for DNA profiling, and never omit to preserve the integrity of the biological specimen during packaging and transportation.

details.text: Never forget to ask the medical officer about collection of seminal evidence such as a vaginal slide and pubic hairs from the victim of sexual assault, and to ask the autopsy surgeon about the collection of postmortem samples for DNA profiling if required for the investigation.

details.text: In sexual offence cases always have the victim examined by a physician, using a Sexual Assault Evidence Collection Kit to collect evidence from the victim and following the kit's instructions carefully so that maximum benefit is obtained from the evidence collected.

steps.title: Obtain authenticated reference samples from victim and accused

steps.text: Collect hair with root (dry, or wet with blood/semen/saliva) from the crime scene, weapon or clothing with tweezers/forceps into white or butter paper and pack in a paper envelope; if hair is found attached in dry blood or on a weapon, do NOT remove the hair — pack the entire substrate intact, and if the object is small, mark it, wrap it in clean brown paper and pack it in cotton cloth; if recovered hairs are wet, allow them to dry in shade and never wash them; collect reference hair samples of 50-100 hairs from the victim and suspects and forward them; submit without any delay.

details.text: Collect plucked, pulled-out or fallen hairs for DNA profiling — cut hairs, being dead material, are useless for the purpose; collect each group of hairs, with respect to their origin, in separate packaging; hairs mixed with blood, tissue or semen must always be allowed to air dry before packaging.
details.citation: Director, Forensic Science Laboratory, UP Police - Crime Scene (Protocol) Management (English section)

details.text: Recover all hair present; where possible pick up hairs with the fingers or small forceps, wrap them in paper, place that in a larger envelope, seal it and mark the outer envelope; if hair is stuck in dried blood or adhering to metal or a piece of glass, do not attempt to remove it — if the object is small, mark it, wrap it and seal it in an envelope, and if the object is large, wrap the area bearing the hair thoroughly in paper so hairs are not dislodged and lost in transit.
details.citation: UP Police - Crime Investigation Tips/Guidance for Investigating Officers - TRANSLATED FROM HINDI

details.text: Known-sample method: have the person bend over a large clean sheet of paper and rub or massage the hair/scalp so that loose hairs fall onto the paper, and use the same method for other body areas; 50-100 hairs are desired for a head-hair sample and 30-60 from the pubic region; do not cut the hairs; if the person is a suspect, take samples from all parts of the body; in rape cases also obtain a combed hair sample from the victim's pubic region.

steps.text: Clean and wash bones/teeth to remove any debris, allow them to dry completely in air, roll/pack in brown paper and envelope, and seal in cotton cloth or cardboard boxes; bone samples should be dry and clean and no chemical preservative is required — never add preservatives like formalin; send intact bones in order of preference: (i) femur (ii) tibia (iii) humerus (iv) teeth (molar) (v) ribs; completely burned bones are not useful for DNA analysis; submit without any delay.

details.text: Never omit to send bones for examination if skeletal remains are found at the crime scene, to get an opinion about sex, approximate age, stature and height; do not hesitate to recover even the smallest bones, as they may be evidence of poisoning, injuries and relation to causation of death.

steps.text: For dried blood, semen, vomit, sputum or other body-fluid stains (crust/stain/spatter) on unmovable surfaces such as a floor or concrete wall: moisten the dry stain for 5-10 minutes with PBS or distilled water, collect the moistened stain with a foam tipped swab / FTA card / gauze piece, air dry the swab and pack it in a paper envelope; use a separate swab for each spot, dry in shade and pack each spot separately in its own packet/envelope — never swab stains at different places with a single cloth; never use direct sunlight, a hot air blower or a heater to dry swabs; submit without any delay.

details.text: Moisten dry/old stains with PBS buffer and leave for 5 minutes, then collect the stain with an FTA card or tipped foam surface swab; use only swabs / FTA card / gauze piece to collect semi-dry or liquid body fluids; air dry the stain/swab before packaging.

details.text: If a dried stain is on a small solid object, send the entire labelled and packaged object; if on a large solid object, cover the stained area with clean paper and seal the edges down with tape; if sending the whole object is impractical, scrape the stain onto a clean piece of paper which is folded and placed in an envelope (never scrape directly into the envelope), using a clean washed and dried knife washed again before each separate stain; do not mix dried stains — one stain per envelope; never attempt to wipe or wash dried stains off an object with a moistened cloth or paper; if the stain is on clothing, wrap the item in clean paper, place it in a box or brown paper bag, seal and label it, and do not attempt to remove the stain from the cloth.

steps.text: For a wet stained movable object: thoroughly air dry at room temperature, collect the item as it is, and pack it in a paper bag/envelope or a cardboard/shipping box depending on its size. For stains on a weapon, firearm, bullet or small object (household utensils, stones, bricks): allow the stains to dry, collect the item directly, and pack and seal it in a cardboard/shipping box sealed with evidence tape. For stains on vehicle upholstery, carpet, wallpaper or wood: cut out the stained area, allow it to dry in shade, package each cutting separately, and also collect an unstained cutting from the adjacent area as a control. Submit without any delay.

details.text: Never hesitate to send the vehicle itself to the laboratory for examination if it carries traces of blood on it.

steps.text: FTA (Flinders Technology Associates) cards may be used for DNA sample collection, allowing collection, room-temperature storage, shipping and processing, with simple collection, convenient room-temperature storage/transport and safe handling. Blood: place the kit contents on a clean dry surface, wear gloves, unfold the protective flap to expose the printed circle, clean the finger with an alcohol wipe, prick it with the lancet, press the finger to deposit a drop of blood in the printed circle without touching the card, never oversaturate (DNA cannot be recovered from an FTA card saturated with too much blood), dry fully for 1-2 hours at room temperature, then close the cover and insert the card with a desiccant packet into the multi-barrier pouch and the pouch into the mailing envelope. Buccal: soak the sterile foam tipped applicator by running it on the inside cheek for 30 seconds and repeat with the opposite side, then lift the paper cover of the indicating FTA card, apply pressure and rock the applicator side to side three times within the sample circle and repeat with the other side (the pink area turns white indicating transfer), dry the card completely at room temperature and pouch it with desiccant.

steps.text: Do not attempt to fit a recovered tool into the questioned mark or to make test marks before the laboratory examination — doing so can alter the questioned mark or the tool, destroy the lines of transferred paint or other stains on the tool, transfer additional material onto it, and render the laboratory examination worthless; wrap the entire contaminated or edged portion of the tool in paper so that fine or sharp edges are protected from contact; as far as possible send the whole object bearing the tool mark, and if that is not possible sketch or photograph the marked area (the photograph will not substitute for comparison but helps the laboratory determine how the mark was made) and, if possible, cut out and send the marked portion; a cast should be made only by a person with adequate experience, since a poor cast is useless and improper technique can destroy the mark; pack small marked objects wrapped in clean paper inside envelopes or boxes, protect the important area of larger objects by wrapping it in paper, and crate large objects against transit damage.

details.text: Never omit to look for tool marks on doors and windows, footprints and shoeprints on the floor, and tyre marks around the house or shop in housebreaking cases, and never overlook footprints, shoeprints and tool marks at the points of entry and exit in arson cases; never forget to take specimen fingerprints, footprints, shoeprints or tyre marks from the suspect and from his shoes and vehicle; never omit to use a proper scale during photography of footprints, shoeprints, tyre marks and tool marks.

steps.text: The primary precaution in all cases is to prevent adding fingerprints to the evidence and to prevent destroying those already present: touch the object as little as possible and then only in areas where identifiable latent prints are unlikely, such as rough surfaces; gloves or a handkerchief may be used to pick up exhibits but unnecessary contact must be avoided, since careless use of cloth may wipe off or smudge the prints actually present; mark all latent-print evidence in a distinctive manner, exercising care so that the prints are not damaged; mark lifted developed latents or seal/mount them in marked envelopes, and photograph developed latents both with and without a scale and identification markings; place large objects bearing latents (glass, metal articles, firearms) on wood or cardboard fastened tightly, or on a pegboard, so they cannot shift or contact other objects in transport; stand bottles and glasses upright on a board in the bottom of a box, held by nails or through a hole in a piece of cardboard; place papers and documents bearing latents individually in cellophane or manila envelopes sandwiched between two pieces of cardboard, wrapped and boxed for despatch.

details.text: Always ask the fingerprint expert to visit the crime scene in cases of house breaking for locating, developing and lifting possible fingerprints.

steps.text: Always adopt general forensic and procedural principles while dealing with electronic evidence and never omit to take the assistance of a trained person while conducting the search, collection and preservation; ensure that no change takes place in the status of the evidence and avoid touching the keyboard or clicking the mouse to recover data or explore the contents; obtain information about the purpose of the system from the person concerned, ascertain the names of the owner and users along with the passwords required to access the system, and get information about any off-site data storage, any unique security scheme or destructive device, and documentation explaining the hardware or software installed; record all actions taken at the scene regarding the monitor, computer, printer and other peripherals; photograph the monitor screen and record the information displayed; remove the power source cable from the computer end instead of from the wall outlet; record the make, model and serial numbers of all devices; mark and label all connectors and cable ends before packaging to allow exact reassembly; package magnetic media in an antistatic container and package multiple computer systems separately so that they can be reassembled as found; pack the collected digital exhibits in a cardboard box with thermocol support inside a Faraday bag.

steps.text: Pick up threads and long fibres with the fingers, place them in a paper packet and then in an envelope which is sealed and marked — never place loose fibres directly into a mailing envelope, where they can be lost or destroyed; if the fibres are short or few in number, wrap the area or the entire bearing object in paper and send the whole exhibit; pick up fibres on tape only if the laboratory in your jurisdiction authorises it and advises that it is necessary; if threads or fibres are recovered, send all clothing of the persons from which they might have originated for comparison; for person-to-person or person-to-object contact comparisons keep each item of each person's clothing strictly separate — spread each garment on a clean sheet of paper, mark the exhibit and wrap it in separate paper — because if one person's garment touches another's or is laid on a surface in contact with the other suspect's clothing the comparison may become meaningless, the examination having value only where it is known that no contact occurred before or after the crime.

steps.text: Never avoid asking for postmortem in cases of unnatural and suspicious deaths; never hide important and relevant positive or negative findings to be submitted to the autopsy surgeon; check that all important points referred to in the postmortem proforma are duly attended to, verify that there is no discrepancy between the injuries and other significant marks in your findings and the medical or autopsy report, and inform the coroner or magistrate of any discrepancy; always procure the preliminary opinion of the medical officer about the medico-legal exhibits before sending them to the forensic laboratory; ensure that appropriate preservatives have been used for viscera, blood, tissues and other samples — all viscera and stomach washing in normal saline and the tissues of internal organs in formalin for histopathology; ensure the skin piece or area affected by snake bite or injection has been preserved, and ask the autopsy surgeon to preserve the trachea in burn cases for carbon particles and the tibia bone for diatom examination in suspicious drowning cases; always avoid unnecessary delay in dispatching postmortem exhibits such as viscera, stomach contents and blood to the chemical laboratory.

steps.text: Store biological evidence by the temperature tables — short term is up to 72 hours, long term is more than 72 hours. Liquid blood: frozen = NEVER (both tables); refrigerated (2-8 degrees C) = best short and long term; temperature controlled (15.5-24 degrees C) = less than 24 hours short term only. Urine: frozen (at or below -10 degrees C) = best; refrigerated = less than 24 hours. Dry biological stained items: temperature controlled = best; room temperature = acceptable short term. Wet bloody items that cannot be dried (short term only): frozen = best, refrigerated = acceptable, temperature controlled = less than 24 hours. Bones: short term frozen, temperature controlled and room temperature all acceptable; long term temperature controlled = best. Hair: temperature controlled = best, room temperature = acceptable. Swab with biological material: refrigerated = best when wet, temperature controlled = best when dried. Vaginal smears: temperature controlled = best. Buccal swabs: temperature controlled = best, room temperature = less than 24 hours short term. Feces: frozen = best. DNA extracts (long term): frozen = best (liquid), refrigerated = acceptable (liquid), temperature controlled = acceptable (dried).
steps.deadline: Short-term storage is defined as up to 72 hours and long-term as more than 72 hours (up_pictorial_forensic_sop p.20)

details.text: Keep wet biological material refrigerated at 4 degrees Celsius and submit it to the laboratory at the earliest; wet blood samples must be preserved in a suitable anticoagulant such as EDTA.

steps.text: Route each exhibit to the correct FSL discipline: Physics (glass, paint, rags/cloth shreds, marks of feet, shoes, tools and tyres, numbers erased on a vehicle, valuable gadgets); Questioned Documents (erasure, loss or alteration of handwriting, over-writing, secret writing, typewriting and printed matter, ink and paper, stamp impressions, fax, carbon and xerox copies, rubber stamps and seals); Firearms/Ballistics (firearms and their parts, cartridges, bullets, pellets, clothing and other material affected by firing); Computer Forensics (software, hardware, computer peripherals, communication equipment, and material relating to crypto currency, pornography and software piracy); Forensic Engineering (material from substandard construction of buildings, roads and dams, train or air accidents, failed machines and structures — each item wrapped and sealed separately, grease stains kept from contact with other material, important stains MAY be protected with aluminium foil); Narcotics (narcotic drugs and psychotropic substances, adulterated liquor and toddy); Chemistry (adulterated petrol, HSD, oil, detergent, cosmetics and cement, explosive material, arson and fire residues, unknown chemicals); Toxicology (poisons, medicines and intoxicants); Serology (blood, saliva, other body fluids and skin tissue — fluids converted into stains and packed separately in sterile paper envelopes or cardboard boxes; the page banner lists the common biological evidence as blood, semen, saliva, teeth, bone, urine, soft tissue and hair with root and shaft); Biomedical (skull, skeletal remains, skin, tissue); DNA (blood, blood stains and swabs, semen and semen stains, medical slides and swabs, bones, tissue, hair, teeth, saliva, skeletal remains); Biology (hair, fibre, semen and semen stains, medical slides and swabs, diatom, tobacco products and other plant material, pollen, leaves, wood, seeds, fruits, flowers, insects, faeces — dried in shade and packed separately); Forensic Psychology (the person of the suspect, witness or complainant, referred with the consent of the Court, a medical certificate if there is any medical problem, the FIR, and the crime scene sketch or photographs).
legal_basis: NDPS Act, Excise Act and central excise duty matters, Copyright Act, Patent Act and 'Piracy Act' as printed in the source discipline table

steps.text: Limit access to the evidence storage facility or location so as to assure that items of evidence cannot be switched or tampered with throughout the chain of custody; provide a safe facility that limits access to vulnerable evidence; secure firearms and narcotics and controlled substances in a separate space from other evidence and strictly enforce and supervise access to that space; keep inventory records of the location where the evidence is stored (e.g. shelf number or bin), the date/time and identity of the person who stored it, and every removal and return of evidence from storage; classify any location where evidence may be stored for 72 hours or less as temporary storage and any location where it may be stored for more than 72 hours as long term or more permanent storage.

steps.text: Maintain a chain of custody document recording the chronological history of every item of evidence: the name or initials of the individual collecting the evidence, each person or entity subsequently having custody of it, the dates the items were collected or transferred, the agency and case number, the victim's or suspect's name, and a brief description of the item.

details.text: The chain of custody is the identification of the person or agency having custody of evidence and of the place where it is kept, in chronological order, from the time of collection to destruction, in a formal WRITTEN process; the record must also reflect the dates on which and a brief reason for which evidence is transferred from one location or person to another (e.g. delivery to laboratory, viewing of evidence by court, viewing of evidence by IO), and access to the storage facility must be limited so that items cannot be switched or tampered with.

details.text: 'Evidence' means property that may be related to a crime and/or that may implicate or clear a person of a crime — an object, a biological sample found on such an item or at a scene, a latent print on an item, or a cell phone or computer. The record identifies three roles: the Evidence Collector (who initially took possession, custody or control for evidentiary purposes), the Evidence Custodian (responsible for evidence processing at a given location — property and evidence room, hospital, court, crime laboratory) and every Evidence Handler (any person who has had the evidence in his possession at any point of time). The documentation must include a description of the evidence, the unique case identifier (e.g. FIR number, PS), where the evidence was collected (location, address), where it was stored (location, address), the person having possession and for what purpose, what was done to it (e.g. analysis or re-packaging), and the date and time of both incident and collection; also record the manner in which each item was wrapped, bagged or boxed.

steps.text: Follow the fifteen-stage custody flow: (1) identification, collection and preservation of evidence at the crime scene by the forensic experts and the investigation officer; (2) handover of evidence by the forensic experts to the IO; (3) documentation of the evidences by the IO with the help of the forensic experts; (4) deposition in the Maalkhana (police property store room) by the IO; (5) submission to the FSL for analysis via special messenger by the forwarding officer; (6) receiving of the evidences by the receipt section of the FSL; (7) receiving in the concerned division by its laboratory assistant; (8) handover to the expert/scientist by the laboratory assistant; (9) analysis by the expert/scientist; (10) handover back to the laboratory assistant after analysis; (11) collection by the special messenger from the laboratory assistant/dispatch; (12) handover to the IO by the special messenger; (13) submission in the Maalkhana by the IO; (14) production in the Court during hearing by the IO; (15) deposition in the Maalkhana till further order of the Court.

bsa_refs.title: Facts which are occasion, cause or effect of facts in issue or relevant facts
bsa_refs.summary: Section 5 makes relevant the facts that surround a fact in issue or a relevant fact rather than constituting it. In one unnumbered sentence it covers five categories, of which the first three are qualified by the words "immediate or otherwise": facts that are the occasion of the fact in issue or relevant fact, facts that are its cause and facts that are its effect, whether immediate or otherwise; facts that constitute the state of things under which it happened; and facts that afforded an opportunity for its occurrence or transaction. The sentence itself groups those five into the three limbs listed as the key requirements below - occasion, cause or effect; the state of things; and opportunity. The section says only that such facts are relevant; it says nothing about the weight to be given to them. The illustrations treat as relevant facts the victim going to a fair with money in his possession shortly before a robbery and showing it or mentioning that he had it to third persons, marks on the ground produced by a struggle at or near the place where the murder was committed, and the state of B's health before the symptoms ascribed to poison together with habits of B known to A which afforded an opportunity for the administration of poison.
key_requirements: Facts which are the occasion, cause or effect, whether immediate or otherwise, of a relevant fact or a fact in issue are relevant.
Facts which constitute the state of things under which the fact in issue or relevant fact happened are relevant.
Facts which afforded an opportunity for the occurrence or transaction of the fact in issue or relevant fact are relevant.
bsa_refs.investigation_relevance: This is the provision that carries the IO's scene and circumstance evidence: physical traces such as marks on the ground produced by a struggle at or near the place of the offence, the state of things at the scene, and the events that created the opportunity for the offence are all relevant, and should therefore be photographed, measured, seized and described in the panchnama. The IO should equally collect the lead-up facts - the victim's movements, what property the victim was carrying and to whom the victim showed it or mentioned that he had it, and the victim's condition before the offence: in a poisoning case, the state of the victim's health before the symptoms ascribed to poison, which is relevant whether or not the accused knew of it. Separately, and carrying its own qualifiers, any habit of the victim known to the accused which afforded an opportunity for the offence is relevant and should be collected. The section establishes relevancy only; proof and weight still have to be built by other means.

bsa_refs.title: Opinions of experts
bsa_refs.summary: Section 39 makes expert opinion a relevant fact. s.39(1) provides that when the Court has to form an opinion on a point of foreign law, of science or art, or any other field, or as to identity of handwriting or finger impressions, the opinions of persons specially skilled in that subject are relevant facts, and it labels such persons "experts". s.39(2) deals separately with electronic material: where the Court has to form an opinion on any matter relating to information transmitted or stored in any computer resource or any other electronic or digital form, the opinion of the Examiner of Electronic Evidence referred to in section 79A of the Information Technology Act, 2000 is a relevant fact. The Explanation to s.39(2) provides that such an Examiner of Electronic Evidence shall be an expert. The illustrations cover opinion on symptoms produced by a poison, opinion on symptoms showing unsoundness of mind and the accused's capacity to know the nature of the act, and comparison of a disputed document with another document proved or admitted to have been written by the same person.
key_requirements: The opinions of persons specially skilled in foreign law, science or art, any other field, or in questions as to identity of handwriting or finger impressions are relevant facts when the Court has to form an opinion on that point.
Persons specially skilled in such a field are called experts.

Where the Court has to form an opinion on any matter relating to information transmitted or stored in any computer resource or any other electronic or digital form, the opinion of the Examiner of Electronic Evidence referred to in section 79A of the Information Technology Act, 2000 is a relevant fact.
For the purposes of sub-section (2), an Examiner of Electronic Evidence shall be an expert.
bsa_refs.investigation_relevance: The IO should route every scientific, medical, ballistic, chemical, handwriting or finger-impression question to a person specially skilled in that field and place the basis of that skill on record, since it is skill in the subject that makes the opinion relevant. For anything transmitted or stored in a computer resource or in any other electronic or digital form, the opinion that s.39(2) makes relevant is that of an Examiner of Electronic Evidence notified under section 79A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, so electronic exhibits should be sent to such an Examiner; and, as illustration (c) shows, a handwriting comparison requires the IO to also supply a specimen document that is proved or admitted to have been written by the suspected author.

bsa_refs.title: Primary evidence
bsa_refs.summary: Section 57 defines primary evidence as the document itself produced for the inspection of the Court, and then extends that definition through seven Explanations. Explanation 1 makes each part of a document executed in several parts primary evidence of the document. Explanation 2 makes each counterpart, executed by one or some of the parties only, primary evidence as against the parties executing it. Explanation 3 applies only where a number of documents are all made by one uniform process, as in the case of printing, lithography or photography: each is then primary evidence of the contents of the rest, but where they are all copies of a common original they are not primary evidence of the contents of the original. Explanations 4 to 7 carry the definition into electronic material: where an electronic or digital record is created or stored and that storage occurs simultaneously or sequentially in multiple files, each such file is primary evidence (Explanation 4); an electronic or digital record produced from proper custody is primary evidence unless it is disputed (Explanation 5); where a video recording is simultaneously stored in electronic form and transmitted or broadcast or transferred to another, each of the stored recordings is primary evidence (Explanation 6); and where an electronic or digital record is stored in multiple storage spaces in a computer resource, each such automated storage, including temporary files, is primary evidence (Explanation 7). An Illustration applies Explanation 3 to placards all printed at one time from one original. The section says what counts as primary evidence; it does not say that contents can be proved only in that way, and the 'unless it is disputed' qualification belongs to Explanation 5 alone.
key_requirements: Primary evidence means the document itself produced for the inspection of the Court.
Where a document is executed in several parts, each part is primary evidence of the document.
Where a document is executed in counterpart, each counterpart executed by one or some of the parties only is primary evidence as against the parties executing it.
Where a number of documents are all made by one uniform process, as in printing, lithography or photography, each is primary evidence of the contents of the rest.
Where such documents are all copies of a common original, they are not primary evidence of the contents of the original.
Where an electronic or digital record is created or stored and that storage occurs simultaneously or sequentially in multiple files, each such file is primary evidence.
Where an electronic or digital record is produced from proper custody, it is primary evidence unless it is disputed.
Where a video recording is simultaneously stored in electronic form and transmitted or broadcast or transferred to another, each of the stored recordings is primary evidence.
Where an electronic or digital record is stored in multiple storage spaces in a computer resource, each such automated storage, including temporary files, is primary evidence.
bsa_refs.investigation_relevance: The IO should seize and produce the document or the device itself wherever that is possible, and should record custody carefully, because under Explanation 5 an electronic or digital record produced from proper custody is primary evidence unless it is disputed. Under Explanations 4 and 7, where an electronic or digital record is created or stored and that storage occurs simultaneously or sequentially in multiple files, or where the record is stored in multiple storage spaces in a computer resource, each such file and each such automated storage, including temporary files, is primary evidence. Explanation 6 is narrower and both of its conditions must be met: it covers a video recording simultaneously stored in electronic form and transmitted or broadcast or transferred to another, and it is each of those stored recordings that is primary evidence; a recording copied afterwards from a stored file is not within Explanation 6, whatever its position under the other Explanations may be. The seizure memo and forwarding note should therefore identify exactly which file, device or storage space is being relied on and how it came into existence. On documents, Explanation 3 operates only where a number of documents are all made by one uniform process, such as printing, lithography or photography; each is then primary evidence of the contents of the rest, but where they are all copies of a common original none of them is primary evidence of the contents of the original. That does not make such a copy worthless, since this section says only what is primary evidence: the contents of the original may still be proved by the original itself, or by secondary evidence where the law permits it, so a copy should not be dropped from the case file merely because it cannot stand as primary evidence of the original.

bsa_refs.title: Cases in which secondary evidence relating to documents may be given
bsa_refs.summary: This section sets out the seven situations, clauses (a) to (g), in which secondary evidence may be given of the existence, condition or contents of a document. They are: the original being in the possession or power of the opponent, of a person beyond the Court's process, or of a person legally bound to produce it, coupled with non-production after the notice mentioned in section 64 (clause (a)); a written admission of the existence, condition or contents (clause (b)); destruction or loss of the original, or inability to produce it in reasonable time for a reason not arising from the party's own default or neglect (clause (c)); an original not easily movable (clause (d)); a public document within the meaning of section 74 (clause (e)); a document of which a certified copy is permitted to be given in evidence (clause (f)); and numerous accounts or documents which cannot conveniently be examined in Court where the fact to be proved is the general result of the whole collection (clause (g)). The Explanation then limits the kind of secondary evidence allowed under each head: any secondary evidence for clauses (a), (c) and (d); only the written admission for clause (b); only a certified copy for clauses (e) and (f); and, for clause (g), evidence of the general result by a skilled person who has examined the documents. The modality throughout is permissive - secondary evidence 'may' be given in these cases.
key_requirements: Secondary evidence may be given of the existence, condition, or contents of a document in the cases listed in clauses (a) to (g).

Secondary evidence may be given when the original is shown or appears to be in the possession or power of the person against whom it is sought to be proved, of any person out of reach of or not subject to the process of the Court, or of any person legally bound to produce it.
In such a case secondary evidence may be given only when, after the notice mentioned in section 64, such person does not produce the original.

Secondary evidence may be given when the existence, condition or contents of the original have been proved to be admitted in writing by the person against whom it is proved or by his representative in interest.

Secondary evidence may be given when the original has been destroyed or lost, or when the party offering evidence of its contents cannot, for any other reason not arising from his own default or neglect, produce it in reasonable time.
Secondary evidence may be given when the original is of such a nature as not to be easily movable.
Secondary evidence may be given when the original is a public document within the meaning of section 74.
Secondary evidence may be given when the original is a document of which a certified copy is permitted by this Adhiniyam, or by any other law in force in India, to be given in evidence.

Secondary evidence may be given when the originals consist of numerous accounts or other documents which cannot conveniently be examined in Court and the fact to be proved is the general result of the whole collection.
For clauses (a), (c) and (d), any secondary evidence of the contents of the document is admissible.
For clause (b), the written admission is admissible.
For clause (e) or (f), a certified copy of the document, but no other kind of secondary evidence, is admissible.
For clause (g), evidence may be given as to the general result of the documents by any person who has examined them and who is skilled in the examination of such document.
bsa_refs.investigation_relevance: This is the gateway the prosecution uses whenever the original document is not on the record, so the case diary must carry the facts that fit one of the clauses - the record of loss or destruction for clause (c), proof of the section 64 notice and of non-production for clause (a), the immovability of the original for clause (d), or the public-document character for clause (e). The Explanation is the practical warning: for public documents and for documents where a certified copy is permitted, only a certified copy is admissible, so the IO should obtain and annex the certified copy rather than a photocopy or a photograph.
time_limits: Clause (c) fixes no number of days: the party must be unable, for a reason not arising from his own default or neglect, to produce the original 'in reasonable time'.

bsa_refs.title: Special provisions as to evidence relating to electronic record
bsa_refs.summary: A single-sentence routing provision. It states that the contents of electronic records may be proved in accordance with the provisions of section 63. It creates no conditions of its own and adds nothing beyond pointing to section 63 for the mode of proof. Its modality is permissive, 'may be proved in accordance with', and it contains no words of exclusion of its own such as 'only', 'and no other' or 'and not otherwise'. The section therefore names the section 63 route without, in its own words, ruling out any other; whether that route is exclusive is not settled by this text.
key_requirements: The contents of electronic records may be proved in accordance with the provisions of section 63.
bsa_refs.investigation_relevance: This section routes the proof of the contents of electronic records to section 63, so for any electronic material the IO seizes or obtains he should plan for the section 63 conditions and certificate from the moment of seizure, and should not leave them to be assembled at trial. Note the wording: the section is permissive, 'may be proved in accordance with', and carries no words of exclusion of its own, so any proposition that section 63 is the only way of proving the contents of an electronic record does not come from the words of this section. That is a reason to work to the section 63 requirements in every case rather than to rely on this section as either granting or shutting off an alternative.
