bsa_refs.title: Cases in which secondary evidence relating to documents may be given
bsa_refs.summary: This section sets out the seven situations, clauses (a) to (g), in which secondary evidence may be given of the existence, condition or contents of a document. They are: the original being in the possession or power of the opponent, of a person beyond the Court's process, or of a person legally bound to produce it, coupled with non-production after the notice mentioned in section 64 (clause (a)); a written admission of the existence, condition or contents (clause (b)); destruction or loss of the original, or inability to produce it in reasonable time for a reason not arising from the party's own default or neglect (clause (c)); an original not easily movable (clause (d)); a public document within the meaning of section 74 (clause (e)); a document of which a certified copy is permitted to be given in evidence (clause (f)); and numerous accounts or documents which cannot conveniently be examined in Court where the fact to be proved is the general result of the whole collection (clause (g)). The Explanation then limits the kind of secondary evidence allowed under each head: any secondary evidence for clauses (a), (c) and (d); only the written admission for clause (b); only a certified copy for clauses (e) and (f); and, for clause (g), evidence of the general result by a skilled person who has examined the documents. The modality throughout is permissive - secondary evidence 'may' be given in these cases.
key_requirements: Secondary evidence may be given of the existence, condition, or contents of a document in the cases listed in clauses (a) to (g).

Secondary evidence may be given when the original is shown or appears to be in the possession or power of the person against whom it is sought to be proved, of any person out of reach of or not subject to the process of the Court, or of any person legally bound to produce it.
In such a case secondary evidence may be given only when, after the notice mentioned in section 64, such person does not produce the original.

Secondary evidence may be given when the existence, condition or contents of the original have been proved to be admitted in writing by the person against whom it is proved or by his representative in interest.

Secondary evidence may be given when the original has been destroyed or lost, or when the party offering evidence of its contents cannot, for any other reason not arising from his own default or neglect, produce it in reasonable time.
Secondary evidence may be given when the original is of such a nature as not to be easily movable.
Secondary evidence may be given when the original is a public document within the meaning of section 74.
Secondary evidence may be given when the original is a document of which a certified copy is permitted by this Adhiniyam, or by any other law in force in India, to be given in evidence.

Secondary evidence may be given when the originals consist of numerous accounts or other documents which cannot conveniently be examined in Court and the fact to be proved is the general result of the whole collection.
For clauses (a), (c) and (d), any secondary evidence of the contents of the document is admissible.
For clause (b), the written admission is admissible.
For clause (e) or (f), a certified copy of the document, but no other kind of secondary evidence, is admissible.
For clause (g), evidence may be given as to the general result of the documents by any person who has examined them and who is skilled in the examination of such document.
bsa_refs.investigation_relevance: This is the gateway the prosecution uses whenever the original document is not on the record, so the case diary must carry the facts that fit one of the clauses - the record of loss or destruction for clause (c), proof of the section 64 notice and of non-production for clause (a), the immovability of the original for clause (d), or the public-document character for clause (e). The Explanation is the practical warning: for public documents and for documents where a certified copy is permitted, only a certified copy is admissible, so the IO should obtain and annex the certified copy rather than a photocopy or a photograph.
time_limits: Clause (c) fixes no number of days: the party must be unable, for a reason not arising from his own default or neglect, to produce the original 'in reasonable time'.

bsa_refs.title: Special provisions as to evidence relating to electronic record
bsa_refs.summary: A single-sentence routing provision. It states that the contents of electronic records may be proved in accordance with the provisions of section 63. It creates no conditions of its own and adds nothing beyond pointing to section 63 for the mode of proof. Its modality is permissive, 'may be proved in accordance with', and it contains no words of exclusion of its own such as 'only', 'and no other' or 'and not otherwise'. The section therefore names the section 63 route without, in its own words, ruling out any other; whether that route is exclusive is not settled by this text.
key_requirements: The contents of electronic records may be proved in accordance with the provisions of section 63.
bsa_refs.investigation_relevance: This section routes the proof of the contents of electronic records to section 63, so for any electronic material the IO seizes or obtains he should plan for the section 63 conditions and certificate from the moment of seizure, and should not leave them to be assembled at trial. Note the wording: the section is permissive, 'may be proved in accordance with', and carries no words of exclusion of its own, so any proposition that section 63 is the only way of proving the contents of an electronic record does not come from the words of this section. That is a reason to work to the section 63 requirements in every case rather than to rely on this section as either granting or shutting off an alternative.

bsa_refs.title: Admissibility of electronic records
bsa_refs.summary: This is the operative provision for proving electronic records. Operating notwithstanding anything contained in this Adhiniyam, sub-section (1) deems any information contained in an electronic record which is printed on paper, stored, recorded or copied in optical or magnetic media or semiconductor memory and produced by a computer or any communication device, or otherwise stored, recorded or copied in any electronic form (the 'computer output'), to be also a document, if the conditions mentioned in this section are satisfied in relation to the information and computer in question, and makes that output admissible in any proceedings, without further proof or production of the original, as evidence of any contents of the original or of any fact stated therein of which direct evidence would be admissible. What sub-section (1) deems is that the computer output is ALSO a document: it does not deem the output to be the original, and it settles nothing about the truth or the weight of what the record contains. Both the deeming and the admissibility are conditional on the section's conditions being satisfied. (The supplied Gazette text reads 'as evidence or any contents of the original'; that is an apparent typographical error for 'as evidence of any contents of the original', and the latter reading is used here.) Sub-section (2) lays down the four conditions in clauses (a) to (d): production of the output by the computer or communication device during the period over which it was used regularly to create, store or process information for the purposes of any activity regularly carried on over that period by the person having lawful control over its use; regular feeding into the device, in the ordinary course of those activities, of information of the kind contained in the record or of the kind from which it is derived; the device operating properly throughout the material part of that period, or any period in which it was not operating properly or was out of operation during that part not being such as to affect the electronic record or the accuracy of its contents; and the information in the record reproducing or being derived from such information fed in. Sub-section (3) treats all the computers or communication devices used for that purpose during that period, whether in standalone mode, on a computer system, on a computer network, on a computer resource enabling information creation or providing information processing and storage, or through an intermediary, as constituting for the purposes of this section a single computer or communication device, and references in the section are construed accordingly. Sub-section (4) is the certificate provision: in any proceeding where it is desired to give a statement in evidence by virtue of this section, a certificate doing ANY of the following three things shall be submitted along with the electronic record at each instance where it is being submitted for admission, namely (a) identifying the electronic record containing the statement and describing the manner in which it was produced, (b) giving such particulars of any device involved in the production of that record as may be appropriate for the purpose of showing that it was produced by a computer or a communication device referred to in clauses (a) to (e) of sub-section (3), and (c) dealing with any of the matters to which the conditions mentioned in sub-section (2) relate. The certificate must purport to be signed by a person in charge of the computer or communication device or the management of the relevant activities (whichever is appropriate) AND an expert, that is, two signatories, and it shall be evidence of any matter stated in the certificate; for the purposes of that sub-section it is sufficient for a matter to be stated to the best of the knowledge and belief of the person stating it, in the certificate specified in the Schedule (the form of which is not part of the text supplied here). Sub-section (5) clarifies that information is taken to be supplied to the computer or communication device if it is supplied in any appropriate form, whether directly or, with or without human intervention, by means of any appropriate equipment; and that a computer output is taken to have been produced by the device whether produced by it directly or, with or without human intervention, by means of any appropriate equipment or by other electronic means as referred to in clauses (a) to (e) of sub-section (3).
key_requirements: Sub-section (1) operates notwithstanding anything contained in this Adhiniyam.

Information contained in an electronic record which is printed on paper, stored, recorded or copied in optical or magnetic media or semiconductor memory and produced by a computer or any communication device, or otherwise stored, recorded or copied in any electronic form (the computer output), shall be deemed to be also a document, if the conditions mentioned in this section are satisfied in relation to the information and computer in question.

Such computer output shall be admissible in any proceedings, without further proof or production of the original, as evidence of any contents of the original or of any fact stated therein of which direct evidence would be admissible (the supplied Gazette text reads 'as evidence or any contents of the original', an apparent typographical error for 'as evidence of any contents of the original', and the latter reading is used here).

The computer output containing the information must have been produced by the computer or communication device during the period over which that device was used regularly to create, store or process information for the purposes of any activity regularly carried on over that period by the person having lawful control over its use.

During the said period, information of the kind contained in the electronic record, or of the kind from which the information so contained is derived, must have been regularly fed into the computer or communication device in the ordinary course of the said activities.

Throughout the material part of the said period the computer or communication device must have been operating properly, or, if not, any period in which it was not operating properly or was out of operation during that part of the period must not have been such as to affect the electronic record or the accuracy of its contents.
The information contained in the electronic record must reproduce or be derived from such information fed into the computer or communication device in the ordinary course of the said activities.

Where the function of creating, storing or processing information for the purposes of the activity was regularly performed by means of one or more computers or communication devices, whether in standalone mode, on a computer system, on a computer network, on a computer resource enabling information creation or providing information processing and storage, or through an intermediary, all the computers or communication devices used for that purpose during that period shall be treated for the purposes of this section as constituting a single computer or communication device.

In any proceeding where it is desired to give a statement in evidence by virtue of this section, a certificate doing any of the things listed in clauses (a) to (c) of sub-section (4) shall be submitted along with the electronic record.
The certificate shall be submitted along with the electronic record at each instance where it is being submitted for admission.
Clause (a) of sub-section (4): identifying the electronic record containing the statement and describing the manner in which it was produced.

Clause (b) of sub-section (4): giving such particulars of any device involved in the production of that electronic record as may be appropriate for the purpose of showing that the electronic record was produced by a computer or a communication device referred to in clauses (a) to (e) of sub-section (3).
Clause (c) of sub-section (4): dealing with any of the matters to which the conditions mentioned in sub-section (2) relate.
The certificate must purport to be signed by a person in charge of the computer or communication device or the management of the relevant activities (whichever is appropriate) and an expert.
The certificate shall be evidence of any matter stated in the certificate.
For the purposes of sub-section (4) it shall be sufficient for a matter to be stated to the best of the knowledge and belief of the person stating it in the certificate specified in the Schedule.

Information shall be taken to be supplied to a computer or communication device if it is supplied thereto in any appropriate form and whether it is so supplied directly or (with or without human intervention) by means of any appropriate equipment.

A computer output shall be taken to have been produced by a computer or communication device whether it was produced by it directly or (with or without human intervention) by means of any appropriate equipment or by other electronic means as referred to in clauses (a) to (e) of sub-section (3).
bsa_refs.investigation_relevance: Wherever the IO relies on this section to put computer output in evidence - CDRs, CCTV footage, device extractions, printouts, server logs - the record must travel with a sub-section (4) certificate, and it must go with the record each and every time the record is submitted for admission, not merely once at charge-sheet stage. On the text the certificate is one 'doing any of' three things: identifying the record and describing how it was produced, giving particulars of any device involved, and dealing with any of the matters to which the sub-section (2) conditions relate; the statute requires any of the three, but the safe practice is to cover all three. The certificate must purport to be signed by two people, a person in charge of the computer or communication device or the management of the relevant activities (whichever is appropriate) and an expert, and it is the certificate specified in the Schedule, so the IO should line up both signatories before the record is tendered; a matter may be stated in it to the best of the knowledge and belief of the person stating it. At seizure, therefore, the IO should record the facts the signatories will later have to certify: regular use of the device over the relevant period for the activity, who had lawful control over its use, regular feeding of information of that kind in the ordinary course, and the proper working of the device (or that any malfunction or downtime in the material part of the period did not affect the record or the accuracy of its contents). Note the limits of sub-section (1): where the conditions are met it deems the computer output to be also a document and lets it in without further proof or production of the original, but it does not make the output the original and it settles nothing about the truth or weight of the contents.
time_limits: s.63(2)(a): no fixed number of days is prescribed - the relevant period is the period over which the computer or communication device was used regularly to create, store or process information for the purposes of the activity regularly carried on over that period.

s.63(2)(c): the computer or communication device must have been operating properly 'throughout the material part of the said period', or any period in which it was not operating properly or was out of operation during that part must not have been such as to affect the electronic record or the accuracy of its contents. This qualification belongs to clause (c) alone and does not relax clauses (a), (b) or (d).
s.63(4): the certificate must be submitted along with the electronic record 'at each instance where it is being submitted for admission' - a repeating timing requirement, not a one-time filing.

bsa_refs.title: Facts which are occasion, cause or effect of facts in issue or relevant facts
bsa_refs.summary: Section 5 makes relevant the facts that surround a fact in issue or a relevant fact rather than constituting it. In one unnumbered sentence it covers five categories, of which the first three are qualified by the words "immediate or otherwise": facts that are the occasion of the fact in issue or relevant fact, facts that are its cause and facts that are its effect, whether immediate or otherwise; facts that constitute the state of things under which it happened; and facts that afforded an opportunity for its occurrence or transaction. The sentence itself groups those five into the three limbs listed as the key requirements below - occasion, cause or effect; the state of things; and opportunity. The section says only that such facts are relevant; it says nothing about the weight to be given to them. The illustrations treat as relevant facts the victim going to a fair with money in his possession shortly before a robbery and showing it or mentioning that he had it to third persons, marks on the ground produced by a struggle at or near the place where the murder was committed, and the state of B's health before the symptoms ascribed to poison together with habits of B known to A which afforded an opportunity for the administration of poison.
key_requirements: Facts which are the occasion, cause or effect, whether immediate or otherwise, of a relevant fact or a fact in issue are relevant.
Facts which constitute the state of things under which the fact in issue or relevant fact happened are relevant.
Facts which afforded an opportunity for the occurrence or transaction of the fact in issue or relevant fact are relevant.
bsa_refs.investigation_relevance: This is the provision that carries the IO's scene and circumstance evidence: physical traces such as marks on the ground produced by a struggle at or near the place of the offence, the state of things at the scene, and the events that created the opportunity for the offence are all relevant, and should therefore be photographed, measured, seized and described in the panchnama. The IO should equally collect the lead-up facts - the victim's movements, what property the victim was carrying and to whom the victim showed it or mentioned that he had it, and the victim's condition before the offence: in a poisoning case, the state of the victim's health before the symptoms ascribed to poison, which is relevant whether or not the accused knew of it. Separately, and carrying its own qualifiers, any habit of the victim known to the accused which afforded an opportunity for the offence is relevant and should be collected. The section establishes relevancy only; proof and weight still have to be built by other means.

bsa_refs.title: Opinions of experts
bsa_refs.summary: Section 39 makes expert opinion a relevant fact. s.39(1) provides that when the Court has to form an opinion on a point of foreign law, of science or art, or any other field, or as to identity of handwriting or finger impressions, the opinions of persons specially skilled in that subject are relevant facts, and it labels such persons "experts". s.39(2) deals separately with electronic material: where the Court has to form an opinion on any matter relating to information transmitted or stored in any computer resource or any other electronic or digital form, the opinion of the Examiner of Electronic Evidence referred to in section 79A of the Information Technology Act, 2000 is a relevant fact. The Explanation to s.39(2) provides that such an Examiner of Electronic Evidence shall be an expert. The illustrations cover opinion on symptoms produced by a poison, opinion on symptoms showing unsoundness of mind and the accused's capacity to know the nature of the act, and comparison of a disputed document with another document proved or admitted to have been written by the same person.
key_requirements: The opinions of persons specially skilled in foreign law, science or art, any other field, or in questions as to identity of handwriting or finger impressions are relevant facts when the Court has to form an opinion on that point.
Persons specially skilled in such a field are called experts.

Where the Court has to form an opinion on any matter relating to information transmitted or stored in any computer resource or any other electronic or digital form, the opinion of the Examiner of Electronic Evidence referred to in section 79A of the Information Technology Act, 2000 is a relevant fact.
For the purposes of sub-section (2), an Examiner of Electronic Evidence shall be an expert.
bsa_refs.investigation_relevance: The IO should route every scientific, medical, ballistic, chemical, handwriting or finger-impression question to a person specially skilled in that field and place the basis of that skill on record, since it is skill in the subject that makes the opinion relevant. For anything transmitted or stored in a computer resource or in any other electronic or digital form, the opinion that s.39(2) makes relevant is that of an Examiner of Electronic Evidence notified under section 79A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, so electronic exhibits should be sent to such an Examiner; and, as illustration (c) shows, a handwriting comparison requires the IO to also supply a specimen document that is proved or admitted to have been written by the suspected author.

bsa_refs.title: Primary evidence
bsa_refs.summary: Section 57 defines primary evidence as the document itself produced for the inspection of the Court, and then extends that definition through seven Explanations. Explanation 1 makes each part of a document executed in several parts primary evidence of the document. Explanation 2 makes each counterpart, executed by one or some of the parties only, primary evidence as against the parties executing it. Explanation 3 applies only where a number of documents are all made by one uniform process, as in the case of printing, lithography or photography: each is then primary evidence of the contents of the rest, but where they are all copies of a common original they are not primary evidence of the contents of the original. Explanations 4 to 7 carry the definition into electronic material: where an electronic or digital record is created or stored and that storage occurs simultaneously or sequentially in multiple files, each such file is primary evidence (Explanation 4); an electronic or digital record produced from proper custody is primary evidence unless it is disputed (Explanation 5); where a video recording is simultaneously stored in electronic form and transmitted or broadcast or transferred to another, each of the stored recordings is primary evidence (Explanation 6); and where an electronic or digital record is stored in multiple storage spaces in a computer resource, each such automated storage, including temporary files, is primary evidence (Explanation 7). An Illustration applies Explanation 3 to placards all printed at one time from one original. The section says what counts as primary evidence; it does not say that contents can be proved only in that way, and the 'unless it is disputed' qualification belongs to Explanation 5 alone.
key_requirements: Primary evidence means the document itself produced for the inspection of the Court.
Where a document is executed in several parts, each part is primary evidence of the document.
Where a document is executed in counterpart, each counterpart executed by one or some of the parties only is primary evidence as against the parties executing it.
Where a number of documents are all made by one uniform process, as in printing, lithography or photography, each is primary evidence of the contents of the rest.
Where such documents are all copies of a common original, they are not primary evidence of the contents of the original.
Where an electronic or digital record is created or stored and that storage occurs simultaneously or sequentially in multiple files, each such file is primary evidence.
Where an electronic or digital record is produced from proper custody, it is primary evidence unless it is disputed.
Where a video recording is simultaneously stored in electronic form and transmitted or broadcast or transferred to another, each of the stored recordings is primary evidence.
Where an electronic or digital record is stored in multiple storage spaces in a computer resource, each such automated storage, including temporary files, is primary evidence.
bsa_refs.investigation_relevance: The IO should seize and produce the document or the device itself wherever that is possible, and should record custody carefully, because under Explanation 5 an electronic or digital record produced from proper custody is primary evidence unless it is disputed. Under Explanations 4 and 7, where an electronic or digital record is created or stored and that storage occurs simultaneously or sequentially in multiple files, or where the record is stored in multiple storage spaces in a computer resource, each such file and each such automated storage, including temporary files, is primary evidence. Explanation 6 is narrower and both of its conditions must be met: it covers a video recording simultaneously stored in electronic form and transmitted or broadcast or transferred to another, and it is each of those stored recordings that is primary evidence; a recording copied afterwards from a stored file is not within Explanation 6, whatever its position under the other Explanations may be. The seizure memo and forwarding note should therefore identify exactly which file, device or storage space is being relied on and how it came into existence. On documents, Explanation 3 operates only where a number of documents are all made by one uniform process, such as printing, lithography or photography; each is then primary evidence of the contents of the rest, but where they are all copies of a common original none of them is primary evidence of the contents of the original. That does not make such a copy worthless, since this section says only what is primary evidence: the contents of the original may still be proved by the original itself, or by secondary evidence where the law permits it, so a copy should not be dropped from the case file merely because it cannot stand as primary evidence of the original.

bsa_refs.title: Cases in which secondary evidence relating to documents may be given
bsa_refs.summary: This section sets out the seven situations, clauses (a) to (g), in which secondary evidence may be given of the existence, condition or contents of a document. They are: the original being in the possession or power of the opponent, of a person beyond the Court's process, or of a person legally bound to produce it, coupled with non-production after the notice mentioned in section 64 (clause (a)); a written admission of the existence, condition or contents (clause (b)); destruction or loss of the original, or inability to produce it in reasonable time for a reason not arising from the party's own default or neglect (clause (c)); an original not easily movable (clause (d)); a public document within the meaning of section 74 (clause (e)); a document of which a certified copy is permitted to be given in evidence (clause (f)); and numerous accounts or documents which cannot conveniently be examined in Court where the fact to be proved is the general result of the whole collection (clause (g)). The Explanation then limits the kind of secondary evidence allowed under each head: any secondary evidence for clauses (a), (c) and (d); only the written admission for clause (b); only a certified copy for clauses (e) and (f); and, for clause (g), evidence of the general result by a skilled person who has examined the documents. The modality throughout is permissive - secondary evidence 'may' be given in these cases.
key_requirements: Secondary evidence may be given of the existence, condition, or contents of a document in the cases listed in clauses (a) to (g).

Secondary evidence may be given when the original is shown or appears to be in the possession or power of the person against whom it is sought to be proved, of any person out of reach of or not subject to the process of the Court, or of any person legally bound to produce it.
In such a case secondary evidence may be given only when, after the notice mentioned in section 64, such person does not produce the original.

Secondary evidence may be given when the existence, condition or contents of the original have been proved to be admitted in writing by the person against whom it is proved or by his representative in interest.

Secondary evidence may be given when the original has been destroyed or lost, or when the party offering evidence of its contents cannot, for any other reason not arising from his own default or neglect, produce it in reasonable time.
Secondary evidence may be given when the original is of such a nature as not to be easily movable.
Secondary evidence may be given when the original is a public document within the meaning of section 74.
Secondary evidence may be given when the original is a document of which a certified copy is permitted by this Adhiniyam, or by any other law in force in India, to be given in evidence.

Secondary evidence may be given when the originals consist of numerous accounts or other documents which cannot conveniently be examined in Court and the fact to be proved is the general result of the whole collection.
For clauses (a), (c) and (d), any secondary evidence of the contents of the document is admissible.
For clause (b), the written admission is admissible.
For clause (e) or (f), a certified copy of the document, but no other kind of secondary evidence, is admissible.
For clause (g), evidence may be given as to the general result of the documents by any person who has examined them and who is skilled in the examination of such document.
bsa_refs.investigation_relevance: This is the gateway the prosecution uses whenever the original document is not on the record, so the case diary must carry the facts that fit one of the clauses - the record of loss or destruction for clause (c), proof of the section 64 notice and of non-production for clause (a), the immovability of the original for clause (d), or the public-document character for clause (e). The Explanation is the practical warning: for public documents and for documents where a certified copy is permitted, only a certified copy is admissible, so the IO should obtain and annex the certified copy rather than a photocopy or a photograph.
time_limits: Clause (c) fixes no number of days: the party must be unable, for a reason not arising from his own default or neglect, to produce the original 'in reasonable time'.

bsa_refs.title: Special provisions as to evidence relating to electronic record
bsa_refs.summary: A single-sentence routing provision. It states that the contents of electronic records may be proved in accordance with the provisions of section 63. It creates no conditions of its own and adds nothing beyond pointing to section 63 for the mode of proof. Its modality is permissive, 'may be proved in accordance with', and it contains no words of exclusion of its own such as 'only', 'and no other' or 'and not otherwise'. The section therefore names the section 63 route without, in its own words, ruling out any other; whether that route is exclusive is not settled by this text.
key_requirements: The contents of electronic records may be proved in accordance with the provisions of section 63.
bsa_refs.investigation_relevance: This section routes the proof of the contents of electronic records to section 63, so for any electronic material the IO seizes or obtains he should plan for the section 63 conditions and certificate from the moment of seizure, and should not leave them to be assembled at trial. Note the wording: the section is permissive, 'may be proved in accordance with', and carries no words of exclusion of its own, so any proposition that section 63 is the only way of proving the contents of an electronic record does not come from the words of this section. That is a reason to work to the section 63 requirements in every case rather than to rely on this section as either granting or shutting off an alternative.

bsa_refs.title: Admissibility of electronic records
bsa_refs.summary: This is the operative provision for proving electronic records. Operating notwithstanding anything contained in this Adhiniyam, sub-section (1) deems any information contained in an electronic record which is printed on paper, stored, recorded or copied in optical or magnetic media or semiconductor memory and produced by a computer or any communication device, or otherwise stored, recorded or copied in any electronic form (the 'computer output'), to be also a document, if the conditions mentioned in this section are satisfied in relation to the information and computer in question, and makes that output admissible in any proceedings, without further proof or production of the original, as evidence of any contents of the original or of any fact stated therein of which direct evidence would be admissible. What sub-section (1) deems is that the computer output is ALSO a document: it does not deem the output to be the original, and it settles nothing about the truth or the weight of what the record contains. Both the deeming and the admissibility are conditional on the section's conditions being satisfied. (The supplied Gazette text reads 'as evidence or any contents of the original'; that is an apparent typographical error for 'as evidence of any contents of the original', and the latter reading is used here.) Sub-section (2) lays down the four conditions in clauses (a) to (d): production of the output by the computer or communication device during the period over which it was used regularly to create, store or process information for the purposes of any activity regularly carried on over that period by the person having lawful control over its use; regular feeding into the device, in the ordinary course of those activities, of information of the kind contained in the record or of the kind from which it is derived; the device operating properly throughout the material part of that period, or any period in which it was not operating properly or was out of operation during that part not being such as to affect the electronic record or the accuracy of its contents; and the information in the record reproducing or being derived from such information fed in. Sub-section (3) treats all the computers or communication devices used for that purpose during that period, whether in standalone mode, on a computer system, on a computer network, on a computer resource enabling information creation or providing information processing and storage, or through an intermediary, as constituting for the purposes of this section a single computer or communication device, and references in the section are construed accordingly. Sub-section (4) is the certificate provision: in any proceeding where it is desired to give a statement in evidence by virtue of this section, a certificate doing ANY of the following three things shall be submitted along with the electronic record at each instance where it is being submitted for admission, namely (a) identifying the electronic record containing the statement and describing the manner in which it was produced, (b) giving such particulars of any device involved in the production of that record as may be appropriate for the purpose of showing that it was produced by a computer or a communication device referred to in clauses (a) to (e) of sub-section (3), and (c) dealing with any of the matters to which the conditions mentioned in sub-section (2) relate. The certificate must purport to be signed by a person in charge of the computer or communication device or the management of the relevant activities (whichever is appropriate) AND an expert, that is, two signatories, and it shall be evidence of any matter stated in the certificate; for the purposes of that sub-section it is sufficient for a matter to be stated to the best of the knowledge and belief of the person stating it, in the certificate specified in the Schedule (the form of which is not part of the text supplied here). Sub-section (5) clarifies that information is taken to be supplied to the computer or communication device if it is supplied in any appropriate form, whether directly or, with or without human intervention, by means of any appropriate equipment; and that a computer output is taken to have been produced by the device whether produced by it directly or, with or without human intervention, by means of any appropriate equipment or by other electronic means as referred to in clauses (a) to (e) of sub-section (3).
key_requirements: Sub-section (1) operates notwithstanding anything contained in this Adhiniyam.

Information contained in an electronic record which is printed on paper, stored, recorded or copied in optical or magnetic media or semiconductor memory and produced by a computer or any communication device, or otherwise stored, recorded or copied in any electronic form (the computer output), shall be deemed to be also a document, if the conditions mentioned in this section are satisfied in relation to the information and computer in question.

Such computer output shall be admissible in any proceedings, without further proof or production of the original, as evidence of any contents of the original or of any fact stated therein of which direct evidence would be admissible (the supplied Gazette text reads 'as evidence or any contents of the original', an apparent typographical error for 'as evidence of any contents of the original', and the latter reading is used here).

The computer output containing the information must have been produced by the computer or communication device during the period over which that device was used regularly to create, store or process information for the purposes of any activity regularly carried on over that period by the person having lawful control over its use.

During the said period, information of the kind contained in the electronic record, or of the kind from which the information so contained is derived, must have been regularly fed into the computer or communication device in the ordinary course of the said activities.

Throughout the material part of the said period the computer or communication device must have been operating properly, or, if not, any period in which it was not operating properly or was out of operation during that part of the period must not have been such as to affect the electronic record or the accuracy of its contents.
The information contained in the electronic record must reproduce or be derived from such information fed into the computer or communication device in the ordinary course of the said activities.

Where the function of creating, storing or processing information for the purposes of the activity was regularly performed by means of one or more computers or communication devices, whether in standalone mode, on a computer system, on a computer network, on a computer resource enabling information creation or providing information processing and storage, or through an intermediary, all the computers or communication devices used for that purpose during that period shall be treated for the purposes of this section as constituting a single computer or communication device.

In any proceeding where it is desired to give a statement in evidence by virtue of this section, a certificate doing any of the things listed in clauses (a) to (c) of sub-section (4) shall be submitted along with the electronic record.
The certificate shall be submitted along with the electronic record at each instance where it is being submitted for admission.
Clause (a) of sub-section (4): identifying the electronic record containing the statement and describing the manner in which it was produced.

Clause (b) of sub-section (4): giving such particulars of any device involved in the production of that electronic record as may be appropriate for the purpose of showing that the electronic record was produced by a computer or a communication device referred to in clauses (a) to (e) of sub-section (3).
Clause (c) of sub-section (4): dealing with any of the matters to which the conditions mentioned in sub-section (2) relate.
The certificate must purport to be signed by a person in charge of the computer or communication device or the management of the relevant activities (whichever is appropriate) and an expert.
The certificate shall be evidence of any matter stated in the certificate.
For the purposes of sub-section (4) it shall be sufficient for a matter to be stated to the best of the knowledge and belief of the person stating it in the certificate specified in the Schedule.

Information shall be taken to be supplied to a computer or communication device if it is supplied thereto in any appropriate form and whether it is so supplied directly or (with or without human intervention) by means of any appropriate equipment.

A computer output shall be taken to have been produced by a computer or communication device whether it was produced by it directly or (with or without human intervention) by means of any appropriate equipment or by other electronic means as referred to in clauses (a) to (e) of sub-section (3).
bsa_refs.investigation_relevance: Wherever the IO relies on this section to put computer output in evidence - CDRs, CCTV footage, device extractions, printouts, server logs - the record must travel with a sub-section (4) certificate, and it must go with the record each and every time the record is submitted for admission, not merely once at charge-sheet stage. On the text the certificate is one 'doing any of' three things: identifying the record and describing how it was produced, giving particulars of any device involved, and dealing with any of the matters to which the sub-section (2) conditions relate; the statute requires any of the three, but the safe practice is to cover all three. The certificate must purport to be signed by two people, a person in charge of the computer or communication device or the management of the relevant activities (whichever is appropriate) and an expert, and it is the certificate specified in the Schedule, so the IO should line up both signatories before the record is tendered; a matter may be stated in it to the best of the knowledge and belief of the person stating it. At seizure, therefore, the IO should record the facts the signatories will later have to certify: regular use of the device over the relevant period for the activity, who had lawful control over its use, regular feeding of information of that kind in the ordinary course, and the proper working of the device (or that any malfunction or downtime in the material part of the period did not affect the record or the accuracy of its contents). Note the limits of sub-section (1): where the conditions are met it deems the computer output to be also a document and lets it in without further proof or production of the original, but it does not make the output the original and it settles nothing about the truth or weight of the contents.
time_limits: s.63(2)(a): no fixed number of days is prescribed - the relevant period is the period over which the computer or communication device was used regularly to create, store or process information for the purposes of the activity regularly carried on over that period.

s.63(2)(c): the computer or communication device must have been operating properly 'throughout the material part of the said period', or any period in which it was not operating properly or was out of operation during that part must not have been such as to affect the electronic record or the accuracy of its contents. This qualification belongs to clause (c) alone and does not relax clauses (a), (b) or (d).
s.63(4): the certificate must be submitted along with the electronic record 'at each instance where it is being submitted for admission' - a repeating timing requirement, not a one-time filing.

bsa_refs.title: Facts which are occasion, cause or effect of facts in issue or relevant facts
bsa_refs.summary: Section 5 makes relevant the facts that surround a fact in issue or a relevant fact rather than constituting it. In one unnumbered sentence it covers five categories, of which the first three are qualified by the words "immediate or otherwise": facts that are the occasion of the fact in issue or relevant fact, facts that are its cause and facts that are its effect, whether immediate or otherwise; facts that constitute the state of things under which it happened; and facts that afforded an opportunity for its occurrence or transaction. The sentence itself groups those five into the three limbs listed as the key requirements below - occasion, cause or effect; the state of things; and opportunity. The section says only that such facts are relevant; it says nothing about the weight to be given to them. The illustrations treat as relevant facts the victim going to a fair with money in his possession shortly before a robbery and showing it or mentioning that he had it to third persons, marks on the ground produced by a struggle at or near the place where the murder was committed, and the state of B's health before the symptoms ascribed to poison together with habits of B known to A which afforded an opportunity for the administration of poison.
key_requirements: Facts which are the occasion, cause or effect, whether immediate or otherwise, of a relevant fact or a fact in issue are relevant.
Facts which constitute the state of things under which the fact in issue or relevant fact happened are relevant.
Facts which afforded an opportunity for the occurrence or transaction of the fact in issue or relevant fact are relevant.
bsa_refs.investigation_relevance: This is the provision that carries the IO's scene and circumstance evidence: physical traces such as marks on the ground produced by a struggle at or near the place of the offence, the state of things at the scene, and the events that created the opportunity for the offence are all relevant, and should therefore be photographed, measured, seized and described in the panchnama. The IO should equally collect the lead-up facts - the victim's movements, what property the victim was carrying and to whom the victim showed it or mentioned that he had it, and the victim's condition before the offence: in a poisoning case, the state of the victim's health before the symptoms ascribed to poison, which is relevant whether or not the accused knew of it. Separately, and carrying its own qualifiers, any habit of the victim known to the accused which afforded an opportunity for the offence is relevant and should be collected. The section establishes relevancy only; proof and weight still have to be built by other means.

bsa_refs.title: Opinions of experts
bsa_refs.summary: Section 39 makes expert opinion a relevant fact. s.39(1) provides that when the Court has to form an opinion on a point of foreign law, of science or art, or any other field, or as to identity of handwriting or finger impressions, the opinions of persons specially skilled in that subject are relevant facts, and it labels such persons "experts". s.39(2) deals separately with electronic material: where the Court has to form an opinion on any matter relating to information transmitted or stored in any computer resource or any other electronic or digital form, the opinion of the Examiner of Electronic Evidence referred to in section 79A of the Information Technology Act, 2000 is a relevant fact. The Explanation to s.39(2) provides that such an Examiner of Electronic Evidence shall be an expert. The illustrations cover opinion on symptoms produced by a poison, opinion on symptoms showing unsoundness of mind and the accused's capacity to know the nature of the act, and comparison of a disputed document with another document proved or admitted to have been written by the same person.
key_requirements: The opinions of persons specially skilled in foreign law, science or art, any other field, or in questions as to identity of handwriting or finger impressions are relevant facts when the Court has to form an opinion on that point.
Persons specially skilled in such a field are called experts.

Where the Court has to form an opinion on any matter relating to information transmitted or stored in any computer resource or any other electronic or digital form, the opinion of the Examiner of Electronic Evidence referred to in section 79A of the Information Technology Act, 2000 is a relevant fact.
For the purposes of sub-section (2), an Examiner of Electronic Evidence shall be an expert.
bsa_refs.investigation_relevance: The IO should route every scientific, medical, ballistic, chemical, handwriting or finger-impression question to a person specially skilled in that field and place the basis of that skill on record, since it is skill in the subject that makes the opinion relevant. For anything transmitted or stored in a computer resource or in any other electronic or digital form, the opinion that s.39(2) makes relevant is that of an Examiner of Electronic Evidence notified under section 79A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, so electronic exhibits should be sent to such an Examiner; and, as illustration (c) shows, a handwriting comparison requires the IO to also supply a specimen document that is proved or admitted to have been written by the suspected author.

bsa_refs.title: Primary evidence
bsa_refs.summary: Section 57 defines primary evidence as the document itself produced for the inspection of the Court, and then extends that definition through seven Explanations. Explanation 1 makes each part of a document executed in several parts primary evidence of the document. Explanation 2 makes each counterpart, executed by one or some of the parties only, primary evidence as against the parties executing it. Explanation 3 applies only where a number of documents are all made by one uniform process, as in the case of printing, lithography or photography: each is then primary evidence of the contents of the rest, but where they are all copies of a common original they are not primary evidence of the contents of the original. Explanations 4 to 7 carry the definition into electronic material: where an electronic or digital record is created or stored and that storage occurs simultaneously or sequentially in multiple files, each such file is primary evidence (Explanation 4); an electronic or digital record produced from proper custody is primary evidence unless it is disputed (Explanation 5); where a video recording is simultaneously stored in electronic form and transmitted or broadcast or transferred to another, each of the stored recordings is primary evidence (Explanation 6); and where an electronic or digital record is stored in multiple storage spaces in a computer resource, each such automated storage, including temporary files, is primary evidence (Explanation 7). An Illustration applies Explanation 3 to placards all printed at one time from one original. The section says what counts as primary evidence; it does not say that contents can be proved only in that way, and the 'unless it is disputed' qualification belongs to Explanation 5 alone.
key_requirements: Primary evidence means the document itself produced for the inspection of the Court.
Where a document is executed in several parts, each part is primary evidence of the document.
Where a document is executed in counterpart, each counterpart executed by one or some of the parties only is primary evidence as against the parties executing it.
Where a number of documents are all made by one uniform process, as in printing, lithography or photography, each is primary evidence of the contents of the rest.
Where such documents are all copies of a common original, they are not primary evidence of the contents of the original.
Where an electronic or digital record is created or stored and that storage occurs simultaneously or sequentially in multiple files, each such file is primary evidence.
Where an electronic or digital record is produced from proper custody, it is primary evidence unless it is disputed.
Where a video recording is simultaneously stored in electronic form and transmitted or broadcast or transferred to another, each of the stored recordings is primary evidence.
Where an electronic or digital record is stored in multiple storage spaces in a computer resource, each such automated storage, including temporary files, is primary evidence.
bsa_refs.investigation_relevance: The IO should seize and produce the document or the device itself wherever that is possible, and should record custody carefully, because under Explanation 5 an electronic or digital record produced from proper custody is primary evidence unless it is disputed. Under Explanations 4 and 7, where an electronic or digital record is created or stored and that storage occurs simultaneously or sequentially in multiple files, or where the record is stored in multiple storage spaces in a computer resource, each such file and each such automated storage, including temporary files, is primary evidence. Explanation 6 is narrower and both of its conditions must be met: it covers a video recording simultaneously stored in electronic form and transmitted or broadcast or transferred to another, and it is each of those stored recordings that is primary evidence; a recording copied afterwards from a stored file is not within Explanation 6, whatever its position under the other Explanations may be. The seizure memo and forwarding note should therefore identify exactly which file, device or storage space is being relied on and how it came into existence. On documents, Explanation 3 operates only where a number of documents are all made by one uniform process, such as printing, lithography or photography; each is then primary evidence of the contents of the rest, but where they are all copies of a common original none of them is primary evidence of the contents of the original. That does not make such a copy worthless, since this section says only what is primary evidence: the contents of the original may still be proved by the original itself, or by secondary evidence where the law permits it, so a copy should not be dropped from the case file merely because it cannot stand as primary evidence of the original.

bsa_refs.title: Cases in which secondary evidence relating to documents may be given
bsa_refs.summary: This section sets out the seven situations, clauses (a) to (g), in which secondary evidence may be given of the existence, condition or contents of a document. They are: the original being in the possession or power of the opponent, of a person beyond the Court's process, or of a person legally bound to produce it, coupled with non-production after the notice mentioned in section 64 (clause (a)); a written admission of the existence, condition or contents (clause (b)); destruction or loss of the original, or inability to produce it in reasonable time for a reason not arising from the party's own default or neglect (clause (c)); an original not easily movable (clause (d)); a public document within the meaning of section 74 (clause (e)); a document of which a certified copy is permitted to be given in evidence (clause (f)); and numerous accounts or documents which cannot conveniently be examined in Court where the fact to be proved is the general result of the whole collection (clause (g)). The Explanation then limits the kind of secondary evidence allowed under each head: any secondary evidence for clauses (a), (c) and (d); only the written admission for clause (b); only a certified copy for clauses (e) and (f); and, for clause (g), evidence of the general result by a skilled person who has examined the documents. The modality throughout is permissive - secondary evidence 'may' be given in these cases.
key_requirements: Secondary evidence may be given of the existence, condition, or contents of a document in the cases listed in clauses (a) to (g).

Secondary evidence may be given when the original is shown or appears to be in the possession or power of the person against whom it is sought to be proved, of any person out of reach of or not subject to the process of the Court, or of any person legally bound to produce it.
In such a case secondary evidence may be given only when, after the notice mentioned in section 64, such person does not produce the original.

Secondary evidence may be given when the existence, condition or contents of the original have been proved to be admitted in writing by the person against whom it is proved or by his representative in interest.

Secondary evidence may be given when the original has been destroyed or lost, or when the party offering evidence of its contents cannot, for any other reason not arising from his own default or neglect, produce it in reasonable time.
Secondary evidence may be given when the original is of such a nature as not to be easily movable.
Secondary evidence may be given when the original is a public document within the meaning of section 74.
Secondary evidence may be given when the original is a document of which a certified copy is permitted by this Adhiniyam, or by any other law in force in India, to be given in evidence.

Secondary evidence may be given when the originals consist of numerous accounts or other documents which cannot conveniently be examined in Court and the fact to be proved is the general result of the whole collection.
For clauses (a), (c) and (d), any secondary evidence of the contents of the document is admissible.
For clause (b), the written admission is admissible.
For clause (e) or (f), a certified copy of the document, but no other kind of secondary evidence, is admissible.
For clause (g), evidence may be given as to the general result of the documents by any person who has examined them and who is skilled in the examination of such document.
bsa_refs.investigation_relevance: This is the gateway the prosecution uses whenever the original document is not on the record, so the case diary must carry the facts that fit one of the clauses - the record of loss or destruction for clause (c), proof of the section 64 notice and of non-production for clause (a), the immovability of the original for clause (d), or the public-document character for clause (e). The Explanation is the practical warning: for public documents and for documents where a certified copy is permitted, only a certified copy is admissible, so the IO should obtain and annex the certified copy rather than a photocopy or a photograph.
time_limits: Clause (c) fixes no number of days: the party must be unable, for a reason not arising from his own default or neglect, to produce the original 'in reasonable time'.

bsa_refs.title: Special provisions as to evidence relating to electronic record
bsa_refs.summary: A single-sentence routing provision. It states that the contents of electronic records may be proved in accordance with the provisions of section 63. It creates no conditions of its own and adds nothing beyond pointing to section 63 for the mode of proof. Its modality is permissive, 'may be proved in accordance with', and it contains no words of exclusion of its own such as 'only', 'and no other' or 'and not otherwise'. The section therefore names the section 63 route without, in its own words, ruling out any other; whether that route is exclusive is not settled by this text.
key_requirements: The contents of electronic records may be proved in accordance with the provisions of section 63.
bsa_refs.investigation_relevance: This section routes the proof of the contents of electronic records to section 63, so for any electronic material the IO seizes or obtains he should plan for the section 63 conditions and certificate from the moment of seizure, and should not leave them to be assembled at trial. Note the wording: the section is permissive, 'may be proved in accordance with', and carries no words of exclusion of its own, so any proposition that section 63 is the only way of proving the contents of an electronic record does not come from the words of this section. That is a reason to work to the section 63 requirements in every case rather than to rely on this section as either granting or shutting off an alternative.

bsa_refs.title: Admissibility of electronic records
bsa_refs.summary: This is the operative provision for proving electronic records. Operating notwithstanding anything contained in this Adhiniyam, sub-section (1) deems any information contained in an electronic record which is printed on paper, stored, recorded or copied in optical or magnetic media or semiconductor memory and produced by a computer or any communication device, or otherwise stored, recorded or copied in any electronic form (the 'computer output'), to be also a document, if the conditions mentioned in this section are satisfied in relation to the information and computer in question, and makes that output admissible in any proceedings, without further proof or production of the original, as evidence of any contents of the original or of any fact stated therein of which direct evidence would be admissible. What sub-section (1) deems is that the computer output is ALSO a document: it does not deem the output to be the original, and it settles nothing about the truth or the weight of what the record contains. Both the deeming and the admissibility are conditional on the section's conditions being satisfied. (The supplied Gazette text reads 'as evidence or any contents of the original'; that is an apparent typographical error for 'as evidence of any contents of the original', and the latter reading is used here.) Sub-section (2) lays down the four conditions in clauses (a) to (d): production of the output by the computer or communication device during the period over which it was used regularly to create, store or process information for the purposes of any activity regularly carried on over that period by the person having lawful control over its use; regular feeding into the device, in the ordinary course of those activities, of information of the kind contained in the record or of the kind from which it is derived; the device operating properly throughout the material part of that period, or any period in which it was not operating properly or was out of operation during that part not being such as to affect the electronic record or the accuracy of its contents; and the information in the record reproducing or being derived from such information fed in. Sub-section (3) treats all the computers or communication devices used for that purpose during that period, whether in standalone mode, on a computer system, on a computer network, on a computer resource enabling information creation or providing information processing and storage, or through an intermediary, as constituting for the purposes of this section a single computer or communication device, and references in the section are construed accordingly. Sub-section (4) is the certificate provision: in any proceeding where it is desired to give a statement in evidence by virtue of this section, a certificate doing ANY of the following three things shall be submitted along with the electronic record at each instance where it is being submitted for admission, namely (a) identifying the electronic record containing the statement and describing the manner in which it was produced, (b) giving such particulars of any device involved in the production of that record as may be appropriate for the purpose of showing that it was produced by a computer or a communication device referred to in clauses (a) to (e) of sub-section (3), and (c) dealing with any of the matters to which the conditions mentioned in sub-section (2) relate. The certificate must purport to be signed by a person in charge of the computer or communication device or the management of the relevant activities (whichever is appropriate) AND an expert, that is, two signatories, and it shall be evidence of any matter stated in the certificate; for the purposes of that sub-section it is sufficient for a matter to be stated to the best of the knowledge and belief of the person stating it, in the certificate specified in the Schedule (the form of which is not part of the text supplied here). Sub-section (5) clarifies that information is taken to be supplied to the computer or communication device if it is supplied in any appropriate form, whether directly or, with or without human intervention, by means of any appropriate equipment; and that a computer output is taken to have been produced by the device whether produced by it directly or, with or without human intervention, by means of any appropriate equipment or by other electronic means as referred to in clauses (a) to (e) of sub-section (3).
key_requirements: Sub-section (1) operates notwithstanding anything contained in this Adhiniyam.

Information contained in an electronic record which is printed on paper, stored, recorded or copied in optical or magnetic media or semiconductor memory and produced by a computer or any communication device, or otherwise stored, recorded or copied in any electronic form (the computer output), shall be deemed to be also a document, if the conditions mentioned in this section are satisfied in relation to the information and computer in question.

Such computer output shall be admissible in any proceedings, without further proof or production of the original, as evidence of any contents of the original or of any fact stated therein of which direct evidence would be admissible (the supplied Gazette text reads 'as evidence or any contents of the original', an apparent typographical error for 'as evidence of any contents of the original', and the latter reading is used here).

The computer output containing the information must have been produced by the computer or communication device during the period over which that device was used regularly to create, store or process information for the purposes of any activity regularly carried on over that period by the person having lawful control over its use.

During the said period, information of the kind contained in the electronic record, or of the kind from which the information so contained is derived, must have been regularly fed into the computer or communication device in the ordinary course of the said activities.

Throughout the material part of the said period the computer or communication device must have been operating properly, or, if not, any period in which it was not operating properly or was out of operation during that part of the period must not have been such as to affect the electronic record or the accuracy of its contents.
The information contained in the electronic record must reproduce or be derived from such information fed into the computer or communication device in the ordinary course of the said activities.

Where the function of creating, storing or processing information for the purposes of the activity was regularly performed by means of one or more computers or communication devices, whether in standalone mode, on a computer system, on a computer network, on a computer resource enabling information creation or providing information processing and storage, or through an intermediary, all the computers or communication devices used for that purpose during that period shall be treated for the purposes of this section as constituting a single computer or communication device.

In any proceeding where it is desired to give a statement in evidence by virtue of this section, a certificate doing any of the things listed in clauses (a) to (c) of sub-section (4) shall be submitted along with the electronic record.
The certificate shall be submitted along with the electronic record at each instance where it is being submitted for admission.
Clause (a) of sub-section (4): identifying the electronic record containing the statement and describing the manner in which it was produced.

Clause (b) of sub-section (4): giving such particulars of any device involved in the production of that electronic record as may be appropriate for the purpose of showing that the electronic record was produced by a computer or a communication device referred to in clauses (a) to (e) of sub-section (3).
Clause (c) of sub-section (4): dealing with any of the matters to which the conditions mentioned in sub-section (2) relate.
The certificate must purport to be signed by a person in charge of the computer or communication device or the management of the relevant activities (whichever is appropriate) and an expert.
The certificate shall be evidence of any matter stated in the certificate.
For the purposes of sub-section (4) it shall be sufficient for a matter to be stated to the best of the knowledge and belief of the person stating it in the certificate specified in the Schedule.

Information shall be taken to be supplied to a computer or communication device if it is supplied thereto in any appropriate form and whether it is so supplied directly or (with or without human intervention) by means of any appropriate equipment.

A computer output shall be taken to have been produced by a computer or communication device whether it was produced by it directly or (with or without human intervention) by means of any appropriate equipment or by other electronic means as referred to in clauses (a) to (e) of sub-section (3).
bsa_refs.investigation_relevance: Wherever the IO relies on this section to put computer output in evidence - CDRs, CCTV footage, device extractions, printouts, server logs - the record must travel with a sub-section (4) certificate, and it must go with the record each and every time the record is submitted for admission, not merely once at charge-sheet stage. On the text the certificate is one 'doing any of' three things: identifying the record and describing how it was produced, giving particulars of any device involved, and dealing with any of the matters to which the sub-section (2) conditions relate; the statute requires any of the three, but the safe practice is to cover all three. The certificate must purport to be signed by two people, a person in charge of the computer or communication device or the management of the relevant activities (whichever is appropriate) and an expert, and it is the certificate specified in the Schedule, so the IO should line up both signatories before the record is tendered; a matter may be stated in it to the best of the knowledge and belief of the person stating it. At seizure, therefore, the IO should record the facts the signatories will later have to certify: regular use of the device over the relevant period for the activity, who had lawful control over its use, regular feeding of information of that kind in the ordinary course, and the proper working of the device (or that any malfunction or downtime in the material part of the period did not affect the record or the accuracy of its contents). Note the limits of sub-section (1): where the conditions are met it deems the computer output to be also a document and lets it in without further proof or production of the original, but it does not make the output the original and it settles nothing about the truth or weight of the contents.
time_limits: s.63(2)(a): no fixed number of days is prescribed - the relevant period is the period over which the computer or communication device was used regularly to create, store or process information for the purposes of the activity regularly carried on over that period.

s.63(2)(c): the computer or communication device must have been operating properly 'throughout the material part of the said period', or any period in which it was not operating properly or was out of operation during that part must not have been such as to affect the electronic record or the accuracy of its contents. This qualification belongs to clause (c) alone and does not relax clauses (a), (b) or (d).
s.63(4): the certificate must be submitted along with the electronic record 'at each instance where it is being submitted for admission' - a repeating timing requirement, not a one-time filing.

ordinary course of the said activities.

(3) Where over any period, the function of creating, storing or processing information
for the purposes of any activity regularly carried on over that period as mentioned in
clause (a) of sub-section (2) was regularly performed by means of one or more computers or
communication device, whether—
(a) in standalone mode; or
(b) on a computer system; or
(c) on a computer network; or
(d) on a computer resource enabling information creation or providing information
processing and storage; or
(e) through an intermediary,
all the computers or communication devices used for that purpose during that period shall
be treated for the purposes of this section as constituting a single computer or communication
device;

(4) In any proceeding where it is desired to give a statement in evidence by virtue of
this section, a certificate doing any of the following things shall be submitted along with the
electronic record at each instance where it is being submitted for admission, namely:—

a certificate doing any of the following things shall be submitted along with the
electronic record at each instance where it is being submitted for admission,

(a) identifying the electronic record containing the statement and describing
the manner in which it was produced;

(b) giving such particulars of any device involved in the production of that
electronic record as may be appropriate for the purpose of showing that the electronic
record was produced by a computer or a communication device referred to in clauses (a)
to (e) of sub-section (3);

(c) dealing with any of the matters to which the conditions mentioned in
sub-section (2) relate,

and purporting to be signed by a person in charge of the computer or communication
device or the management of the relevant activities (whichever is appropriate) and an expert
shall be evidence of any matter stated in the certificate

for the purposes of this
sub-section it shall be sufficient for a matter to be stated to the best of the knowledge and
belief of the person stating it in the certificate specified in the Schedule.

(a) information shall be taken to be supplied to a computer or communication
device if it is supplied thereto in any appropriate form and whether it is so supplied
directly or (with or without human intervention) by means of any appropriate
equipment;

(b) a computer output shall be taken to have been produced by a computer or
communication device whether it was produced by it directly or (with or without
human intervention) by means of any appropriate equipment or by other electronic
means as referred to in clauses (a) to (e) of sub-section (3).
