bsa_refs.title: Evidence as to affairs of State
bsa_refs.summary: Evidence as to affairs of State. The section bars one class of evidence unless permission is given: no one shall be permitted to give any evidence derived from unpublished official records relating to any affairs of State, except with the permission of the officer at the head of the department concerned. That officer shall give or withhold such permission as he thinks fit. The section lays down no criteria for that decision, prescribes no form for the permission, fixes no time within which it must be made, and states no procedure for challenging a refusal. It is a single sentence with no sub-sections.
key_requirements: No one shall be permitted to give any evidence derived from unpublished official records relating to any affairs of State except with permission.
The permission must be that of the officer at the head of the department concerned.
The head of the department shall give or withhold such permission as he thinks fit.
bsa_refs.investigation_relevance: Where an investigation touches unpublished official records relating to affairs of State, the permission of the officer at the head of the department concerned must be obtained before any evidence derived from those records is given, and the bar applies to anyone giving such evidence, the IO included. The IO should therefore apply for the permission early and place it on the case record alongside the material. That officer gives or withholds the permission as he thinks fit, and the section fixes no time frame for the decision and no procedure for challenging a refusal, so the IO should not build a case that rests solely on such records.
supporting_text: No one shall be permitted to give any evidence derived from unpublished official
except with the permission of the officer at the head
who shall give or withhold such permission as he thinks fit.

bsa_refs.title: Official communications
bsa_refs.summary: The section protects communications made to a public officer in official confidence. Such an officer shall not be compelled to disclose them, but the protection operates only when that officer himself considers that the public interests would suffer by the disclosure. The privilege is therefore personal to the public officer and hinges on his own assessment of harm to public interest. The section is a bar on compulsion only; it does not on its face prohibit voluntary disclosure and it names no approving authority, no form and no period.
key_requirements: No public officer shall be compelled to disclose communications made to him in official confidence.
The protection applies when the public officer considers that the public interests would suffer by the disclosure.
bsa_refs.investigation_relevance: An IO cannot compel a public officer to hand over or speak to a communication received in official confidence where that officer takes the view that disclosure would harm the public interest, so such material should be sought by request and the officer's stated position recorded rather than forced. An IO is himself a public officer, so where he is asked in court to reveal a communication received in official confidence he may claim the same protection if he considers disclosure would injure the public interest.

when he considers that the public interests would suffer by the disclosure.

details.text: Do not search a house or dwelling unit unless there are definite reasons to believe that certain specific things or documents required for the investigation will be found there; keep the number of places to be searched at the bare minimum.
details.citation: Kerala Police - Standard Operating Procedure: Investigation & Prosecution in General (SOP Series), State Police Chief, 01.11.2020

details.text: The law does not require that searches be made by daylight only, but avoid searches after dark as far as possible; where a night search is necessary it may be necessary to take precautions to ensure that the articles of evidentiary value for which the search is made are not discharged or tampered with (as printed).
details.citation: Kerala Police - Standard Operating Procedure: Investigation & Prosecution in General (SOP Series), State Police Chief, 01.11.2020

Confine the search to places within the limits of your own police station.

steps.text: Treat search as an effective tool of investigation while recognising that it is a serious invasion of the liberty of a person. Conduct every search either under a warrant issued by a competent court (searches under Sections 93, 94, 95 and 97 CrPC as printed [now Sections 96, 97, 98 and 100 BNSS]) or, without warrant, only as authorised by the Code or a special Act (Sections 103, 165 and 166 CrPC as printed; for police searches during investigation, Sections 165 and 166 [now Sections 185 and 186 BNSS]). In all circumstances follow the general search provisions (Section 100 CrPC [now Section 103 BNSS]) together with the police-search provision (Section 165 CrPC [now Section 185 BNSS]).

details.text: Searches may be conducted before or after registration of the First Information Report; after the arrest of the accused; after confession; to collect evidence during investigation; on the orders of the Court; or for the maintenance of public peace and order.
details.citation: Kerala Police - Standard Operating Procedure: Investigation & Prosecution in General (SOP Series), State Police Chief, 01.11.2020

details.text: Objects of a search: (a) arrest of a person concealing his presence; (b) recovery of property from arrested offenders to connect them with the offence, or of a weapon; (c) obtaining an article or thing wanted in a case; (d) a person wrongfully confined or missing; (e) discovery of firearms, explosives or other material for prevention and detection of crimes; (f) clues and evidence needed for the investigation.
details.citation: Kerala Police - Standard Operating Procedure: Investigation & Prosecution in General (SOP Series), State Police Chief, 01.11.2020

details.text: Certain special and local Acts, such as the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985, prescribe separate search-and-seizure procedures which the IO must follow in those cases.
details.citation: Kerala Police - Standard Operating Procedure: Investigation & Prosecution in General (SOP Series), State Police Chief, 01.11.2020

details.text: Carry out searches always in strict conformity with law; fully comply with the provisions of Sections 94, 165, 166, 100, 101, 102 and 103 CrPC (as printed in the source).

details.text: Any police officer who seizes property, detains a person in custody, conducts a search or arrests a person illegally, for causing annoyance and without reasonable cause, commits a punishable offence (Section 116, Kerala Police Act, as printed — a state provision cited for the principle).

This applies to every Chapter VII BNSS search/seizure and every Section 185 BNSS investigation search.

conflicts.description: bnss_2023 BNSS 105 (and guj_cid_29_sops_2024 SOP 9 p.36, and bprd_av_recording_sop bprd-av-legal-framework p.11) require forwarding 'without delay'; bprd_av_recording_sop (bprd-av-recording-procedures p.60) sets an outer limit of 'without delay, but not later than 48 hours'.
conflicts.resolution: The law's 'without delay' is the canonical requirement; the 48-hour figure is retained only as the national-advisory administrative outer bound and cannot dilute the statutory standard.

conflicts.description: tripura_sop_bundle (tripura-ndps, p.1) treats videography of the search and seizure as discretionary ('Preferably videograph the entire process of search and seizure'), while bnss_2023 BNSS 105 and delhi_compendium_2024 (Scenario 18, p.164) treat it as mandatory.
conflicts.resolution: The law layer governs: recording is mandatory under BNSS 105. The Tripura 'preferably' reflects the pre-BNSS position and is retained only as a lower-authority variant; it does not reduce the obligation.

steps.text: The general search provisions of Section 103 BNSS — independent witnesses, the search list and the rest — apply to every search made under Section 185 BNSS. Accordingly, before searching, call two or more independent and respectable inhabitants of the locality in which the place to be searched is situated (or of any other locality if an inhabitant of that locality is unavailable or unwilling) to attend and witness the search, and issue them a written order to do so if needed (the two-witness rule and the written order as printed in the state SOP under Section 100(4) CrPC [now BNSS 103(4)]).

details.text: Apply the general provisions of Section 100 CrPC [now BNSS 103] to every search made under Section 165 CrPC [now BNSS 185], and conduct house searches according to that procedure.

details.text: Non-compliance with the written order to witness a search amounts to an offence under Section 187 IPC, as provided under Section 100(8) CrPC (as printed [s.100(8) now BNSS 103(8)]).

details.text: Insist on the witnesses being present throughout the search; when an article or document is discovered, draw the witnesses' attention to all the circumstances relating to it.

details.text: While conducting searches in a computerized environment, prefer computer-literate witnesses.

steps.title: Search Thoroughly and Seize Before the Witnesses
steps.triage_why: General investigative diligence to ensure no evidence is missed.

steps.text: Ensure the legal rights of the person whose premises are searched are respected, since any violation may affect the search adversely. The occupant has the right: (a) to see the warrant of authorization duly signed and sealed by the issuing authority; (b) to verify the identity of each member of the search party; (c) to have at least two respectable and independent residents of the locality as witnesses; (d) to have a personal search of all members of the search party before commencement and at conclusion of the search; (e) to ensure that a personal search of females is carried out by another female only, with strict regard to decency; (f) to have a copy of the search list together with all annexures, for which acknowledgment should be given; (g) to call a medical practitioner if required; and (h) to have the facility of having meals etc. at the normal time.

details.text: Give no unauthorized press publicity about searches; issue strict instructions to members of the raiding party not to divulge any information about searches to unauthorized persons.

Prepare it on the spot during the search, in the prescribed search-list form, indicating the proceedings of the search and the documents and articles seized, and give a copy to the occupant of the premises under acknowledgement.

steps.text: While drawing up the search/seizure memo, record every element needed to prove the recovery: the name, occupation, age and address of each witness; the time, date and place of start of the proceedings; the reason for the search and the authority for it; a graphic description of the search operation in simple plain language (who opened the suitcase, who had the key, from where the incriminating documents or contraband were recovered and how they were concealed); and the date and time of conclusion of the search, recorded before leaving the place of search.
steps.responsible: Investigating Officer / officer writing the memo

details.text: Record the offer of personal search of each member of the search party.
details.citation: Kerala Police - Standard Operating Procedure: Investigation & Prosecution in General (SOP Series), State Police Chief, 01.11.2020

details.text: Before conducting a personal search, ask the person whether he would like to be taken before a gazetted officer, and record the factual position in the memo.
details.citation: Kerala Police - Standard Operating Procedure: Investigation & Prosecution in General (SOP Series), State Police Chief, 01.11.2020

details.text: Incorporate in the memo the presence of the occupants of the premises/person to be searched and, if necessary, identification evidence.
details.citation: Kerala Police - Standard Operating Procedure: Investigation & Prosecution in General (SOP Series), State Police Chief, 01.11.2020

details.text: Mention the description of the place to be searched, e.g. area of flat, number of rooms, telephone number etc.
details.citation: Kerala Police - Standard Operating Procedure: Investigation & Prosecution in General (SOP Series), State Police Chief, 01.11.2020

details.text: Ask the person to be searched to give a declaration of his baggage wherever necessary, e.g. whether he is carrying any contraband.
details.citation: Kerala Police - Standard Operating Procedure: Investigation & Prosecution in General (SOP Series), State Police Chief, 01.11.2020

details.text: Mention where and how the weighing of contraband goods was done, giving gross weight and net weight; mention the value of the contraband to be seized; and mention the number of samples drawn with their weight and identification marks.
details.citation: Kerala Police - Standard Operating Procedure: Investigation & Prosecution in General (SOP Series), State Police Chief, 01.11.2020

details.text: Indicate the location from which the contraband exhibits, samples and documents proposed to be seized/taken over were recovered.
details.citation: Kerala Police - Standard Operating Procedure: Investigation & Prosecution in General (SOP Series), State Police Chief, 01.11.2020

details.text: Indicate in the memo that nothing was taken over other than what has been recorded in the memo, that no damage to property or person was done, and that the entire search proceeding was carried out in a peaceful manner (unless the facts are otherwise).
details.citation: Kerala Police - Standard Operating Procedure: Investigation & Prosecution in General (SOP Series), State Police Chief, 01.11.2020

details.text: Seal the exhibits and contraband, mentioning the seal number, and take an impression of the seal on the memo; take signatures of the witnesses, the officer writing the memo and the person being searched on labels pasted on contraband, exhibits and documents.
details.citation: Kerala Police - Standard Operating Procedure: Investigation & Prosecution in General (SOP Series), State Police Chief, 01.11.2020

details.text: Give a copy of the memo/search list to the person whose premises were searched and obtain his receipt with date and time; to ensure proper identification, mention the complete description of the property seized in the memo.
details.citation: Kerala Police - Standard Operating Procedure: Investigation & Prosecution in General (SOP Series), State Police Chief, 01.11.2020

details.text: For recovery from or seizure of a vehicle: mention its registration number, colour, engine number, chassis number and model; if any part such as wheels, battery or lights is missing, note it in the memo.
details.citation: Kerala Police - Standard Operating Procedure: Investigation & Prosecution in General (SOP Series), State Police Chief, 01.11.2020

details.text: For firearms: mention the make (country made or foreign make), number and any specific writings inscribed on it; prepare a sketch of the recovered arms at the spot and mention in the memo that the sketch has been prepared; seal the arms and mention the mark of the seal in the seizure memo itself.
details.citation: Kerala Police - Standard Operating Procedure: Investigation & Prosecution in General (SOP Series), State Police Chief, 01.11.2020

details.text: For arms like knives, mention complete details in the memo, i.e. the length and breadth of the blade and of the handle.
details.citation: Kerala Police - Standard Operating Procedure: Investigation & Prosecution in General (SOP Series), State Police Chief, 01.11.2020

details.text: For stolen property such as ornaments and watches, mention special marks of identification and weight; mention special identification marks on articles including cloth, and if an article is used, torn or worn out, record that in the memo.
details.citation: Kerala Police - Standard Operating Procedure: Investigation & Prosecution in General (SOP Series), State Police Chief, 01.11.2020

details.text: For recoveries made from a field (a pit) etc., mention the depth dug up; the spot may be photographed and mention of this made in the recovery/seizure memo. For animals recovered, mention their complete description including any deformity.
details.citation: Kerala Police - Standard Operating Procedure: Investigation & Prosecution in General (SOP Series), State Police Chief, 01.11.2020

details.text: For currency notes recovered in trap cases registered under Section 5(ii) of the Prevention of Corruption Act (as printed), mention the number, denomination and serial numbers of the notes.
details.citation: Kerala Police - Standard Operating Procedure: Investigation & Prosecution in General (SOP Series), State Police Chief, 01.11.2020

details.text: Where property is sealed for purposes of identification, record in the memo the handing over of the seal to one of the witnesses of the recovery/seizure, and refer to it in that witness's statement recorded under Section 161 CrPC [now BNSS 180].
details.citation: Kerala Police - Standard Operating Procedure: Investigation & Prosecution in General (SOP Series), State Police Chief, 01.11.2020

bsa_refs.title: Confession to police officer
bsa_refs.summary: Bars proof of confessions connected with the police. Sub-section (1) provides that no confession made to a police officer shall be proved as against a person accused of any offence; the sub-section itself contains no 'unless' and no reference to a Magistrate. Sub-section (2) separately provides that no confession made by any person while he is in the custody of a police officer, unless it is made in the immediate presence of a Magistrate, shall be proved against him; that immediate-presence exception sits inside sub-section (2) and relieves only the custody bar. The proviso to sub-section (2) creates the discovery exception: when any fact is deposed to as discovered in consequence of information received from a person accused of any offence, in the custody of a police officer, so much of that information, whether it amounts to a confession or not, as relates distinctly to the fact discovered may be proved. That permission is worded 'may be proved' - it permits proof of that portion, it does not require it. Both sub-sections bar only confessions.
key_requirements: Sub-section (1): no confession made to a police officer shall be proved as against a person accused of any offence; the sub-section itself states this without any unless or exception and makes no reference to a Magistrate.
Sub-section (2): no confession made by any person while he is in the custody of a police officer shall be proved against him.

The immediate presence of a Magistrate is an exception carried within sub-section (2) and relieves only the custody bar; a confession made in the immediate presence of a Magistrate is outside that bar.

The proviso reaches only information received from a person accused of any offence who is in the custody of a police officer, and only where a fact is deposed to as discovered in consequence of that information.

Where those conditions are met, so much of that information, whether it amounts to a confession or not, as relates distinctly to the fact discovered may be proved; the proviso permits proof of that portion, it does not direct that it be proved.
bsa_refs.investigation_relevance: Subject to the discovery proviso, the IO cannot prove a confession made to him; and a confession made by a person while he is in the custody of a police officer cannot be proved against him unless it was made in the immediate presence of a Magistrate. The bar is confined to confessions, so this section does not by itself exclude statements of the accused that are not confessional, though other law may restrict their use. Sub-section (1) carries no Magistrate exception: the immediate-presence exception sits inside sub-section (2) and relieves only the custody bar, so what it saves is a confession made in a Magistrate's immediate presence by a person in police custody, not a confession made to a police officer. Subject to the discovery proviso, a confession made to a police officer cannot be proved against the accused. The other route on the text is the discovery proviso, which is available only where the information came from a person accused of an offence who was in the custody of a police officer, and only where a fact is deposed to as discovered in consequence of that information; the IO must record the information, effect the recovery, have the discovery deposed to, and confine the portion sought to be proved to so much of the information as relates distinctly to the fact actually discovered. Even then the proviso only permits that portion to be proved.

steps.text: Whenever electronic records are to be produced as evidence in a legal proceeding, produce with them the certificate under Section 63(4)(c) of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam: Part-A (Annexure-1) signed by the person/party having charge of the computer or communication device, or by the person managing the activities concerned, and Part-B (Annexure-2) signed by the expert — each identifying the device and stating the hash value with its algorithm. Where Section 63 BSA has been complied with, electronic or digital records have the very same legal effect and enforceability as any other documents and are admissible without further proof or production of the original.
steps.responsible: Investigating Officer; person having lawful charge of the device (Part-A); Expert (Part-B)
steps.applies_when: Electronic records (in particular secondary computer output) are to be produced in evidence

details.text: Admissibility [s.63(1) BSA]: information in an electronic record generated by a computer or other communication means, or stored/recorded/copied in electronic form, printed on paper, or stored/noted/copied in optical or magnetic media or semiconductor memory ('computer output'), shall be treated as a document and, if the Section 63 conditions are satisfied, is admissible as evidence without any further proof or production of the original.
details.citation: Twenty-Nine Standard Operating Procedures - C.I.D. Crime & Railways, Gujarat Police, circular PRC/Circular-SOP-1/656/2024 dated 29/10/2024

details.text: Condition (a) [s.63(2) BSA]: the computer output containing the information was produced during the period in which the computer/communication means was regularly used for creating, storing or processing information for the purposes of regularly carrying on activities by a person having lawful control over its use.
details.citation: Twenty-Nine Standard Operating Procedures - C.I.D. Crime & Railways, Gujarat Police, circular PRC/Circular-SOP-1/656/2024 dated 29/10/2024

details.text: Conditions (b)-(d) [s.63(2) BSA]: during that period, information of the kind contained in the electronic record (or of the kind from which it is derived) was regularly fed into the computer in the ordinary course of the said activities; during the material part of that period the computer was operating properly, or any malfunction was not such as to affect the electronic records or the accuracy of their particulars; and the information contained in the electronic records is derived from information fed in in the ordinary course.
details.citation: Twenty-Nine Standard Operating Procedures - C.I.D. Crime & Railways, Gujarat Police, circular PRC/Circular-SOP-1/656/2024 dated 29/10/2024

details.text: Multiple computers [s.63(3) BSA]: where more than one computer or communication means was used for creating, storing or processing the information — whether working independently, over a network or through an intermediary medium — they shall all be treated as one larger system and counted as one unit.
details.citation: Twenty-Nine Standard Operating Procedures - C.I.D. Crime & Railways, Gujarat Police, circular PRC/Circular-SOP-1/656/2024 dated 29/10/2024

details.text: Input and output [s.63(5) BSA]: information can be sent into and received from a computer in various forms, directly or indirectly, with or without human intervention, using appropriate equipment; it is not necessary that the computer output be produced directly or only by appropriate equipment.
details.citation: Twenty-Nine Standard Operating Procedures - C.I.D. Crime & Railways, Gujarat Police, circular PRC/Circular-SOP-1/656/2024 dated 29/10/2024

details.text: Section 63(4)(c) BSA 2023 reproduces, with certain modifications, the provision corresponding to Section 65B of the Indian Evidence Act.
details.citation: Twenty-Nine Standard Operating Procedures - C.I.D. Crime & Railways, Gujarat Police, circular PRC/Circular-SOP-1/656/2024 dated 29/10/2024

details.text: Annexure-1 (Part-A) is filled and signed on solemn oath by the party having lawful control of the device: it identifies the device/source (computer/storage media, DVR, mobile, flash drive, CD/DVD, server, cloud, other), brand, model, colour, serial number, IMEI/UIN/UID/MAC/Cloud ID, ownership/maintenance/management/operation status and the proper-functioning declaration, plus the hash value with algorithm (SHA-1/SHA-256/MD5/other legally acceptable standard), with date, time (24-hour format) and place. bsa_refs.title: Admissibility of electronic records
bsa_refs.summary: This is the operative provision for proving electronic records. Operating notwithstanding anything contained in this Adhiniyam, sub-section (1) deems any information contained in an electronic record which is printed on paper, stored, recorded or copied in optical or magnetic media or semiconductor memory and produced by a computer or any communication device, or otherwise stored, recorded or copied in any electronic form (the 'computer output'), to be also a document, if the conditions mentioned in this section are satisfied in relation to the information and computer in question, and makes that output admissible in any proceedings, without further proof or production of the original, as evidence of any contents of the original or of any fact stated therein of which direct evidence would be admissible. What sub-section (1) deems is that the computer output is ALSO a document: it does not deem the output to be the original, and it settles nothing about the truth or the weight of what the record contains. Both the deeming and the admissibility are conditional on the section's conditions being satisfied. (The supplied Gazette text reads 'as evidence or any contents of the original'; that is an apparent typographical error for 'as evidence of any contents of the original', and the latter reading is used here.) Sub-section (2) lays down the four conditions in clauses (a) to (d): production of the output by the computer or communication device during the period over which it was used regularly to create, store or process information for the purposes of any activity regularly carried on over that period by the person having lawful control over its use; regular feeding into the device, in the ordinary course of those activities, of information of the kind contained in the record or of the kind from which it is derived; the device operating properly throughout the material part of that period, or any period in which it was not operating properly or was out of operation during that part not being such as to affect the electronic record or the accuracy of its contents; and the information in the record reproducing or being derived from such information fed in. Sub-section (3) treats all the computers or communication devices used for that purpose during that period, whether in standalone mode, on a computer system, on a computer network, on a computer resource enabling information creation or providing information processing and storage, or through an intermediary, as constituting for the purposes of this section a single computer or communication device, and references in the section are construed accordingly. Sub-section (4) is the certificate provision: in any proceeding where it is desired to give a statement in evidence by virtue of this section, a certificate doing ANY of the following three things shall be submitted along with the electronic record at each instance where it is being submitted for admission, namely (a) identifying the electronic record containing the statement and describing the manner in which it was produced, (b) giving such particulars of any device involved in the production of that record as may be appropriate for the purpose of showing that it was produced by a computer or a communication device referred to in clauses (a) to (e) of sub-section (3), and (c) dealing with any of the matters to which the conditions mentioned in sub-section (2) relate. The certificate must purport to be signed by a person in charge of the computer or communication device or the management of the relevant activities (whichever is appropriate) AND an expert, that is, two signatories, and it shall be evidence of any matter stated in the certificate; for the purposes of that sub-section it is sufficient for a matter to be stated to the best of the knowledge and belief of the person stating it, in the certificate specified in the Schedule (the form of which is not part of the text supplied here). Sub-section (5) clarifies that information is taken to be supplied to the computer or communication device if it is supplied in any appropriate form, whether directly or, with or without human intervention, by means of any appropriate equipment; and that a computer output is taken to have been produced by the device whether produced by it directly or, with or without human intervention, by means of any appropriate equipment or by other electronic means as referred to in clauses (a) to (e) of sub-section (3).
key_requirements: Sub-section (1) operates notwithstanding anything contained in this Adhiniyam.

Information contained in an electronic record which is printed on paper, stored, recorded or copied in optical or magnetic media or semiconductor memory and produced by a computer or any communication device, or otherwise stored, recorded or copied in any electronic form (the computer output), shall be deemed to be also a document, if the conditions mentioned in this section are satisfied in relation to the information and computer in question.

Such computer output shall be admissible in any proceedings, without further proof or production of the original, as evidence of any contents of the original or of any fact stated therein of which direct evidence would be admissible (the supplied Gazette text reads 'as evidence or any contents of the original', an apparent typographical error for 'as evidence of any contents of the original', and the latter reading is used here).

The computer output containing the information must have been produced by the computer or communication device during the period over which that device was used regularly to create, store or process information for the purposes of any activity regularly carried on over that period by the person having lawful control over its use.

During the said period, information of the kind contained in the electronic record, or of the kind from which the information so contained is derived, must have been regularly fed into the computer or communication device in the ordinary course of the said activities.

Throughout the material part of the said period the computer or communication device must have been operating properly, or, if not, any period in which it was not operating properly or was out of operation during that part of the period must not have been such as to affect the electronic record or the accuracy of its contents.
The information contained in the electronic record must reproduce or be derived from such information fed into the computer or communication device in the ordinary course of the said activities.

Where the function of creating, storing or processing information for the purposes of the activity was regularly performed by means of one or more computers or communication devices, whether in standalone mode, on a computer system, on a computer network, on a computer resource enabling information creation or providing information processing and storage, or through an intermediary, all the computers or communication devices used for that purpose during that period shall be treated for the purposes of this section as constituting a single computer or communication device.

In any proceeding where it is desired to give a statement in evidence by virtue of this section, a certificate doing any of the things listed in clauses (a) to (c) of sub-section (4) shall be submitted along with the electronic record.
The certificate shall be submitted along with the electronic record at each instance where it is being submitted for admission.
Clause (a) of sub-section (4): identifying the electronic record containing the statement and describing the manner in which it was produced.

Clause (b) of sub-section (4): giving such particulars of any device involved in the production of that electronic record as may be appropriate for the purpose of showing that the electronic record was produced by a computer or a communication device referred to in clauses (a) to (e) of sub-section (3).
Clause (c) of sub-section (4): dealing with any of the matters to which the conditions mentioned in sub-section (2) relate.
The certificate must purport to be signed by a person in charge of the computer or communication device or the management of the relevant activities (whichever is appropriate) and an expert.
The certificate shall be evidence of any matter stated in the certificate.
For the purposes of sub-section (4) it shall be sufficient for a matter to be stated to the best of the knowledge and belief of the person stating it in the certificate specified in the Schedule.

Information shall be taken to be supplied to a computer or communication device if it is supplied thereto in any appropriate form and whether it is so supplied directly or (with or without human intervention) by means of any appropriate equipment.

A computer output shall be taken to have been produced by a computer or communication device whether it was produced by it directly or (with or without human intervention) by means of any appropriate equipment or by other electronic means as referred to in clauses (a) to (e) of sub-section (3).
bsa_refs.investigation_relevance: Wherever the IO relies on this section to put computer output in evidence - CDRs, CCTV footage, device extractions, printouts, server logs - the record must travel with a sub-section (4) certificate, and it must go with the record each and every time the record is submitted for admission, not merely once at charge-sheet stage. On the text the certificate is one 'doing any of' three things: identifying the record and describing how it was produced, giving particulars of any device involved, and dealing with any of the matters to which the sub-section (2) conditions relate; the statute requires any of the three, but the safe practice is to cover all three. The certificate must purport to be signed by two people, a person in charge of the computer or communication device or the management of the relevant activities (whichever is appropriate) and an expert, and it is the certificate specified in the Schedule, so the IO should line up both signatories before the record is tendered; a matter may be stated in it to the best of the knowledge and belief of the person stating it. At seizure, therefore, the IO should record the facts the signatories will later have to certify: regular use of the device over the relevant period for the activity, who had lawful control over its use, regular feeding of information of that kind in the ordinary course, and the proper working of the device (or that any malfunction or downtime in the material part of the period did not affect the record or the accuracy of its contents). Note the limits of sub-section (1): where the conditions are met it deems the computer output to be also a document and lets it in without further proof or production of the original, but it does not make the output the original and it settles nothing about the truth or weight of the contents.
time_limits: s.63(2)(a): no fixed number of days is prescribed - the relevant period is the period over which the computer or communication device was used regularly to create, store or process information for the purposes of the activity regularly carried on over that period.

s.63(2)(c): the computer or communication device must have been operating properly 'throughout the material part of the said period', or any period in which it was not operating properly or was out of operation during that part must not have been such as to affect the electronic record or the accuracy of its contents. This qualification belongs to clause (c) alone and does not relax clauses (a), (b) or (d).
s.63(4): the certificate must be submitted along with the electronic record 'at each instance where it is being submitted for admission' - a repeating timing requirement, not a one-time filing.

bsa_refs.title: Proof of signature and handwriting of person alleged to have signed or written document produced
bsa_refs.summary: This section states the proof rule for a document said to bear a person's signature or handwriting. Where a document is alleged to be signed by, or to have been written wholly or in part by, any person, the signature or the handwriting of so much of the document as is alleged to be in that person's handwriting must be proved to be in his handwriting. The obligation is mandatory, and it is limited to the portion alleged to be that person's: nothing beyond that portion has to be proved under this section. The section does not itself prescribe the manner in which that proof is to be given, and it names no act to be done by any investigating officer; it operates as a rule of proof on whoever tenders the document and on the Court in receiving it.
key_requirements: If a document is alleged to be signed or to have been written wholly or in part by any person, the signature or the handwriting must be proved to be in his handwriting.
The proof requirement extends only to so much of the document as is alleged to be in that person's handwriting.
bsa_refs.investigation_relevance: Whenever the case rests on a signed or handwritten document - a disputed cheque, a receipt, a threat letter, a register entry, a signed agreement - the IO must build the material that will later establish the signature or handwriting as that person's, because the document does not prove itself. Note the limit: only the part alleged to be in that person's hand needs proving, so the IO should identify precisely which words, entries or signature are attributed to the accused or witness. The section itself prescribes no mode of proof and no step for the IO; nothing about specimen writings, comparison or expert opinion appears in this text, so any such step must be sourced from another provision and not from this one.

steps.text: At the time of seizure, obtain the hash value of the electronic records and make a note of it in the case diary, so that the reliability of the information is preserved. Computing the hash value of electronic records is compulsory, and mentioning the hash value in the certificate under Section 63 of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam is compulsory.
legal_basis: BSA 63
steps.applies_when: Electronic records/digital devices are seized

details.text: Make a forensic image and verify all the digital information by its hash value.
details.citation: State Forensic Science Laboratory UP / Technical Services HQ, Lucknow - A Collection of Standard Operating Procedures for Crime Scene Investigation (pictorial, BNSS/BSA era) - TRANSLATED FROM HINDI

details.text: Use write blockers so that there is no change in the original form of the evidence, and keep the digital information obtained in its original form secure.
details.citation: State Forensic Science Laboratory UP / Technical Services HQ, Lucknow - A Collection of Standard Operating Procedures for Crime Scene Investigation (pictorial, BNSS/BSA era) - TRANSLATED FROM HINDI

details.text: Note the make of the CD (and similar media) along with its serial number.
details.citation: State Forensic Science Laboratory UP / Technical Services HQ, Lucknow - A Collection of Standard Operating Procedures for Crime Scene Investigation (pictorial, BNSS/BSA era) - TRANSLATED FROM HINDI

details.text: Effect the authentication of the electronic record by the use of an asymmetric crypto system and hash function which envelope and transform the initial electronic record into another electronic record, using the most widely used hash functions in tune with international standards - SHA (Secure Hash Algorithm) and MD5 (Message Digest); the SHA-1 hash function is a set of cryptographic hash functions designed by the National Security Agency (NSA), USA, and in India the Centre for Development of Advanced Computing (CDAC) has developed a similar system which can be used after due evaluation.
details.citation: LNJN National Institute of Criminology and Forensic Science, MHA - A Forensic Guide for Crime Investigators: Standard Operating Procedures (marked Restricted)

details.text: Calculate the first hash result at the time of the acquisition of the conversation recorded in the recording device, before the witnesses, using commercially available or open source software such as SHA-1 or MD5, and document the computed hash result.

bsa_refs.title: Admissibility of electronic records
bsa_refs.summary: This is the operative provision for proving electronic records. Operating notwithstanding anything contained in this Adhiniyam, sub-section (1) deems any information contained in an electronic record which is printed on paper, stored, recorded or copied in optical or magnetic media or semiconductor memory and produced by a computer or any communication device, or otherwise stored, recorded or copied in any electronic form (the 'computer output'), to be also a document, if the conditions mentioned in this section are satisfied in relation to the information and computer in question, and makes that output admissible in any proceedings, without further proof or production of the original, as evidence of any contents of the original or of any fact stated therein of which direct evidence would be admissible. What sub-section (1) deems is that the computer output is ALSO a document: it does not deem the output to be the original, and it settles nothing about the truth or the weight of what the record contains. Both the deeming and the admissibility are conditional on the section's conditions being satisfied. (The supplied Gazette text reads 'as evidence or any contents of the original'; that is an apparent typographical error for 'as evidence of any contents of the original', and the latter reading is used here.) Sub-section (2) lays down the four conditions in clauses (a) to (d): production of the output by the computer or communication device during the period over which it was used regularly to create, store or process information for the purposes of any activity regularly carried on over that period by the person having lawful control over its use; regular feeding into the device, in the ordinary course of those activities, of information of the kind contained in the record or of the kind from which it is derived; the device operating properly throughout the material part of that period, or any period in which it was not operating properly or was out of operation during that part not being such as to affect the electronic record or the accuracy of its contents; and the information in the record reproducing or being derived from such information fed in. Sub-section (3) treats all the computers or communication devices used for that purpose during that period, whether in standalone mode, on a computer system, on a computer network, on a computer resource enabling information creation or providing information processing and storage, or through an intermediary, as constituting for the purposes of this section a single computer or communication device, and references in the section are construed accordingly. Sub-section (4) is the certificate provision: in any proceeding where it is desired to give a statement in evidence by virtue of this section, a certificate doing ANY of the following three things shall be submitted along with the electronic record at each instance where it is being submitted for admission, namely (a) identifying the electronic record containing the statement and describing the manner in which it was produced, (b) giving such particulars of any device involved in the production of that record as may be appropriate for the purpose of showing that it was produced by a computer or a communication device referred to in clauses (a) to (e) of sub-section (3), and (c) dealing with any of the matters to which the conditions mentioned in sub-section (2) relate. The certificate must purport to be signed by a person in charge of the computer or communication device or the management of the relevant activities (whichever is appropriate) AND an expert, that is, two signatories, and it shall be evidence of any matter stated in the certificate; for the purposes of that sub-section it is sufficient for a matter to be stated to the best of the knowledge and belief of the person stating it, in the certificate specified in the Schedule (the form of which is not part of the text supplied here). Sub-section (5) clarifies that information is taken to be supplied to the computer or communication device if it is supplied in any appropriate form, whether directly or, with or without human intervention, by means of any appropriate equipment; and that a computer output is taken to have been produced by the device whether produced by it directly or, with or without human intervention, by means of any appropriate equipment or by other electronic means as referred to in clauses (a) to (e) of sub-section (3).

steps.text: Classify every electronic record before production: where the very device in which the electronic record was generated (e.g., the DVR/NVR machine connected to the CCTV camera) is itself produced before the Court, treat its output as primary evidence (Section 57 BSA); where a copy of the computer output, or a copy of any part of it, is collected and produced before the Court (e.g., CCTV footage in a DVR/NVR copied onto a CD/DVD, pen drive or hard disk), treat it as secondary evidence (Section 58 BSA), which requires the Section 63 BSA certificate.

bsa_refs.title: Primary evidence
bsa_refs.summary: Section 57 defines primary evidence as the document itself produced for the inspection of the Court, and then extends that definition through seven Explanations. Explanation 1 makes each part of a document executed in several parts primary evidence of the document. Explanation 2 makes each counterpart, executed by one or some of the parties only, primary evidence as against the parties executing it. Explanation 3 applies only where a number of documents are all made by one uniform process, as in the case of printing, lithography or photography: each is then primary evidence of the contents of the rest, but where they are all copies of a common original they are not primary evidence of the contents of the original. Explanations 4 to 7 carry the definition into electronic material: where an electronic or digital record is created or stored and that storage occurs simultaneously or sequentially in multiple files, each such file is primary evidence (Explanation 4); an electronic or digital record produced from proper custody is primary evidence unless it is disputed (Explanation 5); where a video recording is simultaneously stored in electronic form and transmitted or broadcast or transferred to another, each of the stored recordings is primary evidence (Explanation 6); and where an electronic or digital record is stored in multiple storage spaces in a computer resource, each such automated storage, including temporary files, is primary evidence (Explanation 7). An Illustration applies Explanation 3 to placards all printed at one time from one original. The section says what counts as primary evidence; it does not say that contents can be proved only in that way, and the 'unless it is disputed' qualification belongs to Explanation 5 alone.
key_requirements: Primary evidence means the document itself produced for the inspection of the Court.
Where a document is executed in several parts, each part is primary evidence of the document.
Where a document is executed in counterpart, each counterpart executed by one or some of the parties only is primary evidence as against the parties executing it.
Where a number of documents are all made by one uniform process, as in printing, lithography or photography, each is primary evidence of the contents of the rest.
Where such documents are all copies of a common original, they are not primary evidence of the contents of the original.
Where an electronic or digital record is created or stored and that storage occurs simultaneously or sequentially in multiple files, each such file is primary evidence.
Where an electronic or digital record is produced from proper custody, it is primary evidence unless it is disputed.
Where a video recording is simultaneously stored in electronic form and transmitted or broadcast or transferred to another, each of the stored recordings is primary evidence.
Where an electronic or digital record is stored in multiple storage spaces in a computer resource, each such automated storage, including temporary files, is primary evidence.
bsa_refs.investigation_relevance: The IO should seize and produce the document or the device itself wherever that is possible, and should record custody carefully, because under Explanation 5 an electronic or digital record produced from proper custody is primary evidence unless it is disputed. Under Explanations 4 and 7, where an electronic or digital record is created or stored and that storage occurs simultaneously or sequentially in multiple files, or where the record is stored in multiple storage spaces in a computer resource, each such file and each such automated storage, including temporary files, is primary evidence. Explanation 6 is narrower and both of its conditions must be met: it covers a video recording simultaneously stored in electronic form and transmitted or broadcast or transferred to another, and it is each of those stored recordings that is primary evidence; a recording copied afterwards from a stored file is not within Explanation 6, whatever its position under the other Explanations may be. The seizure memo and forwarding note should therefore identify exactly which file, device or storage space is being relied on and how it came into existence. On documents, Explanation 3 operates only where a number of documents are all made by one uniform process, such as printing, lithography or photography; each is then primary evidence of the contents of the rest, but where they are all copies of a common original none of them is primary evidence of the contents of the original. That does not make such a copy worthless, since this section says only what is primary evidence: the contents of the original may still be proved by the original itself, or by secondary evidence where the law permits it, so a copy should not be dropped from the case file merely because it cannot stand as primary evidence of the original.

bsa_refs.title: Secondary evidence
bsa_refs.summary: Section 58 defines what counts as secondary evidence. It is framed with the word 'includes' and lists eight categories in clauses (i) to (viii): certified copies given under the provisions hereinafter contained; copies made from the original by mechanical processes which in themselves ensure the accuracy of the copy, and copies compared with such copies; copies made from or compared with the original; counterparts of documents as against the parties who did not execute them; oral accounts of the contents of a document given by some person who has himself seen it; oral admissions; written admissions; and the evidence of a person skilled in the examination of such documents who has examined a document whose original consists of numerous accounts or other documents which cannot conveniently be examined in Court. Four illustrations work the definition through. Illustration (a): a photograph of an original is secondary evidence of its contents, though the two have not been compared, if it is proved that the thing photographed was the original. Illustration (b): a copy compared with a copy of a letter made by a copying machine is secondary evidence of the contents of the letter, if it is shown that the copy made by the copying machine was made from the original. Illustration (c): a copy transcribed from a copy, but afterwards compared with the original, is secondary evidence, while the copy not so compared is not secondary evidence of the original, although the copy from which it was transcribed was compared with the original. Illustration (d): neither an oral account of a copy compared with the original, nor an oral account of a photograph or machine-copy of the original, is secondary evidence of the original. The section only defines the categories; it does not by itself permit secondary evidence to be led.
key_requirements: Secondary evidence includes certified copies given under the provisions hereinafter contained.
Secondary evidence includes copies made from the original by mechanical processes which in themselves ensure the accuracy of the copy, and copies compared with such copies.
Secondary evidence includes copies made from or compared with the original.
Secondary evidence includes counterparts of documents as against the parties who did not execute them.
Secondary evidence includes oral accounts of the contents of a document given by some person who has himself seen it.
Secondary evidence includes oral admissions.
Secondary evidence includes written admissions.

Secondary evidence includes the evidence of a person who has examined a document whose original consists of numerous accounts or other documents which cannot conveniently be examined in Court, and who is skilled in the examination of such documents.
A photograph of an original is secondary evidence of its contents, though the two have not been compared, if it is proved that the thing photographed was the original (Illustration (a)).

A copy compared with a copy of a letter made by a copying machine is secondary evidence of the contents of the letter, if it is shown that the copy made by the copying machine was made from the original (Illustration (b)).

A copy transcribed from a copy and afterwards compared with the original is secondary evidence; a copy not so compared is not secondary evidence of the original, although the copy from which it was transcribed was compared with the original (Illustration (c)).
Neither an oral account of a copy compared with the original, nor an oral account of a photograph or machine-copy of the original, is secondary evidence of the original (Illustration (d)).
bsa_refs.investigation_relevance: Where the IO cannot put the original document before the Court, this section identifies which substitutes fall within secondary evidence: certified copies given under the provisions hereinafter contained, copies made from the original by mechanical processes which in themselves ensure the accuracy of the copy and copies compared with such copies, copies made from or compared with the original, counterparts as against the parties who did not execute them, oral or written admissions, an oral account of the contents given by a person who has himself seen the document, and, for originals consisting of numerous accounts or other documents which cannot conveniently be examined in Court, the evidence of a person who has examined the document and who is skilled in the examination of such documents. Three practical traps follow from the illustrations. First, a photograph of a document qualifies only if it is proved that the thing photographed was the original, so the record should show who photographed what and from what. Second, in a chain of copies it is the comparison that saves the copy: a copy transcribed from a copy qualifies only if it was afterwards compared with the original, and it is not enough that the copy it was transcribed from had itself been compared, so where a copy of a copy is seized the comparison with the original should be made and recorded; for a copying-machine copy, it must be shown that the machine copy was made from the original. Third, a witness who merely describes a photocopy or a photograph orally does not give secondary evidence of the original, so the copy itself should be seized. This section only says what secondary evidence is; the occasions on which secondary evidence may actually be given are dealt with elsewhere in the Adhiniyam, not here.

bsa_refs.title: Admissibility of electronic records
bsa_refs.summary: This is the operative provision for proving electronic records. Operating notwithstanding anything contained in this Adhiniyam, sub-section (1) deems any information contained in an electronic record which is printed on paper, stored, recorded or copied in optical or magnetic media or semiconductor memory and produced by a computer or any communication device, or otherwise stored, recorded or copied in any electronic form (the 'computer output'), to be also a document, if the conditions mentioned in this section are satisfied in relation to the information and computer in question, and makes that output admissible in any proceedings, without further proof or production of the original, as evidence of any contents of the original or of any fact stated therein of which direct evidence would be admissible. What sub-section (1) deems is that the computer output is ALSO a document: it does not deem the output to be the original, and it settles nothing about the truth or the weight of what the record contains. Both the deeming and the admissibility are conditional on the section's conditions being satisfied. (The supplied Gazette text reads 'as evidence or any contents of the original'; that is an apparent typographical error for 'as evidence of any contents of the original', and the latter reading is used here.) Sub-section (2) lays down the four conditions in clauses (a) to (d): production of the output by the computer or communication device during the period over which it was used regularly to create, store or process information for the purposes of any activity regularly carried on over that period by the person having lawful control over its use; regular feeding into the device, in the ordinary course of those activities, of information of the kind contained in the record or of the kind from which it is derived; the device operating properly throughout the material part of that period, or any period in which it was not operating properly or was out of operation during that part not being such as to affect the electronic record or the accuracy of its contents; and the information in the record reproducing or being derived from such information fed in. Sub-section (3) treats all the computers or communication devices used for that purpose during that period, whether in standalone mode, on a computer system, on a computer network, on a computer resource enabling information creation or providing information processing and storage, or through an intermediary, as constituting for the purposes of this section a single computer or communication device, and references in the section are construed accordingly. Sub-section (4) is the certificate provision: in any proceeding where it is desired to give a statement in evidence by virtue of this section, a certificate doing ANY of the following three things shall be submitted along with the electronic record at each instance where it is being submitted for admission, namely (a) identifying the electronic record containing the statement and describing the manner in which it was produced, (b) giving such particulars of any device involved in the production of that record as may be appropriate for the purpose of showing that it was produced by a computer or a communication device referred to in clauses (a) to (e) of sub-section (3), and (c) dealing with any of the matters to which the conditions mentioned in sub-section (2) relate. The certificate must purport to be signed by a person in charge of the computer or communication device or the management of the relevant activities (whichever is appropriate) AND an expert, that is, two signatories, and it shall be evidence of any matter stated in the certificate; for the purposes of that sub-section it is sufficient for a matter to be stated to the best of the knowledge and belief of the person stating it, in the certificate specified in the Schedule (the form of which is not part of the text supplied here). Sub-section (5) clarifies that information is taken to be supplied to the computer or communication device if it is supplied in any appropriate form, whether directly or, with or without human intervention, by means of any appropriate equipment; and that a computer output is taken to have been produced by the device whether produced by it directly or, with or without human intervention, by means of any appropriate equipment or by other electronic means as referred to in clauses (a) to (e) of sub-section (3).
key_requirements: Sub-section (1) operates notwithstanding anything contained in this Adhiniyam.

Information contained in an electronic record which is printed on paper, stored, recorded or copied in optical or magnetic media or semiconductor memory and produced by a computer or any communication device, or otherwise stored, recorded or copied in any electronic form (the computer output), shall be deemed to be also a document, if the conditions mentioned in this section are satisfied in relation to the information and computer in question.

Such computer output shall be admissible in any proceedings, without further proof or production of the original, as evidence of any contents of the original or of any fact stated therein of which direct evidence would be admissible (the supplied Gazette text reads 'as evidence or any contents of the original', an apparent typographical error for 'as evidence of any contents of the original', and the latter reading is used here).

The computer output containing the information must have been produced by the computer or communication device during the period over which that device was used regularly to create, store or process information for the purposes of any activity regularly carried on over that period by the person having lawful control over its use.

During the said period, information of the kind contained in the electronic record, or of the kind from which the information so contained is derived, must have been regularly fed into the computer or communication device in the ordinary course of the said activities.

Throughout the material part of the said period the computer or communication device must have been operating properly, or, if not, any period in which it was not operating properly or was out of operation during that part of the period must not have been such as to affect the electronic record or the accuracy of its contents.
The information contained in the electronic record must reproduce or be derived from such information fed into the computer or communication device in the ordinary course of the said activities.

Where the function of creating, storing or processing information for the purposes of the activity was regularly performed by means of one or more computers or communication devices, whether in standalone mode, on a computer system, on a computer network, on a computer resource enabling information creation or providing information processing and storage, or through an intermediary, all the computers or communication devices used for that purpose during that period shall be treated for the purposes of this section as constituting a single computer or communication device.

In any proceeding where it is desired to give a statement in evidence by virtue of this section, a certificate doing any of the things listed in clauses (a) to (c) of sub-section (4) shall be submitted along with the electronic record.
The certificate shall be submitted along with the electronic record at each instance where it is being submitted for admission.
Clause (a) of sub-section (4): identifying the electronic record containing the statement and describing the manner in which it was produced.

Clause (b) of sub-section (4): giving such particulars of any device involved in the production of that electronic record as may be appropriate for the purpose of showing that the electronic record was produced by a computer or a communication device referred to in clauses (a) to (e) of sub-section (3).
Clause (c) of sub-section (4): dealing with any of the matters to which the conditions mentioned in sub-section (2) relate.
The certificate must purport to be signed by a person in charge of the computer or communication device or the management of the relevant activities (whichever is appropriate) and an expert.
The certificate shall be evidence of any matter stated in the certificate.
For the purposes of sub-section (4) it shall be sufficient for a matter to be stated to the best of the knowledge and belief of the person stating it in the certificate specified in the Schedule.

Information shall be taken to be supplied to a computer or communication device if it is supplied thereto in any appropriate form and whether it is so supplied directly or (with or without human intervention) by means of any appropriate equipment.

A computer output shall be taken to have been produced by a computer or communication device whether it was produced by it directly or (with or without human intervention) by means of any appropriate equipment or by other electronic means as referred to in clauses (a) to (e) of sub-section (3).
bsa_refs.investigation_relevance: Wherever the IO relies on this section to put computer output in evidence - CDRs, CCTV footage, device extractions, printouts, server logs - the record must travel with a sub-section (4) certificate, and it must go with the record each and every time the record is submitted for admission, not merely once at charge-sheet stage. On the text the certificate is one 'doing any of' three things: identifying the record and describing how it was produced, giving particulars of any device involved, and dealing with any of the matters to which the sub-section (2) conditions relate; the statute requires any of the three, but the safe practice is to cover all three. The certificate must purport to be signed by two people, a person in charge of the computer or communication device or the management of the relevant activities (whichever is appropriate) and an expert, and it is the certificate specified in the Schedule, so the IO should line up both signatories before the record is tendered; a matter may be stated in it to the best of the knowledge and belief of the person stating it. At seizure, therefore, the IO should record the facts the signatories will later have to certify: regular use of the device over the relevant period for the activity, who had lawful control over its use, regular feeding of information of that kind in the ordinary course, and the proper working of the device (or that any malfunction or downtime in the material part of the period did not affect the record or the accuracy of its contents). Note the limits of sub-section (1): where the conditions are met it deems the computer output to be also a document and lets it in without further proof or production of the original, but it does not make the output the original and it settles nothing about the truth or weight of the contents.
time_limits: s.63(2)(a): no fixed number of days is prescribed - the relevant period is the period over which the computer or communication device was used regularly to create, store or process information for the purposes of the activity regularly carried on over that period.

s.63(2)(c): the computer or communication device must have been operating properly 'throughout the material part of the said period', or any period in which it was not operating properly or was out of operation during that part must not have been such as to affect the electronic record or the accuracy of its contents. This qualification belongs to clause (c) alone and does not relax clauses (a), (b) or (d).
s.63(4): the certificate must be submitted along with the electronic record 'at each instance where it is being submitted for admission' - a repeating timing requirement, not a one-time filing.

bsa_refs.source_note: The Gazette text of sub-section (1) prints "as evidence or any contents of the original". The reading is plainly "as evidence of any contents", which is how the key requirement states it and how the repealed s.65B of the Evidence Act read; the quotation reproduces the print exactly. Flag it if a defence takes a point on it.

steps.text: Take necessary safety measures to prevent damage to or tampering with the electronic records — use device covers, anti-static bags, Faraday bags, etc., to keep the records safe during packaging and transport.
steps.applies_when: Seized digital exhibits are packaged and transported

details.text: Transportation rules: do not bend any disk; place hard disks and circuit boards in anti-static bags; handle all equipment with extra care; place keyboard, leads, mouse and modems in the attached bag; keep all equipment away from magnetic sources like loudspeakers, heated seats and radiation.
details.citation: State Forensic Science Laboratory UP / Technical Services HQ, Lucknow - A Collection of Standard Operating Procedures for Crime Scene Investigation (pictorial, BNSS/BSA era) - TRANSLATED FROM HINDI

details.text: Place labels on them; place personal organizers in paper envelopes; do not place items under heavy objects; an electronic device like a mobile should be packed in containers to avoid direct contact of hot sealing wax while sealing the exhibits.
details.citation: State Forensic Science Laboratory UP / Technical Services HQ, Lucknow - A Collection of Standard Operating Procedures for Crime Scene Investigation (pictorial, BNSS/BSA era) - TRANSLATED FROM HINDI

details.text: Check if the device is stand alone or attached to a network; if the evidence is small and portable such as a cell phone, tablet or telephone interceptor, collect it in an anti-static bag.
details.citation: LNJN National Institute of Criminology and Forensic Science, MHA - A Forensic Guide for Crime Investigators: Standard Operating Procedures (marked Restricted)

details.text: Pack all digital evidence in anti-static packaging; only paper bags and envelopes, cardboard boxes and anti-static containers should be used for packaging digital evidence, and plastic materials must not be used to preserve digital evidence.
details.citation: LNJN National Institute of Criminology and Forensic Science, MHA - A Forensic Guide for Crime Investigators: Standard Operating Procedures (marked Restricted)

details.text: Ensure that all digital evidence is packed in a manner that will prevent it from being bent, scratched or otherwise deformed, and label all containers used to package and store digital evidence clearly and properly.
details.citation: LNJN National Institute of Criminology and Forensic Science, MHA - A Forensic Guide for Crime Investigators: Standard Operating Procedures (marked Restricted)

steps.title: Protect Electronic Records During Packaging and Transport
steps.triage_why: Best practice for evidence preservation, but failure to use a specific bag does not automatically defeat the prosecution if the data remains intact.

steps.text: For CCTV evidence, note the Serial No, Make and Model No etc. of the DVR relating to the incident, then seal and pack it, and pack the collected CCTV footage/DVR in bubble wrap and seal it. If the DVR is installed at a place where it is not possible to seal it as evidence, have the backup of the time and date relating to the incident taken by the technician of the DVR manufacturing company and obtain along with it a certificate conforming to Section 63(4)(c) of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam [BSA 2023 s.63(4)(c); pre-2023 equivalent s.65B(4) Indian Evidence Act 1872].
steps.deadline: Transfer the data from the compact flash card to a permanent memory system as soon as possible for further examination (no fixed number of hours printed; UP FSL SOP, CCTV/DVR precautions)
steps.applies_when: CCTV footage or a DVR/NVR is to be collected

details.text: CCTV is an important instrument as evidence: it captures video images around the clock, and the image can be used to identify the suspect, to show a person's activities at a scene, or to indicate the areas/spots at which a person's presence can be traced.
details.citation: State Forensic Science Laboratory UP / Technical Services HQ, Lucknow - A Collection of Standard Operating Procedures for Crime Scene Investigation (pictorial, BNSS/BSA era) - TRANSLATED FROM HINDI

details.text: Precautions: do not change the time and date on the DVR system; do not install any additional software on it (if extremely necessary, contact the manufacturer); if the required video data appears to have been overwritten, check the backup; ensure the frame rate on recovery is as close as possible to the frame rate at which the footage was recorded; other copies may be prepared from the master evidence; and transfer the data from the compact flash card to a permanent memory system as soon as possible for further examination.
