bsa_refs.title: Admissibility of electronic records
bsa_refs.summary: This is the operative provision for proving electronic records. Operating notwithstanding anything contained in this Adhiniyam, sub-section (1) deems any information contained in an electronic record which is printed on paper, stored, recorded or copied in optical or magnetic media or semiconductor memory and produced by a computer or any communication device, or otherwise stored, recorded or copied in any electronic form (the 'computer output'), to be also a document, if the conditions mentioned in this section are satisfied in relation to the information and computer in question, and makes that output admissible in any proceedings, without further proof or production of the original, as evidence of any contents of the original or of any fact stated therein of which direct evidence would be admissible. What sub-section (1) deems is that the computer output is ALSO a document: it does not deem the output to be the original, and it settles nothing about the truth or the weight of what the record contains. Both the deeming and the admissibility are conditional on the section's conditions being satisfied. (The supplied Gazette text reads 'as evidence or any contents of the original'; that is an apparent typographical error for 'as evidence of any contents of the original', and the latter reading is used here.) Sub-section (2) lays down the four conditions in clauses (a) to (d): production of the output by the computer or communication device during the period over which it was used regularly to create, store or process information for the purposes of any activity regularly carried on over that period by the person having lawful control over its use; regular feeding into the device, in the ordinary course of those activities, of information of the kind contained in the record or of the kind from which it is derived; the device operating properly throughout the material part of that period, or any period in which it was not operating properly or was out of operation during that part not being such as to affect the electronic record or the accuracy of its contents; and the information in the record reproducing or being derived from such information fed in. Sub-section (3) treats all the computers or communication devices used for that purpose during that period, whether in standalone mode, on a computer system, on a computer network, on a computer resource enabling information creation or providing information processing and storage, or through an intermediary, as constituting for the purposes of this section a single computer or communication device, and references in the section are construed accordingly. Sub-section (4) is the certificate provision: in any proceeding where it is desired to give a statement in evidence by virtue of this section, a certificate doing ANY of the following three things shall be submitted along with the electronic record at each instance where it is being submitted for admission, namely (a) identifying the electronic record containing the statement and describing the manner in which it was produced, (b) giving such particulars of any device involved in the production of that record as may be appropriate for the purpose of showing that it was produced by a computer or a communication device referred to in clauses (a) to (e) of sub-section (3), and (c) dealing with any of the matters to which the conditions mentioned in sub-section (2) relate. The certificate must purport to be signed by a person in charge of the computer or communication device or the management of the relevant activities (whichever is appropriate) AND an expert, that is, two signatories, and it shall be evidence of any matter stated in the certificate; for the purposes of that sub-section it is sufficient for a matter to be stated to the best of the knowledge and belief of the person stating it, in the certificate specified in the Schedule (the form of which is not part of the text supplied here). Sub-section (5) clarifies that information is taken to be supplied to the computer or communication device if it is supplied in any appropriate form, whether directly or, with or without human intervention, by means of any appropriate equipment; and that a computer output is taken to have been produced by the device whether produced by it directly or, with or without human intervention, by means of any appropriate equipment or by other electronic means as referred to in clauses (a) to (e) of sub-section (3).
key_requirements: Sub-section (1) operates notwithstanding anything contained in this Adhiniyam.

Information contained in an electronic record which is printed on paper, stored, recorded or copied in optical or magnetic media or semiconductor memory and produced by a computer or any communication device, or otherwise stored, recorded or copied in any electronic form (the computer output), shall be deemed to be also a document, if the conditions mentioned in this section are satisfied in relation to the information and computer in question.

Such computer output shall be admissible in any proceedings, without further proof or production of the original, as evidence of any contents of the original or of any fact stated therein of which direct evidence would be admissible (the supplied Gazette text reads 'as evidence or any contents of the original', an apparent typographical error for 'as evidence of any contents of the original', and the latter reading is used here).

The computer output containing the information must have been produced by the computer or communication device during the period over which that device was used regularly to create, store or process information for the purposes of any activity regularly carried on over that period by the person having lawful control over its use.

During the said period, information of the kind contained in the electronic record, or of the kind from which the information so contained is derived, must have been regularly fed into the computer or communication device in the ordinary course of the said activities.

Throughout the material part of the said period the computer or communication device must have been operating properly, or, if not, any period in which it was not operating properly or was out of operation during that part of the period must not have been such as to affect the electronic record or the accuracy of its contents.
The information contained in the electronic record must reproduce or be derived from such information fed into the computer or communication device in the ordinary course of the said activities.

Where the function of creating, storing or processing information for the purposes of the activity was regularly performed by means of one or more computers or communication devices, whether in standalone mode, on a computer system, on a computer network, on a computer resource enabling information creation or providing information processing and storage, or through an intermediary, all the computers or communication devices used for that purpose during that period shall be treated for the purposes of this section as constituting a single computer or communication device.

In any proceeding where it is desired to give a statement in evidence by virtue of this section, a certificate doing any of the things listed in clauses (a) to (c) of sub-section (4) shall be submitted along with the electronic record.
The certificate shall be submitted along with the electronic record at each instance where it is being submitted for admission.
Clause (a) of sub-section (4): identifying the electronic record containing the statement and describing the manner in which it was produced.

Clause (b) of sub-section (4): giving such particulars of any device involved in the production of that electronic record as may be appropriate for the purpose of showing that the electronic record was produced by a computer or a communication device referred to in clauses (a) to (e) of sub-section (3).
Clause (c) of sub-section (4): dealing with any of the matters to which the conditions mentioned in sub-section (2) relate.
The certificate must purport to be signed by a person in charge of the computer or communication device or the management of the relevant activities (whichever is appropriate) and an expert.
The certificate shall be evidence of any matter stated in the certificate.
For the purposes of sub-section (4) it shall be sufficient for a matter to be stated to the best of the knowledge and belief of the person stating it in the certificate specified in the Schedule.

Information shall be taken to be supplied to a computer or communication device if it is supplied thereto in any appropriate form and whether it is so supplied directly or (with or without human intervention) by means of any appropriate equipment.

A computer output shall be taken to have been produced by a computer or communication device whether it was produced by it directly or (with or without human intervention) by means of any appropriate equipment or by other electronic means as referred to in clauses (a) to (e) of sub-section (3).
bsa_refs.investigation_relevance: Wherever the IO relies on this section to put computer output in evidence - CDRs, CCTV footage, device extractions, printouts, server logs - the record must travel with a sub-section (4) certificate, and it must go with the record each and every time the record is submitted for admission, not merely once at charge-sheet stage. On the text the certificate is one 'doing any of' three things: identifying the record and describing how it was produced, giving particulars of any device involved, and dealing with any of the matters to which the sub-section (2) conditions relate; the statute requires any of the three, but the safe practice is to cover all three. The certificate must purport to be signed by two people, a person in charge of the computer or communication device or the management of the relevant activities (whichever is appropriate) and an expert, and it is the certificate specified in the Schedule, so the IO should line up both signatories before the record is tendered; a matter may be stated in it to the best of the knowledge and belief of the person stating it. At seizure, therefore, the IO should record the facts the signatories will later have to certify: regular use of the device over the relevant period for the activity, who had lawful control over its use, regular feeding of information of that kind in the ordinary course, and the proper working of the device (or that any malfunction or downtime in the material part of the period did not affect the record or the accuracy of its contents). Note the limits of sub-section (1): where the conditions are met it deems the computer output to be also a document and lets it in without further proof or production of the original, but it does not make the output the original and it settles nothing about the truth or weight of the contents.
time_limits: s.63(2)(a): no fixed number of days is prescribed - the relevant period is the period over which the computer or communication device was used regularly to create, store or process information for the purposes of the activity regularly carried on over that period.

s.63(2)(c): the computer or communication device must have been operating properly 'throughout the material part of the said period', or any period in which it was not operating properly or was out of operation during that part must not have been such as to affect the electronic record or the accuracy of its contents. This qualification belongs to clause (c) alone and does not relax clauses (a), (b) or (d).
s.63(4): the certificate must be submitted along with the electronic record 'at each instance where it is being submitted for admission' - a repeating timing requirement, not a one-time filing.

bsa_refs.source_note: The Gazette text of sub-section (1) prints "as evidence or any contents of the original". The reading is plainly "as evidence of any contents", which is how the key requirement states it and how the repealed s.65B of the Evidence Act read; the quotation reproduces the print exactly. Flag it if a defence takes a point on it.
bsa_refs.case_trigger: the accused was seen on CCTV taking the vehicle
bsa_refs.case_action: Obtain the necessary certificate and ensure the computer/device output (CCTV footage) satisfies the admissibility conditions for electronic records.

steps.text: Seize every device and accessory of evidential value, grouped by purpose: for retrieval of the evidence itself — floppy disks, CDs, DVDs, SIM cards, memory cards and pen drives, the mobile phone, and external/removable hard drives; because they help the examination — manuals and computer software, the password paper, and keys and dongles; for comparison of printouts — the printers, printouts and printer papers; so that the system can be reconstructed — the CPU unit, all cables, the power supply unit, the external hard disk, dongles, modems, and the keyboard and mouse. Also search the crime scene for any other valuable evidence such as password paper, diaries and notebooks, and ask the user for any password and record it.
steps.applies_when: Digital devices are found at the scene

details.text: Device-by-device evidential yield (items 1-7): CPU — may itself be proof of theft, forgery etc.; holds all files and information including deleted files and folders, recovered by forensic imaging and analysis. Display monitor (CRT/LCD/TFT) and mobile phone screens if switched on — record everything visible by video/photo and written description. Smart cards, dongles and biometric scanners — card information, user information and other information. Digital cameras — pictures, videos, sound, removable cartridge, time and date stamps. Handheld devices (printed 'Handled Devices': PDAs, electronic organizers, smart phones) — address book, appointment calendar, documents, email, phone book, text and voice messages, email passwords. Hard drives — store all the information. LAN card / NIC — yields the device's MAC address.
details.citation: State Forensic Science Laboratory UP / Technical Services HQ, Lucknow - A Collection of Standard Operating Procedures for Crime Scene Investigation (pictorial, BNSS/BSA era) - TRANSLATED FROM HINDI

details.text: Device-by-device evidential yield (items 8-16): modems, routers, hubs and switches — configuration files hold IP-address information. Servers — last log-in, emails exchanged, material downloaded, pages accessed. Network cables and connectors — trace back to the computers concerned and identify the types of device attached. Pagers — address information, text messages, phone numbers. Printers — number of prints last taken, usage logs with time/date, network identification information, and fingerprints. Removable storage media and devices — files in which evidence may be found. Scanners — the scanning capability can help prove the illegal activity. Telephones — names, text and voice messages, memos, passwords, phone numbers, caller identification data; some store appointment information and work as voice recorders. Copiers — documents in physical and electronic form, user log and time/date data.
details.citation: State Forensic Science Laboratory UP / Technical Services HQ, Lucknow - A Collection of Standard Operating Procedures for Crime Scene Investigation (pictorial, BNSS/BSA era) - TRANSLATED FROM HINDI

details.text: Device-by-device evidential yield (items 17-21): CD and DVD drives — files/data in which evidence may be found. Credit card skimmers — the magnetic-strip track holds cardholder information (card expiry date, user's address, credit card number, user's name). Digital/smart watches — address book, notes, appointment calendar, phone numbers, email. Fax machines — documents, phone numbers, send/receive logs, film cartridge. Keyboard and mouse — examine for finger marks/fingerprints.

steps.title: Identify What to Seize at a Digital Scene
steps.triage_why: Comprehensive seizure strengthens the case, but missing a manual or printer does not typically defeat a murder/robbery prosecution.

steps.text: Carry the Digital Crime Scene Investigation Kit to any scene with digital devices: scene-securing and recording hardware, empty storage media, packaging (anti-static and Faraday bags), a non-magnetic toolkit, and the forensic software set — write blockers, converters/adapters, boot software, forensic imaging software and volatile-data collection software.
steps.responsible: Digital crime scene party / Investigating Officer
steps.applies_when: The scene involves digital/electronic devices (including CCTV/DVR)

details.text: Kit hardware: tape to secure the crime scene (yellow tape); digital camera (DSLR); extra battery/power backup; video camera; note/sketch pad; empty storage media (portable USB hard disk and pen drive); labels/evidence markers; pen and marker; storage container; anti-static bag; Faraday bag; toolkit with non-magnetic screwdrivers, pliers, forceps, scissors, clips, pins and cutter; torch and magnifying glass; rubber gloves.
details.citation: State Forensic Science Laboratory UP / Technical Services HQ, Lucknow - A Collection of Standard Operating Procedures for Crime Scene Investigation (pictorial, BNSS/BSA era) - TRANSLATED FROM HINDI

details.text: Kit software and interfaces: Incident Response Toolkit software; converters/adapters SATA to USB, IDE to USB, SCSI to USB, NVMe to USB and PCIe to USB; write blockers for USB, SATA, IDE and SCSI; boot software (to start the computer so the existing hard disk can be imaged and analysed without tampering); forensic imaging software; volatile-data collection software such as Win32DD, Win64DD, FTK Imager and Crypt Hunter.
details.citation: State Forensic Science Laboratory UP / Technical Services HQ, Lucknow - A Collection of Standard Operating Procedures for Crime Scene Investigation (pictorial, BNSS/BSA era) - TRANSLATED FROM HINDI

details.text: For CCTV/DVR collection additionally take: a laptop with CD/DVD drive, USB port, firewire port, wireless access, media card reader and four-port network switch/hub; an external CD/DVD writer drive (USB/SCSI/firewire); USB and firewire storage devices; a high-capacity hard drive.
details.citation: State Forensic Science Laboratory UP / Technical Services HQ, Lucknow - A Collection of Standard Operating Procedures for Crime Scene Investigation (pictorial, BNSS/BSA era) - TRANSLATED FROM HINDI

details.text: Cabling for CCTV/DVR work: network cable (crossover and straight patch), composite and S-Video cable with RCA to BNC adapter, audio cable (RCA, stereo and mono mini), USB cable, firewire cable (i-Link, 400, 800), power cable and extension cord.
details.citation: State Forensic Science Laboratory UP / Technical Services HQ, Lucknow - A Collection of Standard Operating Procedures for Crime Scene Investigation (pictorial, BNSS/BSA era) - TRANSLATED FROM HINDI

details.text: Also for CCTV/DVR work: write blockers (IDE, firewire) so the original evidence is not altered; blank media (CD-R, DVD-R); a still camera with external storage media; a toolkit (flashlight, mirror, assorted screwdrivers, pen, marker); a digital/analog video recorder; and suitable evidence packing bags (anti-static bags).

steps.title: Equip the Party for a Digital Scene
steps.triage_why: Using a professional kit is sound practice, but the absence of a specific tool doesn't invalidate the case if the evidence is otherwise legally seized.

steps.text: On reaching a scene with digital devices, keep people away from the digital evidence, equipment and power supply, then check whether the system is switched ON. If it is ON and the advice of an expert is available, follow that advice (for imaging volatile and non-volatile data) and then proceed to labelling and photography/videography. If it is ON and no expert advice is available: do not touch the keyboard, do not take advice from the owner, make a note of what is on the screen and photograph it, allow the printer to complete the printing, and remove the power cables from the suspected system. If the system is not switched ON, verify the power state and proceed to labelling and photography/videography.
steps.responsible: First responder / Investigating Officer at the digital scene
steps.applies_when: Digital devices are found at the scene

details.text: If the system is switched on, record everything open and visible on the screen — all graphics and files displayed can be entered as electronic evidence; this evidence can only be recorded through video and photograph and entered by means of a written description.

steps.title: Isolate and triage digital devices by power state
steps.triage_why: Standard operating procedure to prevent volatile data loss; however, in this case, the primary evidence is likely stored CCTV footage (non-volatile).

steps.text: Label and photograph or videograph the equipment, remove all connection cables, document/record all details and remove the equipment, ensuring that all the components have proper exhibit labels attached; then submit all the evidence for forensic examination.
steps.applies_when: Digital devices are being seized

details.text: Documentation of the scene is a very important stage of the investigation: record the physical condition of the computer, the related equipment and the other evidence exactly as found; photography/videography is the best source for sketching and reconstructing the scene of crime.

steps.text: Mention in the case diary the chain of custody (date, time, place, etc.) of all documents, including seized electronic devices, so that it may be duly proved in Court during the trial.

details.text: Label seized articles properly; keep a copy of the label in the case diary; make proper entries in the General Diary; ensure entries in the Property Register; and maintain the chain of custody of seized articles.

steps.stage: Statutory basis of search and seizure
steps.text: Persons in charge of closed place to allow search [BNSS 103]: Whenever any place liable to search or inspection under Chapter VII is closed, any person residing in or being in charge of such place SHALL, on demand of the officer or other person executing the warrant and on production of the warrant, allow him free ingress thereto and afford all reasonable facilities for a search therein; if ingress cannot be so obtained, the executing officer or other person MAY proceed in the manner provided by sub-section (2) of section 44. Where any person in or about such place is reasonably suspected of concealing about his person any article for which search should be made, such person MAY be searched, and if such person is a woman the search SHALL be made by another woman with strict regard to decency. Before making a search under this Chapter the officer or other person about to make it SHALL call upon two or more independent and respectable inhabitants of the locality in which the place to be searched is situate, or of any other locality if no such inhabitant of the said locality is available or is willing to be a witness to the search, to attend and witness the search, and MAY issue an order in writing to them or any of them so to do. The search SHALL be made in their presence, and a list of all things seized in the course of such search and of the places in which they are respectively found SHALL be prepared by such officer or other person and signed by such witnesses, but no person witnessing a search under this section shall be required to attend the Court as a witness of the search unless specially summoned by it. The occupant of the place searched, or some person in his behalf, SHALL in every instance be permitted to attend during the search, and a copy of the list prepared under this section, signed by the said witnesses, SHALL be delivered to such occupant or person.
legal_basis: Section 103 BNSS 2023

steps.stage: Statutory basis of search and seizure
steps.text: Power of police officer to seize certain property [BNSS 106]: Any police officer MAY seize any property which may be alleged or suspected to have been stolen, or which may be found under circumstances which create suspicion of the commission of any offence - the seizure power is permissive and belongs to any police officer. The reporting duties that follow are mandatory: such police officer, if subordinate to the officer in charge of a police station, SHALL forthwith report the seizure to that officer, and every police officer acting under sub-section (1) SHALL forthwith report the seizure to the Magistrate having jurisdiction. Within the same sub-section (3), where the property seized cannot be conveniently transported to the Court, or where there is difficulty in securing proper accommodation for its custody, or where continued retention of the property in police custody may not be considered necessary for the purpose of investigation, he MAY give custody thereof to any person on his executing a bond undertaking to produce the property before the Court as and when required and to give effect to the further orders of the Court as to the disposal of the same. By the proviso, where property seized under sub-section (1) is subject to speedy and natural decay and the person entitled to possession is unknown or absent and the value of such property is less than five hundred rupees, it MAY forthwith be sold by auction under the orders of the Superintendent of Police, and the provisions of sections 503 and 504 shall, as nearly as may be practicable, apply to the net proceeds of such sale.
legal_basis: Section 106 BNSS 2023
steps.deadline: 'Forthwith' - a subordinate police officer's report of the seizure to the officer in charge of the police station (sub-section (2)); 'Forthwith' - every police officer acting under sub-section (1) must report the seizure to the Magistrate having jurisdiction (sub-section (3)); 'Forthwith' - the permissive auction sale of perishable property meeting the proviso conditions, under the orders of the Superintendent of Police

steps.text: When officer in charge of police station may require another to issue search-warrant [BNSS 186]: Sub-section (1) is permissive: an officer in charge of a police station or a police officer not being below the rank of sub-inspector making an investigation "may require" an officer in charge of another police station, whether in the same or a different district, to cause a search to be made in any place, in any case in which the former officer might cause such search to be made, within the limits of his own station. Sub-section (2) is mandatory on the officer who receives the requisition: such officer, on being so required, shall proceed according to the provisions of section 185, and shall forward the thing found, if any, to the officer at whose request the search was made. Sub-section (3) supplies an urgency route in enabling terms - whenever there is reason to believe that the delay occasioned by requiring an officer in charge of another police station to cause a search to be made under sub-section (1) might result in evidence of the commission of an offence being concealed or destroyed, "it shall be lawful for" an officer in charge of a police station or a police officer making any investigation under this Chapter to search, or cause to be searched, any place in the limits of another police station in accordance with the provisions of section 185, as if such place were within the limits of his own police station; this confers lawful authority, it does not compel a search. Sub-section (4) then imposes mandatory post-search intimation: any officer conducting a search under sub-section (3) shall forthwith send notice of the search to the officer in charge of the police station within the limits of which such place is situate, shall also send with such notice a copy of the list (if any) prepared under section 103, and shall also send to the nearest Magistrate empowered to take cognizance of the offence copies of the records referred to in sub-sections (1) and (3) of section 185. Sub-section (5) requires that the owner or occupier of the place searched shall, on application, be furnished free of cost with a copy of any record sent to the Magistrate under sub-section (4).
legal_basis: Section 186 BNSS 2023
steps.deadline: Sub-section (4): notice of a search conducted under sub-section (3) shall be sent "forthwith" to the officer in charge of the police station within the limits of which the searched place is situate. No fixed number of hours is printed anywhere in section 186. (Do not import the "forthwith, but not later than forty-eight hours" figure printed on the same PDF page 73 - that period belongs to section 185(5), which governs copies of records made under section 185(1) or 185(3).)

steps.text: Make no arrest except in accordance with the BNSS or another law in force authorising arrest — an arrest outside these provisions is illegal.

details.text: An IO who fails to comply with the BNSS arrest provisions is liable to departmental disciplinary action under the rules in force.

details.text: Exercise the power of arrest without warrant with utmost care; it takes away individual liberty and human rights must not be violated.

details.text: Before making any arrest, consider whether there are proper grounds for the arrest and whether the arrest is necessary; no person is to be arrested merely because the police possess the power to arrest, and no arbitrary arrest may be made without following due process.

steps.text: Before a warrantless arrest, verify the person falls in a BNSS 35(1) category: (i) commits a cognizable offence in police presence; (ii) credible information received that he has committed a cognizable offence punishable with more than 7 years or death, with reason to believe on the basis of that information that he committed it; (iii) credible information or reasonable suspicion of a cognizable offence punishable up to 7 years, with a recorded necessity ground; (iv) proclaimed offender; (v) possession of suspected stolen property with reasonable suspicion of an offence; (vi) obstructing police in duty or escaping/attempting escape from lawful custody; (vii) armed-forces deserter; (viii) extraditable act committed abroad; (ix) released convict breaching the release-condition rules under s.394(5); (x) requisition (written or oral, specifying the person and the offence or other cause) from another police officer who could lawfully arrest that person without warrant. In a non-cognizable case do not arrest except under a warrant or Magistrate's order (subject to s.39).

(v) Possession of suspected stolen property with reasonable suspicion of an offence.
(vi) Obstructing police in duty or escaping or attempting escape from lawful custody.
(vii) Armed-forces deserter.
(viii) Extraditable act committed abroad.
(ix) Released convict breaching the release-condition rules under s.394(5).
(x) Requisition (written or oral, specifying the person and the offence or other cause) from another police officer who could lawfully arrest that person without warrant.

steps.text: A private person may arrest someone who commits a non-bailable and cognizable offence in his presence, or any proclaimed offender, and must hand the person over to a police officer or take him to the nearest police station without unnecessary delay and within six hours. steps.text: To execute a warrant directed to a police officer beyond the local jurisdiction of the issuing Court, ordinarily take it for endorsement either to an Executive Magistrate or to a police officer not below the rank of officer-in-charge of a police station within whose local limits it is to be executed; the local police shall, if required, assist in executing it (s.79 CrPC [now BNSS 81]). Where the warrant is executed outside the issuing district and the issuing Court is beyond 30 km from the place of execution, produce the arrestee before the Executive Magistrate, District Superintendent of Police or Commissioner of Police in whose jurisdiction the warrant was executed (s.80 CrPC [now BNSS 82]) and obtain that authority's orders for production before the issuing Court.

steps.text: Use handcuffs only, having regard to the nature and gravity of the offence, on a habitual or repeat offender, a person who escaped from custody, or a person accused of organised crime, terrorist act, drug-related crime, illegal possession of arms and ammunition, murder, rape, acid attack, counterfeiting of coins and currency notes, human trafficking, sexual offences against children, or offences against the State (BNSS 43(3)).

details.text: Do not use handcuffs as a form of punishment or to damage the person's reputation, or in a manner causing unnecessary pain or injury; avoid handcuffing for long periods without proper and necessary reason, on persons who are not a danger to themselves or others, or on ill persons for whom handcuffing is hazardous; ensure Article 21 is not violated in any manner and human dignity is not harmed. Make a clear Station Diary entry of the justifiable reasons for handcuffing and of any Court order obtained.
details.citation: Twenty-Nine Standard Operating Procedures - C.I.D. Crime & Railways, Gujarat Police, circular PRC/Circular-SOP-1/656/2024 dated 29/10/2024

details.text: Clearly mention the reasons why handcuffs have been used in the Case Diary; they must also be shown to the court if so required.
details.citation: Kerala Police - Standard Operating Procedure: Investigation & Prosecution in General (SOP Series), State Police Chief, 01.11.2020

details.text: A person arrested in execution of an arrest warrant issued by a magistrate must not be handcuffed unless prior permission has been taken from the magistrate; once produced before the court, the escorting officer must take the court's permission before handcuffing him to and from the court.
details.citation: Kerala Police - Standard Operating Procedure: Investigation & Prosecution in General (SOP Series), State Police Chief, 01.11.2020

details.text: In an arrest without warrant, handcuff only on concrete proof that the person is prone to violence, has a tendency to escape, or is so dangerous and desperate that there is no other practical way to restrain him, and then only till he is taken to the police station and thereafter to the magistrate's court; ideally do not use handcuffs on women, the infirm, bailable-offence accused, juvenile offenders or arrested witnesses (Prem Shanker Shukla; Citizen for Democracy).
details.citation: Kerala Police - Standard Operating Procedure: Investigation & Prosecution in General (SOP Series), State Police Chief, 01.11.2020

conflicts.description: bnss_2023 (BNSS 50) permits the officer or other person making an arrest to take offensive weapons from the arrested person ('may take'), while making delivery of all weapons so taken to the Court or officer mandatory; guj_cid_29_sops_2024 SOP 23 (p.102) renders the same provision as a duty - 'the police officer or other person making an arrest shall, immediately after the arrest, take from the person apprehended the offensive weapons upon his person, and hand over all weapons so taken...'.
conflicts.resolution: BNSS 50 governs as the law layer: taking the offensive weapons is a power ('may take') and only the delivery of the weapons so taken to the Court or officer is mandatory. The Gujarat SOP's mandatory phrasing is recorded here as the binding_gujarat restatement and does not change the canonical requirement.

conflicts.description: The statute and the binding Gujarat SOP differ on whether the search of an arrested person is a power or a duty. BNSS 49(1) is permissive as to the search itself: the officer making the arrest may search such person and place in safe custody all articles other than necessary wearing apparel found upon him, and where any article is seized a receipt shall be given — only the receipt limb (and, under s.49(2), the rule that a woman is searched only by another woman with strict regard to decency) is mandatory. guj_cid_29_sops_2024 SOP 11 p.24-49 (binding_gujarat) instead directs that the officer 'shall search the arrested person forthwith and, after taking proper action, seize all articles found and keep them in safe custody (Section 49(1) BNSS); give a receipt (seizure list) of the seized articles to the arrested person'.
conflicts.resolution: The statute sets the floor and is stated permissively in the canonical text, because a lower-authority source cannot strengthen a higher one. The Gujarat direction is not discarded: within Gujarat, the binding CID SOP requires the search to be made forthwith, so a Gujarat officer must search — but that mandate is a binding_gujarat administrative direction layered on top of BNSS 49, not a requirement of the section itself, and it must not be cited as though the statute compelled it. The mandatory receipt and the woman-searched-by-woman rule are mandatory under the statute in either reading.

conflicts.description: kerala_police_sop_2020 (pp.162, 164, per CrPC 167 as it stood) states the initial remand shall be to judicial custody and police custody can be granted only within the FIRST 15 days of remand; BNSS 187 (2023) allows the 15 days of police custody to be taken in whole or in parts at any time during the initial 40 days (60-day cases) or 60 days (90-day cases).
conflicts.resolution: Canonical text follows BNSS 187 (law); the Kerala first-15-days rule is superseded and retained only inside this conflict record.

conflicts.description: delhi_compendium_2024 (Scenario 11 pp.104 and 108, Scenario 12 p.115) states that under Sec 187 BNSS the IO can take a total of 15 days of Police Custody Remand in parts 'up to 40 days from the date of arrest of the accused'. BNSS 187 makes the 15-day police custody available during the initial forty days only where the total detention period is sixty days; where the offence is punishable with death, imprisonment for life or imprisonment for ten years or more, the window is the initial sixty days of a ninety-day period.
conflicts.resolution: The law layer prevails. The canonical text carries the statutory 40/60-day windows and the 60/90-day outer caps, and the Delhi formulation is retained in details[] and in the source stack as an incomplete statement of the same provision; the two figures have not been averaged. Which window applies in a given case turns on the punishment prescribed for the BNS section invoked, so the IO must check the punishment prescribed for the section actually invoked rather than assume a window.

conflicts.description: delhi_compendium_2024 Scenario 17 p.161 states the IO can take 15 days of Police Custody Remand, in parts, 'up to 60 days from the date of arrest'. BNSS 187 allows the 15 days in whole or in parts only within the initial 40 days (60-day cases) or 60 days (90-day cases) of the detention period.
conflicts.resolution: Canonical text follows BNSS 187 (law). The Delhi 'up to 60 days from the date of arrest' window is superseded and retained only in this conflict record.

steps.text: When the investigation cannot be completed within the 24 hours allowed by BNSS 58 and the accusation appears well-founded, the officer (not below the rank of Sub-Inspector) transmits the case-diary entries to, and forwards the accused before, the nearest Magistrate with a remand application. Total detention pending investigation cannot exceed 90 days for offences punishable with death, life imprisonment or 10 years or more, and 60 days for other offences; on expiry the accused has a right to default bail if he furnishes it. Where no Judicial Magistrate is available, an empowered Executive Magistrate may authorize detention up to 7 days (counted within the overall period). steps.text: After issuing the proclamation, the Court may, for reasons recorded in writing, at any time order attachment of any movable or immovable property (or both) of the proclaimed person; an order made simultaneously with the proclamation requires the Court's satisfaction, by affidavit or otherwise, that he is about to dispose of his property or remove it from the Court's jurisdiction. Before applying, the IO identifies the movable and immovable property of the accused's independent ownership, prepares a detailed list and produces it in Court with the grounds. Attachment modes: movable property and debts by seizure, appointment of a receiver, a written prohibitory order, or any combination; revenue-paying land through the Collector of the district in which it is situated; other immovable property by taking possession, a receiver, or a prohibitory order on rent or delivery. Property outside the ordering Court's district is attached when the order is endorsed by the District Magistrate of the district where the property is situated. Livestock and perishables may be ordered sold at once, the proceeds abiding the Court's order; the attached property is finally disposed of as directed in the final judgment.
legal_basis: BNSS 85

steps.text: The Court publishes a written proclamation requiring the person to appear at a specified place and time not less than 30 days from the date of publication. Publication is made by: (a) public reading in a conspicuous place of the town or village where he ordinarily resides; (b) affixture to a conspicuous part of his house or homestead, or of such town or village; and (c) affixture to a conspicuous part of the Court-house; the Court may also direct publication in a daily newspaper circulating in the place where he ordinarily resides. The Court's written statement that publication was duly made is conclusive evidence of compliance. The IO carries out the execution/publication of the proclamation.
legal_basis: BNSS 84
steps.deadline: Appearance date in the proclamation not less than 30 days from the date of publication

details.text: Gujarat practice: also execute the proclamation personally on the accused or upon any one adult person in his family, obtaining proper acknowledgement where a copy is so given; and affix or paste it, in the presence of at least two independent witnesses, upon the entrance door of the house/dwelling where he resides and at an easily visible place in public buildings such as the Court building and the Panchayat office.
details.citation: Twenty-Nine Standard Operating Procedures - C.I.D. Crime & Railways, Gujarat Police, circular PRC/Circular-SOP-1/656/2024 dated 29/10/2024

sources.citation: Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023

conflicts.description: guj_cid_29_sops_2024 SOP 15 (p.70) lists the modes as personal service on the accused, service on an adult family member, two-witness affixture at the dwelling entrance and public buildings, and optional newspaper publication; BNSS 84 prescribes as mandatory public reading in the town/village, affixture at the house/homestead and affixture at the Court-house, with newspaper publication optional.
conflicts.resolution: Canonical text follows the BNSS 84 mandatory publication modes (law); the SOP 15 personal-service-with-acknowledgement and public-building affixture practice is retained as additional Gujarat procedure in details.

ticks.do: Obtain from the Court a written proclamation requiring the person to appear at a specified place and time not less than 30 days from the date of publication [BNSS 84].
Carry out the execution and publication of the proclamation as the investigating officer.
Publish the proclamation by each of the following means:
sub: (a) Public reading in a conspicuous place of the town or village where he ordinarily resides.
(b) Affixture to a conspicuous part of his house or homestead, or of such town or village.
(c) Affixture to a conspicuous part of the Court-house.
notes: The Court may also direct publication in a daily newspaper circulating in the place where he ordinarily resides.

ticks.do: Obtain the Court's written statement that publication was duly made.
notes: That written statement is conclusive evidence of compliance.

steps.title: Publish the Court's proclamation in the prescribed manner
steps.triage_why: duty of another authority, not the IO

steps.text: If, despite necessary and sufficient efforts, the arrest warrant could not be executed for a period exceeding one month (30 days), apply before the Magistrate for issuing a proclamation of absconding under Section 84 BNSS (precondition: the Court has reason to believe the person against whom the warrant was issued has absconded or is concealing himself so that the warrant cannot be executed).
legal_basis: BNSS 84
steps.deadline: Apply once the warrant has remained unexecuted for a period exceeding one month (30 days) despite necessary and sufficient efforts

ticks.do: Apply before the Magistrate for issuing a proclamation of absconding under Section 84 BNSS once the arrest warrant has remained unexecuted for a period exceeding one month (30 days).
notes: Applies despite necessary and sufficient efforts to execute the warrant.
Precondition: the Court has reason to believe the person against whom the warrant was issued has absconded or is concealing himself so that the warrant cannot be executed.

steps.title: Apply for a proclamation after an unexecuted warrant
steps.triage_why: Procedural step for absconding accused; while important for long-term prosecution, it is not a statutory duty that defeats the case if not done within exactly 30 days.

steps.text: Where the proclamation relates to a person accused of an offence punishable with 10 years' imprisonment or more, life imprisonment or death, and he fails to appear at the specified place and time, the Court may, after making such inquiry as it thinks fit, pronounce him a proclaimed offender and make a declaration to that effect. The publication and conclusive-evidence rules of BNSS 84 apply to that declaration also.
legal_basis: BNSS 84

details.text: If, despite publication/execution of the proclamation, the accused does not appear, the IO shall apply in Court for declaring the proclamation of absconding against him, producing at that time the papers relating to the publication/execution and a copy of the Case Diary; if the Court is satisfied it shall pass the order.
details.citation: Twenty-Nine Standard Operating Procedures - C.I.D. Crime & Railways, Gujarat Police, circular PRC/Circular-SOP-1/656/2024 dated 29/10/2024

details.text: The IO shall obtain from the Court the order declaring the accused a proclaimed offender, carry out the publication/execution of that proclamation in the same manner as above, and produce before the Court the papers showing compliance with the execution work.
details.citation: Twenty-Nine Standard Operating Procedures - C.I.D. Crime & Railways, Gujarat Police, circular PRC/Circular-SOP-1/656/2024 dated 29/10/2024

conflicts.description: guj_cid_29_sops_2024 SOP 15 (p.70) states a person charged with an offence punishable with 10 years or more, life or death who fails to remain present 'shall be declared' a proclaimed offender; BNSS 84 provides that the Court 'may', after making such inquiry as it thinks fit, pronounce the declaration.
conflicts.resolution: Canonical text follows the discretionary wording of BNSS 84 (law); the SOP is read as instructing the IO to seek the declaration, not as compelling the Court.

ticks.do: Establish that the proclamation relates to a person accused of an offence punishable with 10 years' imprisonment or more, life imprisonment or death [BNSS 84].
Establish that he has failed to appear at the specified place and time.
Move the Court to pronounce him a proclaimed offender and make a declaration to that effect.
notes: The Court may do so after making such inquiry as it thinks fit.

ticks.do: Apply the publication and conclusive-evidence rules of BNSS 84 to that declaration also.

steps.title: Obtain a declaration of proclaimed offender status
steps.triage_why: Describes the Court's power to declare a proclaimed offender; this is a judicial action, not an IO's investigative duty.

steps.text: If the accused is suspected to have travelled, or is likely to travel, abroad, seek a Look Out Circular: the IO makes a written request with details and reasons to the officer notified by the MHA circular, who alone gives directions for opening the LOC by passing an order; the request goes in the prescribed proforma to the Deputy Director, Bureau of Immigration, and must carry the approval of an officer not below the notified ranks (District Magistrate or SP of the district concerned, Joint Secretary in the State Government, Deputy Secretary to the Government of India, or the specified equivalents in CBI, NCB, DRI/CBDT/CBEC, IB/BoI, R&AW, NIA, Enforcement Directorate, Protector of Emigrants or the designated Interpol officer); LOCs may also issue as per the directions of any Criminal Court in India. Recourse to an LOC lies in cognizable offences under penal law where the accused deliberately evades arrest or does not appear despite non-bailable warrants and is likely to leave the country (Sumer Singh Salkan v. Asstt. Director, Delhi HC, 11.8.2010).
legal_basis: MHA Office Memorandum No. 25016/31/2010-Imm dated 27.10.2010
steps.deadline: LOC valid one year from the date of issue; renewal must be requested before expiry or the name is automatically removed (exceptions: ban-entry, loss-of-passport, impounding-of-passport, and Court/Interpol LOCs)
steps.applies_when: Accused evading arrest/NBWs with likelihood of leaving or having left India

details.text: An LOC is valid for one year and can be extended before expiry of the one-year period, failing which it is automatically closed by the Immigration Officer concerned; requests must come from the Central or State Government in the prescribed form and only from officers of the specified rank, though criminal courts dealing with criminal law enforcement can issue directions resulting in an LOC (Vikram Sharma v. Union of India, Delhi HC, 26.7.2010).
details.citation: Kerala Police - Standard Operating Procedure: Investigation & Prosecution in General (SOP Series), State Police Chief, 01.11.2020

details.text: The subject of an LOC must join the investigation by appearing before the IO, surrender before the court concerned, or satisfy the court that the LOC was wrongly issued; he may also approach the officer who ordered its issuance. The LOC can be withdrawn by the authority that issued it and can also be rescinded by the trial court where the case is pending, on an application by the person concerned.
details.citation: Kerala Police - Standard Operating Procedure: Investigation & Prosecution in General (SOP Series), State Police Chief, 01.11.2020

details.text: The name and designation of the officer signing the LOC proforma must invariably be mentioned, without which the request will not be entertained.
details.citation: Kerala Police - Standard Operating Procedure: Investigation & Prosecution in General (SOP Series), State Police Chief, 01.11.2020

details.text: Provide the originator's contact details in column VI of the proforma and the contact telephone/mobile number of the respective control room to ensure proper communication and effective follow-up action.
details.citation: Kerala Police - Standard Operating Procedure: Investigation & Prosecution in General (SOP Series), State Police Chief, 01.11.2020

details.text: An LOC cannot be opened unless a minimum of three identifying parameters, apart from sex and nationality, are available — though it can also be issued if the name and passport particulars are available; constantly review LOC requests and proactively provide additional parameters to minimise harassment to genuine passengers.
details.citation: Kerala Police - Standard Operating Procedure: Investigation & Prosecution in General (SOP Series), State Police Chief, 01.11.2020

details.text: The details in column IV regarding 'reason for opening LOC' must invariably be provided, without which the subject will not be arrested/detained; where there is no cognizable offence the subject cannot be detained, arrested or prevented from leaving the country and the agency can only request to be informed about his arrival/departure. The legal liability for action taken by the immigration authorities under the LOC rests with the originating agency.
details.citation: Kerala Police - Standard Operating Procedure: Investigation & Prosecution in General (SOP Series), State Police Chief, 01.11.2020

details.text: Requests cannot emanate from statutory bodies such as the NCW, NHRC and the National Commission for Protection of Children's Rights; such requests with full facts are first brought to the notice of the police, and the SP concerned then makes the LOC request upon an assessment of the situation and strictly per the prescribed procedure.
details.citation: Kerala Police - Standard Operating Procedure: Investigation & Prosecution in General (SOP Series), State Police Chief, 01.11.2020

details.text: In exceptional cases LOCs can be issued without complete parameters and/or case details against CI suspects, terrorists and anti-national elements in the larger national interest.
details.citation: Kerala Police - Standard Operating Procedure: Investigation & Prosecution in General (SOP Series), State Police Chief, 01.11.2020

details.text: The LOC proforma specifies the action expected from the Immigration Check Point: inform of arrival/departure; seize travel documents; prevent entry; prevent departure; or detain and hand over to the local police — alongside personal particulars, physical description, passport details, the reason for opening the LOC (FIR number, sections, police station, district or wanted-by-court details) and the originator's particulars.
details.citation: Kerala Police - Standard Operating Procedure: Investigation & Prosecution in General (SOP Series), State Police Chief, 01.11.2020

details.text: The period of retention specified in the proforma cannot exceed 12 months; renewal requests are made by the competent authority from time to time or yearly.
details.citation: Kerala Police - Standard Operating Procedure: Investigation & Prosecution in General (SOP Series), State Police Chief, 01.11.2020

steps.triage_why: Preventative measure to stop flight; failure to do so is a risk but does not inherently invalidate the evidence or the prosecution's legal standing.

steps.text: Where intimation of the proclamation order has been given to the accused and the absconding accused still does not remain present in Court by the appointed date: if the investigation is in progress, add Section 209 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita 2023 against the accused in the charge-sheet; if the investigation against him has been completed, register a fresh complaint under BNS Section 209 against the person declared an absconder.
legal_basis: BNS 209

Register a fresh complaint under BNS Section 209 against the person declared an absconder where the investigation against him has been completed.

steps.title: Proceed under BNS 209 against a non-appearing absconder
steps.triage_why: Administrative step to add charges for non-appearance; does not affect the primary murder/loot charges.

steps.text: Investigate the cognizable offence and take steps for effecting the arrest of the accused. If, during the investigation, the accused evades arrest or moves about in concealment and does not cooperate, apply to the Court for the issue of an arrest warrant; the IO shall remain personally present in Court and state to the Magistrate the reasonable grounds for issuing it. After obtaining the warrant, the IO may give it to any police officer for execution, and shall mention in the Case Diary the action taken for its execution.

details.text: Where sufficient evidence justifying arrest is collected but the accused is found evading arrest, first issue notices/summons to secure his presence to join the investigation and document all efforts taken; make enquiries with his relatives, friends and other persons likely to be aware of his movements and warn them all against harbouring him; if his presence is still not secured, report the facts and apply to the Court for bailable and non-bailable warrants and take all efforts to trace and arrest him.
details.citation: Kerala Police - Standard Operating Procedure: Investigation & Prosecution in General (SOP Series), State Police Chief, 01.11.2020

details.text: The details of all wanted persons may be uploaded on the State Police website (through the State Crime Records Bureau) and circulated amongst other law-enforcement agencies to compel the person to join the investigation.

steps.title: Obtain and execute a warrant against an evading accused
steps.triage_why: Statutory duty to investigate cognizable offences and effect arrest; failure to pursue the accused in a murder case is a fundamental failure of duty.

steps.text: For a fugitive suspected to be, or likely to go, abroad, additionally seek an Interpol Red Notice through the National Central Bureau using the prescribed Red Notice form (identity particulars; caution indicators such as armed, dangerous, escape risk, suicidal or violent; aliases and nicknames; family details; occupation; languages; regions/countries likely to be visited; identity documents, of which nationality, type and number are mandatory; identification material including photographs, fingerprints, DNA and dental information; physical description; and facts of the case with date, town, country, offence codes and a summary limited to 1000 characters/200 words). For a fugitive wanted for prosecution all fields are mandatory, the arrest warrant should be open dated, and the conduct must be punishable by a maximum deprivation of liberty of at least two years or a more serious penalty; for a fugitive wanted to serve a sentence the person must have at least six months of imprisonment imposed and/or at least six months remaining to be served. A Blue Notice may also be used to collect additional information about a person's identity, location or activities in relation to a crime.
steps.applies_when: Absconder suspected to be, or likely to go, outside India

steps.stage: Specimen signatures, handwriting, finger impressions and voice samples (BNSS 349)
steps.text: Where specimen signatures, finger impressions, handwriting or voice samples are required from any person, including the accused, obtain an order of a Magistrate of the first class who is satisfied that it is expedient for the investigation or proceeding; the person must attend at the specified time and place and furnish the specimen or sample. Ordinarily the person must at some time have been arrested in connection with the investigation or proceeding, but the Magistrate may, for reasons recorded in writing, order specimens or samples from a person who has not been arrested.
legal_basis: Section 349 BNSS 2023
steps.responsible: Magistrate of the first class, on the investigating officer's application
steps.applies_when: Specimen signature, handwriting, finger impression or voice comparison required

conflicts.description: The Delhi compendium prints the provision for taking specimen signatures, finger prints and voice samples as 'section 349 of BNS, 2023' (Scenario 20, p.191). The extraction of that source itself flags the citation, listing it as '349 (specimen signatures, finger prints and voice samples - printed as BNS in source; see notes)'.
conflicts.resolution: Resolved in favour of the law layer. bnss_2023 BNSS 349 ('Power of Magistrate to order person to give specimen signatures or handwriting, etc.') is the provision that empowers a Magistrate of the first class to order any person, including an accused, to give specimen signatures, finger impressions, handwriting or a voice sample, so the compendium's 'BNS' is a misprint for BNSS and the canonical text follows BNSS 349. The compendium's substantive additions - that arrest is not required and that 'any person' covers the complainant and witnesses - agree with BNSS 349, which records the same expansion, and are retained as detail.

conflicts.description: delhi_compendium_2024 states that 'as per Section 349 BNSS, the IO can take samples of handwriting, specimen signatures, finger impressions and voice impressions of any person, including the accused person, without effecting his/their arrest' (Scenario 17 p.160; same statement at Scenario 4 p.42 and Scenario 13 p.128), which reads as a police power and omits the Magistrate entirely; bnss_2023 BNSS 349 vests the power in a Magistrate of the first class who is satisfied that it is expedient, and permits an order against an unarrested person only for reasons recorded in writing.
conflicts.resolution: The law layer prevails: the canonical text keeps the first-class Magistrate's order as mandatory. The two are not blended. The point the compendium was correctly making - that BNSS 349 extends to persons who have not been arrested - survives, but only with the statutory condition that the Magistrate records his reasons in writing.

conflicts.description: delhi_compendium_2024 Scenario 17 p.160 states that 'As per Section 349 BNSS, the IO can take samples of handwriting, specimen signatures, finger impressions and voice impressions of any person, including the accused person, without effecting his/their arrest', omitting the requirement of an order of a Magistrate of the first class. Section 349 BNSS in fact requires such an order, and permits it in respect of a person who has not been arrested only for reasons recorded in writing by the Magistrate.
conflicts.resolution: Law prevails: specimens or samples under Section 349 BNSS may be taken only on the order of a Magistrate of the first class. The Delhi wording is read as making the point that arrest is not a precondition, not as dispensing with the Magistrate's order.

steps.text: Arrest on refusal to give name and residence [BNSS 39]: Where any person who, in the presence of a police officer, has committed or has been accused of committing a non-cognizable offence refuses on demand of such officer to give his name and residence, or gives a name or residence which such officer has reason to believe to be false, the statute says he MAY be arrested by such officer - the arrest is permissive and its stated purpose is limited, 'in order that his name or residence may be ascertained'. When the true name and residence have been ascertained, he SHALL be released on a bond or bail bond, to appear before a Magistrate if so required. If such person is not resident in India, the bail bond shall be secured by a surety or sureties resident in India. If the true name and residence are not ascertained within twenty-four hours from the time of arrest, or if he fails to execute the bond or bail bond or, if so required, to furnish sufficient sureties, he shall forthwith be forwarded to the nearest Magistrate having jurisdiction.
legal_basis: Section 39 BNSS 2023
steps.deadline: Twenty-four hours from the time of arrest - if the true name and residence are not ascertained within this period, the person shall forthwith be forwarded to the nearest Magistrate having jurisdiction (sub-section (3)); 'Forthwith' - forwarding to the nearest Magistrate having jurisdiction once sub-section (3) is triggered

steps.stage: Statutory basis of arrest and identification
steps.text: Search of place entered by person sought to be arrested [BNSS 44]: If any person acting under a warrant of arrest, or any police officer having authority to arrest, has reason to believe that the person to be arrested has entered into, or is within, any place, any person residing in or being in charge of such place SHALL, on demand of such person acting as aforesaid or such police officer, allow him free ingress thereto and afford all reasonable facilities for a search therein. If ingress cannot be obtained under sub-section (1), the statute says it SHALL BE LAWFUL - an enabling permission, not a command - in any case for a person acting under a warrant, and in any case in which a warrant may issue but cannot be obtained without affording the person to be arrested an opportunity of escape, for a police officer to enter such place and search therein, and, in order to effect an entrance, to break open any outer or inner door or window of any house or place, if after notification of his authority and purpose and demand of admittance duly made he cannot otherwise obtain admittance. Where the place is an apartment in the actual occupancy of a female (not being the person to be arrested) who according to custom does not appear in public, such person or police officer SHALL before entering give her notice that she is at liberty to withdraw and SHALL afford her every reasonable facility for withdrawing, and MAY then break open the apartment and enter it. Any police officer or other person authorised to make an arrest MAY also break open any outer or inner door or window of any house or place in order to liberate himself or any other person who, having lawfully entered for the purpose of making an arrest, is detained therein.
legal_basis: Section 44 BNSS 2023

steps.text: Identification of person arrested [BNSS 54]: Where a person is arrested on a charge of committing an offence and his identification by any other person or persons is considered necessary for the purpose of investigation of such offence, the Court having jurisdiction MAY, on the request of the officer in charge of a police station, direct the person so arrested to subject himself to identification by any person or persons in such manner as the Court may deem fit. The power is the Court's and is discretionary; the officer in charge of a police station does not order the identification himself, he requests it. Where the person identifying the person arrested is mentally or physically disabled, such process of identification SHALL take place under the supervision of a Magistrate, who shall take appropriate steps to ensure that such person identifies the person arrested using methods that person is comfortable with, and the identification process SHALL be recorded by any audio-video electronic means. The section has no sub-sections; it is a single provision with one proviso.
legal_basis: Section 54 BNSS 2023

steps.text: Examine witnesses as early as possible — memory fades with lapse of time, and belated examination risks witnesses enriching their account from what they hear from others or filling gaps from imagination — but do not begin interrogation of witnesses until the place of occurrence has been carefully inspected, the scene-of-crime map prepared, searches made and exhibits preserved.

steps.text: Where witnesses could not be contacted within reasonable time and have forgotten all or a substantial part of the occurrence, revive lost memory in two ways: (i) the association method — link the occurrence to a memorable event of about the same date (a sensational political event for an educated witness, a village festival for a rustic villager); (ii) place the witness amidst the surroundings in which he first made his observations — it is advantageous to examine all important witnesses on the spot. Never suggest anything to make the witness testify to matters outside his personal knowledge: trustworthy testimony must come spontaneously, not from suggestions or feelers thrown at him.

steps.text: Identify the class of witness and apply the matching handling technique: (i) interested witnesses (stand to gain from a successful investigation) — tap them fully but do not repose implicit faith without preliminary verification; they are prone to exaggerate, so guard against half-truths lest a false charge be unwittingly brought before a court; (ii) hostile witnesses (stand to lose; generally drawn from the suspect's friends, relatives, associates, receivers or well-wishers) — deal with them tactfully, courteously and firmly, give no advance intimation, take them by surprise and examine them at a place away from friends, associates, lawyers and relations; (iii) disinterested witnesses — devoid of personal motive, their evidence deserves the highest credence but they rarely come forward of their own accord; fix a time convenient to them, develop a common ground of conversation, and approach with utmost civility and politeness without provoking their apathy; (iv) lying witnesses — find the motive for the false information (lack of or incorrect observation, self-interest, interest in the suspect) and shape questions accordingly; let an intentional liar talk as much as he likes until he contradicts himself on material points; (v) unwilling witnesses — discover the cause of the aversion in each case and take steps to remove it; (vi) nervous witnesses — pick up information slowly and gradually, point by point in a systematic fashion, in a conversational manner and in their own surroundings, never with a volley of interrogatories; (vii) child witnesses — use a friendly, almost fatherly tone, ask for their own experiences and not what they heard, keep it a brief and simple conversation, and never put leading or suggestive questions (children tend to answer them affirmatively without understanding their implications); (viii) female witnesses — examine at their residence in the presence of a relation or guardian, with a high standard of decorum and courtesy, requisitioning the services of women police.

steps.text: Have the TI parade conducted preferably by a Magistrate, in a separate place within the jail premises (a parade held in the police station is admissible if there is separate space to conduct it), and hold it without unnecessary delay, as early as possible; explain any delay to the Magistrate with a request to record it in his TI parade report, and also explain the delay in the Case Diary. Police should abstain from conducting TI parades: a parade conducted by a police officer attracts Section 162 CrPC [now BNSS 181], which makes the evidence inadmissible, and identification statements recorded before police, if signed, are hit by the same bar. The Magistrate's memorandum of the TI proceedings is admissible under Section 80 of the Evidence Act without any proof, and the record he makes can be used as a statement under Section 164 CrPC [now BNSS 183]; follow the instructions issued by the State Government for the guidance of Magistrates and jail authorities regarding the conduct of identification proceedings.

details.text: The value of TI evidence is very high when it can be established that the witness, while being examined at the trial, corroborates such evidence; statements made by witnesses in the course of TI proceedings are admissible for the purpose of corroboration under Section 157 of the Evidence Act.

steps.title: Hold the TI parade before a Magistrate without delay
steps.triage_why: TI parades are a matter of prudence to strengthen identification; however, direct identification in court is legally permissible.

steps.text: Test Identification (TI) is the process by which the identity of persons, things or animals concerned in the offence is established as a matter of prudence; it has a two-fold objective — to satisfy the Investigating Officer that a person arrested but not previously known to the witness is concerned in the crime (or that a particular item of property is connected with the case), and to enable the witnesses to satisfy themselves that the person they suspect is really the one they saw in connection with the crime. Hold a TI parade when: (i) the accused was not known to the witnesses before the occurrence; (ii) the witness had the opportunity to observe the accused during the commission of the crime; and (iii) there were sufficient surrounding circumstances facilitating identification of the accused at the time of occurrence. There is no necessity to hold a parade where the accused is well known to the witness. When a witness says he can identify property, accused persons or others connected with the case, record their description in detail, examine the witness properly and record his statement first, and then request the Magistrate to conduct the identification parade (test identification is relevant under Section 9 of the Evidence Act).
legal_basis: Section 9 Indian Evidence Act, 1872

bsa_refs.title: Examination of witnesses
bsa_refs.summary: Examination of witnesses. The section is purely definitional and fixes the names of the three stages of witness examination. s.142(1) provides that the examination of a witness by the party who calls him shall be called his examination-in-chief. s.142(2) provides that the examination of a witness by the adverse party shall be called his cross-examination. s.142(3) provides that the examination of a witness, subsequent to the cross-examination, by the party who called him, shall be called his re-examination. The section therefore does fix who conducts each stage, and it does place re-examination after the cross-examination; what it lays down nothing about is the scope or the content of any of the three examinations. It does not provide that a cross-examination or a re-examination will in fact take place, and it imposes no obligation on any party. The supplied statutory text ends with a Gazette running header and rows of underscores; those are extraction and printing artefacts, not statutory content, and the operative text is only the three definitional sub-sections.
key_requirements: The examination of a witness by the party who calls him shall be called his examination-in-chief.
The examination of a witness by the adverse party shall be called his cross-examination.
The examination of a witness, subsequent to the cross-examination, by the party who called him, shall be called his re-examination.
bsa_refs.investigation_relevance: The section creates no duty and no power for the investigating officer: it does not require him to collect, verify or annex anything, and it imposes no obligation on any party. Its only value in an investigation file is vocabulary, so that an officer reading a trial record or a later evidence provision knows that examination by the party calling the witness is the examination-in-chief, examination by the adverse party is the cross-examination, and examination by the calling party after the cross-examination is the re-examination. The section does not itself provide that any witness will be cross-examined; the working expectation that prosecution witnesses face cross-examination comes from trial practice and from other provisions, not from s.142, and is therefore not a basis for treating this section as bearing on the IO's own work.

bsa_refs.title: Confession to police officer
bsa_refs.summary: Bars proof of confessions connected with the police. Sub-section (1) provides that no confession made to a police officer shall be proved as against a person accused of any offence; the sub-section itself contains no 'unless' and no reference to a Magistrate. Sub-section (2) separately provides that no confession made by any person while he is in the custody of a police officer, unless it is made in the immediate presence of a Magistrate, shall be proved against him; that immediate-presence exception sits inside sub-section (2) and relieves only the custody bar. The proviso to sub-section (2) creates the discovery exception: when any fact is deposed to as discovered in consequence of information received from a person accused of any offence, in the custody of a police officer, so much of that information, whether it amounts to a confession or not, as relates distinctly to the fact discovered may be proved. That permission is worded 'may be proved' - it permits proof of that portion, it does not require it. Both sub-sections bar only confessions.
key_requirements: Sub-section (1): no confession made to a police officer shall be proved as against a person accused of any offence; the sub-section itself states this without any unless or exception and makes no reference to a Magistrate.
Sub-section (2): no confession made by any person while he is in the custody of a police officer shall be proved against him.

The immediate presence of a Magistrate is an exception carried within sub-section (2) and relieves only the custody bar; a confession made in the immediate presence of a Magistrate is outside that bar.

The proviso reaches only information received from a person accused of any offence who is in the custody of a police officer, and only where a fact is deposed to as discovered in consequence of that information.

Where those conditions are met, so much of that information, whether it amounts to a confession or not, as relates distinctly to the fact discovered may be proved; the proviso permits proof of that portion, it does not direct that it be proved.
bsa_refs.investigation_relevance: Subject to the discovery proviso, the IO cannot prove a confession made to him; and a confession made by a person while he is in the custody of a police officer cannot be proved against him unless it was made in the immediate presence of a Magistrate. The bar is confined to confessions, so this section does not by itself exclude statements of the accused that are not confessional, though other law may restrict their use. Sub-section (1) carries no Magistrate exception: the immediate-presence exception sits inside sub-section (2) and relieves only the custody bar, so what it saves is a confession made in a Magistrate's immediate presence by a person in police custody, not a confession made to a police officer. Subject to the discovery proviso, a confession made to a police officer cannot be proved against the accused. The other route on the text is the discovery proviso, which is available only where the information came from a person accused of an offence who was in the custody of a police officer, and only where a fact is deposed to as discovered in consequence of that information; the IO must record the information, effect the recovery, have the discovery deposed to, and confine the portion sought to be proved to so much of the information as relates distinctly to the fact actually discovered. Even then the proviso only permits that portion to be proved.

steps.text: Handle extra-judicial confessions for what they are worth: (i) a confession before members of the public is not given much weight in court — the courts require the exact words used by the accused as nearly as possible and some other supporting evidence, so never remain satisfied with this sort of evidence alone, though in conjunction with other evidence it has great value in fixing guilt; (ii) if an accused on being arrested is willing to confess to a police officer, record it in the case diary, as far as practicable in the accused's same words and in the first person, with the officer's certificate at the end that it was correctly recorded — such a confession is not admissible except under Section 27 of the Evidence Act, and only so much of the statement as leads to the discovery is reproduced in the recovery mahazar, which is attested by witnesses; (iii) record the accused's version even if the statement does not amount to a confession, since it may help further investigation and collection of evidence.
