steps.text: Never build the case on the confession of a co-accused: it is very weak evidence requiring corroboration, is not substantive evidence against the other accused, and no conviction of the other accused can be based on it even where it led to the discovery of a material fact under Section 27 of the Evidence Act. It may be considered under Section 30 of the Evidence Act only by the court trying the case, and only when: (i) the statement is a confession of the person who makes it; (ii) it affects the confessing prisoner and his fellow prisoner; (iii) the confessor is tried jointly with the others; (iv) the trial is for the same offence (an offence under the same section of law); (v) the joint trial is a legal one; and (vi) the confession is proved. The Investigating Officer must be able to show that the maker implicated himself in all the offences in which he implicates the co-accused, and must make all efforts to collect other collateral and corroborative evidence to support the case.
legal_basis: Section 30 Indian Evidence Act, 1872

steps.text: When the accused narrates his involvement to the police (for investigative use), recording of the confession can be done in one of three ways — sentence by sentence, stage by stage, or heard completely and then drawn up as a comprehensive statement — keeping in mind: (i) name, parentage, residence etc. of the suspect and associates; (ii) acts showing motive and preparation for the crime; (iii) actual commission of the crime with details of time and manner; (iv) subsequent conduct — details of retreat, division and disposal of property; (v) information on the same lines regarding previous offences; (vi) names and activities of receivers, accomplices and harbourers. The IO may record just the relevant information, which may give further clues to the crime; the exercise may become infructuous if the accused, once produced in court, decides not to confess, but details obtained from him earlier may still be useful in further unfolding the truth.

steps.text: Treat statements recorded by police under Section 161 CrPC [now BNSS 180] as non-substantive evidence: they are not evidence for the prosecution, cannot be used against the accused, and shall not be used for any purpose except to contradict a prosecution witness in the manner provided by Section 145 of the Evidence Act under the proviso to Section 162(1) CrPC [now BNSS 181] — the defence may so use them, and the Public Prosecutor may with the court's permission, including to cross-examine a prosecution witness who turns hostile; a part so used may also be used in re-examination, but only to explain matters referred to in cross-examination. An omission to state a fact may amount to a contradiction if it appears significant and otherwise relevant in the context (a question of fact). The bar does not apply to statements falling within Section 32(1) of the Evidence Act [now BSA 2023 s.26(a)] (dying declarations) or to Section 27 discoveries, which the prosecution can use as evidence; and the relevant portions of a hostile witness's evidence remain usable in appropriate situations, at least to corroborate the evidence of other independent witnesses in material particulars.
legal_basis: Section 162 CrPC [now BNSS 181]
Sections 27 and 32(1) Indian Evidence Act, 1872
Section 145 Indian Evidence Act, 1872

bsa_refs.title: Cases in which statement of relevant fact by person who is dead or cannot be found, etc., is relevant
bsa_refs.summary: Makes certain out-of-court statements of an unavailable person relevant facts in themselves. The opening paragraph sets the gateway for every clause: the maker must be dead, or cannot be found, or has become incapable of giving evidence, or is a person whose attendance cannot be procured without an amount of delay or expense which under the circumstances of the case appears to the Court unreasonable. Clause (a) covers a statement by a person as to the cause of his death, or as to any of the circumstances of the transaction which resulted in his death, in cases in which the cause of that person's death comes into question, and makes such statements relevant whether or not he was under expectation of death when he made them and whatever the nature of the proceeding in which the cause of his death comes into question. Clause (b) covers a statement made by such a person in the ordinary course of business, and in particular an entry or memorandum made by him in books kept in the ordinary course of business or in the discharge of professional duty, an acknowledgement written or signed by him of the receipt of money, goods, securities or property of any kind, a document used in commerce written or signed by him, or the date of a letter or other document usually dated, written or signed by him; the gateway is the ordinary course of business, and the words 'in the discharge of professional duty' qualify the books kept rather than opening a separate gateway. Clause (c) covers a statement against the maker's pecuniary or proprietary interest, or which if true would expose him or would have exposed him to a criminal prosecution or to a suit for damages. Clause (d) covers a statement of opinion as to the existence of any public right or custom or matter of public or general interest of whose existence he would have been likely to be aware, made before any controversy as to that right, custom or matter had arisen. Clause (e) covers a statement as to the existence of a relationship by blood, marriage or adoption where the maker had special means of knowledge of that relationship and the statement was made before the question in dispute was raised. Clause (f) covers a statement as to such a relationship between persons deceased, made in a will or deed relating to the affairs of the family to which the deceased belonged, in a family pedigree, or upon a tombstone, family portrait or other thing on which such statements are usually made, and made before the question in dispute was raised. Clause (g) covers a statement contained in any deed, will or other document relating to a transaction of the kind specified in clause (a) of section 11, and clause (h) a statement made by a number of persons expressing feelings or impressions on their part relevant to the matter in question. The section carries illustrations (a) to (n).
key_requirements: Written or verbal statements of relevant facts made by a person who is dead, who cannot be found, who has become incapable of giving evidence, or whose attendance cannot be procured without an amount of delay or expense which under the circumstances of the case appears to the Court unreasonable, are themselves relevant facts in the cases set out in clauses (a) to (h); this unavailability gateway applies to every clause.

Clause (a): where the cause of a person's death comes into question, his statement as to the cause of his death, or as to any of the circumstances of the transaction which resulted in his death, is relevant.

Clause (a) further provides that such statements are relevant whether or not the maker was, at the time when they were made, under expectation of death, and whatever the nature of the proceeding in which the cause of his death comes into question.

Clause (b): a statement made by such a person in the ordinary course of business is relevant, and in particular an entry or memorandum made by him in books kept in the ordinary course of business or in the discharge of professional duty, an acknowledgement written or signed by him of the receipt of money, goods, securities or property of any kind, a document used in commerce written or signed by him, or the date of a letter or other document usually dated, written or signed by him. The gateway is the ordinary course of business; 'in the discharge of professional duty' qualifies the books kept and is not an independent gateway.

Clause (c): a statement against the pecuniary or proprietary interest of the person making it, or which if true would expose him or would have exposed him to a criminal prosecution or to a suit for damages, is relevant.

Clause (d): a statement giving such a person's opinion as to the existence of any public right or custom or matter of public or general interest, of the existence of which he would have been likely to be aware, is relevant, and only where it was made before any controversy as to that right, custom or matter had arisen.

Clause (e): a statement as to the existence of a relationship by blood, marriage or adoption is relevant only where the person making it had special means of knowledge of that relationship and the statement was made before the question in dispute was raised.

Clause (f): a statement as to the existence of a relationship by blood, marriage or adoption between persons deceased is relevant only where it is made in a will or deed relating to the affairs of the family to which any such deceased person belonged, or in a family pedigree, or upon a tombstone, family portrait or other thing on which such statements are usually made, and only where it was made before the question in dispute was raised.
Clause (g): a statement contained in any deed, will or other document which relates to a transaction of the kind specified in clause (a) of section 11 is relevant.
Clause (h): a statement made by a number of persons and expressing feelings or impressions on their part relevant to the matter in question is relevant.
bsa_refs.investigation_relevance: This is the dying declaration provision. Under clause (a), a statement by the deceased as to the cause of his death or as to any of the circumstances of the transaction which resulted in his death is relevant where the cause of death comes into question, whether or not he was under expectation of death and whatever the proceeding, so the IO must record it fully, preserve it, and be ready to prove the ground of unavailability relied on: death, that the maker cannot be found, incapacity to give evidence, or that attendance cannot be procured without delay or expense the Court finds unreasonable in the circumstances. That unavailability gateway applies to every clause, not only clause (a). For the business, interest, relationship, public-right and document clauses the IO must seize the original entry, book, acknowledgement, deed, pedigree or memorial and collect evidence of when and by whom the statement was made. Clause (b) turns on the statement having been made in the ordinary course of business, so the IO should establish that course of business and not merely that the maker was discharging a professional duty; the professional-duty words qualify the books kept. Clause (d) additionally requires that the maker be a person who, if the public right, custom or matter existed, would have been likely to be aware of its existence, and it fails if the statement post-dates the controversy as to that right, custom or matter. Clause (e) additionally requires that the maker had special means of knowledge of the relationship, and clause (f) is confined to relationships between persons deceased and to statements made in a will or deed relating to family affairs, a family pedigree, a tombstone, family portrait or other thing on which such statements are usually made; under both, the statement must pre-date the question in dispute. Clause (g) cross-refers to clause (a) of section 11, which is not set out here, so nothing about its content can be worked out from this section alone. The section fixes relevance only, and the unreasonableness of delay or expense is for the Court.
time_limits: Clause (d): the statement must have been made before any controversy as to the public right, custom or matter had arisen.
Clause (e): the statement must have been made before the question in dispute was raised.
Clause (f): the statement must have been made before the question in dispute was raised.
supporting_text:
Statements, written or verbal, of relevant facts made by a person who is dead, or
who cannot be found, or who has become incapable of giving evidence, or whose attendance
cannot be procured without an amount of delay or expense which under the circumstances
of the case appears to the Court unreasonable, are themselves relevant facts in the following
cases, namely:—

(a) when the statement is made by a person as to the cause of his death, or as
to any of the circumstances of the transaction which resulted in his death, in cases in
which the cause of that person's death comes into question.

Such statements are
relevant whether the person who made them was or was not, at the time when they
were made, under expectation of death, and whatever may be the nature of the
proceeding in which the cause of his death comes into question;

(b) when the statement was made by such person in the ordinary course of
business, and in particular when it consists of any entry or memorandum made by him
in books kept in the ordinary course of business, or in the discharge of professional
duty; or of an acknowledgement written or signed by him of the receipt of money,
goods, securities or property of any kind; or of a document used in commerce written
or signed by him; or of the date of a letter or other document usually dated, written or
signed by him;

(d) when the statement gives the opinion of any such person, as to the existence
of any public right or custom or matter of public or general interest, of the existence of
which, if it existed, he would have been likely to be aware, and when such statement
was made before any controversy as to such right, custom or matter had arisen;

(e) when the statement relates to the existence of any relationship by blood,
marriage or adoption between persons as to whose relationship by blood, marriage or
adoption the person making the statement had special means of knowledge, and
when the statement was made before the question in dispute was raised;

(f) when the statement relates to the existence of any relationship by blood,
marriage or adoption between persons deceased, and is made in any will or deed
relating to the affairs of the family to which any such deceased person belonged, or in
any family pedigree, or upon any tombstone, family portrait or other thing on which
such statements are usually made, and when such statement was made before the
question in dispute was raised;

(g) when the statement is contained in any deed, will or other document which
relates to any such transaction as is specified in clause (a) of section 11;

(h) when the statement was made by a number of persons, and expressed
feelings or impressions on their part relevant to the matter in question.

steps.text: Select two or more independent and respectable persons as panch witnesses. After preparation of the panchnama, have the panchas read its contents; if a panch is illiterate, read the panchnama over to him and make an endorsement on it that the contents were read over to him. Where there was no source of light at the time of making the panchnama, mention how the source of light was managed to prepare it (guidance may be taken from Section 100(4) and (5) CrPC [now BNSS 103]). Where there is no eye witness to the offence and the case rests wholly on circumstantial evidence, the panchnama carries immense value.
legal_basis: Section 100(4)-(5) CrPC [now BNSS 103]

steps.text: Apply the settled credibility principles when selecting and citing witnesses: a related witness is not equivalent to an interested witness — a witness is 'interested' only where he derives some benefit from the litigation or from seeing the accused punished — and relationship alone does not affect credibility or justify rejection of the testimony as a matter of rule; an injured witness has a special status in law with a built-in guarantee of his presence at the scene (probe what he was doing there at that hour, his relation to the parties, and how he came to be injured) and his testimony can be acted upon even without corroboration absent grounds for rejection based on major contradictions and discrepancies; an eye-witness must have been capable of adequate vision with light adequate enough to see and identify, and must not be a stock witness — appreciation of his evidence depends on the accuracy of his original observation, the correctness and extent of what he remembers, and his veracity; the evidence of police officials cannot be discarded merely because it is not corroborated by an independent witness or because they belong to the police force (Kripal Singh v. The State of Rajasthan 2019 All SCR (Online) 145), though the rule of prudence requires a greater degree of scrutiny and, as a precaution, corroboration by some independent witness; courts insist on the testimony of an independent witness only where some doubt exists — non-examination of an independent witness is not a serious lacuna where the prosecution evidence inspires confidence (independent witnesses are often unwilling to come forward, leaving the prosecution to fall back on friends and family of the victim); the evidence of interested and of trap witnesses is not discarded but scrutinized with utmost care and caution; and chance-witness evidence may be reliable or unreliable depending on the circumstances.

steps.text: Where the eyewitness account and the medical evidence diverge, remember that medical evidence does not itself establish the guilt or innocence of the accused — it provides expert opinion based upon objective, indisputable facts which helps evaluate the reliability and credibility of other witnesses — and that conviction cannot be based solely on medical evidence, which must be corroborated by other evidence. On a conflict of opinion between experts, obtain further opinion from senior experts. Where the eyewitness account is found credible and trustworthy, medical evidence pointing to alternative possibilities is not accepted as conclusive; where the two are not of exactly similar opinion yet both lead to the same story there is no contradiction (Jheena v. State of M.P. 1986 Cri LJ 1375 (MP)); the Court first examines the discrepancies carefully and makes every effort at a harmonious construction of the medical and eyewitness evidence — but on a contradiction between ocular testimony and medical evidence, ocular testimony is neither accepted nor rejected at the instance of the medical evidence and the accused gets the benefit of doubt (Mahar Singh v. State of Punjab AIR 1981 SC 1578).

steps.stage: Statutory rules on statements to the police
steps.text: Statements to police and use thereof [BNSS 181]: Sub-section (1) is prohibitory: no statement made by any person to a police officer in the course of an investigation under this Chapter shall, if reduced to writing, be signed by the person making it; nor shall any such statement or any record thereof, whether in a police diary or otherwise, or any part of such statement or record, be used for any purpose, save as hereinafter provided, at any inquiry or trial in respect of any offence under investigation at the time when such statement was made. The proviso creates a narrow permissive exception: when any witness is called for the prosecution in such inquiry or trial whose statement has been reduced into writing as aforesaid, any part of his statement, if duly proved, "may be used by the accused, and with the permission of the Court, by the prosecution, to contradict such witness" in the manner provided by section 148 of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 - this is an option, not an obligation, and the prosecution's use additionally needs the Court's permission. And when any part of such statement is so used, any part thereof may also be used in the re-examination of such witness, but for the purpose only of explaining any matter referred to in his cross-examination. Sub-section (2) provides that nothing in the section shall be deemed to apply to any statement falling within the provisions of clause (a) of section 26 of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023, or to affect the provisions of the proviso to sub-section (2) of section 23 of that Adhiniyam. The Explanation states that an omission to state a fact or circumstance in the statement referred to in sub-section (1) "may amount to contradiction" if the same appears to be significant and otherwise relevant having regard to the context in which such omission occurs, and whether any omission amounts to a contradiction in the particular context shall be a question of fact.
legal_basis: Section 181 BNSS 2023

(Editorial note for KB use only, NOT printed in section 181: the statements in question are those a police officer may reduce into writing under section 180(3); section 181 itself does not cite section 180.)

bsa_refs.title: Cases in which statement of relevant fact by person who is dead or cannot be found, etc., is relevant
bsa_refs.summary: Makes certain out-of-court statements of an unavailable person relevant facts in themselves. The opening paragraph sets the gateway for every clause: the maker must be dead, or cannot be found, or has become incapable of giving evidence, or is a person whose attendance cannot be procured without an amount of delay or expense which under the circumstances of the case appears to the Court unreasonable. Clause (a) covers a statement by a person as to the cause of his death, or as to any of the circumstances of the transaction which resulted in his death, in cases in which the cause of that person's death comes into question, and makes such statements relevant whether or not he was under expectation of death when he made them and whatever the nature of the proceeding in which the cause of his death comes into question. Clause (b) covers a statement made by such a person in the ordinary course of business, and in particular an entry or memorandum made by him in books kept in the ordinary course of business or in the discharge of professional duty, an acknowledgement written or signed by him of the receipt of money, goods, securities or property of any kind, a document used in commerce written or signed by him, or the date of a letter or other document usually dated, written or signed by him; the gateway is the ordinary course of business, and the words 'in the discharge of professional duty' qualify the books kept rather than opening a separate gateway. Clause (c) covers a statement against the maker's pecuniary or proprietary interest, or which if true would expose him or would have exposed him to a criminal prosecution or to a suit for damages. Clause (d) covers a statement of opinion as to the existence of any public right or custom or matter of public or general interest of whose existence he would have been likely to be aware, made before any controversy as to that right, custom or matter had arisen. Clause (e) covers a statement as to the existence of a relationship by blood, marriage or adoption where the maker had special means of knowledge of that relationship and the statement was made before the question in dispute was raised. Clause (f) covers a statement as to such a relationship between persons deceased, made in a will or deed relating to the affairs of the family to which the deceased belonged, in a family pedigree, or upon a tombstone, family portrait or other thing on which such statements are usually made, and made before the question in dispute was raised. Clause (g) covers a statement contained in any deed, will or other document relating to a transaction of the kind specified in clause (a) of section 11, and clause (h) a statement made by a number of persons expressing feelings or impressions on their part relevant to the matter in question. The section carries illustrations (a) to (n).
key_requirements: Written or verbal statements of relevant facts made by a person who is dead, who cannot be found, who has become incapable of giving evidence, or whose attendance cannot be procured without an amount of delay or expense which under the circumstances of the case appears to the Court unreasonable, are themselves relevant facts in the cases set out in clauses (a) to (h); this unavailability gateway applies to every clause.

Clause (a): where the cause of a person's death comes into question, his statement as to the cause of his death, or as to any of the circumstances of the transaction which resulted in his death, is relevant.

Clause (a) further provides that such statements are relevant whether or not the maker was, at the time when they were made, under expectation of death, and whatever the nature of the proceeding in which the cause of his death comes into question.

Clause (b): a statement made by such a person in the ordinary course of business is relevant, and in particular an entry or memorandum made by him in books kept in the ordinary course of business or in the discharge of professional duty, an acknowledgement written or signed by him of the receipt of money, goods, securities or property of any kind, a document used in commerce written or signed by him, or the date of a letter or other document usually dated, written or signed by him. The gateway is the ordinary course of business; 'in the discharge of professional duty' qualifies the books kept and is not an independent gateway.

Clause (c): a statement against the pecuniary or proprietary interest of the person making it, or which if true would expose him or would have exposed him to a criminal prosecution or to a suit for damages, is relevant.

Clause (d): a statement giving such a person's opinion as to the existence of any public right or custom or matter of public or general interest, of the existence of which he would have been likely to be aware, is relevant, and only where it was made before any controversy as to that right, custom or matter had arisen.

Clause (e): a statement as to the existence of a relationship by blood, marriage or adoption is relevant only where the person making it had special means of knowledge of that relationship and the statement was made before the question in dispute was raised.

Clause (f): a statement as to the existence of a relationship by blood, marriage or adoption between persons deceased is relevant only where it is made in a will or deed relating to the affairs of the family to which any such deceased person belonged, or in a family pedigree, or upon a tombstone, family portrait or other thing on which such statements are usually made, and only where it was made before the question in dispute was raised.
Clause (g): a statement contained in any deed, will or other document which relates to a transaction of the kind specified in clause (a) of section 11 is relevant.
Clause (h): a statement made by a number of persons and expressing feelings or impressions on their part relevant to the matter in question is relevant.
bsa_refs.investigation_relevance: This is the dying declaration provision. Under clause (a), a statement by the deceased as to the cause of his death or as to any of the circumstances of the transaction which resulted in his death is relevant where the cause of death comes into question, whether or not he was under expectation of death and whatever the proceeding, so the IO must record it fully, preserve it, and be ready to prove the ground of unavailability relied on: death, that the maker cannot be found, incapacity to give evidence, or that attendance cannot be procured without delay or expense the Court finds unreasonable in the circumstances. That unavailability gateway applies to every clause, not only clause (a). For the business, interest, relationship, public-right and document clauses the IO must seize the original entry, book, acknowledgement, deed, pedigree or memorial and collect evidence of when and by whom the statement was made. Clause (b) turns on the statement having been made in the ordinary course of business, so the IO should establish that course of business and not merely that the maker was discharging a professional duty; the professional-duty words qualify the books kept. Clause (d) additionally requires that the maker be a person who, if the public right, custom or matter existed, would have been likely to be aware of its existence, and it fails if the statement post-dates the controversy as to that right, custom or matter. Clause (e) additionally requires that the maker had special means of knowledge of the relationship, and clause (f) is confined to relationships between persons deceased and to statements made in a will or deed relating to family affairs, a family pedigree, a tombstone, family portrait or other thing on which such statements are usually made; under both, the statement must pre-date the question in dispute. Clause (g) cross-refers to clause (a) of section 11, which is not set out here, so nothing about its content can be worked out from this section alone. The section fixes relevance only, and the unreasonableness of delay or expense is for the Court.
time_limits: Clause (d): the statement must have been made before any controversy as to the public right, custom or matter had arisen.
Clause (e): the statement must have been made before the question in dispute was raised.
Clause (f): the statement must have been made before the question in dispute was raised.

bsa_refs.title: Cross-examination as to previous statements in writing
bsa_refs.summary: This section governs confronting a witness in cross-examination with his own earlier statements that are in writing or were reduced into writing. It permits such cross-examination on writings relevant to matters in question without the writing first being shown to the witness or being proved. It then imposes one condition: where the cross-examiner intends to contradict the witness by the writing, the witness's attention must be drawn to the specific parts to be used for contradiction before the writing can be proved. The section is a single undivided provision with no numbered sub-sections.
key_requirements: A witness may be cross-examined as to previous statements made by him in writing or reduced into writing which are relevant to matters in question.
Such cross-examination may be conducted without the writing being shown to the witness or being proved.

If it is intended to contradict the witness by the writing, his attention must be called, before the writing can be proved, to those parts of it which are to be used for the purpose of contradicting him.
bsa_refs.investigation_relevance: The IO's own written record of what a witness said is the raw material this section operates on, so statements must be recorded accurately, attributable to that witness, and the original writing preserved and produced with the case papers. The IO should flag the precise passages likely to be used for contradiction, because contradiction is barred until the witness's attention has been drawn to those specific parts.

steps.stage: Statutory rules on statements to the police
steps.text: No inducement to be offered [BNSS 182]: Sub-section (1) is an absolute prohibition: no police officer or other person in authority shall offer or make, or cause to be offered or made, any such inducement, threat or promise as is mentioned in section 22 of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023. Sub-section (2) imposes the mirror-image prohibition on suppression, and widens the class of persons bound by dropping the words "in authority": "But no police officer or other person shall prevent, by any caution or otherwise, any person from making in the course of any investigation under this Chapter any statement which he may be disposed to make of his own free will". The section therefore bars the officer both from procuring a statement by inducement, threat or promise and from discouraging or cautioning a willing person out of making one. The single proviso qualifies only sub-section (2): "Provided that nothing in this sub-section shall affect the provisions of sub-section (4) of section 183" - that is, the requirement that a confession be recorded in the manner provided in section 316, be signed by the person making it, and carry the Magistrate's memorandum at the foot of the record (verified against section 183(4) as printed on PDF page 71).
legal_basis: Section 182 BNSS 2023

bsa_refs.title: Confession caused by inducement, threat, coercion or promise, when irrelevant in criminal proceeding
bsa_refs.summary: Makes a confession by an accused person irrelevant in a criminal proceeding where the making of the confession appears to the Court to have been caused by any inducement, threat, coercion or promise having reference to the charge against the accused person, proceeding from a person in authority and sufficient, in the opinion of the Court, to give the accused person grounds which would appear to him reasonable for supposing that by making it he would gain any advantage or avoid any evil of a temporal nature in reference to the proceedings against him. All four elements must be present. The first proviso makes a confession relevant if it is made after the impression caused by that inducement, threat, coercion or promise has, in the opinion of the Court, been fully removed; it does not retrospectively validate a confession already made while the impression still subsisted. The second proviso operates only on a confession that is otherwise relevant, and preserves it even though it was made under a promise of secrecy, or in consequence of a deception practised on the accused person for the purpose of obtaining it, or when he was drunk, or because it was made in answer to questions which he need not have answered, whatever may have been the form of those questions, or because he was not warned that he was not bound to make such confession and that evidence of it might be given against him; it does not rescue a confession caught by the main clause. Causation, the sufficiency of the inducement, threat, coercion or promise, and whether the impression has been fully removed are each expressly assigned to the Court, while the reasonableness of the grounds is measured by what would appear reasonable to the accused person himself. The section has no numbered sub-sections: the two rules following the main clause are provisos.
key_requirements: A confession made by an accused person is irrelevant in a criminal proceeding if the making of the confession appears to the Court to have been caused by any inducement, threat, coercion or promise having reference to the charge against the accused person.

That inducement, threat, coercion or promise must proceed from a person in authority and be sufficient, in the opinion of the Court, to give the accused person grounds which would appear to him reasonable for supposing that by making it he would gain any advantage or avoid any evil of a temporal nature in reference to the proceedings against him.

First proviso: a confession is relevant if it is made after the impression caused by any such inducement, threat, coercion or promise has, in the opinion of the Court, been fully removed; the confession must be made after the removal, so a later removal does not make relevant a confession already made while the impression subsisted.

Second proviso: a confession that is otherwise relevant does not become irrelevant merely because it was made under a promise of secrecy, or in consequence of a deception practised on the accused person for the purpose of obtaining it.

Second proviso, continued: nor does such an otherwise relevant confession become irrelevant merely because he was drunk, or because it was made in answer to questions which he need not have answered, whatever may have been the form of those questions, or because he was not warned that he was not bound to make such confession and that evidence of it might be given against him.
bsa_refs.investigation_relevance: A confession the prosecution relies on can be shut out if the Court finds that its making was caused by an inducement, threat, coercion or promise having reference to the charge, proceeding from a person in authority - a description capable of covering the investigating officer and supervisory officers, the section not defining the term - and sufficient, in the Court's opinion, to give the accused person grounds which would appear to him reasonable for supposing that by making it he would gain any advantage or avoid any evil of a temporal nature in reference to the proceedings against him. All four elements are required, so the IO must avoid any offer of advantage and any pressure referable to the charge, and should be in a position to place before the Court the circumstances in which the confession was made. Where such an impression has been created, only a confession made after that impression has, in the Court's opinion, been fully removed is relevant; a confession made while it still subsisted is not saved by the later removal. The second proviso means that a promise of secrecy, a deception practised to obtain the confession, the accused's drunkenness, questioning he need not have answered, or the absence of a warning does not by itself make an otherwise relevant confession irrelevant, but it operates only on a confession that is otherwise relevant and does not cure one caught by the main clause. Whether the confession is relevant is decided by the Court, not by the IO.

steps.stage: Case diary: writing, format and contents
steps.text: Every police officer making an investigation shall day by day enter his proceedings in the case diary in the prescribed form, setting forth the time the information reached him, the times he began and closed investigation, the places visited, and a statement of the circumstances ascertained. Write the diary promptly, on the very day of investigation, and dispatch it without delay: failure to write day-by-day the facts discovered gives rise to the suspicion that those circumstances did not exist, and delay leads to suspicion by the Court and adversely affects the IO and the prosecution, while day-to-day writing attaches sanctity and credibility to the evidence collected. Changing or delaying case diaries is strictly prohibited.
legal_basis: Section 172(1) CrPC [now BNSS 192]
steps.deadline: Day by day - on the very day of investigation, dispatched without delay

details.text: Daily investigation diary entries (zimni) must be completed with respect to date and time and must show the statements of witnesses.

details.text: The case diary helps successor IOs understand the case, enables senior officers to guide and supervise the investigation, aids the prosecutor before the Court, and lets the IO refresh his memory at trial.

steps.stage: Case diary: writing, format and contents
steps.text: Fill every column of the case diary (FIR number, sections, CD serial number and date, times of commencement/conclusion, FIR date, complainant, accused, property lost/recovered with value and nature, deceased, places visited, persons examined and their total number, day's investigation details) and record in it: the time information reached the IO and its gist; the scene visit with description, sketch map, index and photographs; a true record of scene observations with a statement and reasons for the circumstances ascertained; places visited chronologically with date and time; the daily proceedings of investigation; consultation of police-station records and its outcome; details of inquests, searches, seizures, arrests and witness examinations with their places; witness particulars with the complete s.161 CrPC [now BNSS 180] statements inserted; every step including dispatch of the accused, reports, documents and seized articles to experts with dates and times of dispatch and receipt and their opinions; and every addition or alteration of sections of law or of accused brought to the notice of the competent Court by petition. Record witness-statement gists in the third person, clearly mention the grounds of warrantless searches and of arrests, describe scene objects by reference to objects having a fixed position, note the fact of photography/videography, draw the map or plan on a separate sheet with distances as accurate as possible, maintain a correct record of time throughout, mention every clue (even if it appears of no value at the time) and the methods adopted by the suspects, and end each day's diary with a note of further actions yet to be taken and of the dispatch and means of dispatch of copies to superior officers.

details.text: For departmental record and supervision also enter: information sent to departmental superiors; requisition of experts' services; references to crime records; verification of complicity of possible criminals; Hue and Cry notices and inquiry slips; disposal of manpower and equipment; clues found and action taken to preserve, develop and submit them for expert examination; verification of statements and alibis; theories formed and reasons for discarding any; lines of further investigation proposed; final probabilities on conclusion of investigation.

steps.text: For removing, adding or bringing to light the name of any accused during the investigation, the IO records the action and its evidential basis in the case diary (no prior written approval of a designated supervisory officer is required) and the diaries are sent without delay to the supervisory officers for monitoring; if the supervisory officer finds the action wrong or unsupported by sufficient evidence he records his objection with reasons and issues clear directions to the IO. conflicts.description: DG Circular 66/2015 (up_major_crimes_handbook, up-handbook-circulars-p46-p65 p.48) abolishes the earlier requirement of prior written approval for adding, removing or bringing to light an accused's name (SP for murder/rape, Addl SP for dacoity/loot/dowry death, Circle Officer for other crimes), whereas DG Circular 03/2013 (up-handbook-circulars-p106-p116 p.107) requires the SP in charge to record his clear opinion on deleting or adding accused names before the charge sheet/final report in murder and rape cases.
conflicts.resolution: Both are same-tier state_advisory circulars from one document, so the ladder cannot separate them; they are separated by stage and by recency. The later DG 66/2015 governs mid-investigation name changes - no prior approval, supervisory control operating through case-diary monitoring - and is the canonical text here. DG 03/2013's SP opinion survives only as the concluding-report vetting step in murder and rape (canonical step core-documentation-supervision-sp-opinion-final-report), not as a prior approval for changes made during investigation.

steps.text: Record the statements of the informant, victim/injured and other important witnesses of fact at the earliest, as far as possible within 24 hours of FIR registration; if that is not possible, furnish a separate written explanation for the late recording of each witness's statement along with that statement. steps.text: Never close an investigation without having collected the substantive/material evidence, and never send a charge sheet to court without the expert opinion the case requires. Do not base the investigation only on oral evidence - collect physical evidence (body secretions such as blood, sweat, spit, saliva for DNA sampling, and thumb/foot prints) and send the samples to the FSL without delay in the initial stage of the investigation.

steps.text: Apply the three key quality points in every investigation in principle (implementing them first in murder and rape, and extending them to other heinous crimes once the working methods have stabilised): (1) protect the scene of crime, have it photographed and have evidence collected from it by the field unit; (2) serve notice on witnesses under s.160 CrPC [now BNSS 179] and record their statements under s.161 CrPC [now BNSS 180] with an audio/video recording under s.161(3); and (3) ensure active participation of supervisory officers in the investigation. The first responder to reach the spot shall put yellow tape around the scene and prevent any unauthorised person from entering it; the field unit collects the necessary evidence in the IO's presence; keep one copy of the scene photographs with the case diary and the second with the Special Report file. Police officers of other stations or units who reach the scene and obtain information about the incident must transmit it by report to the police station concerned so that it is incorporated in the investigation.

steps.text: Write case diaries promptly in the prescribed form and dispatch them without delay. Prepare each date's case diary, with the witness statements, in duplicate: the original is retained by the IO in the case file at the station and the duplicate goes to the supervisory officer (SDPO), who scrutinises it, gives the IO the necessary instructions and retains it in the office file; where the investigating Sub-Inspector is himself the SHO of the police station, forward the case diaries directly to the SDPO concerned.

details.text: Kerala routing variants: where a Circle Inspector exists he scrutinises the diary and sends it to the Sub-Divisional Officer, who files it after scrutiny; CI-investigated cases go to his immediate superior on the day of the case diary itself (in grave crimes one copy to the DCRB, one to the Sub-Divisional Office and one retained, the diary being handed over to the police station after the Final Report); SDPO/DySP-investigated cases go to the DCRB on the day of the case diary itself, with DPC/SP-level verification and instructions.

steps.stage: Case diary: custody, confidentiality and court use
steps.text: Treat every case diary as confidential until the final disposal of the case including the appeal, if any, or until the expiry of the period of appeal. The IO and his superiors shall ensure the physical safety of the case diary and its contents; permit no access to any unauthorized person, particularly the accused, their agents or their counsel (the accused cannot claim an unfettered right to inspect the case diary: Balakram v. State of Uttarakhand, 2017(5) SCALE 220). Access is limited to: the IO; the officer in charge of the police station; any police officer superior to him; the Court Officer (the senior-most prosecuting officer and his junior deputed to prosecute the case); staff specially authorised to deal with such diaries; and any other officer authorised by the Superintendent of Police.
steps.deadline: Confidential until final disposal including appeal, or expiry of the appeal period

steps.stage: Case diary: custody, confidentiality and court use
steps.text: Know the legal position on court use of the case diary: any Criminal Court may send for the diaries of a case under inquiry or trial and use them, not as evidence in the case, but to aid it in such inquiry or trial (s.172(2) CrPC [now BNSS 192]) - including to discover relevant evidence, put necessary questions to a witness, clear up ambiguities in evidence, see whether a witness has turned hostile, decide whether police-custody remand is necessary, decide bail (without disclosing the contents of the case diary in bail orders passed during investigation), see whether there is a case justifying framing of a charge, and summon additional persons as accused. Neither the accused nor his agents are entitled to call for or see the diaries merely because the Court refers to them; the privilege goes only if the police officer who made them uses them to refresh his memory or the Court uses them to contradict him - and then the accused may see only the particular entry referred to and so much of the diary as, in the Court's opinion, is necessary for full understanding of that entry, and no more. The prosecution cannot use the case diary as supporting evidence, and it cannot be used to refresh the memory of, or to contradict, any witness other than the police officer who made it; the prosecution may, with the Court's permission, use a recorded statement to contradict a hostile witness (s.162 CrPC).
legal_basis: Section 172(2),(3) CrPC [now BNSS 192]
Sections 145, 159, 160, 161 Indian Evidence Act, 1872

steps.text: Keep case diaries in the personal custody of the IO; he or a police officer deputed by him takes them to court on hearing dates, and the Prosecutor peruses them at the time of preparing the charge sheet or before/on the hearing date; the IO may also take the case diary in person to the Public Prosecutor to brief him on the case. In cases committed to the Court of Sessions send the diary to the Public Prosecutor under acknowledgement; on disposal he returns it to the SHO through the Court Officer. Whenever the CD file is transferred from one office to another, maintain the Movement Register of the CD File (on the lines of the Local Delivery Book), clearly giving the details and dates of transfer and taking the signature of the person receiving the file in each office without fail; supervisory officers monitor the movement of CD files from time to time.

steps.text: To oppose bail effectively, present before the court a clear written report incorporating the evidence against the accused, his role in the offence and his criminal history, together with the relevant records, and establish coordination with the concerned Public Prosecutor. A bail order passed by ignoring the relevant facts, evidence and law presented by the prosecution, or by considering irrelevant facts, evidence and law, is legally flawed; if the order is so flawed, or the accused while on bail influences prosecution evidence, intimidates or threatens the victim, the victim's family or prosecution witnesses, tampers with or vitiates evidence, violates the conditions of bail or otherwise misuses it, or creates law and order problems, ensure legal proceedings including cancellation of his bail.

details.text: Bail factors the court weighs (State of U.P. v. Amarmani Tripathi): prima facie or reasonable ground to believe the accused committed the offence; nature and gravity of the charge; severity of the punishment on conviction; danger of the accused absconding; character, behaviour, means, position and standing of the accused; likelihood of the offence being repeated; reasonable apprehension of the witnesses being tampered with; and danger of justice being thwarted.

details.text: Kalyan Chandra Sarkar v. Rajesh Ranjan: bail discretion must be exercised judiciously and not as a matter of course, the order indicating reasons for the prima facie conclusion, and considering the nature of the accusation and severity of punishment, the nature of supporting evidence, reasonable apprehension of tampering with witnesses or threat to the complainant, and prima facie satisfaction in support of the charge.

steps.text: With the police report, submit to the Magistrate as many duly listed copies of the report and the accompanying documents as are necessary for furnishing to the accused (a report and documents submitted through electronic communication are deemed duly served). Where proceedings are commenced on a police report the Magistrate shall, without delay and in any case within 14 days from the date the accused is produced or appears, furnish free of cost to the accused and to the victim (if represented by an advocate) copies of the police report, the FIR recorded under BNSS 173, the BNSS 180(3) statements of all persons the prosecution proposes to examine (excluding any part whose exclusion the police officer has requested under BNSS 193(7)), the confessions and statements recorded under BNSS 183, and any other document or relevant extract forwarded with the police report under BNSS 193(6); where a document is too voluminous the Magistrate may instead order copies to be furnished electronically or allow inspection in Court personally or through an advocate.

steps.text: Treat the heinous/sensational crimes designated in the State's police regulations (together with the other categories placed in the Special Report category from time to time by order or circular) as Special Report cases upon their registration at the police station: send information immediately to senior officers, open a Special Report file, and investigate the case in depth and in a time-bound manner under closer and deeper supervision by senior officers, the investigator receiving correct guidance. The Circle Officer writes the Special Report case file (supervision notes) in his own hand, and where the investigator is a gazetted officer the Dy.SP/Additional SP completes the file personally with appropriate directions; all successive progress reports are approved every month by the district SSP/SP only - not cursorily by the Additional SP - and range/zone-level supervisors open their own Special Report crime files, monitor them every month and issue directions to subordinates. Along with the quality of investigation ensure one-hundred-percent arrest of the accused; take departmental action against investigators who show laxity in investigation and against officers who take no interest in supervision work, adverse remarks in the annual confidential assessment of negligent supervising officers being considered. Zonal IGs and Range DIGs shall, at the time of district inspections or visits, also review the case files of some Special Report crimes whose monitoring is not being done by them.
steps.deadline: Information to senior officers immediately on registration; progress reports approved monthly by the district SSP/SP; range/zone monitoring every month
steps.responsible: SHO; Circle Officer; Dy.SP/Addl SP; district SSP/SP; Range DIG; Zonal IG
steps.applies_when: Crimes designated as Special Report cases under the State's police regulations

conflicts.description: The circulars disagree on which paragraph of the Police Regulations designates the Special Report crimes: DG Circulars 73/2007 (up-handbook-circulars-p106-p116 p.112), 15/2008 (p.111), 44/2015 (up-handbook-circulars-p46-p65 p.55) and 40/2016 (up-handbook-circulars-p26-p45 p.35) all cite paragraph 101, while ADG Circular 12/2001 (up-handbook-circulars-p106-p116 p.114) cites paragraph 100.
conflicts.resolution: All are same-tier state_advisory sources within one document. The canonical text is worded generically ('the crimes designated in the State's police regulations'), so the paragraph-number variance does not change the requirement; the later and more numerous circulars (paragraph 101) are the operative citation and the variance is recorded here for traceability rather than resolved by the ladder.

ticks.do: Treat the heinous or sensational crimes designated in the State's police regulations as Special Report cases upon their registration at the police station.
notes: This includes the other categories placed in the Special Report category from time to time by order or circular.

ticks.do: Send information immediately to senior officers, open a Special Report file, and investigate the case in depth and in a time-bound manner under closer and deeper supervision by senior officers.
notes: The investigator is to receive correct guidance.

ticks.do: Write the Special Report case file (supervision notes) in your own hand as the Circle Officer.
Complete the file personally as the Dy.SP or Additional SP with appropriate directions where the investigator is a gazetted officer.
Obtain approval of all successive progress reports every month from the district SSP/SP only.
notes: Such reports are not to be approved cursorily by the Additional SP.

ticks.do: Discharge the range and zone level supervision duties:
sub: Open your own Special Report crime files at range and zone level
Monitor them every month and issue directions to subordinates
Review, at the time of district inspections or visits, the case files of some Special Report crimes whose monitoring is not being done by you

ticks.do: Ensure one-hundred-percent arrest of the accused along with the quality of investigation.
Take departmental action against investigators who show laxity in investigation and against officers who take no interest in supervision work.
notes: Adverse remarks in the annual confidential assessment of negligent supervising officers are to be considered.

steps.title: Open and supervise Special Report crime files
steps.triage_why: Internal police regulations regarding 'Special Report' categories are administrative requirements for supervision, not statutory duties that affect the legality of the prosecution.

steps.text: Run a standing pendency-review ladder for investigations: the SHO/Inspector-in-charge reviews at his own level all investigations, including special crime cases, pending more than 45 days and sends a weekly report showing the reasons for pendency to the Circle Officer; the Circle Officer holds at least 2 order rooms per month for his circle and sends the Additional SP a monthly list of all investigations pending more than 3 months with reasons; the Additional SP holds a monthly order room reviewing that 3-month list and forwards the list of investigations pending more than 6 months, with reasons, to the SSP/SP; the SSP/SP holds an order room at least once a month reviewing the over-6-month cases in depth, takes action against the investigators at fault, and sends the list to the Range DIG, who reviews each such investigation in depth and obtains a weekly progress report from the SSP/SP. Where pendency is due to awaited FSL or other expert reports in serious crime, the SSP/SP, Range DIG and Zonal IG shall themselves establish coordination with the FSL and expert units and have the reports obtained promptly; the Circle Officer, Additional SP and SSP/SP take action according to the rules against negligent investigators whose cases are found pending without reason, and Range DIGs and Zonal IGs review compliance during their tours and report negligence to headquarters.
steps.deadline: SHO report weekly (>45 days); CO at least 2 order rooms per month and a monthly list of cases over 3 months; Addl SP monthly order room; SSP/SP order room at least once a month (>6 months); Range DIG weekly progress reports
steps.responsible: SHO; Circle Officer; Additional SP; SSP/SP; Range DIG; Zonal IG

steps.title: Run the pendency review ladder for pending investigations
steps.triage_why: This describes a supervisory review mechanism (pendency ladder) for the SHO/Circle Officer, not a step for the IO to perform in the investigation.

steps.text: Transfer of an investigation is ordered only by the district SSP/SP - never at Circle Officer or Additional SP level and, as a rule, never on the request of the accused party - by a written speaking order, a copy of which must invariably be sent to the range-level supervisory officer, and only once within the district (from one police station to another or to the Crime Branch). The SSP/SP personally supervises transferred investigations and ensures they are completed impartially within 2 months for heinous crimes and 1 month for ordinary crimes. Transfer outside the district is done only once, by the range-level officer (with a copy of the order to the zonal officer), who likewise supervises to the same time limits. Transfer orders are not ordinarily issued from state police headquarters or zonal level and may be issued from there only where the impartiality of the investigation is in doubt; re-transfer of an investigation requires the approval of the state police chief on a reasoned proposal routed through the supervisory chain with recommendations. Higher formations compile lists of transferred investigations, obtain the explanation of the officer concerned where the time limits are exceeded, and report quarterly.
steps.deadline: Transferred investigations: heinous crimes within 2 months, ordinary crimes within 1 month; quarterly compilation to state headquarters
steps.responsible: District SSP/SP; Range DIG; Zonal IG

steps.text: The district police chief shall hold a monthly orderly room at the headquarters of every circle/tehsil (in proper uniform, without summoning the personnel to district headquarters) reviewing the status of disposal of investigations, part-pending investigations, disposal of applications, and the arrest of warrantees, wanted criminals and criminals carrying declared rewards. Every IO attends with his own case diary and investigation register for in-depth review; the SP obtains a written certificate from all Circle Officers who, after examining the crime registers, report the pendency of investigations, part-pending cases, arrests remaining and the reasons, and where negligence is being committed; the officers with the most pending cases are proceeded against. A compliance report is sent by the 2nd of each month, the Range DIG reviews these points during his tours and reports negligence to the police chief, and the status of cases in which charge sheets remain to be filed is reviewed as a campaign.
steps.deadline: Every month; compliance report by the 2nd of the month
steps.responsible: District SSP/SP; Circle Officers; Range DIG

steps.text: Supervisory officers who receive a copy of the FIR shall read its contents and ensure prompt receipt of the case diaries; as and when diaries are received, note the date and initial them, read them promptly and thoroughly and pass remarks wherever necessary - remarks being more advisory in form than fault-finding unless there are glaring omissions and commissions. Record the gist of the case diaries in your own hand in the crime register or the Special Report file (with approval by an officer senior to you) together with specific, meaningful and reasoned directions that set the direction of the investigation; do not record only general and vague directions as a ritual formality. Supervision must not remain limited to directing quick disposal - it must evaluate the quality and fairness of the investigation - and supervisory officers must use their training, experience and legal knowledge to make effective and meaningful interventions.
legal_basis: Section 158 CrPC (cited in the source as the provision under which the supervisory officer monitors case diaries)

details.text: Case diaries and the documents enclosed with them may be used for preparing the prescribed periodical Progress Reports; the supervisory officer records a gist of the contents in the running note sheet, which need not be forwarded unless specially called for.

steps.text: In all cases the IO shall adhere to strict compliance with the provisions of the criminal procedure law, the Police Act and the Regulations relating to investigation, and superior police authorities shall develop an effective monitoring system to ensure that compliance, curing willful and intentional violations at the earliest and taking appropriate action against the erring IO. bsa_refs.title: Opinion as to handwriting and signature, when relevant
bsa_refs.summary: Section 41 makes non-expert opinion on authorship relevant in two situations. s.41(1) provides that when the Court has to form an opinion as to who wrote or signed a document, the opinion of any person acquainted with the handwriting of the supposed writer, that it was or was not written or signed by that person, is a relevant fact. The Explanation to s.41(1) fixes when a person counts as acquainted: he has seen that person write; or he has received documents purporting to be written by that person in answer to documents written by himself or under his authority and addressed to that person; or, in the ordinary course of business, documents purporting to be written by that person have habitually been submitted to him. The illustration confirms that such witnesses qualify even though they never saw the writer write. s.41(2) covers electronic signatures: the opinion of the Certifying Authority which issued the Electronic Signature Certificate is a relevant fact.
key_requirements: The opinion of any person acquainted with the handwriting of the supposed writer, that a document was or was not written or signed by that person, is a relevant fact.

A person is acquainted with another's handwriting when he has seen that person write, or when he has received documents purporting to be written by that person in answer to documents written by himself or under his authority and addressed to that person.
A person is also acquainted with another's handwriting when, in the ordinary course of business, documents purporting to be written by that person have been habitually submitted to him.
When the Court has to form an opinion as to the electronic signature of any person, the opinion of the Certifying Authority which has issued the Electronic Signature Certificate is a relevant fact.
bsa_refs.investigation_relevance: To prove who wrote or signed a disputed document the IO can rely on ordinary witnesses, not only handwriting experts, but the statement must bring out how the witness became acquainted with the handwriting, in one of the three ways the Explanation lists, otherwise the opinion does not qualify. Where an electronic signature is disputed, the IO should approach the Certifying Authority that issued the Electronic Signature Certificate and obtain its opinion, and annex the certificate details to the case papers.

steps.text: Report how submitted. [BNSS 177]: Every report sent to a Magistrate under section 176 SHALL, if the State Government so directs, be submitted through such superior officer of police as the State Government, by general or special order, appoints in that behalf. The routing requirement is conditional on a State Government direction existing, but is mandatory once that direction exists. Such superior officer MAY give such instructions to the officer in charge of the police station as he thinks fit, and SHALL, after recording such instructions on such report, transmit the same without delay to the Magistrate. The instruction-giving is therefore permissive while the recording-and-transmission is mandatory.

bsa_refs.title: Confession to police officer
bsa_refs.summary: Bars proof of confessions connected with the police. Sub-section (1) provides that no confession made to a police officer shall be proved as against a person accused of any offence; the sub-section itself contains no 'unless' and no reference to a Magistrate. Sub-section (2) separately provides that no confession made by any person while he is in the custody of a police officer, unless it is made in the immediate presence of a Magistrate, shall be proved against him; that immediate-presence exception sits inside sub-section (2) and relieves only the custody bar. bsa_refs.title: Admissibility of electronic records
bsa_refs.summary: This is the operative provision for proving electronic records. Operating notwithstanding anything contained in this Adhiniyam, sub-section (1) deems any information contained in an electronic record which is printed on paper, stored, recorded or copied in optical or magnetic media or semiconductor memory and produced by a computer or any communication device, or otherwise stored, recorded or copied in any electronic form (the 'computer output'), to be also a document, if the conditions mentioned in this section are satisfied in relation to the information and computer in question, and makes that output admissible in any proceedings, without further proof or production of the original, as evidence of any contents of the original or of any fact stated therein of which direct evidence would be admissible. What sub-section (1) deems is that the computer output is ALSO a document: it does not deem the output to be the original, and it settles nothing about the truth or the weight of what the record contains. Both the deeming and the admissibility are conditional on the section's conditions being satisfied. (The supplied Gazette text reads 'as evidence or any contents of the original'; that is an apparent typographical error for 'as evidence of any contents of the original', and the latter reading is used here.) Sub-section (2) lays down the four conditions in clauses (a) to (d): production of the output by the computer or communication device during the period over which it was used regularly to create, store or process information for the purposes of any activity regularly carried on over that period by the person having lawful control over its use; regular feeding into the device, in the ordinary course of those activities, of information of the kind contained in the record or of the kind from which it is derived; the device operating properly throughout the material part of that period, or any period in which it was not operating properly or was out of operation during that part not being such as to affect the electronic record or the accuracy of its contents; and the information in the record reproducing or being derived from such information fed in. Sub-section (3) treats all the computers or communication devices used for that purpose during that period, whether in standalone mode, on a computer system, on a computer network, on a computer resource enabling information creation or providing information processing and storage, or through an intermediary, as constituting for the purposes of this section a single computer or communication device, and references in the section are construed accordingly. Sub-section (4) is the certificate provision: in any proceeding where it is desired to give a statement in evidence by virtue of this section, a certificate doing ANY of the following three things shall be submitted along with the electronic record at each instance where it is being submitted for admission, namely (a) identifying the electronic record containing the statement and describing the manner in which it was produced, (b) giving such particulars of any device involved in the production of that record as may be appropriate for the purpose of showing that it was produced by a computer or a communication device referred to in clauses (a) to (e) of sub-section (3), and (c) dealing with any of the matters to which the conditions mentioned in sub-section (2) relate. The certificate must purport to be signed by a person in charge of the computer or communication device or the management of the relevant activities (whichever is appropriate) AND an expert, that is, two signatories, and it shall be evidence of any matter stated in the certificate; for the purposes of that sub-section it is sufficient for a matter to be stated to the best of the knowledge and belief of the person stating it, in the certificate specified in the Schedule (the form of which is not part of the text supplied here). Sub-section (5) clarifies that information is taken to be supplied to the computer or communication device if it is supplied in any appropriate form, whether directly or, with or without human intervention, by means of any appropriate equipment; and that a computer output is taken to have been produced by the device whether produced by it directly or, with or without human intervention, by means of any appropriate equipment or by other electronic means as referred to in clauses (a) to (e) of sub-section (3).

Such computer output shall be admissible in any proceedings, without further proof or production of the original, as evidence of any contents of the original or of any fact stated therein of which direct evidence would be admissible (the supplied Gazette text reads 'as evidence or any contents of the original', an apparent typographical error for 'as evidence of any contents of the original', and the latter reading is used here).

The computer output containing the information must have been produced by the computer or communication device during the period over which that device was used regularly to create, store or process information for the purposes of any activity regularly carried on over that period by the person having lawful control over its use.

During the said period, information of the kind contained in the electronic record, or of the kind from which the information so contained is derived, must have been regularly fed into the computer or communication device in the ordinary course of the said activities.

In any proceeding where it is desired to give a statement in evidence by virtue of this section, a certificate doing any of the things listed in clauses (a) to (c) of sub-section (4) shall be submitted along with the electronic record.
The certificate shall be submitted along with the electronic record at each instance where it is being submitted for admission.
Clause (a) of sub-section (4): identifying the electronic record containing the statement and describing the manner in which it was produced.

Clause (b) of sub-section (4): giving such particulars of any device involved in the production of that electronic record as may be appropriate for the purpose of showing that the electronic record was produced by a computer or a communication device referred to in clauses (a) to (e) of sub-section (3).

The certificate must purport to be signed by a person in charge of the computer or communication device or the management of the relevant activities (whichever is appropriate) and an expert.
The certificate shall be evidence of any matter stated in the certificate.
For the purposes of sub-section (4) it shall be sufficient for a matter to be stated to the best of the knowledge and belief of the person stating it in the certificate specified in the Schedule.

bsa_refs.investigation_relevance: Wherever the IO relies on this section to put computer output in evidence - CDRs, CCTV footage, device extractions, printouts, server logs - the record must travel with a sub-section (4) certificate, and it must go with the record each and every time the record is submitted for admission, not merely once at charge-sheet stage. On the text the certificate is one 'doing any of' three things: identifying the record and describing how it was produced, giving particulars of any device involved, and dealing with any of the matters to which the sub-section (2) conditions relate; the statute requires any of the three, but the safe practice is to cover all three. The certificate must purport to be signed by two people, a person in charge of the computer or communication device or the management of the relevant activities (whichever is appropriate) and an expert, and it is the certificate specified in the Schedule, so the IO should line up both signatories before the record is tendered; a matter may be stated in it to the best of the knowledge and belief of the person stating it. At seizure, therefore, the IO should record the facts the signatories will later have to certify: regular use of the device over the relevant period for the activity, who had lawful control over its use, regular feeding of information of that kind in the ordinary course, and the proper working of the device (or that any malfunction or downtime in the material part of the period did not affect the record or the accuracy of its contents). Note the limits of sub-section (1): where the conditions are met it deems the computer output to be also a document and lets it in without further proof or production of the original, but it does not make the output the original and it settles nothing about the truth or weight of the contents.

This qualification belongs to clause (c) alone and does not relax clauses (a), (b) or (d).
s.63(4): the certificate must be submitted along with the electronic record 'at each instance where it is being submitted for admission' - a repeating timing requirement, not a one-time filing.

bsa_refs.title: Proof of signature and handwriting of person alleged to have signed or written document produced
bsa_refs.summary: This section states the proof rule for a document said to bear a person's signature or handwriting. Where a document is alleged to be signed by, or to have been written wholly or in part by, any person, the signature or the handwriting of so much of the document as is alleged to be in that person's handwriting must be proved to be in his handwriting. The obligation is mandatory, and it is limited to the portion alleged to be that person's: nothing beyond that portion has to be proved under this section. The section does not itself prescribe the manner in which that proof is to be given, and it names no act to be done by any investigating officer; it operates as a rule of proof on whoever tenders the document and on the Court in receiving it.
key_requirements: If a document is alleged to be signed or to have been written wholly or in part by any person, the signature or the handwriting must be proved to be in his handwriting.
The proof requirement extends only to so much of the document as is alleged to be in that person's handwriting.
bsa_refs.investigation_relevance: Whenever the case rests on a signed or handwritten document - a disputed cheque, a receipt, a threat letter, a register entry, a signed agreement - the IO must build the material that will later establish the signature or handwriting as that person's, because the document does not prove itself. Note the limit: only the part alleged to be in that person's hand needs proving, so the IO should identify precisely which words, entries or signature are attributed to the accused or witness. The section itself prescribes no mode of proof and no step for the IO; nothing about specimen writings, comparison or expert opinion appears in this text, so any such step must be sourced from another provision and not from this one.

bsa_refs.title: Confession to police officer
bsa_refs.summary: Bars proof of confessions connected with the police. Sub-section (1) provides that no confession made to a police officer shall be proved as against a person accused of any offence; the sub-section itself contains no 'unless' and no reference to a Magistrate. Sub-section (2) separately provides that no confession made by any person while he is in the custody of a police officer, unless it is made in the immediate presence of a Magistrate, shall be proved against him; that immediate-presence exception sits inside sub-section (2) and relieves only the custody bar. The proviso to sub-section (2) creates the discovery exception: when any fact is deposed to as discovered in consequence of information received from a person accused of any offence, in the custody of a police officer, so much of that information, whether it amounts to a confession or not, as relates distinctly to the fact discovered may be proved. That permission is worded 'may be proved' - it permits proof of that portion, it does not require it. Both sub-sections bar only confessions.
