Sub-section (2): no confession made by any person while he is in the custody of a police officer shall be proved against him.

The immediate presence of a Magistrate is an exception carried within sub-section (2) and relieves only the custody bar; a confession made in the immediate presence of a Magistrate is outside that bar.

The proviso reaches only information received from a person accused of any offence who is in the custody of a police officer, and only where a fact is deposed to as discovered in consequence of that information.

Where those conditions are met, so much of that information, whether it amounts to a confession or not, as relates distinctly to the fact discovered may be proved; the proviso permits proof of that portion, it does not direct that it be proved.
bsa_refs.investigation_relevance: Subject to the discovery proviso, the IO cannot prove a confession made to him; and a confession made by a person while he is in the custody of a police officer cannot be proved against him unless it was made in the immediate presence of a Magistrate. The bar is confined to confessions, so this section does not by itself exclude statements of the accused that are not confessional, though other law may restrict their use. Sub-section (1) carries no Magistrate exception: the immediate-presence exception sits inside sub-section (2) and relieves only the custody bar, so what it saves is a confession made in a Magistrate's immediate presence by a person in police custody, not a confession made to a police officer. Subject to the discovery proviso, a confession made to a police officer cannot be proved against the accused. bsa_refs.title: Admissibility of electronic records
bsa_refs.summary: This is the operative provision for proving electronic records. Operating notwithstanding anything contained in this Adhiniyam, sub-section (1) deems any information contained in an electronic record which is printed on paper, stored, recorded or copied in optical or magnetic media or semiconductor memory and produced by a computer or any communication device, or otherwise stored, recorded or copied in any electronic form (the 'computer output'), to be also a document, if the conditions mentioned in this section are satisfied in relation to the information and computer in question, and makes that output admissible in any proceedings, without further proof or production of the original, as evidence of any contents of the original or of any fact stated therein of which direct evidence would be admissible. What sub-section (1) deems is that the computer output is ALSO a document: it does not deem the output to be the original, and it settles nothing about the truth or the weight of what the record contains. Both the deeming and the admissibility are conditional on the section's conditions being satisfied. (The supplied Gazette text reads 'as evidence or any contents of the original'; that is an apparent typographical error for 'as evidence of any contents of the original', and the latter reading is used here.) Sub-section (2) lays down the four conditions in clauses (a) to (d): production of the output by the computer or communication device during the period over which it was used regularly to create, store or process information for the purposes of any activity regularly carried on over that period by the person having lawful control over its use; regular feeding into the device, in the ordinary course of those activities, of information of the kind contained in the record or of the kind from which it is derived; the device operating properly throughout the material part of that period, or any period in which it was not operating properly or was out of operation during that part not being such as to affect the electronic record or the accuracy of its contents; and the information in the record reproducing or being derived from such information fed in. Sub-section (3) treats all the computers or communication devices used for that purpose during that period, whether in standalone mode, on a computer system, on a computer network, on a computer resource enabling information creation or providing information processing and storage, or through an intermediary, as constituting for the purposes of this section a single computer or communication device, and references in the section are construed accordingly. Sub-section (4) is the certificate provision: in any proceeding where it is desired to give a statement in evidence by virtue of this section, a certificate doing ANY of the following three things shall be submitted along with the electronic record at each instance where it is being submitted for admission, namely (a) identifying the electronic record containing the statement and describing the manner in which it was produced, (b) giving such particulars of any device involved in the production of that record as may be appropriate for the purpose of showing that it was produced by a computer or a communication device referred to in clauses (a) to (e) of sub-section (3), and (c) dealing with any of the matters to which the conditions mentioned in sub-section (2) relate. The certificate must purport to be signed by a person in charge of the computer or communication device or the management of the relevant activities (whichever is appropriate) AND an expert, that is, two signatories, and it shall be evidence of any matter stated in the certificate; for the purposes of that sub-section it is sufficient for a matter to be stated to the best of the knowledge and belief of the person stating it, in the certificate specified in the Schedule (the form of which is not part of the text supplied here). Sub-section (5) clarifies that information is taken to be supplied to the computer or communication device if it is supplied in any appropriate form, whether directly or, with or without human intervention, by means of any appropriate equipment; and that a computer output is taken to have been produced by the device whether produced by it directly or, with or without human intervention, by means of any appropriate equipment or by other electronic means as referred to in clauses (a) to (e) of sub-section (3).
key_requirements: Sub-section (1) operates notwithstanding anything contained in this Adhiniyam.

Information contained in an electronic record which is printed on paper, stored, recorded or copied in optical or magnetic media or semiconductor memory and produced by a computer or any communication device, or otherwise stored, recorded or copied in any electronic form (the computer output), shall be deemed to be also a document, if the conditions mentioned in this section are satisfied in relation to the information and computer in question.

Such computer output shall be admissible in any proceedings, without further proof or production of the original, as evidence of any contents of the original or of any fact stated therein of which direct evidence would be admissible (the supplied Gazette text reads 'as evidence or any contents of the original', an apparent typographical error for 'as evidence of any contents of the original', and the latter reading is used here).

The computer output containing the information must have been produced by the computer or communication device during the period over which that device was used regularly to create, store or process information for the purposes of any activity regularly carried on over that period by the person having lawful control over its use.

During the said period, information of the kind contained in the electronic record, or of the kind from which the information so contained is derived, must have been regularly fed into the computer or communication device in the ordinary course of the said activities.

Throughout the material part of the said period the computer or communication device must have been operating properly, or, if not, any period in which it was not operating properly or was out of operation during that part of the period must not have been such as to affect the electronic record or the accuracy of its contents.
The information contained in the electronic record must reproduce or be derived from such information fed into the computer or communication device in the ordinary course of the said activities.

Where the function of creating, storing or processing information for the purposes of the activity was regularly performed by means of one or more computers or communication devices, whether in standalone mode, on a computer system, on a computer network, on a computer resource enabling information creation or providing information processing and storage, or through an intermediary, all the computers or communication devices used for that purpose during that period shall be treated for the purposes of this section as constituting a single computer or communication device.

In any proceeding where it is desired to give a statement in evidence by virtue of this section, a certificate doing any of the things listed in clauses (a) to (c) of sub-section (4) shall be submitted along with the electronic record.
The certificate shall be submitted along with the electronic record at each instance where it is being submitted for admission.
Clause (a) of sub-section (4): identifying the electronic record containing the statement and describing the manner in which it was produced.

Clause (b) of sub-section (4): giving such particulars of any device involved in the production of that electronic record as may be appropriate for the purpose of showing that the electronic record was produced by a computer or a communication device referred to in clauses (a) to (e) of sub-section (3).
Clause (c) of sub-section (4): dealing with any of the matters to which the conditions mentioned in sub-section (2) relate.
The certificate must purport to be signed by a person in charge of the computer or communication device or the management of the relevant activities (whichever is appropriate) and an expert.
The certificate shall be evidence of any matter stated in the certificate.
For the purposes of sub-section (4) it shall be sufficient for a matter to be stated to the best of the knowledge and belief of the person stating it in the certificate specified in the Schedule.

Information shall be taken to be supplied to a computer or communication device if it is supplied thereto in any appropriate form and whether it is so supplied directly or (with or without human intervention) by means of any appropriate equipment.

A computer output shall be taken to have been produced by a computer or communication device whether it was produced by it directly or (with or without human intervention) by means of any appropriate equipment or by other electronic means as referred to in clauses (a) to (e) of sub-section (3).
bsa_refs.investigation_relevance: Wherever the IO relies on this section to put computer output in evidence - CDRs, CCTV footage, device extractions, printouts, server logs - the record must travel with a sub-section (4) certificate, and it must go with the record each and every time the record is submitted for admission, not merely once at charge-sheet stage. On the text the certificate is one 'doing any of' three things: identifying the record and describing how it was produced, giving particulars of any device involved, and dealing with any of the matters to which the sub-section (2) conditions relate; the statute requires any of the three, but the safe practice is to cover all three. The certificate must purport to be signed by two people, a person in charge of the computer or communication device or the management of the relevant activities (whichever is appropriate) and an expert, and it is the certificate specified in the Schedule, so the IO should line up both signatories before the record is tendered; a matter may be stated in it to the best of the knowledge and belief of the person stating it. At seizure, therefore, the IO should record the facts the signatories will later have to certify: regular use of the device over the relevant period for the activity, who had lawful control over its use, regular feeding of information of that kind in the ordinary course, and the proper working of the device (or that any malfunction or downtime in the material part of the period did not affect the record or the accuracy of its contents). Note the limits of sub-section (1): where the conditions are met it deems the computer output to be also a document and lets it in without further proof or production of the original, but it does not make the output the original and it settles nothing about the truth or weight of the contents.

Sub-section (1) carries no Magistrate exception: the immediate-presence exception sits inside sub-section (2) and relieves only the custody bar, so what it saves is a confession made in a Magistrate's immediate presence by a person in police custody, not a confession made to a police officer. Subject to the discovery proviso, a confession made to a police officer cannot be proved against the accused. The other route on the text is the discovery proviso, which is available only where the information came from a person accused of an offence who was in the custody of a police officer, and only where a fact is deposed to as discovered in consequence of that information; the IO must record the information, effect the recovery, have the discovery deposed to, and confine the portion sought to be proved to so much of the information as relates distinctly to the fact actually discovered. Even then the proviso only permits that portion to be proved.

bsa_refs.title: Admissibility of electronic records
bsa_refs.summary: This is the operative provision for proving electronic records. Operating notwithstanding anything contained in this Adhiniyam, sub-section (1) deems any information contained in an electronic record which is printed on paper, stored, recorded or copied in optical or magnetic media or semiconductor memory and produced by a computer or any communication device, or otherwise stored, recorded or copied in any electronic form (the 'computer output'), to be also a document, if the conditions mentioned in this section are satisfied in relation to the information and computer in question, and makes that output admissible in any proceedings, without further proof or production of the original, as evidence of any contents of the original or of any fact stated therein of which direct evidence would be admissible. What sub-section (1) deems is that the computer output is ALSO a document: it does not deem the output to be the original, and it settles nothing about the truth or the weight of what the record contains. Both the deeming and the admissibility are conditional on the section's conditions being satisfied. (The supplied Gazette text reads 'as evidence or any contents of the original'; that is an apparent typographical error for 'as evidence of any contents of the original', and the latter reading is used here.) Sub-section (2) lays down the four conditions in clauses (a) to (d): production of the output by the computer or communication device during the period over which it was used regularly to create, store or process information for the purposes of any activity regularly carried on over that period by the person having lawful control over its use; regular feeding into the device, in the ordinary course of those activities, of information of the kind contained in the record or of the kind from which it is derived; the device operating properly throughout the material part of that period, or any period in which it was not operating properly or was out of operation during that part not being such as to affect the electronic record or the accuracy of its contents; and the information in the record reproducing or being derived from such information fed in. Sub-section (3) treats all the computers or communication devices used for that purpose during that period, whether in standalone mode, on a computer system, on a computer network, on a computer resource enabling information creation or providing information processing and storage, or through an intermediary, as constituting for the purposes of this section a single computer or communication device, and references in the section are construed accordingly. Sub-section (4) is the certificate provision: in any proceeding where it is desired to give a statement in evidence by virtue of this section, a certificate doing ANY of the following three things shall be submitted along with the electronic record at each instance where it is being submitted for admission, namely (a) identifying the electronic record containing the statement and describing the manner in which it was produced, (b) giving such particulars of any device involved in the production of that record as may be appropriate for the purpose of showing that it was produced by a computer or a communication device referred to in clauses (a) to (e) of sub-section (3), and (c) dealing with any of the matters to which the conditions mentioned in sub-section (2) relate. The certificate must purport to be signed by a person in charge of the computer or communication device or the management of the relevant activities (whichever is appropriate) AND an expert, that is, two signatories, and it shall be evidence of any matter stated in the certificate; for the purposes of that sub-section it is sufficient for a matter to be stated to the best of the knowledge and belief of the person stating it, in the certificate specified in the Schedule (the form of which is not part of the text supplied here). Sub-section (5) clarifies that information is taken to be supplied to the computer or communication device if it is supplied in any appropriate form, whether directly or, with or without human intervention, by means of any appropriate equipment; and that a computer output is taken to have been produced by the device whether produced by it directly or, with or without human intervention, by means of any appropriate equipment or by other electronic means as referred to in clauses (a) to (e) of sub-section (3).

Such computer output shall be admissible in any proceedings, without further proof or production of the original, as evidence of any contents of the original or of any fact stated therein of which direct evidence would be admissible (the supplied Gazette text reads 'as evidence or any contents of the original', an apparent typographical error for 'as evidence of any contents of the original', and the latter reading is used here).

The computer output containing the information must have been produced by the computer or communication device during the period over which that device was used regularly to create, store or process information for the purposes of any activity regularly carried on over that period by the person having lawful control over its use.

During the said period, information of the kind contained in the electronic record, or of the kind from which the information so contained is derived, must have been regularly fed into the computer or communication device in the ordinary course of the said activities.

Throughout the material part of the said period the computer or communication device must have been operating properly, or, if not, any period in which it was not operating properly or was out of operation during that part of the period must not have been such as to affect the electronic record or the accuracy of its contents.
The information contained in the electronic record must reproduce or be derived from such information fed into the computer or communication device in the ordinary course of the said activities.

Where the function of creating, storing or processing information for the purposes of the activity was regularly performed by means of one or more computers or communication devices, whether in standalone mode, on a computer system, on a computer network, on a computer resource enabling information creation or providing information processing and storage, or through an intermediary, all the computers or communication devices used for that purpose during that period shall be treated for the purposes of this section as constituting a single computer or communication device.

In any proceeding where it is desired to give a statement in evidence by virtue of this section, a certificate doing any of the things listed in clauses (a) to (c) of sub-section (4) shall be submitted along with the electronic record.
The certificate shall be submitted along with the electronic record at each instance where it is being submitted for admission.
Clause (a) of sub-section (4): identifying the electronic record containing the statement and describing the manner in which it was produced.

Clause (b) of sub-section (4): giving such particulars of any device involved in the production of that electronic record as may be appropriate for the purpose of showing that the electronic record was produced by a computer or a communication device referred to in clauses (a) to (e) of sub-section (3).
Clause (c) of sub-section (4): dealing with any of the matters to which the conditions mentioned in sub-section (2) relate.
The certificate must purport to be signed by a person in charge of the computer or communication device or the management of the relevant activities (whichever is appropriate) and an expert.
The certificate shall be evidence of any matter stated in the certificate.
For the purposes of sub-section (4) it shall be sufficient for a matter to be stated to the best of the knowledge and belief of the person stating it in the certificate specified in the Schedule.

A computer output shall be taken to have been produced by a computer or communication device whether it was produced by it directly or (with or without human intervention) by means of any appropriate equipment or by other electronic means as referred to in clauses (a) to (e) of sub-section (3).
bsa_refs.investigation_relevance: Wherever the IO relies on this section to put computer output in evidence - CDRs, CCTV footage, device extractions, printouts, server logs - the record must travel with a sub-section (4) certificate, and it must go with the record each and every time the record is submitted for admission, not merely once at charge-sheet stage. On the text the certificate is one 'doing any of' three things: identifying the record and describing how it was produced, giving particulars of any device involved, and dealing with any of the matters to which the sub-section (2) conditions relate; the statute requires any of the three, but the safe practice is to cover all three. The certificate must purport to be signed by two people, a person in charge of the computer or communication device or the management of the relevant activities (whichever is appropriate) and an expert, and it is the certificate specified in the Schedule, so the IO should line up both signatories before the record is tendered; a matter may be stated in it to the best of the knowledge and belief of the person stating it. Note the limits of sub-section (1): where the conditions are met it deems the computer output to be also a document and lets it in without further proof or production of the original, but it does not make the output the original and it settles nothing about the truth or weight of the contents.

bsa_refs.title: Proof of signature and handwriting of person alleged to have signed or written document produced
bsa_refs.summary: This section states the proof rule for a document said to bear a person's signature or handwriting. Where a document is alleged to be signed by, or to have been written wholly or in part by, any person, the signature or the handwriting of so much of the document as is alleged to be in that person's handwriting must be proved to be in his handwriting. The obligation is mandatory, and it is limited to the portion alleged to be that person's: nothing beyond that portion has to be proved under this section. The section does not itself prescribe the manner in which that proof is to be given, and it names no act to be done by any investigating officer; it operates as a rule of proof on whoever tenders the document and on the Court in receiving it.
key_requirements: If a document is alleged to be signed or to have been written wholly or in part by any person, the signature or the handwriting must be proved to be in his handwriting.
The proof requirement extends only to so much of the document as is alleged to be in that person's handwriting.
bsa_refs.investigation_relevance: Whenever the case rests on a signed or handwritten document - a disputed cheque, a receipt, a threat letter, a register entry, a signed agreement - the IO must build the material that will later establish the signature or handwriting as that person's, because the document does not prove itself. Note the limit: only the part alleged to be in that person's hand needs proving, so the IO should identify precisely which words, entries or signature are attributed to the accused or witness. The section itself prescribes no mode of proof and no step for the IO; nothing about specimen writings, comparison or expert opinion appears in this text, so any such step must be sourced from another provision and not from this one.

bsa_refs.title: Confession to police officer
bsa_refs.summary: Bars proof of confessions connected with the police. Sub-section (1) provides that no confession made to a police officer shall be proved as against a person accused of any offence; the sub-section itself contains no 'unless' and no reference to a Magistrate. Sub-section (2) separately provides that no confession made by any person while he is in the custody of a police officer, unless it is made in the immediate presence of a Magistrate, shall be proved against him; that immediate-presence exception sits inside sub-section (2) and relieves only the custody bar. The proviso to sub-section (2) creates the discovery exception: when any fact is deposed to as discovered in consequence of information received from a person accused of any offence, in the custody of a police officer, so much of that information, whether it amounts to a confession or not, as relates distinctly to the fact discovered may be proved. That permission is worded 'may be proved' - it permits proof of that portion, it does not require it. Both sub-sections bar only confessions.
key_requirements: Sub-section (1): no confession made to a police officer shall be proved as against a person accused of any offence; the sub-section itself states this without any unless or exception and makes no reference to a Magistrate.

The proviso reaches only information received from a person accused of any offence who is in the custody of a police officer, and only where a fact is deposed to as discovered in consequence of that information.

Where those conditions are met, so much of that information, whether it amounts to a confession or not, as relates distinctly to the fact discovered may be proved; the proviso permits proof of that portion, it does not direct that it be proved.

Sub-section (2) separately provides that no confession made by any person while he is in the custody of a police officer, unless it is made in the immediate presence of a Magistrate, shall be proved against him; that immediate-presence exception sits inside sub-section (2) and relieves only the custody bar. The proviso to sub-section (2) creates the discovery exception: when any fact is deposed to as discovered in consequence of information received from a person accused of any offence, in the custody of a police officer, so much of that information, whether it amounts to a confession or not, as relates distinctly to the fact discovered may be proved. That permission is worded 'may be proved' - it permits proof of that portion, it does not require it. Both sub-sections bar only confessions.

The proviso reaches only information received from a person accused of any offence who is in the custody of a police officer, and only where a fact is deposed to as discovered in consequence of that information.

bsa_refs.title: Admissibility of electronic records
bsa_refs.summary: This is the operative provision for proving electronic records. Operating notwithstanding anything contained in this Adhiniyam, sub-section (1) deems any information contained in an electronic record which is printed on paper, stored, recorded or copied in optical or magnetic media or semiconductor memory and produced by a computer or any communication device, or otherwise stored, recorded or copied in any electronic form (the 'computer output'), to be also a document, if the conditions mentioned in this section are satisfied in relation to the information and computer in question, and makes that output admissible in any proceedings, without further proof or production of the original, as evidence of any contents of the original or of any fact stated therein of which direct evidence would be admissible. What sub-section (1) deems is that the computer output is ALSO a document: it does not deem the output to be the original, and it settles nothing about the truth or the weight of what the record contains. Both the deeming and the admissibility are conditional on the section's conditions being satisfied. (The supplied Gazette text reads 'as evidence or any contents of the original'; that is an apparent typographical error for 'as evidence of any contents of the original', and the latter reading is used here.) Sub-section (2) lays down the four conditions in clauses (a) to (d): production of the output by the computer or communication device during the period over which it was used regularly to create, store or process information for the purposes of any activity regularly carried on over that period by the person having lawful control over its use; regular feeding into the device, in the ordinary course of those activities, of information of the kind contained in the record or of the kind from which it is derived; the device operating properly throughout the material part of that period, or any period in which it was not operating properly or was out of operation during that part not being such as to affect the electronic record or the accuracy of its contents; and the information in the record reproducing or being derived from such information fed in. Sub-section (3) treats all the computers or communication devices used for that purpose during that period, whether in standalone mode, on a computer system, on a computer network, on a computer resource enabling information creation or providing information processing and storage, or through an intermediary, as constituting for the purposes of this section a single computer or communication device, and references in the section are construed accordingly. Sub-section (4) is the certificate provision: in any proceeding where it is desired to give a statement in evidence by virtue of this section, a certificate doing ANY of the following three things shall be submitted along with the electronic record at each instance where it is being submitted for admission, namely (a) identifying the electronic record containing the statement and describing the manner in which it was produced, (b) giving such particulars of any device involved in the production of that record as may be appropriate for the purpose of showing that it was produced by a computer or a communication device referred to in clauses (a) to (e) of sub-section (3), and (c) dealing with any of the matters to which the conditions mentioned in sub-section (2) relate. The certificate must purport to be signed by a person in charge of the computer or communication device or the management of the relevant activities (whichever is appropriate) AND an expert, that is, two signatories, and it shall be evidence of any matter stated in the certificate; for the purposes of that sub-section it is sufficient for a matter to be stated to the best of the knowledge and belief of the person stating it, in the certificate specified in the Schedule (the form of which is not part of the text supplied here). Sub-section (5) clarifies that information is taken to be supplied to the computer or communication device if it is supplied in any appropriate form, whether directly or, with or without human intervention, by means of any appropriate equipment; and that a computer output is taken to have been produced by the device whether produced by it directly or, with or without human intervention, by means of any appropriate equipment or by other electronic means as referred to in clauses (a) to (e) of sub-section (3).
key_requirements: Sub-section (1) operates notwithstanding anything contained in this Adhiniyam.

Information contained in an electronic record which is printed on paper, stored, recorded or copied in optical or magnetic media or semiconductor memory and produced by a computer or any communication device, or otherwise stored, recorded or copied in any electronic form (the computer output), shall be deemed to be also a document, if the conditions mentioned in this section are satisfied in relation to the information and computer in question.

Such computer output shall be admissible in any proceedings, without further proof or production of the original, as evidence of any contents of the original or of any fact stated therein of which direct evidence would be admissible (the supplied Gazette text reads 'as evidence or any contents of the original', an apparent typographical error for 'as evidence of any contents of the original', and the latter reading is used here).

The computer output containing the information must have been produced by the computer or communication device during the period over which that device was used regularly to create, store or process information for the purposes of any activity regularly carried on over that period by the person having lawful control over its use.

During the said period, information of the kind contained in the electronic record, or of the kind from which the information so contained is derived, must have been regularly fed into the computer or communication device in the ordinary course of the said activities.

Throughout the material part of the said period the computer or communication device must have been operating properly, or, if not, any period in which it was not operating properly or was out of operation during that part of the period must not have been such as to affect the electronic record or the accuracy of its contents.
The information contained in the electronic record must reproduce or be derived from such information fed into the computer or communication device in the ordinary course of the said activities.

Where the function of creating, storing or processing information for the purposes of the activity was regularly performed by means of one or more computers or communication devices, whether in standalone mode, on a computer system, on a computer network, on a computer resource enabling information creation or providing information processing and storage, or through an intermediary, all the computers or communication devices used for that purpose during that period shall be treated for the purposes of this section as constituting a single computer or communication device.

In any proceeding where it is desired to give a statement in evidence by virtue of this section, a certificate doing any of the things listed in clauses (a) to (c) of sub-section (4) shall be submitted along with the electronic record.
The certificate shall be submitted along with the electronic record at each instance where it is being submitted for admission.
Clause (a) of sub-section (4): identifying the electronic record containing the statement and describing the manner in which it was produced.

Clause (b) of sub-section (4): giving such particulars of any device involved in the production of that electronic record as may be appropriate for the purpose of showing that the electronic record was produced by a computer or a communication device referred to in clauses (a) to (e) of sub-section (3).
Clause (c) of sub-section (4): dealing with any of the matters to which the conditions mentioned in sub-section (2) relate.
The certificate must purport to be signed by a person in charge of the computer or communication device or the management of the relevant activities (whichever is appropriate) and an expert.
The certificate shall be evidence of any matter stated in the certificate.
For the purposes of sub-section (4) it shall be sufficient for a matter to be stated to the best of the knowledge and belief of the person stating it in the certificate specified in the Schedule.

Information shall be taken to be supplied to a computer or communication device if it is supplied thereto in any appropriate form and whether it is so supplied directly or (with or without human intervention) by means of any appropriate equipment.

A computer output shall be taken to have been produced by a computer or communication device whether it was produced by it directly or (with or without human intervention) by means of any appropriate equipment or by other electronic means as referred to in clauses (a) to (e) of sub-section (3).
bsa_refs.investigation_relevance: Wherever the IO relies on this section to put computer output in evidence - CDRs, CCTV footage, device extractions, printouts, server logs - the record must travel with a sub-section (4) certificate, and it must go with the record each and every time the record is submitted for admission, not merely once at charge-sheet stage. On the text the certificate is one 'doing any of' three things: identifying the record and describing how it was produced, giving particulars of any device involved, and dealing with any of the matters to which the sub-section (2) conditions relate; the statute requires any of the three, but the safe practice is to cover all three. The certificate must purport to be signed by two people, a person in charge of the computer or communication device or the management of the relevant activities (whichever is appropriate) and an expert, and it is the certificate specified in the Schedule, so the IO should line up both signatories before the record is tendered; a matter may be stated in it to the best of the knowledge and belief of the person stating it. At seizure, therefore, the IO should record the facts the signatories will later have to certify: regular use of the device over the relevant period for the activity, who had lawful control over its use, regular feeding of information of that kind in the ordinary course, and the proper working of the device (or that any malfunction or downtime in the material part of the period did not affect the record or the accuracy of its contents). Note the limits of sub-section (1): where the conditions are met it deems the computer output to be also a document and lets it in without further proof or production of the original, but it does not make the output the original and it settles nothing about the truth or weight of the contents.
time_limits: s.63(2)(a): no fixed number of days is prescribed - the relevant period is the period over which the computer or communication device was used regularly to create, store or process information for the purposes of the activity regularly carried on over that period.

s.63(2)(c): the computer or communication device must have been operating properly 'throughout the material part of the said period', or any period in which it was not operating properly or was out of operation during that part must not have been such as to affect the electronic record or the accuracy of its contents. This qualification belongs to clause (c) alone and does not relax clauses (a), (b) or (d).
s.63(4): the certificate must be submitted along with the electronic record 'at each instance where it is being submitted for admission' - a repeating timing requirement, not a one-time filing.

What sub-section (1) deems is that the computer output is ALSO a document: it does not deem the output to be the original, and it settles nothing about the truth or the weight of what the record contains. Both the deeming and the admissibility are conditional on the section's conditions being satisfied. (The supplied Gazette text reads 'as evidence or any contents of the original'; that is an apparent typographical error for 'as evidence of any contents of the original', and the latter reading is used here.) Sub-section (2) lays down the four conditions in clauses (a) to (d): production of the output by the computer or communication device during the period over which it was used regularly to create, store or process information for the purposes of any activity regularly carried on over that period by the person having lawful control over its use; regular feeding into the device, in the ordinary course of those activities, of information of the kind contained in the record or of the kind from which it is derived; the device operating properly throughout the material part of that period, or any period in which it was not operating properly or was out of operation during that part not being such as to affect the electronic record or the accuracy of its contents; and the information in the record reproducing or being derived from such information fed in. Sub-section (3) treats all the computers or communication devices used for that purpose during that period, whether in standalone mode, on a computer system, on a computer network, on a computer resource enabling information creation or providing information processing and storage, or through an intermediary, as constituting for the purposes of this section a single computer or communication device, and references in the section are construed accordingly. Sub-section (4) is the certificate provision: in any proceeding where it is desired to give a statement in evidence by virtue of this section, a certificate doing ANY of the following three things shall be submitted along with the electronic record at each instance where it is being submitted for admission, namely (a) identifying the electronic record containing the statement and describing the manner in which it was produced, (b) giving such particulars of any device involved in the production of that record as may be appropriate for the purpose of showing that it was produced by a computer or a communication device referred to in clauses (a) to (e) of sub-section (3), and (c) dealing with any of the matters to which the conditions mentioned in sub-section (2) relate. The certificate must purport to be signed by a person in charge of the computer or communication device or the management of the relevant activities (whichever is appropriate) AND an expert, that is, two signatories, and it shall be evidence of any matter stated in the certificate; for the purposes of that sub-section it is sufficient for a matter to be stated to the best of the knowledge and belief of the person stating it, in the certificate specified in the Schedule (the form of which is not part of the text supplied here). Sub-section (5) clarifies that information is taken to be supplied to the computer or communication device if it is supplied in any appropriate form, whether directly or, with or without human intervention, by means of any appropriate equipment; and that a computer output is taken to have been produced by the device whether produced by it directly or, with or without human intervention, by means of any appropriate equipment or by other electronic means as referred to in clauses (a) to (e) of sub-section (3).
key_requirements: Sub-section (1) operates notwithstanding anything contained in this Adhiniyam.

Information contained in an electronic record which is printed on paper, stored, recorded or copied in optical or magnetic media or semiconductor memory and produced by a computer or any communication device, or otherwise stored, recorded or copied in any electronic form (the computer output), shall be deemed to be also a document, if the conditions mentioned in this section are satisfied in relation to the information and computer in question.

Such computer output shall be admissible in any proceedings, without further proof or production of the original, as evidence of any contents of the original or of any fact stated therein of which direct evidence would be admissible (the supplied Gazette text reads 'as evidence or any contents of the original', an apparent typographical error for 'as evidence of any contents of the original', and the latter reading is used here).

The computer output containing the information must have been produced by the computer or communication device during the period over which that device was used regularly to create, store or process information for the purposes of any activity regularly carried on over that period by the person having lawful control over its use.

During the said period, information of the kind contained in the electronic record, or of the kind from which the information so contained is derived, must have been regularly fed into the computer or communication device in the ordinary course of the said activities.

Throughout the material part of the said period the computer or communication device must have been operating properly, or, if not, any period in which it was not operating properly or was out of operation during that part of the period must not have been such as to affect the electronic record or the accuracy of its contents.
The information contained in the electronic record must reproduce or be derived from such information fed into the computer or communication device in the ordinary course of the said activities.

Where the function of creating, storing or processing information for the purposes of the activity was regularly performed by means of one or more computers or communication devices, whether in standalone mode, on a computer system, on a computer network, on a computer resource enabling information creation or providing information processing and storage, or through an intermediary, all the computers or communication devices used for that purpose during that period shall be treated for the purposes of this section as constituting a single computer or communication device.

In any proceeding where it is desired to give a statement in evidence by virtue of this section, a certificate doing any of the things listed in clauses (a) to (c) of sub-section (4) shall be submitted along with the electronic record.
The certificate shall be submitted along with the electronic record at each instance where it is being submitted for admission.
Clause (a) of sub-section (4): identifying the electronic record containing the statement and describing the manner in which it was produced.

Clause (b) of sub-section (4): giving such particulars of any device involved in the production of that electronic record as may be appropriate for the purpose of showing that the electronic record was produced by a computer or a communication device referred to in clauses (a) to (e) of sub-section (3).
Clause (c) of sub-section (4): dealing with any of the matters to which the conditions mentioned in sub-section (2) relate.
The certificate must purport to be signed by a person in charge of the computer or communication device or the management of the relevant activities (whichever is appropriate) and an expert.
The certificate shall be evidence of any matter stated in the certificate.
For the purposes of sub-section (4) it shall be sufficient for a matter to be stated to the best of the knowledge and belief of the person stating it in the certificate specified in the Schedule.

Information shall be taken to be supplied to a computer or communication device if it is supplied thereto in any appropriate form and whether it is so supplied directly or (with or without human intervention) by means of any appropriate equipment.

A computer output shall be taken to have been produced by a computer or communication device whether it was produced by it directly or (with or without human intervention) by means of any appropriate equipment or by other electronic means as referred to in clauses (a) to (e) of sub-section (3).
bsa_refs.investigation_relevance: Wherever the IO relies on this section to put computer output in evidence - CDRs, CCTV footage, device extractions, printouts, server logs - the record must travel with a sub-section (4) certificate, and it must go with the record each and every time the record is submitted for admission, not merely once at charge-sheet stage. On the text the certificate is one 'doing any of' three things: identifying the record and describing how it was produced, giving particulars of any device involved, and dealing with any of the matters to which the sub-section (2) conditions relate; the statute requires any of the three, but the safe practice is to cover all three. The certificate must purport to be signed by two people, a person in charge of the computer or communication device or the management of the relevant activities (whichever is appropriate) and an expert, and it is the certificate specified in the Schedule, so the IO should line up both signatories before the record is tendered; a matter may be stated in it to the best of the knowledge and belief of the person stating it. At seizure, therefore, the IO should record the facts the signatories will later have to certify: regular use of the device over the relevant period for the activity, who had lawful control over its use, regular feeding of information of that kind in the ordinary course, and the proper working of the device (or that any malfunction or downtime in the material part of the period did not affect the record or the accuracy of its contents). Note the limits of sub-section (1): where the conditions are met it deems the computer output to be also a document and lets it in without further proof or production of the original, but it does not make the output the original and it settles nothing about the truth or weight of the contents.
time_limits: s.63(2)(a): no fixed number of days is prescribed - the relevant period is the period over which the computer or communication device was used regularly to create, store or process information for the purposes of the activity regularly carried on over that period.

s.63(2)(c): the computer or communication device must have been operating properly 'throughout the material part of the said period', or any period in which it was not operating properly or was out of operation during that part must not have been such as to affect the electronic record or the accuracy of its contents. This qualification belongs to clause (c) alone and does not relax clauses (a), (b) or (d).
s.63(4): the certificate must be submitted along with the electronic record 'at each instance where it is being submitted for admission' - a repeating timing requirement, not a one-time filing.

bsa_refs.title: Proof of signature and handwriting of person alleged to have signed or written document produced
bsa_refs.summary: This section states the proof rule for a document said to bear a person's signature or handwriting. Where a document is alleged to be signed by, or to have been written wholly or in part by, any person, the signature or the handwriting of so much of the document as is alleged to be in that person's handwriting must be proved to be in his handwriting. The obligation is mandatory, and it is limited to the portion alleged to be that person's: nothing beyond that portion has to be proved under this section. The section does not itself prescribe the manner in which that proof is to be given, and it names no act to be done by any investigating officer; it operates as a rule of proof on whoever tenders the document and on the Court in receiving it.
key_requirements: If a document is alleged to be signed or to have been written wholly or in part by any person, the signature or the handwriting must be proved to be in his handwriting.
The proof requirement extends only to so much of the document as is alleged to be in that person's handwriting.
bsa_refs.investigation_relevance: Whenever the case rests on a signed or handwritten document - a disputed cheque, a receipt, a threat letter, a register entry, a signed agreement - the IO must build the material that will later establish the signature or handwriting as that person's, because the document does not prove itself. Note the limit: only the part alleged to be in that person's hand needs proving, so the IO should identify precisely which words, entries or signature are attributed to the accused or witness. The section itself prescribes no mode of proof and no step for the IO; nothing about specimen writings, comparison or expert opinion appears in this text, so any such step must be sourced from another provision and not from this one.

bsa_refs.title: Confession to police officer
bsa_refs.summary: Bars proof of confessions connected with the police. Sub-section (1) provides that no confession made to a police officer shall be proved as against a person accused of any offence; the sub-section itself contains no 'unless' and no reference to a Magistrate. Sub-section (2) separately provides that no confession made by any person while he is in the custody of a police officer, unless it is made in the immediate presence of a Magistrate, shall be proved against him; that immediate-presence exception sits inside sub-section (2) and relieves only the custody bar. The proviso to sub-section (2) creates the discovery exception: when any fact is deposed to as discovered in consequence of information received from a person accused of any offence, in the custody of a police officer, so much of that information, whether it amounts to a confession or not, as relates distinctly to the fact discovered may be proved. That permission is worded 'may be proved' - it permits proof of that portion, it does not require it. Both sub-sections bar only confessions.
key_requirements: Sub-section (1): no confession made to a police officer shall be proved as against a person accused of any offence; the sub-section itself states this without any unless or exception and makes no reference to a Magistrate.
Sub-section (2): no confession made by any person while he is in the custody of a police officer shall be proved against him.

The immediate presence of a Magistrate is an exception carried within sub-section (2) and relieves only the custody bar; a confession made in the immediate presence of a Magistrate is outside that bar.

The proviso reaches only information received from a person accused of any offence who is in the custody of a police officer, and only where a fact is deposed to as discovered in consequence of that information.

Where those conditions are met, so much of that information, whether it amounts to a confession or not, as relates distinctly to the fact discovered may be proved; the proviso permits proof of that portion, it does not direct that it be proved.
bsa_refs.investigation_relevance: Subject to the discovery proviso, the IO cannot prove a confession made to him; and a confession made by a person while he is in the custody of a police officer cannot be proved against him unless it was made in the immediate presence of a Magistrate. The bar is confined to confessions, so this section does not by itself exclude statements of the accused that are not confessional, though other law may restrict their use. Sub-section (1) carries no Magistrate exception: the immediate-presence exception sits inside sub-section (2) and relieves only the custody bar, so what it saves is a confession made in a Magistrate's immediate presence by a person in police custody, not a confession made to a police officer. Subject to the discovery proviso, a confession made to a police officer cannot be proved against the accused. The other route on the text is the discovery proviso, which is available only where the information came from a person accused of an offence who was in the custody of a police officer, and only where a fact is deposed to as discovered in consequence of that information; the IO must record the information, effect the recovery, have the discovery deposed to, and confine the portion sought to be proved to so much of the information as relates distinctly to the fact actually discovered. Even then the proviso only permits that portion to be proved.

bsa_refs.title: Proof of signature and handwriting of person alleged to have signed or written document produced
bsa_refs.summary: This section states the proof rule for a document said to bear a person's signature or handwriting. Where a document is alleged to be signed by, or to have been written wholly or in part by, any person, the signature or the handwriting of so much of the document as is alleged to be in that person's handwriting must be proved to be in his handwriting. The obligation is mandatory, and it is limited to the portion alleged to be that person's: nothing beyond that portion has to be proved under this section. The section does not itself prescribe the manner in which that proof is to be given, and it names no act to be done by any investigating officer; it operates as a rule of proof on whoever tenders the document and on the Court in receiving it.
key_requirements: If a document is alleged to be signed or to have been written wholly or in part by any person, the signature or the handwriting must be proved to be in his handwriting.
The proof requirement extends only to so much of the document as is alleged to be in that person's handwriting.
bsa_refs.investigation_relevance: Whenever the case rests on a signed or handwritten document - a disputed cheque, a receipt, a threat letter, a register entry, a signed agreement - the IO must build the material that will later establish the signature or handwriting as that person's, because the document does not prove itself. Note the limit: only the part alleged to be in that person's hand needs proving, so the IO should identify precisely which words, entries or signature are attributed to the accused or witness. The section itself prescribes no mode of proof and no step for the IO; nothing about specimen writings, comparison or expert opinion appears in this text, so any such step must be sourced from another provision and not from this one.

bsa_refs.title: Confession to police officer
bsa_refs.summary: Bars proof of confessions connected with the police. Sub-section (1) provides that no confession made to a police officer shall be proved as against a person accused of any offence; the sub-section itself contains no 'unless' and no reference to a Magistrate. Sub-section (2) separately provides that no confession made by any person while he is in the custody of a police officer, unless it is made in the immediate presence of a Magistrate, shall be proved against him; that immediate-presence exception sits inside sub-section (2) and relieves only the custody bar. The proviso to sub-section (2) creates the discovery exception: when any fact is deposed to as discovered in consequence of information received from a person accused of any offence, in the custody of a police officer, so much of that information, whether it amounts to a confession or not, as relates distinctly to the fact discovered may be proved. That permission is worded 'may be proved' - it permits proof of that portion, it does not require it. Both sub-sections bar only confessions.
key_requirements: Sub-section (1): no confession made to a police officer shall be proved as against a person accused of any offence; the sub-section itself states this without any unless or exception and makes no reference to a Magistrate.
Sub-section (2): no confession made by any person while he is in the custody of a police officer shall be proved against him.

The immediate presence of a Magistrate is an exception carried within sub-section (2) and relieves only the custody bar; a confession made in the immediate presence of a Magistrate is outside that bar.

The proviso reaches only information received from a person accused of any offence who is in the custody of a police officer, and only where a fact is deposed to as discovered in consequence of that information.

Where those conditions are met, so much of that information, whether it amounts to a confession or not, as relates distinctly to the fact discovered may be proved; the proviso permits proof of that portion, it does not direct that it be proved.
bsa_refs.investigation_relevance: Subject to the discovery proviso, the IO cannot prove a confession made to him; and a confession made by a person while he is in the custody of a police officer cannot be proved against him unless it was made in the immediate presence of a Magistrate. The bar is confined to confessions, so this section does not by itself exclude statements of the accused that are not confessional, though other law may restrict their use. Sub-section (1) carries no Magistrate exception: the immediate-presence exception sits inside sub-section (2) and relieves only the custody bar, so what it saves is a confession made in a Magistrate's immediate presence by a person in police custody, not a confession made to a police officer. Subject to the discovery proviso, a confession made to a police officer cannot be proved against the accused. The other route on the text is the discovery proviso, which is available only where the information came from a person accused of an offence who was in the custody of a police officer, and only where a fact is deposed to as discovered in consequence of that information; the IO must record the information, effect the recovery, have the discovery deposed to, and confine the portion sought to be proved to so much of the information as relates distinctly to the fact actually discovered. Even then the proviso only permits that portion to be proved.

bsa_refs.title: Confession to police officer
bsa_refs.summary: Bars proof of confessions connected with the police. Sub-section (1) provides that no confession made to a police officer shall be proved as against a person accused of any offence; the sub-section itself contains no 'unless' and no reference to a Magistrate. Sub-section (2) separately provides that no confession made by any person while he is in the custody of a police officer, unless it is made in the immediate presence of a Magistrate, shall be proved against him; that immediate-presence exception sits inside sub-section (2) and relieves only the custody bar. The proviso to sub-section (2) creates the discovery exception: when any fact is deposed to as discovered in consequence of information received from a person accused of any offence, in the custody of a police officer, so much of that information, whether it amounts to a confession or not, as relates distinctly to the fact discovered may be proved. That permission is worded 'may be proved' - it permits proof of that portion, it does not require it. Both sub-sections bar only confessions.
key_requirements: Sub-section (1): no confession made to a police officer shall be proved as against a person accused of any offence; the sub-section itself states this without any unless or exception and makes no reference to a Magistrate.
Sub-section (2): no confession made by any person while he is in the custody of a police officer shall be proved against him.

The immediate presence of a Magistrate is an exception carried within sub-section (2) and relieves only the custody bar; a confession made in the immediate presence of a Magistrate is outside that bar.

The proviso reaches only information received from a person accused of any offence who is in the custody of a police officer, and only where a fact is deposed to as discovered in consequence of that information.

Where those conditions are met, so much of that information, whether it amounts to a confession or not, as relates distinctly to the fact discovered may be proved; the proviso permits proof of that portion, it does not direct that it be proved.
bsa_refs.investigation_relevance: Subject to the discovery proviso, the IO cannot prove a confession made to him; and a confession made by a person while he is in the custody of a police officer cannot be proved against him unless it was made in the immediate presence of a Magistrate. The bar is confined to confessions, so this section does not by itself exclude statements of the accused that are not confessional, though other law may restrict their use. Sub-section (1) carries no Magistrate exception: the immediate-presence exception sits inside sub-section (2) and relieves only the custody bar, so what it saves is a confession made in a Magistrate's immediate presence by a person in police custody, not a confession made to a police officer. Subject to the discovery proviso, a confession made to a police officer cannot be proved against the accused. The other route on the text is the discovery proviso, which is available only where the information came from a person accused of an offence who was in the custody of a police officer, and only where a fact is deposed to as discovered in consequence of that information; the IO must record the information, effect the recovery, have the discovery deposed to, and confine the portion sought to be proved to so much of the information as relates distinctly to the fact actually discovered. Even then the proviso only permits that portion to be proved.

bsa_refs.title: Admissibility of electronic records
bsa_refs.summary: This is the operative provision for proving electronic records. Operating notwithstanding anything contained in this Adhiniyam, sub-section (1) deems any information contained in an electronic record which is printed on paper, stored, recorded or copied in optical or magnetic media or semiconductor memory and produced by a computer or any communication device, or otherwise stored, recorded or copied in any electronic form (the 'computer output'), to be also a document, if the conditions mentioned in this section are satisfied in relation to the information and computer in question, and makes that output admissible in any proceedings, without further proof or production of the original, as evidence of any contents of the original or of any fact stated therein of which direct evidence would be admissible. What sub-section (1) deems is that the computer output is ALSO a document: it does not deem the output to be the original, and it settles nothing about the truth or the weight of what the record contains. Both the deeming and the admissibility are conditional on the section's conditions being satisfied. (The supplied Gazette text reads 'as evidence or any contents of the original'; that is an apparent typographical error for 'as evidence of any contents of the original', and the latter reading is used here.) Sub-section (2) lays down the four conditions in clauses (a) to (d): production of the output by the computer or communication device during the period over which it was used regularly to create, store or process information for the purposes of any activity regularly carried on over that period by the person having lawful control over its use; regular feeding into the device, in the ordinary course of those activities, of information of the kind contained in the record or of the kind from which it is derived; the device operating properly throughout the material part of that period, or any period in which it was not operating properly or was out of operation during that part not being such as to affect the electronic record or the accuracy of its contents; and the information in the record reproducing or being derived from such information fed in. Sub-section (3) treats all the computers or communication devices used for that purpose during that period, whether in standalone mode, on a computer system, on a computer network, on a computer resource enabling information creation or providing information processing and storage, or through an intermediary, as constituting for the purposes of this section a single computer or communication device, and references in the section are construed accordingly. Sub-section (4) is the certificate provision: in any proceeding where it is desired to give a statement in evidence by virtue of this section, a certificate doing ANY of the following three things shall be submitted along with the electronic record at each instance where it is being submitted for admission, namely (a) identifying the electronic record containing the statement and describing the manner in which it was produced, (b) giving such particulars of any device involved in the production of that record as may be appropriate for the purpose of showing that it was produced by a computer or a communication device referred to in clauses (a) to (e) of sub-section (3), and (c) dealing with any of the matters to which the conditions mentioned in sub-section (2) relate. The certificate must purport to be signed by a person in charge of the computer or communication device or the management of the relevant activities (whichever is appropriate) AND an expert, that is, two signatories, and it shall be evidence of any matter stated in the certificate; for the purposes of that sub-section it is sufficient for a matter to be stated to the best of the knowledge and belief of the person stating it, in the certificate specified in the Schedule (the form of which is not part of the text supplied here). Sub-section (5) clarifies that information is taken to be supplied to the computer or communication device if it is supplied in any appropriate form, whether directly or, with or without human intervention, by means of any appropriate equipment; and that a computer output is taken to have been produced by the device whether produced by it directly or, with or without human intervention, by means of any appropriate equipment or by other electronic means as referred to in clauses (a) to (e) of sub-section (3).
key_requirements: Sub-section (1) operates notwithstanding anything contained in this Adhiniyam.

Information contained in an electronic record which is printed on paper, stored, recorded or copied in optical or magnetic media or semiconductor memory and produced by a computer or any communication device, or otherwise stored, recorded or copied in any electronic form (the computer output), shall be deemed to be also a document, if the conditions mentioned in this section are satisfied in relation to the information and computer in question.

Such computer output shall be admissible in any proceedings, without further proof or production of the original, as evidence of any contents of the original or of any fact stated therein of which direct evidence would be admissible (the supplied Gazette text reads 'as evidence or any contents of the original', an apparent typographical error for 'as evidence of any contents of the original', and the latter reading is used here).

The computer output containing the information must have been produced by the computer or communication device during the period over which that device was used regularly to create, store or process information for the purposes of any activity regularly carried on over that period by the person having lawful control over its use.

During the said period, information of the kind contained in the electronic record, or of the kind from which the information so contained is derived, must have been regularly fed into the computer or communication device in the ordinary course of the said activities.

Throughout the material part of the said period the computer or communication device must have been operating properly, or, if not, any period in which it was not operating properly or was out of operation during that part of the period must not have been such as to affect the electronic record or the accuracy of its contents.
The information contained in the electronic record must reproduce or be derived from such information fed into the computer or communication device in the ordinary course of the said activities.

Where the function of creating, storing or processing information for the purposes of the activity was regularly performed by means of one or more computers or communication devices, whether in standalone mode, on a computer system, on a computer network, on a computer resource enabling information creation or providing information processing and storage, or through an intermediary, all the computers or communication devices used for that purpose during that period shall be treated for the purposes of this section as constituting a single computer or communication device.

In any proceeding where it is desired to give a statement in evidence by virtue of this section, a certificate doing any of the things listed in clauses (a) to (c) of sub-section (4) shall be submitted along with the electronic record.
The certificate shall be submitted along with the electronic record at each instance where it is being submitted for admission.
Clause (a) of sub-section (4): identifying the electronic record containing the statement and describing the manner in which it was produced.

Clause (b) of sub-section (4): giving such particulars of any device involved in the production of that electronic record as may be appropriate for the purpose of showing that the electronic record was produced by a computer or a communication device referred to in clauses (a) to (e) of sub-section (3).
Clause (c) of sub-section (4): dealing with any of the matters to which the conditions mentioned in sub-section (2) relate.
The certificate must purport to be signed by a person in charge of the computer or communication device or the management of the relevant activities (whichever is appropriate) and an expert.
The certificate shall be evidence of any matter stated in the certificate.
For the purposes of sub-section (4) it shall be sufficient for a matter to be stated to the best of the knowledge and belief of the person stating it in the certificate specified in the Schedule.

Information shall be taken to be supplied to a computer or communication device if it is supplied thereto in any appropriate form and whether it is so supplied directly or (with or without human intervention) by means of any appropriate equipment.

A computer output shall be taken to have been produced by a computer or communication device whether it was produced by it directly or (with or without human intervention) by means of any appropriate equipment or by other electronic means as referred to in clauses (a) to (e) of sub-section (3).
bsa_refs.investigation_relevance: Wherever the IO relies on this section to put computer output in evidence - CDRs, CCTV footage, device extractions, printouts, server logs - the record must travel with a sub-section (4) certificate, and it must go with the record each and every time the record is submitted for admission, not merely once at charge-sheet stage. On the text the certificate is one 'doing any of' three things: identifying the record and describing how it was produced, giving particulars of any device involved, and dealing with any of the matters to which the sub-section (2) conditions relate; the statute requires any of the three, but the safe practice is to cover all three. The certificate must purport to be signed by two people, a person in charge of the computer or communication device or the management of the relevant activities (whichever is appropriate) and an expert, and it is the certificate specified in the Schedule, so the IO should line up both signatories before the record is tendered; a matter may be stated in it to the best of the knowledge and belief of the person stating it. At seizure, therefore, the IO should record the facts the signatories will later have to certify: regular use of the device over the relevant period for the activity, who had lawful control over its use, regular feeding of information of that kind in the ordinary course, and the proper working of the device (or that any malfunction or downtime in the material part of the period did not affect the record or the accuracy of its contents). Note the limits of sub-section (1): where the conditions are met it deems the computer output to be also a document and lets it in without further proof or production of the original, but it does not make the output the original and it settles nothing about the truth or weight of the contents.
time_limits: s.63(2)(a): no fixed number of days is prescribed - the relevant period is the period over which the computer or communication device was used regularly to create, store or process information for the purposes of the activity regularly carried on over that period.

s.63(2)(c): the computer or communication device must have been operating properly 'throughout the material part of the said period', or any period in which it was not operating properly or was out of operation during that part must not have been such as to affect the electronic record or the accuracy of its contents. This qualification belongs to clause (c) alone and does not relax clauses (a), (b) or (d).
s.63(4): the certificate must be submitted along with the electronic record 'at each instance where it is being submitted for admission' - a repeating timing requirement, not a one-time filing.

bsa_refs.title: Proof of signature and handwriting of person alleged to have signed or written document produced
bsa_refs.summary: This section states the proof rule for a document said to bear a person's signature or handwriting. Where a document is alleged to be signed by, or to have been written wholly or in part by, any person, the signature or the handwriting of so much of the document as is alleged to be in that person's handwriting must be proved to be in his handwriting. The obligation is mandatory, and it is limited to the portion alleged to be that person's: nothing beyond that portion has to be proved under this section. The section does not itself prescribe the manner in which that proof is to be given, and it names no act to be done by any investigating officer; it operates as a rule of proof on whoever tenders the document and on the Court in receiving it.
key_requirements: If a document is alleged to be signed or to have been written wholly or in part by any person, the signature or the handwriting must be proved to be in his handwriting.
The proof requirement extends only to so much of the document as is alleged to be in that person's handwriting.
bsa_refs.investigation_relevance: Whenever the case rests on a signed or handwritten document - a disputed cheque, a receipt, a threat letter, a register entry, a signed agreement - the IO must build the material that will later establish the signature or handwriting as that person's, because the document does not prove itself. Note the limit: only the part alleged to be in that person's hand needs proving, so the IO should identify precisely which words, entries or signature are attributed to the accused or witness. The section itself prescribes no mode of proof and no step for the IO; nothing about specimen writings, comparison or expert opinion appears in this text, so any such step must be sourced from another provision and not from this one.
