bsa_refs.title: Confession to police officer
bsa_refs.summary: Bars proof of confessions connected with the police. Sub-section (1) provides that no confession made to a police officer shall be proved as against a person accused of any offence; the sub-section itself contains no 'unless' and no reference to a Magistrate. Sub-section (2) separately provides that no confession made by any person while he is in the custody of a police officer, unless it is made in the immediate presence of a Magistrate, shall be proved against him; that immediate-presence exception sits inside sub-section (2) and relieves only the custody bar. The proviso to sub-section (2) creates the discovery exception: when any fact is deposed to as discovered in consequence of information received from a person accused of any offence, in the custody of a police officer, so much of that information, whether it amounts to a confession or not, as relates distinctly to the fact discovered may be proved. That permission is worded 'may be proved' - it permits proof of that portion, it does not require it. Both sub-sections bar only confessions.
key_requirements: Sub-section (1): no confession made to a police officer shall be proved as against a person accused of any offence; the sub-section itself states this without any unless or exception and makes no reference to a Magistrate.
Sub-section (2): no confession made by any person while he is in the custody of a police officer shall be proved against him.

The immediate presence of a Magistrate is an exception carried within sub-section (2) and relieves only the custody bar; a confession made in the immediate presence of a Magistrate is outside that bar.

The proviso reaches only information received from a person accused of any offence who is in the custody of a police officer, and only where a fact is deposed to as discovered in consequence of that information.

Where those conditions are met, so much of that information, whether it amounts to a confession or not, as relates distinctly to the fact discovered may be proved; the proviso permits proof of that portion, it does not direct that it be proved.
bsa_refs.investigation_relevance: Subject to the discovery proviso, the IO cannot prove a confession made to him; and a confession made by a person while he is in the custody of a police officer cannot be proved against him unless it was made in the immediate presence of a Magistrate. The bar is confined to confessions, so this section does not by itself exclude statements of the accused that are not confessional, though other law may restrict their use. Sub-section (1) carries no Magistrate exception: the immediate-presence exception sits inside sub-section (2) and relieves only the custody bar, so what it saves is a confession made in a Magistrate's immediate presence by a person in police custody, not a confession made to a police officer. Subject to the discovery proviso, a confession made to a police officer cannot be proved against the accused. The other route on the text is the discovery proviso, which is available only where the information came from a person accused of an offence who was in the custody of a police officer, and only where a fact is deposed to as discovered in consequence of that information; the IO must record the information, effect the recovery, have the discovery deposed to, and confine the portion sought to be proved to so much of the information as relates distinctly to the fact actually discovered. Even then the proviso only permits that portion to be proved.

bsa_refs.title: Admissibility of electronic records
bsa_refs.summary: This is the operative provision for proving electronic records. Operating notwithstanding anything contained in this Adhiniyam, sub-section (1) deems any information contained in an electronic record which is printed on paper, stored, recorded or copied in optical or magnetic media or semiconductor memory and produced by a computer or any communication device, or otherwise stored, recorded or copied in any electronic form (the 'computer output'), to be also a document, if the conditions mentioned in this section are satisfied in relation to the information and computer in question, and makes that output admissible in any proceedings, without further proof or production of the original, as evidence of any contents of the original or of any fact stated therein of which direct evidence would be admissible. What sub-section (1) deems is that the computer output is ALSO a document: it does not deem the output to be the original, and it settles nothing about the truth or the weight of what the record contains. Both the deeming and the admissibility are conditional on the section's conditions being satisfied. (The supplied Gazette text reads 'as evidence or any contents of the original'; that is an apparent typographical error for 'as evidence of any contents of the original', and the latter reading is used here.) Sub-section (2) lays down the four conditions in clauses (a) to (d): production of the output by the computer or communication device during the period over which it was used regularly to create, store or process information for the purposes of any activity regularly carried on over that period by the person having lawful control over its use; regular feeding into the device, in the ordinary course of those activities, of information of the kind contained in the record or of the kind from which it is derived; the device operating properly throughout the material part of that period, or any period in which it was not operating properly or was out of operation during that part not being such as to affect the electronic record or the accuracy of its contents; and the information in the record reproducing or being derived from such information fed in. Sub-section (3) treats all the computers or communication devices used for that purpose during that period, whether in standalone mode, on a computer system, on a computer network, on a computer resource enabling information creation or providing information processing and storage, or through an intermediary, as constituting for the purposes of this section a single computer or communication device, and references in the section are construed accordingly. Sub-section (4) is the certificate provision: in any proceeding where it is desired to give a statement in evidence by virtue of this section, a certificate doing ANY of the following three things shall be submitted along with the electronic record at each instance where it is being submitted for admission, namely (a) identifying the electronic record containing the statement and describing the manner in which it was produced, (b) giving such particulars of any device involved in the production of that record as may be appropriate for the purpose of showing that it was produced by a computer or a communication device referred to in clauses (a) to (e) of sub-section (3), and (c) dealing with any of the matters to which the conditions mentioned in sub-section (2) relate. Sub-section (5) clarifies that information is taken to be supplied to the computer or communication device if it is supplied in any appropriate form, whether directly or, with or without human intervention, by means of any appropriate equipment; and that a computer output is taken to have been produced by the device whether produced by it directly or, with or without human intervention, by means of any appropriate equipment or by other electronic means as referred to in clauses (a) to (e) of sub-section (3).

bsa_refs.title: Admissibility of electronic records
bsa_refs.summary: This is the operative provision for proving electronic records. Operating notwithstanding anything contained in this Adhiniyam, sub-section (1) deems any information contained in an electronic record which is printed on paper, stored, recorded or copied in optical or magnetic media or semiconductor memory and produced by a computer or any communication device, or otherwise stored, recorded or copied in any electronic form (the 'computer output'), to be also a document, if the conditions mentioned in this section are satisfied in relation to the information and computer in question, and makes that output admissible in any proceedings, without further proof or production of the original, as evidence of any contents of the original or of any fact stated therein of which direct evidence would be admissible. What sub-section (1) deems is that the computer output is ALSO a document: it does not deem the output to be the original, and it settles nothing about the truth or the weight of what the record contains. Both the deeming and the admissibility are conditional on the section's conditions being satisfied. (The supplied Gazette text reads 'as evidence or any contents of the original'; that is an apparent typographical error for 'as evidence of any contents of the original', and the latter reading is used here.) Sub-section (2) lays down the four conditions in clauses (a) to (d): production of the output by the computer or communication device during the period over which it was used regularly to create, store or process information for the purposes of any activity regularly carried on over that period by the person having lawful control over its use; regular feeding into the device, in the ordinary course of those activities, of information of the kind contained in the record or of the kind from which it is derived; the device operating properly throughout the material part of that period, or any period in which it was not operating properly or was out of operation during that part not being such as to affect the electronic record or the accuracy of its contents; and the information in the record reproducing or being derived from such information fed in. Sub-section (3) treats all the computers or communication devices used for that purpose during that period, whether in standalone mode, on a computer system, on a computer network, on a computer resource enabling information creation or providing information processing and storage, or through an intermediary, as constituting for the purposes of this section a single computer or communication device, and references in the section are construed accordingly. Sub-section (4) is the certificate provision: in any proceeding where it is desired to give a statement in evidence by virtue of this section, a certificate doing ANY of the following three things shall be submitted along with the electronic record at each instance where it is being submitted for admission, namely (a) identifying the electronic record containing the statement and describing the manner in which it was produced, (b) giving such particulars of any device involved in the production of that record as may be appropriate for the purpose of showing that it was produced by a computer or a communication device referred to in clauses (a) to (e) of sub-section (3), and (c) dealing with any of the matters to which the conditions mentioned in sub-section (2) relate. The certificate must purport to be signed by a person in charge of the computer or communication device or the management of the relevant activities (whichever is appropriate) AND an expert, that is, two signatories, and it shall be evidence of any matter stated in the certificate; for the purposes of that sub-section it is sufficient for a matter to be stated to the best of the knowledge and belief of the person stating it, in the certificate specified in the Schedule (the form of which is not part of the text supplied here). Sub-section (5) clarifies that information is taken to be supplied to the computer or communication device if it is supplied in any appropriate form, whether directly or, with or without human intervention, by means of any appropriate equipment; and that a computer output is taken to have been produced by the device whether produced by it directly or, with or without human intervention, by means of any appropriate equipment or by other electronic means as referred to in clauses (a) to (e) of sub-section (3).
key_requirements: Sub-section (1) operates notwithstanding anything contained in this Adhiniyam.

Information contained in an electronic record which is printed on paper, stored, recorded or copied in optical or magnetic media or semiconductor memory and produced by a computer or any communication device, or otherwise stored, recorded or copied in any electronic form (the computer output), shall be deemed to be also a document, if the conditions mentioned in this section are satisfied in relation to the information and computer in question.

Such computer output shall be admissible in any proceedings, without further proof or production of the original, as evidence of any contents of the original or of any fact stated therein of which direct evidence would be admissible (the supplied Gazette text reads 'as evidence or any contents of the original', an apparent typographical error for 'as evidence of any contents of the original', and the latter reading is used here).

The computer output containing the information must have been produced by the computer or communication device during the period over which that device was used regularly to create, store or process information for the purposes of any activity regularly carried on over that period by the person having lawful control over its use.

During the said period, information of the kind contained in the electronic record, or of the kind from which the information so contained is derived, must have been regularly fed into the computer or communication device in the ordinary course of the said activities.

Throughout the material part of the said period the computer or communication device must have been operating properly, or, if not, any period in which it was not operating properly or was out of operation during that part of the period must not have been such as to affect the electronic record or the accuracy of its contents.
The information contained in the electronic record must reproduce or be derived from such information fed into the computer or communication device in the ordinary course of the said activities.

Where the function of creating, storing or processing information for the purposes of the activity was regularly performed by means of one or more computers or communication devices, whether in standalone mode, on a computer system, on a computer network, on a computer resource enabling information creation or providing information processing and storage, or through an intermediary, all the computers or communication devices used for that purpose during that period shall be treated for the purposes of this section as constituting a single computer or communication device.

In any proceeding where it is desired to give a statement in evidence by virtue of this section, a certificate doing any of the things listed in clauses (a) to (c) of sub-section (4) shall be submitted along with the electronic record.
The certificate shall be submitted along with the electronic record at each instance where it is being submitted for admission.
Clause (a) of sub-section (4): identifying the electronic record containing the statement and describing the manner in which it was produced.

Clause (b) of sub-section (4): giving such particulars of any device involved in the production of that electronic record as may be appropriate for the purpose of showing that the electronic record was produced by a computer or a communication device referred to in clauses (a) to (e) of sub-section (3).
Clause (c) of sub-section (4): dealing with any of the matters to which the conditions mentioned in sub-section (2) relate.
The certificate must purport to be signed by a person in charge of the computer or communication device or the management of the relevant activities (whichever is appropriate) and an expert.
The certificate shall be evidence of any matter stated in the certificate.
For the purposes of sub-section (4) it shall be sufficient for a matter to be stated to the best of the knowledge and belief of the person stating it in the certificate specified in the Schedule.

Information shall be taken to be supplied to a computer or communication device if it is supplied thereto in any appropriate form and whether it is so supplied directly or (with or without human intervention) by means of any appropriate equipment.

A computer output shall be taken to have been produced by a computer or communication device whether it was produced by it directly or (with or without human intervention) by means of any appropriate equipment or by other electronic means as referred to in clauses (a) to (e) of sub-section (3).
bsa_refs.investigation_relevance: Wherever the IO relies on this section to put computer output in evidence - CDRs, CCTV footage, device extractions, printouts, server logs - the record must travel with a sub-section (4) certificate, and it must go with the record each and every time the record is submitted for admission, not merely once at charge-sheet stage. On the text the certificate is one 'doing any of' three things: identifying the record and describing how it was produced, giving particulars of any device involved, and dealing with any of the matters to which the sub-section (2) conditions relate; the statute requires any of the three, but the safe practice is to cover all three. The certificate must purport to be signed by two people, a person in charge of the computer or communication device or the management of the relevant activities (whichever is appropriate) and an expert, and it is the certificate specified in the Schedule, so the IO should line up both signatories before the record is tendered; a matter may be stated in it to the best of the knowledge and belief of the person stating it. At seizure, therefore, the IO should record the facts the signatories will later have to certify: regular use of the device over the relevant period for the activity, who had lawful control over its use, regular feeding of information of that kind in the ordinary course, and the proper working of the device (or that any malfunction or downtime in the material part of the period did not affect the record or the accuracy of its contents). Note the limits of sub-section (1): where the conditions are met it deems the computer output to be also a document and lets it in without further proof or production of the original, but it does not make the output the original and it settles nothing about the truth or weight of the contents.
time_limits: s.63(2)(a): no fixed number of days is prescribed - the relevant period is the period over which the computer or communication device was used regularly to create, store or process information for the purposes of the activity regularly carried on over that period.

s.63(2)(c): the computer or communication device must have been operating properly 'throughout the material part of the said period', or any period in which it was not operating properly or was out of operation during that part must not have been such as to affect the electronic record or the accuracy of its contents. This qualification belongs to clause (c) alone and does not relax clauses (a), (b) or (d).
s.63(4): the certificate must be submitted along with the electronic record 'at each instance where it is being submitted for admission' - a repeating timing requirement, not a one-time filing.

Information contained in an electronic record which is printed on paper, stored, recorded or copied in optical or magnetic media or semiconductor memory and produced by a computer or any communication device, or otherwise stored, recorded or copied in any electronic form (the computer output), shall be deemed to be also a document, if the conditions mentioned in this section are satisfied in relation to the information and computer in question.

Such computer output shall be admissible in any proceedings, without further proof or production of the original, as evidence of any contents of the original or of any fact stated therein of which direct evidence would be admissible (the supplied Gazette text reads 'as evidence or any contents of the original', an apparent typographical error for 'as evidence of any contents of the original', and the latter reading is used here).

The computer output containing the information must have been produced by the computer or communication device during the period over which that device was used regularly to create, store or process information for the purposes of any activity regularly carried on over that period by the person having lawful control over its use.

During the said period, information of the kind contained in the electronic record, or of the kind from which the information so contained is derived, must have been regularly fed into the computer or communication device in the ordinary course of the said activities.

Throughout the material part of the said period the computer or communication device must have been operating properly, or, if not, any period in which it was not operating properly or was out of operation during that part of the period must not have been such as to affect the electronic record or the accuracy of its contents.
The information contained in the electronic record must reproduce or be derived from such information fed into the computer or communication device in the ordinary course of the said activities.

Where the function of creating, storing or processing information for the purposes of the activity was regularly performed by means of one or more computers or communication devices, whether in standalone mode, on a computer system, on a computer network, on a computer resource enabling information creation or providing information processing and storage, or through an intermediary, all the computers or communication devices used for that purpose during that period shall be treated for the purposes of this section as constituting a single computer or communication device.

In any proceeding where it is desired to give a statement in evidence by virtue of this section, a certificate doing any of the things listed in clauses (a) to (c) of sub-section (4) shall be submitted along with the electronic record.
The certificate shall be submitted along with the electronic record at each instance where it is being submitted for admission.
Clause (a) of sub-section (4): identifying the electronic record containing the statement and describing the manner in which it was produced.

Clause (b) of sub-section (4): giving such particulars of any device involved in the production of that electronic record as may be appropriate for the purpose of showing that the electronic record was produced by a computer or a communication device referred to in clauses (a) to (e) of sub-section (3).
Clause (c) of sub-section (4): dealing with any of the matters to which the conditions mentioned in sub-section (2) relate.
The certificate must purport to be signed by a person in charge of the computer or communication device or the management of the relevant activities (whichever is appropriate) and an expert.
The certificate shall be evidence of any matter stated in the certificate.
For the purposes of sub-section (4) it shall be sufficient for a matter to be stated to the best of the knowledge and belief of the person stating it in the certificate specified in the Schedule.

Information shall be taken to be supplied to a computer or communication device if it is supplied thereto in any appropriate form and whether it is so supplied directly or (with or without human intervention) by means of any appropriate equipment.

A computer output shall be taken to have been produced by a computer or communication device whether it was produced by it directly or (with or without human intervention) by means of any appropriate equipment or by other electronic means as referred to in clauses (a) to (e) of sub-section (3).
bsa_refs.investigation_relevance: Wherever the IO relies on this section to put computer output in evidence - CDRs, CCTV footage, device extractions, printouts, server logs - the record must travel with a sub-section (4) certificate, and it must go with the record each and every time the record is submitted for admission, not merely once at charge-sheet stage. On the text the certificate is one 'doing any of' three things: identifying the record and describing how it was produced, giving particulars of any device involved, and dealing with any of the matters to which the sub-section (2) conditions relate; the statute requires any of the three, but the safe practice is to cover all three. The certificate must purport to be signed by two people, a person in charge of the computer or communication device or the management of the relevant activities (whichever is appropriate) and an expert, and it is the certificate specified in the Schedule, so the IO should line up both signatories before the record is tendered; a matter may be stated in it to the best of the knowledge and belief of the person stating it. At seizure, therefore, the IO should record the facts the signatories will later have to certify: regular use of the device over the relevant period for the activity, who had lawful control over its use, regular feeding of information of that kind in the ordinary course, and the proper working of the device (or that any malfunction or downtime in the material part of the period did not affect the record or the accuracy of its contents). Note the limits of sub-section (1): where the conditions are met it deems the computer output to be also a document and lets it in without further proof or production of the original, but it does not make the output the original and it settles nothing about the truth or weight of the contents.
time_limits: s.63(2)(a): no fixed number of days is prescribed - the relevant period is the period over which the computer or communication device was used regularly to create, store or process information for the purposes of the activity regularly carried on over that period.

s.63(2)(c): the computer or communication device must have been operating properly 'throughout the material part of the said period', or any period in which it was not operating properly or was out of operation during that part must not have been such as to affect the electronic record or the accuracy of its contents. This qualification belongs to clause (c) alone and does not relax clauses (a), (b) or (d).
s.63(4): the certificate must be submitted along with the electronic record 'at each instance where it is being submitted for admission' - a repeating timing requirement, not a one-time filing.

bsa_refs.title: Proof of signature and handwriting of person alleged to have signed or written document produced
bsa_refs.summary: This section states the proof rule for a document said to bear a person's signature or handwriting. Where a document is alleged to be signed by, or to have been written wholly or in part by, any person, the signature or the handwriting of so much of the document as is alleged to be in that person's handwriting must be proved to be in his handwriting. The obligation is mandatory, and it is limited to the portion alleged to be that person's: nothing beyond that portion has to be proved under this section. The section does not itself prescribe the manner in which that proof is to be given, and it names no act to be done by any investigating officer; it operates as a rule of proof on whoever tenders the document and on the Court in receiving it.
key_requirements: If a document is alleged to be signed or to have been written wholly or in part by any person, the signature or the handwriting must be proved to be in his handwriting.
The proof requirement extends only to so much of the document as is alleged to be in that person's handwriting.
bsa_refs.investigation_relevance: Whenever the case rests on a signed or handwritten document - a disputed cheque, a receipt, a threat letter, a register entry, a signed agreement - the IO must build the material that will later establish the signature or handwriting as that person's, because the document does not prove itself. Note the limit: only the part alleged to be in that person's hand needs proving, so the IO should identify precisely which words, entries or signature are attributed to the accused or witness. The section itself prescribes no mode of proof and no step for the IO; nothing about specimen writings, comparison or expert opinion appears in this text, so any such step must be sourced from another provision and not from this one.

steps.stage: Joinder of charges and split charge-sheets
steps.text: Three offences of the same kind committed within a year may be charged together (Section 219 Cr.P.C.). Offences are of the same kind when punishable with the same amount of punishment under the same section of the IPC or of any special or local law; an offence under Section 379 IPC is deemed of the same kind as one under Section 380 IPC, and an offence is deemed of the same kind as an attempt to commit it where the attempt is itself an offence.
legal_basis: Section 219 CrPC

details.text: Distinguish 'same kind' from 'same offence' (Lalu Prasad Yadav, AIR 2017 SC 3389, 'Fodder Scam'): defalcations in different treasuries were distinct offences, though of the same kind, by different sets of accused, requiring separate charges and separate trials; defalcation across different treasuries, years, amounts, allotment letters, supply orders and suppliers is not the same transaction.
details.citation: Kerala Police - Standard Operating Procedure: Investigation & Prosecution in General (SOP Series), State Police Chief, 01.11.2020

details.text: There may be a larger conspiracy and a smaller one developing in successive stages involving different accused; where defalcations are made in various years by combinations of different accused there can be separate trials (Ram Lal Narang v. State (Delhi Administration), 1979(2) SCC 322: AIR 1979 SC 1791).

steps.text: Classify the referred report under the correct category - Non-Cognizable, Mistake of Fact, Civil Nature, False, or Undetectable - because the consequences differ for each.

details.text: Non-Cognizable: if investigation of a cognizable offence reveals a non-cognizable offence, the report is deemed a complaint per Section 2(d) CrPC; submit a Final Report Non-Cognizable - the parties are then free to contest in a court of law, or the Magistrate may take cognizance on the Final Report itself and summon the accused to stand trial (India Carat Pvt. Ltd. v. State of Karnataka, 1989 Cr.L.J. 963 SC).
details.citation: Kerala Police - Standard Operating Procedure: Investigation & Prosecution in General (SOP Series), State Police Chief, 01.11.2020

details.text: Mistake of Fact: where the case was started because of misrepresentation of facts and the investigator learns the correct state of facts, submit the Final Report as Mistake of Fact for dismissing the case.

details.text: Civil Nature: if the investigation reveals the case relates to a civil dispute, dispose of it as of civil nature.
details.citation: Kerala Police - Standard Operating Procedure: Investigation & Prosecution in General (SOP Series), State Police Chief, 01.11.2020

details.text: False: when the investigation shows the complainant's case to be false, submit the Final Report as False; the complainant should be prosecuted under Section 182 or 221 IPC or the corresponding State Police Act provision (printed in the source as Section 117(d) of the Kerala Police Act).
details.citation: Kerala Police - Standard Operating Procedure: Investigation & Prosecution in General (SOP Series), State Police Chief, 01.11.2020

details.text: Undetectable: if despite all efforts the case is not detected, submit a Final Report Undetectable; whenever the accused is traced and arrested, the case is opened again.

steps.text: When preparing a final report: type it in double space with a dark ink impression and number the paragraphs; make the enquiry thorough and complete with information adequate on all points; keep allegations, facts, available evidence, opinions and comments separate and succinct; avoid repetition, list the allegations in proper order in clear and definite form and discuss each separately in detail; keep the analysis of facts separate from the opinion, with a clear conclusion on each allegation and each accused, naming each accused and his accused number in the final recommendation; state clearly with reasons any necessary witness who could not be examined or document that could not be obtained; and incorporate the expert's opinion, or at least the relevant portion, in the report.

conflicts.description: kerala_police_sop_2020 (kerala-final-report, p.234) records, on Rama Chaudhury v. State of Bihar (AIR 2009 SC 2308), that the law does not mandate prior permission of the Magistrate for further investigation, though it is good to inform the Court; bnss_2023 (BNSS 193) requires the court's permission for further investigation during trial and caps it at ninety days, extendable by the court.
conflicts.resolution: The BNSS requirement governs, being the law layer and highest authority: obtain the court's permission and complete the further investigation within ninety days unless the court extends it. The Kerala position states the pre-2023 law under Section 173(8) CrPC and is retained in details[] only as the historical rule; its practice of informing the court is subsumed by the BNSS permission requirement.

steps.stage: Conduct of the trial - assisting the prosecutor
steps.text: Watch the cross-examination of prosecution witnesses and give the prosecutor valid inputs and suggestions where a witness has been made to give a misleading statement, or where a point has been purposefully left obscure, so that it can be cleared in re-examination.

details.text: Examination of witnesses is governed by the Indian Evidence Act: Section 137 lays down the three stages - examination-in-chief, cross-examination and re-examination - and Section 138 the order of examination. Cross-examination is a statutory right to test veracity, extract truth and expose falsehood; the prosecutor's function is to assist the Court on legal and admissible evidence.

steps.stage: The investigating officer in the witness box
steps.text: Go to the witness box ready with the case diaries and witness statements and hand the case diaries over immediately if the Court calls for them, since delay may draw an adverse inference on the IO's conduct. Appear in uniform even if working in a Special Unit, salute the Court on entering and leaving the Court and the witness box, and keep the decorum of the Court. After taking the oath, narrate the statement chronologically - from receipt of information and registration of the case, through the steps adopted and evidence collected, up to filing of the charge sheet - and mention witnesses, exhibits and material objects in the chronological order marked in Court (PW, Exhibit P, MO). Give short answers in simple language, never answer hastily without understanding the question and do not delay unduly, since lengthy answers open fresh rounds of questions. An officer who investigated only part of the case should depose about his own role and its handover alone, and not about investigation done by other officers unless verified by him.

steps.stage: The investigating officer in the witness box
steps.text: Remain calm and do not argue with the defence counsel, while still ensuring your points reach the Court. Understand the question patiently and answer only after it is completed; answer looking at the Judge, and if the question is unclear bring it to the Court's notice. Never turn towards the prosecution counsel when questioned by the adverse party, as it suggests reliance on the prosecutor for the reply. Do not take offence at the nature of the questions, and if a question is unnecessarily vexatious represent the matter to the Court and seek its protection. Be vigilant against questions framed so that only 'Yes' or 'No' can be answered - give a suitable explanation instead, and if counsel insists, seek the Court's permission to suffix an explanation.

steps.text: Report the progress of cases in Courts, including appeals and revisions, regularly through Court Diaries in the prescribed form, in duplicate - one copy to the Public Prosecutor and one to the District Police Chief. The Court Diary forwarded by the District Police Chief must invariably contain: (i) names of prosecution or defence witnesses summoned or examined; (ii) how the witnesses fared and a gist of their evidence, and where a witness turns hostile, that fact with the District Police Chief's comment on how the damage will be remedied; (iii) how the case proceeded; (iv) what proceedings are due on the next hearing date; (v) reasons for any adjournment, indicating whether granted at the request of prosecution or defence or because the Court could not take up the case; and (vi) where adjournment was occasioned by non-production of witnesses, the reasons for it.
steps.responsible: Prosecuting Officers in charge of the cases; District Police Chief on forwarding

details.text: The Court Diary should be detailed; if in any extreme exigency adjournment is sought by the prosecution - which should normally be avoided - the diary should contain full reasons for it.

steps.stage: After judgment - scrutiny, appeal and revision
steps.text: Drive the appeal process against an acquittal to time. In a Sessions case the Public Prosecutor reports to the Collector and the Superintendent of Police soon after the judgment with his recommendation; where he considers an appeal or revision should be filed he obtains certified copies of the necessary records and forwards them with his report direct to the Advocate General, sending a copy to the District Collector, who promptly addresses the Home Department for instructions to the Advocate General. In Magistrate court acquittals the Assistant Public Prosecutor sends the proposal to the District Collector through the Superintendent of Police, obtaining certified copies of depositions and other records promptly. The District Collector, after consulting the Public Prosecutor if necessary, sends a report to the Government in the Home Department with a copy to the Director General of Prosecutions; his report must reach the Government within 45 days of the judgment, and if he decides no appeal is needed he immediately informs the Superintendent of Police. Where the District Police Chief is of the view that grounds exist, he sends a report to the State Police Chief through proper channel to move the Government.
steps.deadline: District Collector's report to the Government within 45 days of the judgment
steps.responsible: SHO / Inspector of Police concerned coordinates all these steps in time
steps.applies_when: The trial ended in acquittal and an appeal is under consideration

steps.text: Never recommend an appeal or revision mechanically without analysis of the judgment. While examining a case for appeal against acquittal or discharge, keep in mind the decisions of the High Courts and the Supreme Court on the scope of the Appellate Court's power to interfere under Section 378 Cr.P.C., and weigh: (i) the trial court's views on the credibility of witnesses; (ii) the appellate court's reluctance to disturb findings of fact recorded by the court which saw and heard the witnesses; (iii) the accused's right to the benefit of doubt; and (iv) any other factor the Public Prosecutor considers relevant.

steps.text: Do not use 'appeal' and 'revision' loosely or interchangeably. Sections 372 to 394 Cr.P.C. deal with appeals and Sections 395 to 405 Cr.P.C. with revisions. An appeal is a legal right by which the appellant approaches a higher Court for review or reversal of the verdict below on legal and/or factual grounds, and lies both against conviction and against acquittal (Section 378(2) Cr.P.C.). A revision invokes the supervisory jurisdiction of a higher Court to examine the correctness, legality or propriety of any finding, sentence or order of an inferior Court; under Section 397 Cr.P.C. the High Court cannot re-appreciate evidence in revision and interferes only in exceptional cases of real and substantial injustice.

ticks.do: Do not use 'appeal' and 'revision' loosely or interchangeably.
Locate appeals in Sections 372 to 394 Cr.P.C. and revisions in Sections 395 to 405 Cr.P.C.
Treat an appeal as a legal right by which the appellant approaches a higher Court for review or reversal of the verdict below on legal and/or factual grounds.
Note that an appeal lies both against conviction and against acquittal under Section 378(2) Cr.P.C.
Treat a revision as an invocation of the supervisory jurisdiction of a higher Court over the correctness, legality or propriety of any finding, sentence or order of an inferior Court.
Remember that under Section 397 Cr.P.C. the High Court cannot re-appreciate evidence in revision and interferes only in exceptional cases of real and substantial injustice.

steps.title: Distinguish appeal from revision correctly
steps.triage_why: This is a legal definition distinguishing 'appeal' from 'revision'.

steps.stage: After judgment - scrutiny, appeal and revision
steps.text: Do not seek review or modification of a judgment once it has been signed. Under Section 362 Cr.P.C. the criminal court becomes functus officio the moment the disposal order is signed, and the order cannot be altered except to correct a clerical or arithmetical error. The prohibition is absolute - even the High Court, exercising its inherent power under Section 482 Cr.P.C., has no authority or jurisdiction to alter the judgment (Hari Singh Mann v. Harbhajan Singh Bajwa & Ors, AIR 2001 SC 43; Chhanni v. State of U.P., AIR 2006 SC 3051).
legal_basis: Section 362 CrPC
Section 482 CrPC

conflicts.description: BNSS 107 (bnss/sec_107.json, key_requirements) frames the matter as a power: where the IO 'has reason to believe' property is proceeds of crime he 'may', with SP/CP approval, apply for attachment. Gujarat SOP 24 (guj_cid_29_sops_2024, SOP 24, p.107) casts the antecedent identification as a duty — the IO 'shall identify such properties'.
conflicts.resolution: No factual conflict, only a modal one: the statute confers the power and supplies the 'derived or obtained, directly or indirectly' standard, while the binding Gujarat SOP makes identification mandatory for Gujarat officers. Both are marked operative and the mandatory 'shall identify' is retained on the authority of the binding Gujarat SOP, not attributed to BNSS 107.

conflicts.description: Approving authority: BNSS 107 (bnss/sec_107.json, key_requirements) requires the 'Prior approval of SP or Commissioner of Police' — a single officer in the alternative, according to jurisdiction. Gujarat SOP 24 (SOP 24, p.108) directs a detailed report 'addressed to the concerned Superintendent of Police and Commissioner of Police' and approval from 'their' hands, which read literally requires both.
conflicts.resolution: The statute governs the requirement: approval of the Superintendent of Police OR the Commissioner of Police having jurisdiction suffices, and the canonical text uses the statutory 'or'. The SOP's 'and' formulation is preserved verbatim in details[] as the Gujarat reporting practice; the two were not blended into a single requirement.

steps.text: After considering the explanation, if any, given by the person and the material/evidence available, and after giving the person(s) a reasonable opportunity of being heard, the Court/Magistrate may pass an order attaching the property. If the person does not appear before the Court/Magistrate within the fourteen days specified in the show-cause notice, or does not make a representation in his own case, the order may be passed ex parte. Where the Court/Magistrate is of the opinion that issuing the show-cause notice would defeat the object of the attachment or forfeiture, an interim ex parte order directing attachment or seizure of the property may issue, and it remains in force until the distribution order under BNSS 107(6) is passed.
legal_basis: BNSS 107

details.text: The Court/Magistrate, after considering any explanation given by the person and the material/evidence available, and after giving the person(s) a reasonable opportunity of being heard, may pass an order taking the properties into attachment if satisfied the property was purchased out of proceeds of crime; if the person does not appear within the 14-day period, or does not make a representation in his own case, the Court/Magistrate may proceed to pass an ex parte order.

conflicts.description: Content of the interim ex parte order: BNSS 107 (bnss/sec_107.json, summary) says 'an interim ex parte attachment/seizure may issue where notice would defeat the object'. Gujarat SOP 24 (SOP 24, p.108) says the interim ex parte order directs 'attachment or forfeiture of the property'. Forfeiture at the interim stage is a materially heavier consequence than seizure.
conflicts.resolution: The statute wins the canonical text: the interim ex parte order directs attachment or SEIZURE. The SOP's 'attachment or forfeiture' wording is retained verbatim in details[] with its source; the two were not blended. Both sources agree the interim order lasts until the sub-clause (6) distribution order.

steps.text: If the accused/suspect or any other person refuses or shows unwillingness to give a specimen signature, handwriting, thumb impression or voice sample: the IO shall make an application to the Court concerned setting out the necessary reasons for obtaining such specimens.

details.text: Source's record of the pre-BNSS legal position on compelling a voice sample: the Allahabad High Court in Ritesh Sinha v. State of UP and Anr. (Criminal Misc. Appl. 3272 of 2010) ruled that there is no illegality in asking any person to give a sample of his voice for the purpose of comparison; on challenge the Supreme Court's two-judge bench could not decide the issue - Justice Aftab Alam reversed the Allahabad High Court order while Justice Ranjana Desai upheld it - and the matter was referred to a higher bench, undecided as of 31/07/2015. The power of a Magistrate to order specimen signatures, handwriting, finger impressions and voice samples, including from a person not arrested, is now expressly provided by BNSS s.349.

steps.text: The specimen signature, handwriting or thumb impression shall be obtained on paper of the same type and size as the paper of the disputed document, and with the same type of ink as that with which the disputed document was made.

steps.text: The specimens/impressions shall be taken after seating the person giving them in a manner convenient to him; once a specimen/impression has been obtained on one sheet, that sheet shall be taken back from him immediately, and only thereafter shall the specimen/impression be taken on the next sheet.

steps.triage_why: Prevents the subject from copying the disputed document, strengthening the case, but is a technicality of collection.

steps.stage: S.O.P. for taking specimen signature, handwriting, voice sample, etc. (Section 349 BNSS)
steps.text: The IO shall seize the specimen samples/impressions desirably in 6 sets of 6 specimens each — a total of 36 specimens — and a separate clear mark shall be given to each set.

steps.text: Only the disputed original document shall be sent to the F.S.L. for examination; under no circumstances is a copy of the original document to be sent.

steps.text: If the handwriting, signature or thumb impression on a seized document is that of a deceased person, then for verification and comparison, whatever original documents bearing the handwriting, signature and thumb impression of that deceased person are available shall be seized.

steps.stage: S.O.P. for taking specimen signature, handwriting, voice sample, etc. (Section 349 BNSS)
steps.text: Specimens of natural writing shall be taken in the same language as the disputed document.

steps.text: If, despite due diligence, the person summoned cannot be found, serve by delivering his copy of the summons to some adult member of his family residing with him; that person must invariably sign an acknowledgement of receipt on the reverse side of the second copy (Section 66).

steps.text: On information of a death, determine at once whether it falls within BNSS 194(1), which requires a police inquest: a person has committed suicide; has been killed by another person, by an animal, by machinery or by an accident; or has died in circumstances raising a reasonable suspicion that some other person has committed an offence. details.text: Gujarat SOP 12 enumerates the same trigger as six death cases: (1) suicide; (2) murder committed by an unknown person; (3) death caused by any animal; (4) death caused by machinery; (5) death caused by an accident; (6) death in circumstances raising suspicion that some other person has committed an offence.

conflicts.description: BNSS 194(1) makes the second trigger category a person 'killed by another person', without qualification, whereas Gujarat SOP 12 (p.57) renders that category as 'a murder has been committed by an unknown person', which would exclude a killing by a known person from the inquest trigger.
conflicts.resolution: Law prevails over the Gujarat binding SOP. The canonical text uses the BNSS 194(1) formulation ('killed by another person'), so an inquest is required whether or not the killer is known.

steps.text: On receiving information that a person has committed suicide, been killed by another person or by an animal, died by a weapon or accident, or died in circumstances raising reasonable suspicion of an offence, forthwith intimate the nearest Executive Magistrate empowered to hold inquests and proceed to the place where the body lies. There, draw up the report of the apparent cause of death (the inquest report / panchnama) in the presence of two or more respectable inhabitants of the neighbourhood, recording the particulars of the wounds, fractures, bruises and other marks of injury visible on the body and the manner or weapon by which they appear to have been inflicted; have the report signed by the police officer and the other concurring persons and forward it to the District Magistrate or the Sub-divisional Magistrate within 24 hours.
legal_basis: BNSS 194
steps.deadline: Intimation to the Executive Magistrate forthwith; signed inquest report to the DM/SDM within 24 hours
steps.responsible: Officer in charge of the police station / specially empowered officer

conflicts.description: BNSS 195 (read with BNSS 179) exempts from attendance at the police station a male under fifteen or above sixty, any woman, a mentally or physically disabled person and a person suffering from acute illness, whereas the UP handbook (p.7) states the protection simply as 'women and children' - wider as to children (it would cover boys aged fifteen to eighteen, whom the statute does not exempt) and silent as to men above sixty, disabled persons and the acutely ill.
conflicts.resolution: Law prevails for the canonical text, which keeps the full BNSS list of categories. The UP formulation is not a contradiction of a fact but a wider protective practice for children; it is retained as a detail and may be followed as good practice, and it cannot be read as narrowing the statutory exemptions for men above sixty, disabled persons or the acutely ill.

steps.text: After reaching the scene and verifying/confirming that the property offence has actually occurred, inform the senior officers and call the crime team and the videographer to the scene of crime (in the snatching scenario the compendium requires the photo/videographer to be called). Call a Forensic Expert to the scene where the offence registered carries a heavy punishment: attempt to commit robbery when armed with a deadly weapon, the punishment for which is not less than 7 years, and house-breaking by night, punishable with imprisonment which may extend up to 10 years. Where the offence is punishable with 3 years' imprisonment and fine (snatching), a Forensic Expert is not needed to be called to the Scene of Crime; however the IO may request the assistance of Forensic Experts if the circumstances dictate so.
steps.deadline: Immediately after verification and confirmation of the offence
steps.applies_when: All property offences in this module; whether a Forensic Expert is called, and whether the full crime team or only the photo/videographer is summoned, depends on the offence registered

steps.stage: Scene examination: break-in and offender traces
steps.text: The weapon of offence — whether used for entry and found at the scene, or found on an accused apprehended at the spot — should not be touched by anyone. The first one to examine it should be the finger print proficient along with the Forensic Expert, so that any chance prints present on the weapon, and any traces of shards of glass or other metal present on the weapon used to break open a passage into the premises, are not damaged; the same shall also be done for the deadly weapon being carried by the accused. The IO shall then perform a cursory search of the accused and seize the weapon(s) carried by him with the help of Forensic Experts so that chance prints can be lifted from them, and a sketch of the recovered weapon of offence should be carefully prepared.
steps.responsible: Investigating Officer with the finger print proficient and the Forensic Expert

conflicts.description: The same document prescribes different chargesheet-to-Scrutiny periods across the three property scenarios: 'within 45 days of the arrest' in delhi_compendium_2024, Scenario 14 (snatching), p.137, but 'within 75 days of the arrest' in Scenario 15 (attempt robbery armed with deadly weapon), p.144 and in Scenario 16 (house-breaking by night), p.151.
conflicts.resolution: Not averaged or blended. The two figures are kept separate and tied to the offence registered, because the compendium states them scenario-wise and the gravity of the offence differs (3 years for snatching; not less than 7 years and up to 10 years for the other two). No higher-authority source in this bucket fixes an internal scrutiny period — the only law file here is BNSS 107 — so the advisory figures stand as offence-specific; the statutory limits for completing investigation and filing the final report are governed by the core final-report bucket (BNSS 190/193).

steps.stage: Do's and Don'ts for the IO
steps.text: DON'T: there should be no delay in reaching the scene of crime/occurrence, lest crucial evidence should be lost.
legal_basis: Section 302 IPC [now BNS 103(1)] — punishment for murder: death, or imprisonment for life, and also liable to fine

Section 304B IPC [now BNS 80] — dowry death, where the death of a woman is caused by any burns or bodily injury or occurs otherwise than under normal circumstances within seven years of her marriage and it is shown that soon before her death she was subjected to cruelty or harassment by her husband or any relative of her husband for or in connection with any demand for dowry
Section 174 CrPC [now BNSS 194] — police to enquire and report on suicide etc.; report signed and forwarded forthwith to the District Magistrate or Sub-divisional Magistrate

Section 176 CrPC [now BNSS 196] — inquiry by Magistrate into cause of death; power to disinter and examine a body; relatives to be informed and allowed to remain present ('relative' means parents, children, brothers, sisters and spouse)
Section 327 IPC [now BNS 119(1)] — voluntarily causing hurt to extort property, or to constrain to an illegal act (imprisonment up to ten years and fine)
Section 323 IPC [now BNS 115(2)] — punishment for voluntarily causing hurt (except the case provided for by s.334 IPC): imprisonment up to one year, or fine up to one thousand rupees, or both
Section 284 IPC [now BNS 286] — punishment for careless handling of poisonous substances

Sections 299, 302, 304A, 306, 307, 309, 324, 326, 328 and 489A IPC [now BNS 100, 103, 106(1), 108, 109, no direct BNS equivalent for 309 (BNS 226 covers only attempt to suicide to compel or restrain a public servant), 118(1), 118(2), 123 and 178 respectively] — offences relating to administration of poisonous substances
Poisons Act 1919; Drugs Act 1940; Drugs and Magic Remedies Act 1954; Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act 1985; Pharmacy Act 1948 — possession, sale and control of poisons

Motor Vehicles Act 1988 — driving or attempting to drive with alcohol exceeding 30 mg per 100 ml of blood detected by breath analyser, or under the influence of a drug so as to be incapable of exercising proper control over the vehicle
steps.deadline: No delay, lest crucial evidence should be lost

legal_basis: Section 302 IPC [now BNS 103(1)] — punishment for murder: death, or imprisonment for life, and fine (PDF 334)

Section 304 IPC [now BNS 105] — punishment for culpable homicide not amounting to murder: imprisonment for life or up to ten years where the act is done with intention to cause death or such bodily injury as is likely to cause death; up to ten years, or fine, or both, where done only with knowledge that it is likely to cause death (PDF 334-335)

Section 307 IPC [now BNS 109] — attempt to murder: up to ten years and fine; imprisonment for life if hurt is caused; and where a life convict offending under this section causes hurt, he may be punished with death (PDF 335)
Section 308 IPC [now BNS 110] — attempt to commit culpable homicide: up to three years, or fine, or both; up to seven years if hurt is caused (PDF 335)
Section 336 IPC [now BNS 125] — act so rashly or negligently as to endanger human life or the personal safety of others: up to three months, or fine up to Rs. 250, or both (PDF 335)
Section 337 IPC [now BNS 125(a)] — causing hurt by an act endangering life or personal safety of others: up to six months, or fine up to Rs. 500, or both (PDF 335)

Section 25 Arms Act 1959 — punishment for contravention of ss.3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 17, 24A, 24B (acquiring, possession, carrying, manufacture, sale, transfer, conversion, repair, testing, proving, import, export, shortening of barrel, etc.). The Arms Act is a separate central statute and is unaffected by the 2023 codes — no BNS equivalent applies (PDF 336)

Section 27 Arms Act 1959 — punishment for using arms: use of arms/ammunition in contravention of s.5 — not less than three years and up to seven years and fine; use of prohibited arms/ammunition in contravention of s.7 — not less than seven years up to imprisonment for life and fine; and where such use or act results in the death of any other person — punishable with death (PDF 336)

Section 157 CrPC [now BNSS 176] — officer in charge of the police station, having recorded the information and forwarded the report to the Magistrate, shall proceed in person (or send a subordinate) to the spot to investigate the facts (PDF 336)
Arms Act 1959 — statutory definitions of 'arms' and 'ammunition' relied on when framing queries to the ballistic expert about fired ammunition and live ammunition (PDF 373, PDF 375)

State of Orissa vs. Ramachandra, AIR 1965 Orissa 175 — cited in the guide (printed as 'state of Orissa vs. Ramachandra AIR, 1965 Orissa 175') and described by the guide as 'a ruling of the Supreme Court of India' that an IO can ask the medical officer to take an x-ray of the body and recover the projectiles; note that the citation as printed is to an Orissa High Court report, so the 'Supreme Court' attribution is the guide's own and should be checked before being relied on in court (PDF 371)

steps.text: Forensic queries to put to the laboratory for Death due to weapons other than firearms (homicide u/s 302 IPC [now BNS 103]) — section 3.5.5 'Likely Queries to be Raised (may vary from case to case)', medico-legal queries at PDF 74 and forensic-expert queries at PDF 75: Cause, manner and mode of death (medico-legal examiner); Nature and cause of injuries (medico-legal examiner); Time since death (medico-legal examiner); Age and other identifying features of the deceased (medico-legal examiner); Whether blood is present on the exhibits; if yes, its species of origin and grouping; Whether fingerprints lifted from the scene match the suspect's fingerprints; Whether foot/footwear marks lifted from the scene match the suspect's foot/footwear marks; Identification and comparison of hair, fibre and botanical evidence for connecting the victim, suspect and crime scene or suspected vehicle with each other; Whether DNA profiling of the deceased matches the reference samples for establishing identity of the deceased; Whether the torn button or piece of cloth matches the garments recovered from the suspect; Whether the cut mark/hole present on the garment of the deceased can be caused by the weapon recovered from the suspect or crime scene; Whether stains of grease/paint/soil present on the clothing of the deceased match samples collected from the crime scene; Whether vegetable stains on the clothing of the deceased match that of the plant present at the scene; Whether pollen grains are present in nasal secretion and match the pollen grains in the surrounding area of the crime scene

details.text: Samples required: Exhibits bearing suspected blood; liquid blood on cotton gauze cloth air dried in shade, or a few drops on an FTA card

details.text: Samples required: Scraped/chipped bloodstains, or swabs on cotton gauze, plus material from a representative unstained area as control
details.citation: LNJN National Institute of Criminology and Forensic Science, MHA - A Forensic Guide for Crime Investigators: Standard Operating Procedures (marked Restricted)

details.text: Samples required: Blood-soaked soil, hair or grass air dried, with unstained soil as control
details.citation: LNJN National Institute of Criminology and Forensic Science, MHA - A Forensic Guide for Crime Investigators: Standard Operating Procedures (marked Restricted)

details.text: Samples required: Bloodstained portion of the weapon (knife, axe, bullet, stick) wrapped in clean paper, in a cloth bag or paper envelope depending on size
details.citation: LNJN National Institute of Criminology and Forensic Science, MHA - A Forensic Guide for Crime Investigators: Standard Operating Procedures (marked Restricted)

details.text: Samples required: Bloodstained garments air dried in shade, each wrapped separately in clean paper, in a thick paper envelope or cotton cloth bag
details.citation: LNJN National Institute of Criminology and Forensic Science, MHA - A Forensic Guide for Crime Investigators: Standard Operating Procedures (marked Restricted)

details.text: Samples required: Post-mortem blood on a cotton gauze pad or FTA card
details.citation: LNJN National Institute of Criminology and Forensic Science, MHA - A Forensic Guide for Crime Investigators: Standard Operating Procedures (marked Restricted)

details.text: Samples required: Soft organs/tissues in Dimethylsulphoxide (DMSO) or normal saline, never in formalin
details.citation: LNJN National Institute of Criminology and Forensic Science, MHA - A Forensic Guide for Crime Investigators: Standard Operating Procedures (marked Restricted)

details.text: Samples required: Intact long bone in order of preference femur, tibia, humerus, teeth (molar), ribs — cleaned, dried, rolled in brown paper envelope and sealed in cotton cloth — for DNA profiling of unidentified bodies

details.text: Samples required: Hair strands lifted with forceps having plastic covering on the tip, in paper folds; control hair by combing, with method and site of collection stated in the forwarding letter

details.text: Samples required: Fingerprint lifts on adhesive tape, or the whole article packed in a strong cardboard/wooden box; suspect's specimen fingerprints

details.text: Samples required: Fibre, botanical evidence (leaves, flowers, diatoms, pollen grains, wood splinters, seeds, plant fragments) and entomological evidence (insects, maggots, eggs)

details.citation: LNJN National Institute of Criminology and Forensic Science, MHA - A Forensic Guide for Crime Investigators: Standard Operating Procedures (marked Restricted)

steps.text: Establish the method of search based on investigative theory, size of area to be searched and other factors: zonal method (area divided into squares/sectors with an officer assigned to each zone), spiral or circle method (effective in a small area, beginning from the centre or the perimeter and moving in a circular path), wheel method (searchers gather at the centre and move radially outwards, with the drawback of spoiling evidence at the centre and ever increasing distance between searchers), grid method (best procedure for a large area, searchers moving parallel to one another and covering the same area twice), or cross-hatch method (two dimensional — the scene is covered length wise and then width wise).

steps.stage: Evidence law: Relevancy of facts forming part of same transaction
steps.text: The IO should record the whole surrounding episode, not just the act charged: what the accused, the victim and the bystanders said and did at the incident or so shortly before or after it that it belongs to the same transaction, as illustration (a) shows. Do not drop connected events from the case diary or charge-sheet merely because they happened at a different time or a different place, and in multi-act or multi-location offences collect each component act since it can be proved as part of the general transaction even where the accused was not present at all of them.

bsa_refs.title: Relevancy of facts forming part of same transaction
bsa_refs.summary: Section 4 makes facts relevant that are not themselves in issue but are so connected with a fact in issue or a relevant fact that they form part of the same transaction. The section has no sub-sections; it is a single rule with a built-in clarification that relevance survives a difference of time or place, so events at different times and in different places can still belong to one transaction. The illustrations apply this to what was said or done by the accused, the victim or bystanders at or shortly around a beating, to the several component acts of an armed insurrection even where the accused was not present at all of them, to a chain of letters in a correspondence, and to each successive delivery in a chain of deliveries.
key_requirements: Facts not themselves in issue are relevant where they are so connected with a fact in issue or a relevant fact as to form part of the same transaction.
The connecting test is that the facts form part of the same transaction as the fact in issue or relevant fact.
Such facts remain relevant whether they occurred at the same time and place or at different times and places.
bsa_refs.investigation_relevance: The IO should record the whole surrounding episode, not just the act charged: what the accused, the victim and the bystanders said and did at the incident or so shortly before or after it that it belongs to the same transaction, as illustration (a) shows. Do not drop connected events from the case diary or charge-sheet merely because they happened at a different time or a different place, and in multi-act or multi-location offences collect each component act since it can be proved as part of the general transaction even where the accused was not present at all of them.

bsa_refs.title: Motive, preparation and previous or subsequent conduct
bsa_refs.summary: Section 6 makes motive, preparation and conduct relevant. Sub-section (1) makes relevant any fact that shows or constitutes a motive or preparation for a fact in issue or a relevant fact. Sub-section (2) makes relevant the conduct of a party or of a party's agent in reference to the suit or proceeding or to any fact in issue or relevant fact, and also the conduct of a person against whom an offence is the subject of the proceeding, but only where that conduct influences or is influenced by a fact in issue or relevant fact, and it applies whether the conduct was previous or subsequent. Explanation 1 excludes statements from "conduct" unless they accompany and explain acts other than statements, while preserving their relevancy under any other section. Explanation 2 makes relevant any statement made to a person, or in his presence and hearing, which affects his relevant conduct. Illustrations (e), (h) and (i) treat fabricating, destroying or concealing evidence, procuring the absence of witnesses, absconding and possessing the proceeds of the crime as relevant conduct.
key_requirements: Any fact which shows or constitutes a motive or preparation for a fact in issue or a relevant fact is relevant under sub-section (1).
The conduct of any party, or of any agent to any party, to a suit or proceeding, in reference to that proceeding or to any fact in issue or relevant fact, is relevant under sub-section (2).
The conduct of any person against whom an offence is the subject of the proceeding is likewise relevant under sub-section (2).
Such conduct is relevant only if it influences or is influenced by a fact in issue or a relevant fact.
Conduct is relevant whether it was previous or subsequent to the fact in issue or relevant fact.
Under Explanation 1 the word "conduct" in this section does not include statements.
Statements are treated as conduct only where they accompany and explain acts other than statements, and Explanation 1 does not affect their relevancy under any other section of the Adhiniyam.
Under Explanation 2, where a person's conduct is relevant, a statement made to him or in his presence and hearing which affects that conduct is relevant.

bsa_refs.title: Facts necessary to explain or introduce fact in issue or relevant facts
bsa_refs.summary: Section 7 makes relevant a set of supporting or framing facts, in a single unnumbered provision with five limbs. Facts are relevant if they are necessary to explain or introduce a fact in issue or a relevant fact, if they support or rebut an inference suggested by such a fact, if they establish the identity of anything or of a person whose identity is relevant, if they fix the time or place at which a fact in issue or relevant fact happened, or if they show the relation of the parties by whom any such fact was transacted. The relevance is expressly limited: such facts are relevant only in so far as they are necessary for that purpose. Illustration (c) shows the limit in operation - the fact that the accused had sudden and urgent business explaining a sudden departure is relevant, but the details of that business are not, except so far as needed to show it was sudden and urgent.
key_requirements: Facts necessary to explain or introduce a fact in issue or a relevant fact are relevant.
Facts which support or rebut an inference suggested by a fact in issue or a relevant fact are relevant.
Facts which establish the identity of anything, or of a person whose identity is relevant, are relevant.
Facts which fix the time or place at which a fact in issue or relevant fact happened are relevant.
Facts which show the relation of the parties by whom any such fact was transacted are relevant, and all such facts are relevant only in so far as they are necessary for that purpose.

bsa_refs.title: Facts bearing upon opinions of experts
bsa_refs.summary: Section 40 is a single-limb rule that widens relevancy around expert opinion. It provides that facts which would not otherwise be relevant become relevant if they either support or are inconsistent with the opinions of experts. That extension operates only where the expert opinion in question is itself relevant. The illustrations show the point: symptoms exhibited by other persons poisoned by the same poison, and the behaviour of other similarly situated harbours that had no sea-wall.
key_requirements: Facts not otherwise relevant are relevant if they support or are inconsistent with the opinions of experts.
Such facts are relevant only when the expert opinions concerned are themselves relevant.

steps.stage: Evidence law: Oral evidence to be direct
steps.text: The IO must identify and record the person who actually perceived each fact and, for each witness, capture which sense carried the perception, since a witness relaying what someone else saw or heard does not satisfy the directness rule. For opinion material the IO must line up the person who actually holds the opinion, and should preserve and be ready to produce any material thing whose existence or condition the witnesses describe, because the Court may call for it.

bsa_refs.title: Oral evidence to be direct
bsa_refs.summary: This section requires that oral evidence be direct in all cases, and then spells out what 'direct' means for four kinds of fact. Clause (i) requires that a fact which could be seen be spoken to by a witness who says he saw it; clause (ii) requires that a fact which could be heard be spoken to by a witness who says he heard it; clause (iii) requires that a fact perceivable by any other sense or manner be spoken to by a witness who says he perceived it by that sense or in that manner; clause (iv) requires that an opinion, or the grounds of an opinion, come from the person who holds that opinion on those grounds. The first proviso permits expert opinions in a treatise commonly offered for sale, and the grounds of those opinions, to be proved by producing the treatise where the author is dead, cannot be found, has become incapable of giving evidence, or cannot be called without delay or expense the Court regards as unreasonable. The second proviso permits the Court, if it thinks fit, to require production of a material thing other than a document for its inspection when oral evidence refers to that thing's existence or condition.
key_requirements: Oral evidence shall, in all cases whatever, be direct.
A fact which could be seen must be proved by the evidence of a witness who says he saw it.
A fact which could be heard must be proved by the evidence of a witness who says he heard it.
A fact which could be perceived by any other sense or in any other manner must be proved by the evidence of a witness who says he perceived it by that sense or in that manner.
An opinion, or the grounds on which that opinion is held, must be proved by the evidence of the person who holds that opinion on those grounds.

Expert opinions in a treatise commonly offered for sale, and their grounds, may be proved by producing the treatise if the author is dead, cannot be found, has become incapable of giving evidence, or cannot be called without an amount of delay or expense the Court regards as unreasonable.
Where oral evidence refers to the existence or condition of a material thing other than a document, the Court may, if it thinks fit, require production of that thing for its inspection.

steps.stage: Evidence law: Court may presume existence of certain facts
steps.text: Nothing here is a presumption the Court must draw, so an IO cannot rely on it as proof: recovery of stolen property must still be documented so that possession is shown to be 'soon after the theft' and the accused's explanation for possession is recorded and tested, and any approver or accomplice statement must be backed by independent corroboration on material particulars. bsa_refs.title: Court may presume existence of certain facts
bsa_refs.summary: s.119(1) gives the Court a discretionary power to presume the existence of any fact it thinks likely to have happened, judged against the common course of natural events, human conduct and public and private business as they relate to the particular case. The sub-section carries nine illustrations of presumptions the Court may draw, including recent possession of stolen goods pointing to theft or guilty receipt, an accomplice being unworthy of credit unless corroborated in material particulars, regular performance of judicial and official acts, following of the common course of business, and adverse inference from evidence withheld or from refusal to answer a question one is not legally compelled to answer. s.119(2) requires the Court to also have regard to a listed set of countervailing facts when deciding whether those maxims apply, each keyed to a specific illustration (for example the shop-keeper who continually receives rupees in business, the interrupted postal course, or the bond in the obligor's hands that he may have stolen). The whole section is permissive as to the presumption ('may presume') and mandatory only as to considering the counter-examples ('shall also have regard').
key_requirements: The Court may presume the existence of any fact which it thinks likely to have happened, regard being had to the common course of natural events, human conduct and public and private business in their relation to the facts of the particular case.
The Court may presume that a man in possession of stolen goods soon after the theft is either the thief or has received the goods knowing them to be stolen, unless he can account for his possession.
The Court may presume that an accomplice is unworthy of credit unless he is corroborated in material particulars.
The Court may presume that judicial and official acts have been regularly performed.
